## 5. What the bill penalises

5.1. The utility bills the site on kilovolt-amperes as well as kilowatt-hours, so a poor power factor costs money every month even when nothing is wrong with the plant. Large compressor motors pull the factor down; the capacitor bank in the switch room pushes it back up.

5.2. The bank is rated at 360 kvar in six automatic steps. The site's target is a monthly average of 0.98. The utility adds a surcharge to any month that averages below 0.90, and gives a small rebate for any month above 0.95.

5.3. When the bank was first installed it had four steps and a lower rating, and the target was 0.95; the extra steps were added in April 2026 after two summer bills carried the surcharge.

5.4. The controller's display, which shows the kvar switched in on each step, is read at every monthly energy review. A step that will not switch in is reported to the electrical supervisor the same day.

5.5. Capacitor cans are never touched until the bank has been isolated and left for the discharge time printed on its door.

## Power factor

The capacitor bank is sized in kvar for the first year's load: 240 in four steps. Target monthly average 0.95.

BADDI DEPOT SWITCH ROOM CARD

Taped inside the switch room door at the Baddi pharma depot in Himachal Pradesh.

WHAT THE BILL CHARGES FOR
The state utility bills Baddi on kVAh, so a lagging load costs money every month even when the plant is healthy. The depot's chillers and the two air handlers in the pharma rooms pull the factor down.

THE BANK IN THE CORNER
The capacitor bank beside the main panel is sized at 150 kvar in three steps, switched automatically. The depot aims for a monthly average of 0.95. The utility adds a surcharge when a month averages below 0.85; there is no rebate at Baddi.

CHECKS
The maintenance technician reads the controller display every Monday and writes the steps in service in the switch room book. A step that does not come in is reported to the regional engineer the same day. Fuses are replaced only by the electrical contractor, with the bank isolated and the discharge time on the door allowed to pass.

KEEP CLEAR
Nothing is stored in the switch room: no cartons, no ladders, no spare pallets. The floor in front of the panels is marked with yellow tape and kept clear for one metre.

AFTER A POWER CUT
After any outage, check that every step has come back in before leaving the room. If the display shows a fault, do not reset it; phone the regional engineer.

Questions to the regional engineering desk, extension 562.

## 11. When the grid is told to give way

11.1. In the paddy season and in very cold spells the utility may order large consumers to reduce their load for set hours. Such a curtailment order arrives by e-mail and by phone to the site manager, who tells the engineering lead and the shift lead at once.

11.2. The site's sanctioned load is 1,450 kW against a contract demand of 1,200 kVA. During an order, loads are switched off in this sequence until the site is under the figure the order gives: first the office and canteen air conditioning, then the yard and apron lighting except the gate, then the softening plant, and only last the ambient store's ventilation. Refrigeration, the frozen block and the controls are never shed.

11.3. If shedding all of those still leaves the site above the figure, the generators take the essential load and the site draws only what the order allows from the grid.

11.4. Each curtailment is logged with the order number, the hours, the loads shed and the diesel used, and the sanctioned figures are reviewed with the utility once a year in the light of that log.

## 3. Behind the chain-link fence

3.1. The 2 MVA transformer in the substation yard is oil-filled, and its oil is usually the first thing to fail without anyone noticing. Moisture and sludge pull down the oil's dielectric strength long before anything trips.

3.2. A sample is drawn by the approved testing laboratory every six months, in March and September, with the unit on load. The breakdown voltage must read at least 50 kV. A sample below that is filtered on site within seven days and drawn again after filtering.

3.3. The 2025 commissioning note allowed a yearly sample and a lower pass figure; both were tightened after the first monsoon, when condensation was found in the breather.

3.4. The laboratory's report is filed in the substation folder and copied to the engineering lead together with the dielectric figure from each of the last four samples, so that a slow decline is visible before it becomes a failure.

3.5. Nobody opens the transformer enclosure except the electrical supervisor or the utility's linesman, and never alone.

## Utility orders

The sanctioned load is 1,200 kW. On a curtailment order, switch off first the ambient store ventilation, then the yard lights, then the office air conditioning.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

# Ludhiana DC safety rules (opening issue)

Issued for the opening of Ludhiana DC.

## Collapse

The site has two defibrillator units, at the gate cabin and in the canteen. A first aider checks each aed once a month.

## Generators

Two sets, automatic changeover, tested monthly. Bulk tank dipped weekly.

## 9. Cold work

9.1. The frozen block at Ludhiana runs at -25 C, colder than most of the company's freezers, and the body loses heat there faster than people expect. Cold slows thinking before it slows hands, which is why the rules below do not depend on how anyone feels.

9.2. Nobody works inside the frozen block for longer than 40 minutes at a stretch, even in a full freezer suit. A 20-minute rewarming break in the canteen or the warm room follows each stretch, with a hot drink available.

9.3. The shift lead keeps the break board for the frozen block and moves names on it; the workers do not keep their own time.

9.4. Signs of hypothermia, such as uncontrolled shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness or confusion, mean the person leaves the cold at once with a colleague and is checked by a first aider. A person who has shown those signs does not go back into the cold that shift.

9.5. In 2025 the stretch was an hour and the rewarming break fifteen minutes, and two cases of mild hypothermia followed; both were changed after the first winter.

## Plant water

Condenser water comes from the borewell through the softener, and its tds is checked. Softened water must stay below 800 ppm, tested monthly.

## 14. Near misses and hazards

14.1. A near miss is anything that could have hurt someone but did not. Near misses are reported on the yellow cards kept beside every clocking machine, or by telling the shift lead, who writes the card.

14.2. The safety officer reads every card within two working days, decides what action is needed and posts the result on the canteen board, without the reporter's name unless they asked for it to be shown.

14.3. A person who reports a near miss is thanked, not blamed. Shift leads who discourage reporting are themselves reported to the site manager.

14.4. The number of near-miss cards is reported to the safety council each month. A falling number is investigated as carefully as a rising one.

## 6. How findings are graded

6.1. Every finding is graded high, medium or low by the engagement lead and confirmed by the head of the team. High means a control has failed in a way that could cause a material loss, a breach of law or a harm to a customer's product; low means an improvement that would be nice to have.

6.2. A finding of high severity goes to the auditee's department head in a draft report. The auditee's written response, with an action, an owner and a date, is due within 10 working days. Medium findings are due within 20 working days and low within 30.

6.3. An agreed action on a high finding is due for completion within 90 days of the final report, unless the board agrees a longer date.

6.4. The grade is the auditor's decision. A department may argue with it in its response, and the argument is printed in the final report beside the grade, but the grade is not lowered to get a response signed.

6.5. A finding of medium severity repeated from the previous audit of the same area is raised to high.

## 11. After the stock has left

11.1. Responsibility for a batch does not end at the dispatch bay. The store must be able to find every unit it has handled, and it must deal properly with what comes back.

11.2. Twice a year, in March and September, the store runs a mock recall on a batch chosen by the RP without warning. The exercise starts when she names the batch to the shift QA officer. Every unit of the chosen batch must be found and named — on a shelf, on a vehicle or at a consignee — inside four hours of the exercise starting. The result, with the time taken and any unit that could not be found, goes to the customer who owns the batch.

11.3. Hospitals and distributors send product back for many reasons — over-ordering, a ward closing, a wrong delivery — and none of those reasons makes it fit to be resold. Nothing returned goes back into saleable stock unless it comes back within 72 hours of delivery, with an unbroken logger record from our hands to the consignee's and back, and the Responsible Person signs the release; everything else is destroyed. Returned product waits in the quarantine cage while the decision is made.

11.4. A real recall, as opposed to a practice one, is run by the customer. The store's part is to stop dispatch of the batch at once, list every unit it holds and every unit it has sent, and hold any returned units in quarantine until the customer instructs.

11.5. Complaints from hospitals about a product's quality are passed to the customer the same day. The store does not reply to the complaint itself, and does not offer an opinion on it.

## 11. Following up actions

11.1. Every agreed action from every report goes into the actions register, with its owner, its due date and its finding's grade. The register is updated by the team on the first working day of each month from the evidence owners send in.

11.2. An action is closed only on evidence. An e-mail saying "done" is not evidence; a revised procedure, a changed system setting, a signed balance check or a trained-staff list is.

11.3. Overdue actions on high findings are listed by name in each quarterly report to the board, together with the owner's explanation. Overdue actions on medium findings are listed by count.

11.4. Each high finding is tested again by the team about six months after its action is closed, to confirm the fix has held. A fix that has not held reopens the finding at its original grade.

11.5. Owners may ask for one extension of an action date, in writing, before it falls due. A second extension needs the board's agreement.

## 12. Closing an engagement and reporting

12.1. Fieldwork ends with an exit meeting at which the engagement lead goes through every finding with the department head, before anything is written down as final. Nothing should appear in a final report that the department hears of for the first time on paper.

12.2. The final report is issued within 15 working days of that meeting, to the department head, the Chief Financial Officer and the Managing Director, and to the chair of the board's audit committee, which reads every final report at its next quarterly sitting.

12.3. Until this programme the report was allowed 30 working days, and too many reports arrived after the people involved had forgotten the details.

12.4. The committee may call any department head to explain an overdue action in person, and may ask why any report missed its date after the exit meeting.

## 17. Changes to this manual

17.1. Revision 1 (September 2025) was issued when the store opened. Revision 2 (December 2025) added the generator test after a power failure in the first month. Revision 3 (May 2026) changed several frequencies and limits after the store's first full season, and recorded the reasons beside each change.

17.2. The QA lead reviews this manual every April and after any critical deviation, failed customer audit or change to the building. The RP approves each revision.

17.3. Staff send suggested changes to the QA lead at any time. Each suggestion gets an answer, whether or not it is taken up.

17.4. A revised manual is issued with a one-page note of what changed. Every person who works in a product zone signs that they have read the note within a week of issue.

## 15. Customer audits

15.1. Customers may audit the store on ten working days' notice, and for cause at shorter notice. The RP or the QA lead hosts every audit; the store manager joins for the operational parts.

15.2. An auditor may see any record about the customer's own stock and any part of the building. An auditor may not see another customer's stock records or another customer's audit reports.

15.3. The store answers each audit finding within 20 working days with a corrective action, an owner and a date. Answers are written by the QA lead and signed by the RP.

15.4. Findings from customer audits are added to the store's own corrective action register, so that one customer's finding fixes the problem for every customer.

15.5. A customer may ask to observe a mock recall or a self-inspection walk. The request is granted where the customer's own batch is chosen or where the walk does not expose another customer's records.

## 5. The ride to the hub

5.1. Most chilled returns come back in vehicles that delivered something else first. Putting returns on that backhaul is cheaper than sending an empty van, but a chilled carton that has already been out of the customer's fridge is fragile, and every extra stop warms it.

5.2. A chilled return rides on a delivering vehicle only if Fleet Control's plan puts that vehicle at the hub within 6 hours of the collection. Where it cannot, a dedicated pickup is sent instead, however small the load.

5.3. Fleet Control records the planned arrival time on the collection note, and the receiving team writes the actual arrival time beside it, so that the rule can be checked month by month.

5.4. The interim note allowed a longer window, and the hub's first summer showed that it was too long.

5.5. Frozen returns are never added to backhaul unless the delivering body is itself frozen; consolidation of frozen and chilled returns in one body is not allowed.

5.6. Planners may combine several customers' returns on one dedicated pickup, but the consolidation is planned by Fleet Control and never arranged by drivers on the road.

## 18. Training and competence

18.1. Analysts are trained on each method by the laboratory head and authorised in writing only after they have run the method on samples of known result and reached the expected answer three times.

18.2. Each analyst's competence is checked again every year on every method they are authorised for, using blind samples prepared by the laboratory head. An analyst who fails a check is suspended from that method until retrained and checked again.

18.3. Analysts attend at least two external training days a year, chosen with the laboratory head. Notes from each day are shared with the rest of the team at the next weekly meeting.

18.4. The laboratory keeps a training file for each analyst showing every sign-off, every annual check and every course attended.

## 9. When something goes out of range

9.1. A temperature excursion affecting Vetrix's stock is notified to Vetrix's named quality contact within the time the company's customer notification matrix sets for patient-critical stock. Vetrix's vaccines are treated as patient critical for this purpose.

9.2. Quillfern investigates every excursion under its own procedures and shares the investigation report with Vetrix's quality contact on request.

9.3. The decision whether affected stock may be released, returned or destroyed is Vetrix's, taken on Quillfern's records. Quillfern does not destroy Vetrix's stock without Vetrix's written instruction.

9.4. Excursions are listed in the monthly report with their status until each is closed.

## 11. Making things sterile

11.1. Used cultures, plates and swabs are made safe before they leave the laboratory. Glassware and media are sterilised before use.

11.2. Both jobs are done in the autoclave in the washing room. A standard load runs at 121 C for 20 minutes once the whole load has reached that temperature, and every cycle's printout is kept.

11.3. Every week a biological indicator, a spore strip carrying a known number of heat-resistant bacteria, is placed in the middle of a full load. After the cycle the strip is incubated; any growth means the cycle failed, the week's loads are repeated, and the machine is serviced before it is used again.

11.4. Until February 2026 the spore test was done monthly, which would have let three weeks of unsafe waste leave the building after a failure.

11.5. Only trained analysts load and unload the autoclave, wearing heat-resistant gloves and a face shield, and nobody opens the door before the pressure gauge reads zero.

## 9. Measuring small volumes

9.1. Microbiology depends on measuring small volumes of sample and diluent accurately. An error of a few per cent in a single pipette stroke becomes a large error in the count.

9.2. Every pipette in use is checked every three months by weighing the water it delivers on the laboratory balance, at its nominal volume and at a tenth of it, ten times each. The mean must be within 1 per cent of the nominal volume, and the spread within the maker's figure.

9.3. One that fails is labelled out of use and sent to the maker's service agent; one dropped on the floor is checked before it is used again, whatever it looks like.

9.4. The gravimetric check uses the laboratory balance, which is itself checked every morning with a certified weight and calibrated every year by an outside laboratory.

9.5. Results of every check are kept in the equipment file, and gravimetric figures are plotted so that drift shows.

## 12. Reporting results

12.1. Every result is checked by a second analyst against the raw data before it is reported. The checker signs the worksheet.

12.2. Reports go to the person who asked for the test, with a copy to the QA officer for the site concerned. They show the laboratory number, the sample, the method, the result, the date of testing and the name of the analyst.

12.3. A result outside the limit the requester gave is phoned through on the day, before the written report, and the call is recorded.

12.4. Reports state what was tested and what was found. They do not say whether stock should be released or destroyed; that decision belongs to QA.

12.5. A report that has to be corrected is reissued with a new revision number and a note of what changed. The old report is withdrawn, not deleted.

## 12. Invoicing

12.1. Quillfern invoices Vetrix monthly in arrears, with separate invoices for storage, handling and transport, within five working days of the month's end.

12.2. Service credits appear as a separate line on the next handling invoice, with a reference to the month and the measure that earned them.

12.3. Vetrix pays each invoice within 45 days of its date. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days; the undisputed part is paid on time.

## 13. Changing this schedule

13.1. Either company may propose a change to this schedule in writing. A proposed change is discussed at the next monthly review and decided by the senior group or, between its meetings, by written agreement of the account manager and Vetrix's head of supply chain.

13.2. A change takes effect from the first day of the month after it is agreed, never backwards.

13.3. Each revision of this schedule carries a table of changes on its last page.

## 3. Ordering

3.1. Vetrix's distributors and stores place orders through Vetrix's order portal, which passes them to Quillfern's warehouse system every thirty minutes between 06:00 and 22:00.

3.2. Orders received by 12:00 are dispatched the same day where the delivery point is within the day-route network, and the next working day otherwise. The routes are listed in the annex and reviewed every quarter.

3.3. An order may be changed or cancelled by Vetrix until it has been picked. After picking, a change is treated as a new order and the picked stock is returned to its location.

3.4. Vetrix's customer service team tells Quillfern by e-mail of any order that needs special handling, such as a delivery to a government store that receives only on certain days.

## What RF-119 may carry

RF-119 runs the Guwahati dairy and chilled-grocery circuit. Milk and paneer are
its normal load.

RF-119 may carry vaccines or insulin **only** inside a validated passive
shipper, because the body has no cradle and no second compartment to separate
pharma from dairy stock. A passive shipper is hired per trip and the charge is a
line on [the H2 2026 rate card](12-rate-card-2026-h2.md); Fleet Control raises
the hire request, not the customer service agent. Without a shipper, RF-119 is
refused for pharma critical stock whatever the urgency, and
[the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy](08-driver-hours-and-safety-policy.md)
clause 1.3 is the reason no manager may overrule that at the gate.

The temperature limits for whatever RF-119 carries are set by
[the Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md). This
file sets none.

## What RF-118 may carry

RF-118 is a chilled asset. It may carry vaccines, insulin, milk and paneer. It
must not be loaded with frozen food: the body cannot hold the frozen target and
the frozen profile belongs to [RF-120](18-reefer-RF-120-asset-file.md).

This file sets no temperature limit of its own. Every limit and every excursion
duration for the products RF-118 carries is in
[the Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md), and
the sensor configuration is documented in
[the legacy sensor threshold file](02-sensor-thresholds.yaml). Where this file
and the SOP appear to differ, the SOP wins.

## Monsoon working

RF-119 works Guwahati through the monsoon. Rain cover over rear pallets is
mandatory during monsoon unloading, and since June 2026 the handling is billed
to the customer as a line on [the rate card](12-rate-card-2026-h2.md) rather
than absorbed. The yard rule about not idling inside the small yard after 21:30
is in [Dock scheduling rules 2026](13-dock-scheduling-rules-2026.md).

On 18 April 2026 RF-119 reached Guwahati without a rain cover over the rear
pallets and the night team reported it to Riniki Bora by phone. No stock was
lost. Stores now keeps two spare covers in the RF-119 cab locker.

twice received a Nagpur pharma booking on RF-119 that was meant for RF-118, so

## 5. The cold source

5.1. Chilled kits are kept cold by sealed phase-change packs that melt at +3 C, holding the food near that temperature until they have melted. They are conditioned in the Kondhwa cold room for at least 24 hours before use.

5.2. Every chilled kit carries two packs of 600 g each, one under the food and one on top. A kit with frozen items as well carries a third pack, conditioned at -21 C, packed against the frozen items behind the divider.

5.3. The pilot carried three smaller packs and the food between them warmed first.

5.4. Each pcm brick is checked at the line for leaks and swelling and discarded if either is found. Packs are reused only when they come back intact through the box returns, and each pcm brick is retired after 30 uses.

5.5. Gel and ice packs from any other source are never used in a Thali Box kit.

## 6. Who may use one

6.1. A K7 may be used only by a person with a login issued by the IT desk. Logins are personal; a shift lead does not sign in for a picker so the picker can start sooner.

6.2. Contract and agency workers do not get permanent logins. Agency staff on the scanners are some of the busiest users on a peak night, and each one is given a temporary sign-in for the shift at the shift lead's request to the desk. The desk issues them a day credential that stops working twelve hours after it is first used. A new one is issued for each shift worked.

6.3. Personal phones are a separate matter. Many staff would rather scan with their own phone than walk to the rack, and on the pilot some did. No personal phone may run the scanning app or hold a Quillfern login, even for one shift when a K7 has failed; the user takes a spare from the cradle rack or waits.

6.4. Customer staff and auditors may look at a K7's screen with a Quillfern user beside them. They do not operate it.

6.5. Trainees from the Waluj workshop use a K7 only with their trainer's login running, and only for the exercises in their module.

## 6. Paperwork and labels

6.1. Every kit carries a recipe card set, an ingredient list and an allergen card, all printed by Thali Box and supplied to the line in packs of fifty.

6.2. The shipper's end-of-line label shows the customer's name and address, the delivery day and window, the order number and a barcode for the driver.

6.3. A second, larger label on the lid shows the earliest use-by date of any item in the kit. The date is printed in characters at least 6 mm high, so that it can be read by someone standing at the door without bending.

6.4. The pilot printed it smaller, and complaints showed that customers did not read it.

6.5. Every shipper also carries an sscc label so that the kit can be traced through the van and the returns system. The label follows the gs1 standard so that both companies' scanners read it, and a kit whose sscc does not scan is relabelled; the gs1 company prefix used is Thali Box's own.

6.6. Labels are printed on direct-thermal stock that survives condensation. A label that smudges at the line test is reprinted before the kit leaves.

## 9. Bringing the kit home again

9.1. The liner and the cold packs are expensive and can be used again; the outer shipper is collected too, so that customers are not left with a bulky box, even though it is recyclable. The programme asks every customer to hand the whole kit back, empty, at their next delivery or by pickup from the door.

9.2. Customers pay a refundable deposit of Rs. 80 on the first kit they order. The amount is refunded in full if the box comes back within 14 days of delivery, in a condition the hub can reuse, and is kept if it does not.

9.3. The pilot's deposit was smaller and gave less time, and too many boxes stayed in customers' homes.

9.4. Outer shippers that cannot be reused are flattened at the Bhosari hub and sent for recycling; they are recyclable board with water-based ink. Liners that cannot be reused are sent to the moulder, who takes them back as raw material.

9.5. Customer service handles questions about refunds; the van drivers do not discuss money at the door.

## Outer

Three-ply corrugated slotted box, tested by bct. Compression strength at least 300 kgf.

## Cold source

## 8. Weather and the road

8.1. Riders do not ride in a red weather warning. The hub lead watches the
warnings and stops runs before they start.

8.2. In the monsoon every carrier wears its rain cover, and riders carry a
spare cover in the under-seat box.

8.3. In April and May the midday heat is hard on riders and on carriers. Runs
are planned so that no carrier is in the sun at a long stop, and riders carry
drinking water.

8.4. Riders keep to the speed limits of the roads they ride on and never ride
on a footpath to reach a door.

8.5. A road closure or a rally that blocks a route is reported to the hub, and
the hub lead re-plans the run; the rider does not find a way round on his own.

## 7. Proving a design before it is used

7.1. No new packaging component, and no change to an existing one, goes into service until a complete kit built with it has passed a transit test at the Product Testing Laboratory.

7.2. The test follows an ista procedure adapted for meal kits. A kit is built with dummy food packs and a logger, conditioned, and then dropped ten times from 60 cm onto its faces, edges and corners in a set order. It passes if nothing has leaked, the lid is still seated and the logger shows the food stayed in range for the full doorstep period the programme promises.

7.3. The pilot's simulation used fewer and lower drops and passed a box that failed on the road.

7.4. A simulation of the doorstep follows the drops: the kit stands in a chamber that cycles between the hottest and most humid conditions recorded in Pune in May and the coolest night.

7.5. Results of each ista run are written up by the laboratory and signed by the packaging engineer and Thali Box's product manager before the component is released.

## Transit test

Kits pass an ista-style test of 6 drops from 45 cm, followed by a doorstep simulation in the chamber.

## 4. Keeping the heat out

4.1. Inside every shipper sits a moulded expanded polystyrene box with a fitted lid, made of eps beads. It is the only insulation in the kit, and the whole thermal performance of the kit depends on it.

4.2. The liner's walls, base and lid are 30 mm thick, moulded at a density of 20 kg per cubic metre, and its lid fits with a lip that overlaps the walls by at least 10 mm.

4.3. The pilot used thinner walls to save space in the van and kits ran warm on afternoon doorsteps.

4.4. Liners with cracks, chipped lips or a lid that does not seat are rejected at the line. The polystyrene moulder replaces rejected units in the next delivery without charge.

4.5. Every eps liner carries the moulder's lot number on its base so that a complaint can be traced to a mould. The liner is the component customers are asked to return, under section 9.

## 1. What the programme does

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and
in the slot the patient booked.

1.2. The programme started on 1 August 2025 with nine riders and about 300 drops
a week. By April 2026 it had 26 riders and about 1,100 drops a week across Pune
and Pimpri-Chinchwad.

1.3. Only insulin pens, cartridges and vials are carried. Vaccines and other
cold medicines are not carried unless Nirmaya adds them by a written change
signed by both sides, and no such change has been signed.

1.4. Quillfern does not advise patients on their medicine. A patient who asks a
rider how much to take, or whether a pen is the right one, is given the Nirmaya
care-desk number printed on the delivery slip.

1.5. Nirmaya owns the stock and the patient relationship. Quillfern owns the
cold chain from the hub to the door, and is answerable for it.

# Last-Mile Programme Manual

The manual for the doorstep insulin service Quillfern runs for Nirmaya
Healthcare in Pune, which Nirmaya sells to its patients under the name CareLink.
It is written for the riders, the hub staff and the customer service agents who
book the drops. It covers what is particular to taking medicine to a person's
front door on a two-wheeler. Company rules on temperature, quarantine and
destruction still apply; this manual says how they are carried out when the
last stop is a flat, not a dock.

## 11. Vans and handling

11.1. Kits travel to customers in chilled vans running at +4 C. Kits are loaded in delivery order, stacked no more than five high, with heavier kits at the bottom.

11.2. Drivers carry kits by the handles moulded into the shipper, never by the strapping, and never throw a kit onto a doorstep.

11.3. A kit that is dropped from a height in the van or at the door is reported by the driver and checked at the next stop for damage. A kit with a cracked liner is taken back to Kondhwa.

11.4. Vans carry no other customer's goods while kits are on board.

## 18. Trying new materials

18.1. Both companies want to replace foamed plastics with materials that compost or are easier to recycle. Several suppliers have offered insulated boxes made of moulded pulp, wool and straw, and starch foams.

18.2. A new material is tried first in the laboratory, then in a small trial of no more than two hundred kits on one delivery route, with the customers on that route told in a note in the kit that they are helping with a trial.

18.3. A trial material is adopted only if it matches the current kit's results in the transit test and in the doorstep complaint rate over at least eight weeks, and if its cost has been agreed by Thali Box.

18.4. Results of every trial, including failed ones, are written up and kept with this book, so that the same material is not tried twice without a reason.

## 11. Complaints from the person at home

11.1. A patient who complains to a rider is given the Nirmaya care-desk number.
The rider writes down what was said and tells the hub lead before the end of the
shift.

11.2. Complaints that reach Quillfern directly are passed to Nirmaya's care desk
the same day, with the rider's note and the run sheet.

11.3. A complaint about a rider's behaviour or riding goes to the hub lead and
to HR. The rider is told what the complaint says and is asked for his account
before anything is decided.

11.4. Quillfern does not reply to a patient in writing. Written replies come
from Nirmaya.

## 13. Concerns raised in confidence

13.1. Staff, customers and suppliers may raise a concern about fraud, bribery or serious misconduct in confidence, by e-mail to the team's confidential mailbox or by letter to the head of the team at head office. The mailbox is read only by the head of the team.

13.2. Every concern is acknowledged within three working days where the sender has given a way to reply. Anonymous concerns are looked into as far as the information allows; they are never ignored because the sender cannot be asked questions.

13.3. A person who raises a concern in good faith is not disciplined, moved or disadvantaged for it, even if the concern turns out to be mistaken. A manager who tries to find out who raised a concern is reported to the board chair.

13.4. Investigations of concerns are separate from the year's plan. They are run by the head of the team with HR and, where needed, outside lawyers, and are reported to the board chair rather than through the normal report route.

# Internal Audit: interim charter and working rules

Issued when the Internal Audit team was set up, to cover its first months until the first annual programme was approved.

## 17. Working with the other auditors

17.1. The statutory auditors may rely on Internal Audit's work where they judge it reliable. The head of the team meets the statutory audit partner twice a year, shares the plan in April and the year's reports in January, and gives them access to working papers on request.

17.2. Customer auditors and certification bodies are not given Internal Audit reports. If a customer asks whether Quillfern has an internal audit function, the account manager may say that it does and what it covers in general terms.

17.3. Where a customer's audit finding overlaps with an engagement in the plan, the engagement lead reads the customer's report and its agreed actions before fieldwork, so that the department is not asked the same questions twice and the two sets of actions do not contradict each other.

17.4. Findings from the insurers' surveys and from regulators' inspections are added to the risk register when the team plans the next year. They are not repeated as Internal Audit findings unless the team has tested the matter itself.

17.5. Nothing Internal Audit learns from another auditor's work is passed on outside the company without the head of the team's approval and, where the work belongs to someone else, that party's agreement.

18.1. The team keeps its plan, its engagement files, the actions register, the confidential concerns log and its reports to the board in its restricted folder. Access is limited to the three members of the team; the board chair may ask for any file.

18.2. The concerns log is kept separately from engagement files and is encrypted. Entries name the concern, the date, the steps taken and the outcome, and they never name the person who raised it unless that person agreed in writing.

## By post

Mark the envelope "Private: head of Internal Audit" and send it to head office.

## Cash floats

Each site's petty cash imprest is Rs. 10,000. Internal Audit counts it once a year by surprise. Shortages above Rs. 1,000 are reported to Finance.

Nobody audits a function they worked in during the previous 12 months. Engagement leads change after five consecutive audits of the same area; rotation is planned by the head of the team. Threats to independence go to the board chair.

The team reports to the board on audit matters and to the Chief Financial Officer for administration. It runs no process and signs nothing for another department.

## 13. Forms and printed stationery

13.1. Stores holds the printed pads of every QCL form used on the floor, from the
customer intimation form to the wash register. Each pad carries the form number
and the revision printed at its foot.

13.2. When QA issues a new revision of a form, Stores withdraws every pad of the
earlier revision from the DC shelves in the same week and sends the withdrawn
pads to QA to be counted and shredded. Two revisions of one form are never on a
shelf at the same time.

13.3. Forms are issued to shift leads by the pad, never by the loose sheet, so
that a used pad can be matched to the shift that used it.

13.4. Stores reorders a form when its stock falls to three months' use. The
print order goes through Finance like any other purchase.

13.5. Dispatch notes are printed with running numbers. Stores records the first
and last number of each box issued to a gate, as it does for other numbered

# Quillfern Cold Chain Glossary

Plain meanings for expressions used on site. Short forms are defined in the document that uses them, never here, so an expression below appears in its long form only.

back-to-cold — the moment a staged pallet crosses back over the cold-room threshold; staging time stops here.
chlorine contact time — the minutes a sanitising solution must stay wet on a reefer floor before rinsing; wiping it dry early starts the count again.
dead zone — a stretch of road where the telematics unit cannot report; the USB logger covers it and the gap is recorded as missing, never filled in.
door open minutes — the total minutes a cold-room or reefer door stood open in one shift, summed from the door sensor; a measure of load, not a fault.
holding lane B — the covered waiting lane at Nagpur for pharma and frozen vehicles that miss their dock time; nothing is unloaded there.
mean kinetic temperature — the single steady temperature that would give stock the same total heat stress as the uneven record it actually saw; stability letters are written against it, not against the average.
pre-cool hold time — the minutes an empty reefer body is held at loading temperature, doors shut, before the first pallet goes in.
probe grid — the layout of loggers used when a room is mapped; each position is named by rack, bay and height, such as A1-high.
relief point — a named fuel plaza or rest area on a qualified route where a relief driver or a mobile service van can meet the vehicle.
seal watch — time a driver spends guarding a sealed vehicle; it is duty time and never counts as rest.
shipper conditioning time — the hours a passive shipper's gel packs must sit at their set temperature before the shipper may leave with stock.
stability budget remaining — the minutes above the high limit that a customer's stability letter still allows for one lot, once every earlier excursion on that lot is subtracted.
warm pallet — night-shift name for a pallet whose logger has alarmed but whose excursion QA has not yet confirmed; it is handled as quarantine stock until QA decides.
white tag — the RELEASED tag fixed beside a red hold tag when QA lets stock out of quarantine; the red tag stays on.

# Stores and Consumables Standard

How Stores receives, holds and issues the consumables that cold-chain work runs
on: seals, red sleeve packets, spare loggers, gel packs, dry ice, protective
equipment and forms. It covers the main store at Nagpur and the smaller stores
cages at Guwahati and Coimbatore. It does not say how any of these items is used
on the job; the documents that govern their use do that.

## 21. Returns to suppliers

21.1. Faulty goods are returned to the supplier with a return note on the
supplier's own form where the supplier has one, and on QCL-F-45 where it does
not.

21.2. Stores keeps a copy of every return note and follows up any return that
has not been credited or replaced within thirty days.

21.3. Returned numbered stock is listed by number on the return note, so that the
numbers can never reappear on a Quillfern shelf.

21.4. A supplier who has had three returns in a year is raised at the annual
supplier review, whatever the reason for the returns.

## 24. Review of this standard

24.1. Nalini Patil reviews this standard every July with QA and Finance, and
sooner when a new consumable is introduced or a supplier changes.

24.2. A change to how an item is used is made in the document that governs its
use, not here. This standard changes only how Stores receives, holds, issues and
counts the item.

24.3. Each revision is issued with a note of what changed. The storekeepers at
Nagpur and the cage leads at Guwahati and Coimbatore sign that they have read it
within a week.

24.4. The earlier revision is withdrawn from the Stores counter and the shared
drive on the day the new one is issued, so that nobody works from two versions
at the same time.

## 23. Contacts

23.1. The Nagpur store phone is on the Operations extension list. Out of hours,
the night shift lead holds the emergency cupboard key, as in section 2.

23.2. Questions about whether an item is fit to use go to QA. Questions about
whether an item may be bought go to Finance. Stores answers questions about
where an item is and how many are left.

## 8. Finding where warmth gets in

8.1. When the room has held its set point for 48 hours, the envelope is surveyed from outside for places where cold escapes: panel joints, door frames, pipe and cable penetrations, and the junction between wall panels and floor.

8.2. The survey is done by thermography, with an infrared camera, at night or on a dull day when the outside walls are not heated by the sun. Any joint that shows more than 3 C colder than the panel face beside it is marked, resealed and surveyed again.

8.3. The handover note of 2025 allowed a larger difference before resealing, and two joints it allowed are now visibly iced.

8.4. The images are saved with the room number, the date and the camera's serial number, and printed on the commissioning record with each marked joint circled.

8.5. A second thermography survey with the same infrared camera is done six months after handover, in the opposite season, and its images are compared with the first.

## 13. After handover

13.1. The contractor's defects liability period runs for twelve months from practical completion. Faults found in that period are reported to the contractor in writing by the engineering lead, and the contractor's response time is the one written in its contract.

13.2. The plant is serviced in its first year by the contractor who built it, under the contract, and from the second year by the company's approved service partner for refrigeration, unless the two are the same firm.

13.3. The engineering lead reviews the room's alarm history, energy use and defrost behaviour at three months and at twelve months after handover, and writes a short note of anything that needs changing.

13.4. A room that has been altered after handover, by moving racking, replacing an evaporator or changing doors, is treated as a new room for the tests that the change could affect.

## 5. Taking the air out

5.1. Air and moisture left in a refrigeration system turn into acid and sludge that shorten the life of every component. Before charging, the system is put under vacuum with a pump connected at both the high and low sides.

5.2. The system is pumped down to 500 micron. The pump is then isolated and the system left; it passes if the gauge stays below 1,000 for 30 minutes. A rise above that means moisture or a leak, and the pumping continues or the leak is found.

5.3. The 2025 handover note took the contractor's default figures, which were looser on both counts.

5.4. The gauge used is electronic, connected as close to the system as the hose allows, and never read through the pump's own dial. The readings at isolation, at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes go on the test sheet.

5.5. Pumping is never stopped early because the contractor's crew is due elsewhere. A rushed vacuum is the commonest fault the engineering team finds in other people's plant, and the micron figure is the one most often written down without being read.

## What went wrong

1. **Acknowledging an alarm is not containing an excursion.** The alarm was
   acknowledged in four minutes and nobody walked to the room for another
   sixty-seven. The procedure has said this since its first issue; the app makes
   the wrong action the easy one.

2. **The condenser fan had failed twelve days earlier** and the work order sat
   unassigned. The room held band on a cool night and lost it on a warm one, so
   nothing alarmed until the weather changed.

3. **The spare logger bin was empty.** The second reading came from a hand-held
   probe, which this procedure does not accept as a basis for release.

4. The night shift handover note recorded "C1 running warm, watching it" on two
   previous nights. It was never escalated because a handover note is not a
   quality event and nobody made it one.

## 12. Signing the room into service

12.1. Commissioning ends with a single signed record that gathers every test sheet, every calibration certificate, the as-built drawings, the closed list and the fire contractor's certificate.

12.2. Every test on the record must have been witnessed, and the record carries two signatories for each: the site QA lead and the refrigeration contractor's engineer. The customer whose stock the room will hold may send an observer, whose name is recorded, but the observer does not sign.

12.3. The 2025 note asked for one signature, the contractor's, and nobody from Quillfern could later say who had watched the pressure test.

12.4. A test that was not witnessed by both signatories is void, and is repeated. Neither signature may be added later by phone or by e-mail.

12.5. Once the record is complete the room passes to the site QA lead for temperature mapping.

## The tests

Every test in the plan, from the pressure and tightness tests to the temperature runs, is watched by three signatories: our site QA lead, the refrigeration contractor's engineer and the customer's validation manager. None may sign a test they did not watch.

## Copies

Copies of every signed sheet go to the customer and to our QA office on the day of the test. The full record is bound and handed over in two copies when the last test is signed, one for each company.

# Dera Bassi pharma store: who signs the rooms over

For the two chilled rooms being built inside the Dera Bassi pharma store, which will hold one customer's biologics under a dedicated contract.

## 14. Records

14.1. The signed commissioning record, the test sheets and the thermal images are kept for the life of the room and three years after it is demolished or converted.

14.2. Copies go to the site QA lead, who keeps them with the room's mapping studies, and to the site manager, who keeps them with the lease or the title documents.

14.3. Nothing in the record is rewritten after signing. A correction is a new sheet that refers to the old one and is signed in the same way.

## 4. Proving the pipework is tight

4.1. Refrigerant pipework is tested for tightness before any insulation is applied over it and before any refrigerant is admitted. A leak found after the pipes are lagged costs days; one found before costs minutes.

4.2. Every brazed joint is inspected by eye and then the whole system is charged with dry nitrogen at one and a half times its design pressure, isolated from the cylinder and left. The pressure must hold for 24 hours with no fall beyond what the change in ambient temperature explains.

4.3. The first Ludhiana build was held for half that time, and a slow leak at a valve body showed itself only after the room was in service.

4.4. A fall that cannot be explained is searched for with soap solution, joint by joint, and the whole test repeated after repair, from the start.

4.5. The test pressure, ambient temperature, gauge serial and times are recorded at the start, after one hour, and at the end. The nitrogen is vented outdoors and never into a closed room; every brazed repair is followed by a fresh test.

## Why the customer signs

The customer paid for the rooms and its regulator inspects them, so its contract asks for a bigger part in accepting them than our usual customers take.

## 18. Costs and the commissioning budget

18.1. Commissioning has its own line in every project budget, separate from construction. It pays for the engineering team's time, the calibration of instruments, the hire of a heat camera where the team's own is in use elsewhere, refrigerant losses during testing, and the electricity used while the room runs empty.

18.2. Repeat tests caused by a contractor's failure are charged to that contractor under its contract. Repeat tests caused by a change Quillfern asked for are charged to the project.

18.3. The engineering lead reports commissioning spend against budget to Finance at the end of each month of the project, and explains any line that has gone over.

## Delays

If the customer's validation manager cannot attend a planned test, the test is moved rather than run without them. The contractor is told at least a day ahead.

## If someone cannot come

The customer may name a deputy in writing, before the test, to sign in its validation manager's place. We may not; our QA lead's deputy must be named on the plan.

# Ludhiana DC utilities note (commissioning issue)

Written while Ludhiana DC was being commissioned, so that the first shift leads and the electrical supervisor had something to work to before a full manual existed.

## Mapping

Temperature mapping follows handover and is run by our QA team with the customer's validation manager present.

## Why pellets

Quillfern used to buy dry ice in blocks. Blocks had to be broken with a mallet on the dock, and two hand injuries in 2024 came from exactly that.
The blocks came in 12 kg slabs, and staff carried the slabs by hand because no
tote was used for them. The chest lid has two handles. Vidarbha Gases rated
pellets as easier to meter by the kg, and pellets of 16 mm from Vidarbha Gases
replaced blocks in 2024.

## Why a second pair of hands

The tote handles are rated for 12 kg, so one person with a full tote is already at the limit of the handles.
A dropped tote on a wet dock scatters pellets that people then pick up with the
wrong gloves.

## Taking it out

1. Sign the pellets out on QCL-F-26 with the kg, the job and your name.
2. Scoop the pellets into an insulated tote. Never put dry ice in a sealed box, a flask or a drum with a screw lid.
3. A load above 10 kg is carried by two people.
4. Dry ice never travels in a driver's cab, and never goes into cold room C2 or C3.

## 5. Instruments that travel south

5.1. Coimbatore has no calibration chamber and no bench master logger. Those
live at Nagpur. What Coimbatore does have is one lab-certified hand-held
thermometer, serial HP-C00, kept locked in the DC manager's cabinet.

5.2. Every hand-held thermometer in daily use at Coimbatore is checked against
HP-C00 every 14 days: both tips go into the same stirred jug of crushed ice and
water, and the two readings must agree within 0.5 C. The shift lead writes both
readings on QCL-F-12 and sends a photograph of the sheet to the Nagpur QA desk.

5.3. The shorter interval is deliberate. Coimbatore has no bench to catch a
drifting instrument quickly, and a second jug check costs nothing but ten
minutes.

5.4. HP-C00 itself goes to Metrosure Labs, Pune, by courier every 12 months.
While it is away, the Nagpur QA desk sends a loan instrument ahead of it, so the
site is never without a certified thermometer.

5.5. USB loggers are not checked at Coimbatore at all. Every spare logger for a
Coimbatore red sleeve is checked at the Nagpur bench and arrives in its sleeve
already stickered. A logger that has been out of date on the shelf is sent back
to Nagpur, never re-used on the strength of a local jug check.

5.6. Infrared guns are used at Coimbatore only to find a warm carton quickly.
They are never the reading that decides anything.

## 6. The shed by the wash pad

6.1. Coimbatore buys dry ice for two jobs only: emergency packing for a
restaurant chain whose own freezer has failed, and top-up of a frozen body that
has to wait on the apron.

6.2. The dry-ice chest stands in the open-sided store shed beside the wash pad,
not inside any building. The shed has a roof and no walls on two sides, so
carbon dioxide does not collect there the way it does in a closed store. For
that reason there is no carbon dioxide monitor at Coimbatore. The chest is never
moved indoors, even in heavy rain.

6.3. Supply and handling at Coimbatore:

| supplier | Kovai Industrial Gases fills the chest with 60 kg every Tuesday |

## 12. Scrap, waste and returns

12.1. Cardboard, stretch wrap and broken pallets are separated at the back of
the south block. A scrap dealer from Kovaipudur collects cardboard and wrap
every Tuesday and pays by the kg.

12.2. Broken pallets are stacked by the east wall for the pallet repairer, who
comes on the first working day of each month.

12.3. The old chest freezer from the closed dairy room still stands by the
scrap pile. It is not used for anything and it is not to be sold until Finance
writes it off.

12.4. Customer returns are received at dock 2 and checked against the return
challan. Frozen returns go into CBE-FROZEN only after the shift lead has
checked the logger with the Nagpur QA desk on the phone.

12.5. Spoiled stock is not scrap. It follows the spoilage and destruction rules
of the SOP, and it is never given to the scrap dealer, whatever its weight.

6.4. The two-person figure is lower at Coimbatore than elsewhere because the
path from the shed to the apron crosses the wash pad, which is wet for most of
the day.

6.5. Dry ice never goes into CBE-PHARMA, never into the closed dairy room, and
never into a cab. Unused pellets go back to the chest in the same shift.

# Dry ice at Quillfern: why the present rules

## Why it stays out of C2 and C3

On the night of 12 March 2025 dry ice trays were set outside the inner curtain
of C2 to hold the room down. The intention was good, but the trays masked the room reading at the curtain and put the vials nearest the door at risk of dropping below +2.0 C.
A pharma room is protected by containment and quarantine, not by cooling it from
the outside.

# Ranjangaon pharma depot: medical waste leaving the site

Pinned at the waste store door of the Ranjangaon pharma depot. It covers broken vials, spilled injectables and medicines the owner has told us to destroy.

## 9. Destruction

9.1. Food judged C is destroyed through the hub's licensed food-waste contractor, who collects twice a week. Packaging that carries a customer's brand is destroyed with the food, never sent for recycling.

9.2. Pharmaceutical stock for destruction leaves the hub only with the waste contractor's signed manifest, which lists every batch and quantity. The hub's copy is kept with the return number.

9.3. The licensed contractor must destroy the stock within 30 days of collection from the hub and send a certificate naming the batches within 15 days of destruction. The incineration plant used is named on the contract and may not be changed without the QA lead's agreement.

9.4. A certificate of incineration that has not arrived 50 days after collection is chased by the hub manager in writing, and the account manager is told.

9.5. Nothing is destroyed or put on a manifest while a customer's claim or an insurer's survey that concerns it is still open, unless QA rules that keeping it is a hazard.

# Ranjangaon pharma depot - medical waste leaving the site

## How fast it is destroyed

Under the contractor's licence, the waste must reach the common treatment facility and go through incineration within 48 hours of collection from the depot. The contractor sends a monthly certificate covering all collections in the month.

## Destruction

Pharmaceutical stock leaves for destruction with the contractor's manifest. Incineration must take place within 60 days of collection.

## If something goes wrong

A bag that splits, a box that is punctured, or a collection that does not arrive on its day is reported to the QA officer at once. A spill is cleaned with the spill kit hung beside the waste store, wearing the gloves and apron from the same hook, and the cleaning materials go into a fresh yellow bag.

If the contractor's driver cannot produce his licence copy or his vehicle permit at the gate, the waste stays in the store and the QA officer phones the contractor's office. Waste is never handed to anyone else who offers to take it.

## 18. Security of the hub

18.1. The hub is fenced, lit and guarded round the clock by a contract security firm. The gate keeps a register of every vehicle and every visitor, and visitors wear a badge and are escorted.

18.2. Returned goods are attractive to thieves because people assume nobody counts them. They are counted at every step, and the counts are compared every night by the shift lead before handover.

18.3. The locked bay, the waste store and the laboratory each have their own key. Keys are signed for in the key register at the gate, and the waste store key is never held by the waste contractor.

18.4. Staff may not buy, take or be given returned goods of any kind, even goods judged for destruction. A breach is treated as theft from the customer, whatever the goods were worth.

## Packing

Waste goes into the colour-coded bags and puncture-proof boxes supplied by the biomedical waste contractor. Each bag is tied, labelled with the date and weighed on the store scale.

# Bhosari hub: interim rules for returned goods

Interim rules for the first months of the Bhosari hub, until the returns manual is issued.

## 15. The hub's own measures

15.1. The hub is judged on how fast it decides, not on how much it holds. Each month the hub manager reports the share of lines judged within the time in section 7, the share of chilled returns that reached the hub within the time in section 5, the number of lines still waiting for an owner's decision, and the age of the oldest of them.

15.2. The report also counts returns that arrived without a valid number, broken seals found at the dock, damage found at receiving that was not noted at collection, and certificates overdue from the waste contractor.

15.3. The measures are read at the operations review each month, alongside the measures of the other sites. A measure that misses its target for three months running gets a written recovery plan from the hub manager, agreed with the operations head.

15.4. Customers are not sent the hub's measures as they stand. An account manager may draw on them for a customer's own service report.

## Collection

The contractor collects twice a week. Every collection travels with the contractor's manifest, listing each bag by weight and colour; the depot keeps the carbon copy, signed by the driver.

## 5. Growing what is there

5.1. The laboratory counts bacteria, yeasts and moulds on food samples and on surface swabs, so that QA can decide whether a product, a liner or a body is fit to use.

5.2. For the total viable count, the prepared sample is spread on plate count agar and the plates are incubated at 30 C for 72 hours before they are read. Coliforms, yeasts and moulds follow their own methods, listed in the laboratory's method file.

5.3. Until January 2026 the count was read after 48 hours at a higher temperature, which missed slow growers from chilled foods.

5.4. Each incubator is checked twice a day with a reference thermometer, and its reading written on the sheet on its door. One that has drifted more than 1 C from its set point is taken out of use until it has been serviced, and plates inside it are moved to the spare incubator.

5.5. Every batch of agar is tested with a known organism before it is used for samples.

## 4. Samples arriving

4.1. Samples are received at the reception counter by an analyst, who checks them against the request form, labels each one with a laboratory number and records the condition and temperature on arrival.

4.2. Chilled samples arrive in a cooled box with a temperature indicator; frozen samples arrive in a frozen box. A sample that arrives warm, leaking or unlabelled is recorded as received in that condition and the requester is asked whether to test it anyway.

4.3. Samples are stored at their proper temperature in the laboratory's own fridges and freezers, which are separate from the hub's stores and carry their own loggers.

4.4. Food and packaging samples from customers belong to the customer. Nothing is used for anything other than the test requested, and nothing is eaten, taken home or given away.

## What we count

Dry feed carries far fewer bacteria than fresh food, and the feed companies want a quick screen rather than a full analysis. We count total bacteria and moulds on every lot received.

For the small testing room at the Moshi feed warehouse, where we check the dry animal feed and premixes we store for two feed companies.

## 11. Making things sterile

11.1. Used cultures, plates and swabs are made safe before they leave the laboratory. Glassware and media are sterilised before use.

11.2. Both jobs are done in the autoclave in the washing room. A standard load runs at 121 C for 20 minutes once the whole load has reached that temperature, and every cycle's printout is kept.

11.3. Every week a biological indicator, a spore strip carrying a known number of heat-resistant bacteria, is placed in the middle of a full load. After the cycle the strip is incubated; any growth means the cycle failed, the week's loads are repeated, and the machine is serviced before it is used again.

11.4. Until February 2026 the spore test was done monthly, which would have let three weeks of unsafe waste leave the building after a failure.

11.5. Only trained analysts load and unload the autoclave, wearing heat-resistant gloves and a face shield, and nobody opens the door before the pressure gauge reads zero.

## Outside testing

Anything beyond a count, such as salmonella or toxins, goes to an accredited outside laboratory on the feed company's list.

## Results

Results go to the warehouse QA officer by e-mail the day they are read. A lot whose count is above the feed company's limit is held, and the feed company decides what happens to it.

## 9. Counting the money

9.1. Every Quillfern site holds a petty cash float for small purchases that cannot wait for a purchase order: courier charges, a replacement padlock, tea for a visiting inspector. It is an imprest: topped back up to a fixed figure against vouchers, never increased because a month was busy.

9.2. The float is Rs. 15,000 at each site and Rs. 25,000 at head office. Internal Audit counts it by surprise twice a year at every site, with the custodian present, and reconciles cash plus vouchers to the fixed figure.

9.3. A petty cash shortage of more than Rs. 500 is reported to the head of Finance the same day, with the custodian's written explanation.

9.4. The counts in 2025 were yearly and each imprest smaller; both changed in this programme.

## How much

The office's petty cash is kept at Rs. 8,000. It works as an imprest: every voucher spent is replaced from the bank at the end of the month, so the box always returns to the same total.

## Cash floats

Each site's petty cash imprest is Rs. 10,000. Internal Audit counts it once a year by surprise. Shortages above Rs. 1,000 are reported to Finance.

# Internal Audit Programme 2026-27

## 1. Why there is an internal audit team

1.1. Until 2025 Quillfern had no internal audit function of its own. The statutory auditors came once a year, customers audited the sites that held their stock, and certification bodies looked at the quality system, but nobody inside the company was paid to ask, across all departments, whether the controls people relied on were actually working.

1.2. The board set up the Internal Audit team in August 2025, reporting to the board on audit matters and to the Chief Financial Officer for day-to-day administration. This programme is the team's plan for the year from April 2026 to March 2027 and the rulebook it works to.

1.3. The programme is written for three readers. The board needs to know what will be looked at and why. Department heads need to know what will be asked of their teams and when. And the auditors themselves need one place where the working rules are written down, so that two auditors on the same kind of job reach the same kind of conclusion.

1.4. Internal Audit does not run any process, approve any transaction or sign any document on behalf of another department. An auditor who is asked to "just sign this while you're here" declines, however small the item. The team's value lies in having no part in what it examines.

1.5. Nothing in this programme changes an operating procedure. Where an engagement finds that a procedure is unclear or unworkable, the report says so and the procedure's owner decides what to change.

## 4. Starting an engagement

4.1. Each engagement begins with a planning memo, written by the engagement lead and agreed by the head of the team. The memo sets out the scope, the period covered, the controls to be tested, the people to be interviewed and the days allowed.

4.2. The department head receives a notification letter at least ten working days before fieldwork begins, with the memo's scope and a list of documents to be ready. Surprise work, such as a cash count, is the only exception, and it is listed in the memo even though the department is not told.

4.3. An opening meeting is held on the first day of fieldwork. The department head or a named deputy attends, and so does anyone whose work will be tested. The meeting goes through the scope and agrees who will be the contact for document requests.

4.4. Requests for documents are made in writing through the agreed contact and logged by the auditor. A request still unanswered after five working days is raised with the department head; after ten, with the head of the team.

## 8. Agreeing the figures with the customer

8.1. A customer who returns goods usually raises a debit note against Quillfern or against its own supplier, and the reconciliation of that note with what the hub received is the last job on any return.

8.2. Customer service compares each debit note with the hub's receipt records within 5 working days of the note arriving. Any difference of more than 2 per cent in quantity or value goes to the account manager, who settles it with the customer before a credit note is raised.

8.3. A smaller discrepancy is settled by customer service from the hub's records, which are the count of record.

8.4. The reconciliation is kept with the return number in the returns system, so that an auditor can follow one return from the collection note to the credit note without asking anyone.

8.5. A discrepancy caused by a count error at collection is reported to Fleet Control as a driver coaching matter, not as a dispute with the customer.

## 5. The ride to the hub

5.1. Most chilled returns come back in vehicles that delivered something else first. Putting returns on that backhaul is cheaper than sending an empty van, but a chilled carton that has already been out of the customer's fridge is fragile, and every extra stop warms it.

5.2. A chilled return rides on a delivering vehicle only if Fleet Control's plan puts that vehicle at the hub within 6 hours of the collection. Where it cannot, a dedicated pickup is sent instead, however small the load.

5.3. Fleet Control records the planned arrival time on the collection note, and the receiving team writes the actual arrival time beside it, so that the rule can be checked month by month.

5.4. The interim note allowed a longer window, and the hub's first summer showed that it was too long.

5.5. Frozen returns are never added to backhaul unless the delivering body is itself frozen; consolidation of frozen and chilled returns in one body is not allowed.

5.6. Planners may combine several customers' returns on one dedicated pickup, but the consolidation is planned by Fleet Control and never arranged by drivers on the road.

## 1. What the programme does

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and
in the slot the patient booked.

1.2. The programme started on 1 August 2025 with nine riders and about 300 drops
a week. By April 2026 it had 26 riders and about 1,100 drops a week across Pune
and Pimpri-Chinchwad.

1.3. Only insulin pens, cartridges and vials are carried. Vaccines and other
cold medicines are not carried unless Nirmaya adds them by a written change
signed by both sides, and no such change has been signed.

1.4. Quillfern does not advise patients on their medicine. A patient who asks a
rider how much to take, or whether a pen is the right one, is given the Nirmaya
care-desk number printed on the delivery slip.

1.5. Nirmaya owns the stock and the patient relationship. Quillfern owns the
cold chain from the hub to the door, and is answerable for it.

## 9. Pay

9.1. Riders are paid a monthly wage for their shifts, with a small per-drop
addition. The addition is the same for every drop and is not tied to time.

9.2. There is no payment for early arrival and no penalty for a drop that comes
back because the patient was out.

9.3. Fuel for the two-wheelers is paid by Quillfern through a fuel card. Riders
do not pay for fuel from their own money.

9.4. Overtime is paid at the company rate and approved by the hub lead before
the shift is extended, not afterwards.

# Last-Mile Programme Manual

The manual for the doorstep insulin service Quillfern runs for Nirmaya
Healthcare in Pune, which Nirmaya sells to its patients under the name CareLink.
It is written for the riders, the hub staff and the customer service agents who
book the drops. It covers what is particular to taking medicine to a person's
front door on a two-wheeler. Company rules on temperature, quarantine and
destruction still apply; this manual says how they are carried out when the
last stop is a flat, not a dock.

## Without a number

A parcel brought back by a rider without any authorisation from the care desk is accepted, logged on the returns sheet with the rider's name and put in the grey tote. The rider is not blamed; the care desk is asked why the number was missing.

## How long the number lasts

A return number at Kharadi lasts 7 days from the day the care desk raises it. A parcel that reaches the dark store after that is not put back on the shelf; it goes in the grey tote by the pharmacist's desk until the care desk confirms.

## 13. Bikes and kit care

13.1. The two-wheelers are leased and serviced by the leasing company every
3,000 km. The hub lead books the service.

13.2. The rider checks tyres, brakes, lights and the carrier rack before every
shift and writes the check on the shift sheet.

13.3. A two-wheeler with a fault is not ridden. The hub keeps one spare machine
for that reason.

13.4. Helmets are replaced after any fall, whether or not they look damaged.

# Kharadi e-pharmacy dark store: taking back a customer's order

For the pickers and riders at the dark store we run in Kharadi for an online pharmacy. Medicines bought online come back here when a patient refuses delivery or the pharmacy cancels an order.

## Before anything comes back

The online pharmacy's care desk raises a return in its own system and sends us the return number by e-mail. The number is the rma for that order, and it is printed on the rider's run sheet next to the address.

## Records

The returns sheet is scanned at the end of each day and sent to the care desk. Paper sheets are kept in the pharmacist's drawer for a month.

## 11. Complaints from the person at home

11.1. A patient who complains to a rider is given the Nirmaya care-desk number.
The rider writes down what was said and tells the hub lead before the end of the
shift.

11.2. Complaints that reach Quillfern directly are passed to Nirmaya's care desk
the same day, with the rider's note and the run sheet.

11.3. A complaint about a rider's behaviour or riding goes to the hub lead and
to HR. The rider is told what the complaint says and is asked for his account
before anything is decided.

11.4. Quillfern does not reply to a patient in writing. Written replies come
from Nirmaya.

## 7. Setting some aside

7.1. A result can be challenged weeks after it was reported, by a customer, an insurer or a supplier who disagrees with it, and the only fair answer to a challenge is retesting the same material.

7.2. Before testing begins, the analyst divides every food sample and sets aside a portion, sealed and labelled with the laboratory number. Each retained aliquot is stored frozen at -20 C for 90 days after the report is issued, and then destroyed unless someone has asked for it to be kept.

7.3. The first revision of this manual kept portions for 30 days, and two challenges arrived after they had gone, leaving nothing for retesting.

7.4. A request to keep an aliquot longer is made to the laboratory head in writing, with the reason, and is listed in the freezer register.

7.5. Packaging samples are not divided; the tested sample itself is kept, retained in the same way for 90 days, on the shelf in the store room.

# Product Testing Laboratory Manual

## 1. Purpose

1.1. The Product Testing Laboratory is Quillfern's own small laboratory, on the mezzanine of the Bhosari hub. It opened in October 2025 to answer questions that the company used to send to outside laboratories at a cost of days and money: whether a cleaned surface is clean, whether a returned food pack is still sound, whether a new packaging design keeps a meal kit cold on a doorstep, and whether a component from a new supplier is as strong as its certificate says.

1.2. This manual says what the laboratory does, how samples reach it, how tests are run and reported, how the laboratory proves that its results can be trusted, and how it keeps its people safe. It is written for the laboratory's analysts, for the QA officers and engineers who send it samples, and for customers' auditors who want to know how a result was reached.

1.3. The laboratory is not accredited for regulatory testing. Results it reports are for Quillfern's own decisions and for customers who have agreed in writing to rely on them. Where a law or a customer requires an accredited result, the sample goes to an accredited outside laboratory, and this laboratory only prepares and ships it.

1.4. Revision 2 changes several test conditions and checking frequencies after the laboratory's first six months, and adds the section on comparison with other laboratories. Each changed section says what it replaced.

## Portions kept

An aliquot of every food sample is frozen for retesting. Portions are kept for 30 days after the report.

## 18. Training and competence

18.1. Analysts are trained on each method by the laboratory head and authorised in writing only after they have run the method on samples of known result and reached the expected answer three times.

18.2. Each analyst's competence is checked again every year on every method they are authorised for, using blind samples prepared by the laboratory head. An analyst who fails a check is suspended from that method until retrained and checked again.

18.3. Analysts attend at least two external training days a year, chosen with the laboratory head. Notes from each day are shared with the rest of the team at the next weekly meeting.

18.4. The laboratory keeps a training file for each analyst showing every sign-off, every annual check and every course attended.

## 6. Quick checks on cleanliness

6.1. Not every cleanliness check can wait three days for a plate count. For surfaces that have just been cleaned, such as the inside of a returned meal-kit liner or a reefer floor before loading, the laboratory uses a rapid swab that gives a reading in seconds.

6.2. The swab detects atp, the energy molecule present in food residue and living cells, and the hand-held reader reports it in rlu. A reading of 100 or below is a pass. From 101 to 300 the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again; above 300 it fails, and the cleaning itself is reviewed.

6.3. Until March 2026 the laboratory's pass line was higher, and liners that passed were later found carrying mould.

6.4. A swab reading measures cleanliness, not safety. A surface that passes still goes through any microbiological test that QA has asked for.

6.5. The atp reader is checked each morning with the maker's control swabs, which give a known rlu figure. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

## 5. What the bill penalises

5.1. The utility bills the site on kilovolt-amperes as well as kilowatt-hours, so a poor power factor costs money every month even when nothing is wrong with the plant. Large compressor motors pull the factor down; the capacitor bank in the switch room pushes it back up.

5.2. The bank is rated at 360 kvar in six automatic steps. The site's target is a monthly average of 0.98. The utility adds a surcharge to any month that averages below 0.90, and gives a small rebate for any month above 0.95.

5.3. When the bank was first installed it had four steps and a lower rating, and the target was 0.95; the extra steps were added in April 2026 after two summer bills carried the surcharge.

5.4. The controller's display, which shows the kvar switched in on each step, is read at every monthly energy review. A step that will not switch in is reported to the electrical supervisor the same day.

5.5. Capacitor cans are never touched until the bank has been isolated and left for the discharge time printed on its door.
