THE BANK IN THE CORNER
The capacitor bank beside the main panel is sized at 150 kvar in three steps, switched automatically. The depot aims for a monthly average of 0.95. The utility adds a surcharge when a month averages below 0.85; there is no rebate at Baddi.

CHECKS

KEEP CLEAR
Nothing is stored in the switch room: no cartons, no ladders, no spare pallets. The floor in front of the panels is marked with yellow tape and kept clear for one metre.

AFTER A POWER CUT
After any outage, check that every step has come back in before leaving the room. If the display shows a fault, do not reset it; phone the regional engineer.

## 11. When the grid is told to give way

11.1. In the paddy season and in very cold spells the utility may order large consumers to reduce their load for set hours. Such a curtailment order arrives by e-mail and by phone to the site manager, who tells the engineering lead and the shift lead at once.

11.2. The site's sanctioned load is 1,450 kW against a contract demand of 1,200 kVA. During an order, loads are switched off in this sequence until the site is under the figure the order gives: first the office and canteen air conditioning, then the yard and apron lighting except the gate, then the softening plant, and only last the ambient store's ventilation. Refrigeration, the frozen block and the controls are never shed.

11.3. If shedding all of those still leaves the site above the figure, the generators take the essential load and the site draws only what the order allows from the grid.

11.4. Each curtailment is logged with the order number, the hours, the loads shed and the diesel used, and the sanctioned figures are reviewed with the utility once a year in the light of that log.

## 18. Training and competence

18.1. Analysts are trained on each method by the laboratory head and authorised in writing only after they have run the method on samples of known result and reached the expected answer three times.

18.2. Each analyst's competence is checked again every year on every method they are authorised for, using blind samples prepared by the laboratory head. An analyst who fails a check is suspended from that method until retrained and checked again.

18.3. Analysts attend at least two external training days a year, chosen with the laboratory head. Notes from each day are shared with the rest of the team at the next weekly meeting.

18.4. The laboratory keeps a training file for each analyst showing every sign-off, every annual check and every course attended.

## 8. Sunlight on the chilled block

8.1. The roof of the chilled block carries a grid-tied solar plant of 480 kWp, feeding the site's own load through the main switchboard. It cuts the daytime bill; nothing in the site's plans counts on it during an outage.

8.2. Dust from the ring road and smoke from stubble fires settle on the glass within days, and soiling is the plant's largest avoidable loss. It is estimated each week by comparing a cleaned reference panel with its neighbour.

8.3. The panels are washed every fifteen days from October to June, and after any dust storm, using demineralised water and soft brushes only; detergent and pressure washers are never used. In the monsoon months the rain does most of the work and washing is monthly. A soiling estimate above three per cent brings the next wash forward.

8.4. The plant has four inverter units. Each is checked once a month for string currents and alarm history, and its log is downloaded to the engineering share; an inverter fault is reported to the solar contractor the same day.

8.5. Nobody walks on the panels; the roof walkways are the only way across, and the roof is closed in rain and wind.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The laboratory head reviews this manual every June and whenever a method, a piece of equipment or a customer requirement changes.

16.2. Each revision is explained to the analysts at a briefing, and each analyst signs that they have read it.

16.3. Suggestions for changes come from analysts, from the people who send samples and from customers' auditors. Each suggestion is answered in writing by the laboratory head within a month, whether or not it is taken up, and the answers are kept with the manual's revision file.

## 8. Finding where warmth gets in

8.1. When the room has held its set point for 48 hours, the envelope is surveyed from outside for places where cold escapes: panel joints, door frames, pipe and cable penetrations, and the junction between wall panels and floor.

8.2. The survey is done by thermography, with an infrared camera, at night or on a dull day when the outside walls are not heated by the sun. Any joint that shows more than 3 C colder than the panel face beside it is marked, resealed and surveyed again.

8.3. The handover note of 2025 allowed a larger difference before resealing, and two joints it allowed are now visibly iced.

8.4. The images are saved with the room number, the date and the camera's serial number, and printed on the commissioning record with each marked joint circled.

8.5. A second thermography survey with the same infrared camera is done six months after handover, in the opposite season, and its images are compared with the first.

## 7. Bringing the temperature down

7.1. A new frozen chamber cannot be cooled as fast as the plant would allow. Water left in new concrete and in the insulation joints freezes, expands and lifts the floor if the room is cooled too quickly, and repairing a heaved floor means emptying the room for months.

7.2. A new chilled chamber is brought straight to its set point. A new freezer is first held at +2 C for 24 hours to let the floor and panels settle, and then brought below 0 C at no more than 2 C per hour until it reaches its set point.

7.3. The controller is programmed with this ramp before the plant starts, and the programme is printed and signed.

7.4. The first Ludhiana freezer was allowed twice that rate; its floor showed hairline cracks at two expansion joints within a year.

7.5. The floor heater mat is proven working before the pulldown begins, and the room temperature is logged every hour during the pulldown, so that the gradient actually achieved can be compared with the programmed one. Any hour faster than the programme stops the process, and any gradient steeper than planned is investigated before cooling resumes.

## What RF-118 may carry

RF-118 is a chilled asset. It may carry vaccines, insulin, milk and paneer. It
must not be loaded with frozen food: the body cannot hold the frozen target and
the frozen profile belongs to [RF-120](18-reefer-RF-120-asset-file.md).

This file sets no temperature limit of its own. Every limit and every excursion
duration for the products RF-118 carries is in
[the Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md), and
the sensor configuration is documented in
[the legacy sensor threshold file](02-sensor-thresholds.yaml). Where this file
and the SOP appear to differ, the SOP wins.

## 2. The team

2.1. The team is three people. Malavika Rane, a chartered accountant who spent eleven years in a firm of auditors before joining, heads it. Ishaan Kale covers finance and procurement engagements. Pooja Natu, who came from a pharmaceutical quality background, covers operations and the sites.

2.2. Engagements that need knowledge the team lacks, such as refrigeration plant or information security, borrow an expert from inside the company for the days needed, or hire one from outside with the board's agreement. A borrowed expert works under the engagement lead's direction and signs the working papers they contribute to.

2.3. The team sits at head office but spends roughly half its working days at the sites. Travel is booked through the normal travel desk and charged to the Internal Audit cost centre, never to the site being audited.

2.4. Each auditor completes at least forty hours of training a year. The record is kept by the head of the team and shown to the board in the annual report.

## 8. Keeping the auditors clean

8.1. An auditor does not audit their own past work, because independence is the whole value of the team. Nobody is placed on an engagement covering a function they worked in, or a decision they took part in, during the previous 24 months. The head of the team checks this when staffing each engagement and records the check in the planning memo.

8.2. Familiarity creeps in slowly, so rotation of leads is planned. An engagement lead takes the same site or department for at most three consecutive audits, after which another auditor leads it; each rotation is fixed a year ahead.

8.3. An auditor who has a family or financial interest in a supplier, a customer or a member of staff whose work is being examined declares it before fieldwork begins. A declared interest usually means a change of staffing, and it never means silence.

8.4. The head of the team reports any threat to the team's independence directly to the board chair, without going through management.

# Reefer asset file RF-118

Asset **RF-118** is an owned chilled reefer based at Nagpur DC. It is one of the
two pilot assets named in the 2025 telematics cutover, the other being cold room
C2 — see [Telematics Vendor Decision 2026](11-decision-telematics-vendor-2026.md).

⚠ Write the asset number as RF-118 on every dispatch note, challan and seal
photo. RF-119 and RF-120 are different vehicles with different profiles, and the
three numbers differ by one digit. A wrong digit on a challan has twice sent a
dairy crate run to a frozen body.

## 10. Racking and the empty room

10.1. Racking is erected after the tightness and evacuation tests and before the temperature tests, so that the room is tested in the form in which it will be used. Racking erected later means testing again.

10.2. Racking is inspected and load-signed by the racking supplier, who fixes load notices to the end of every run. Nobody places a pallet on racking that does not carry its notice.

10.3. Evaporator air paths are checked against the racking layout. A rack run that blocks an evaporator's throw is moved before the room is accepted.

10.4. Sprinklers and smoke detection, where the room has them, are tested by the fire contractor and signed off separately. The commissioning record notes the fire contractor's certificate number but does not repeat its contents.

## Known history

On the night of 9 February 2026 the Tessaline display on RF-118 jumped between
9.8 C and 3.4 C inside one minute while a hand-held gun read 3.4 C and a spare
logger read 3.6 C on the same insulin carton. The night team kept the original
sensor in place and put the spare logger next to the product, which is what
section 9 of [the SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md) requires, and refused
the driver's request to restart the app. The sensor was re-seated on 11 February
2026 under maintenance ticket NGP-MNT-731 and the alarm history was not closed
until QA had the export.

RF-118 also appears in the Nagpur night handover log for 18 October 2025, when
its driver asked what Compliance-Red means. Fleet Control has since printed the
escalation groups on the RF-118 cab card.

## 13. What customers are told

13.1. Customers hear about their returns from customer service, never from the hub directly. The hub sends customer service a daily report of what arrived, what was judged and what left, and customer service passes on what each customer needs to know.

13.2. A customer who calls the hub is given the customer service number politely and is not told anything about the goods over the phone.

13.3. Customers are never promised a credit, a replacement or a destruction date by hub staff. Those promises are made, if at all, by account managers after Finance has agreed.

13.4. Customer auditors who wish to see their returns at Bhosari are escorted by the hub manager or the QA officer on duty and see only their own goods and records.

## 12. People and training

12.1. Everyone who handles returns at the hub completes the company induction and the hub's own half-day course on receiving, labelling and the returns system before handling stock alone.

12.2. The QA officers on duty at Bhosari are trained by the QA function and hold the same authority as QA officers at any other site. They do not take instructions on pharmaceutical decisions from the hub manager or from account managers.

12.3. Receiving clerks are trained to say "I'll check and come back to you" to drivers and customers who ask what will happen to returned goods. The answer comes from customer service.

12.4. Agency staff may count and move cartons but may not scan them into the returns system or judge them.

12.5. Training is refreshed every year and whenever this manual changes.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The hub manager reviews this manual every July with the QA lead and the customer service lead, and sooner when a customer's contract or a company procedure changes what the hub must do.

16.2. Each revision is issued with a short note of what changed and why. Hub staff sign that they have read the note within a week of issue.

## Hours

The hub is open 08:00 to 20:00, Monday to Saturday.

## After hours

The hub does not receive visitors on Sundays or after 23:00.

## Chilled returns

Chilled returns may ride on a delivering vehicle's backhaul. The vehicle must reach the hub within 10 hours of collection. Consolidation of several customers' returns is arranged by Fleet Control.

## Debit notes

Customer service completes the reconciliation of each debit note with the hub's records within 10 working days. Any discrepancy is recorded; a difference above 5 per cent goes to the account manager.

## 7. Bringing the temperature down

7.1. A new frozen chamber cannot be cooled as fast as the plant would allow. Water left in new concrete and in the insulation joints freezes, expands and lifts the floor if the room is cooled too quickly, and repairing a heaved floor means emptying the room for months.

7.2. A new chilled chamber is brought straight to its set point. A new freezer is first held at +2 C for 24 hours to let the floor and panels settle, and then brought below 0 C at no more than 2 C per hour until it reaches its set point.

7.3. The controller is programmed with this ramp before the plant starts, and the programme is printed and signed.

7.4. The first Ludhiana freezer was allowed twice that rate; its floor showed hairline cracks at two expansion joints within a year.

7.5. The floor heater mat is proven working before the pulldown begins, and the room temperature is logged every hour during the pulldown, so that the gradient actually achieved can be compared with the programmed one. Any hour faster than the programme stops the process, and any gradient steeper than planned is investigated before cooling resumes.

## 14. Training and coaching for drivers

14.1. Every new owned-reefer driver rides two supervised runs with an experienced
driver before driving alone. One of the two is a night run.

14.2. The supervised runs cover the cab card, the takeover walk-round, the seal
routine, the red sleeve, the gate checklist for pharma runs and the way to speak
to Fleet Control on the phone. The experienced driver signs the new driver's
training sheet at the end of each run.

14.3. Telematics coaching calls are held within two working days of an alert, as
the policy says. The coach asks what happened before saying anything about what
should have happened.

14.4. Drivers who complete a year with no safety non-conformance receive a
certificate from the Fleet head, presented at the Nagpur driver meeting. The
certificate carries no money and is not tied to arrival times.

14.5. The Nagpur driver meeting is held on the last Saturday of each month in
the driver rest room. Attendance is paid duty time. Drivers on the road that day
receive the notes on their phone.

## 15. Route changes and diversions

15.1. A driver does not change the planned route on his own judgement unless the
road ahead is closed or unsafe. He stops, calls Fleet Control, and follows the
diversion Fleet Control gives.

15.2. Fleet Control checks any diversion against the lane record for that trip,
because a diversion may take the vehicle through a dead zone or past no safe
stopping place.

15.3. A diversion that adds a toll, a ghat road or a city centre is written on
the dispatch note with the reason.

15.4. Customer service is told of any diversion that will change the arrival
window, and tells the customer. The driver does not tell the customer himself.

15.5. Festivals, elections and large public events close roads without much
notice. Planners check the week's public calendar on Thursday when they build
the plan, and Fleet Control checks it again each morning.

## 6. Hiring

6.1. The DC starts with 72 people on the payroll on the day of first receipt: a site manager, a QA lead and two QA officers, an engineering lead and five technicians, six shift leads, forty-two warehouse staff, eight fleet and gate staff, and seven office staff for customer service, finance and HR. Contract security and cleaning are not counted.

6.2. The satellite starts with 18, mostly shift staff, with its own site lead and one technician seconded from the DC.

6.3. By the end of the first year the DC is planned to grow to 104, in line with signed volume, not ahead of it.

6.4. Recruitment is local wherever possible. Supervisors and the first QA officers are seconded from other Quillfern sites for six months so that the new team learns from people who have done the work before.

6.5. Every new joiner completes the company induction before handling stock, whatever the pressure of the opening weeks.

## 4. Taking over a vehicle

4.1. The driver taking over a vehicle walks round it with the driver handing
over, or with the shift lead if the vehicle was parked empty.

4.2. The walk-round covers tyres and wheel nuts, lights, mirrors, the reefer
unit's display and alarm light, the rear door hasp, the cab locker and the red
sleeve, the fire extinguisher, and the wheel chocks.

4.3. Any damage found on the walk-round is photographed and written on the
takeover sheet before the vehicle moves. Damage found later is presumed to have
happened on the later driver's watch.

4.4. The cab card is checked for the current Fleet Control, QA desk and
Compliance-Red numbers. A cab card printed before the Tessaline cutover is
replaced before the vehicle leaves.

4.5. The driver checks that the Tessaline unit shows the vehicle's own asset
number. Units have been swapped between vehicles in the workshop and not
re-labelled.

## 13. What it costs and when it pays

13.1. The board approved capital spending of Rs. 46 crore for the region: Rs. 31 crore for the DC's fit-out, racking, refrigeration and power, Rs. 6 crore for the satellite, and Rs. 9 crore for the owned fleet.

13.2. Running costs in the first year are budgeted at Rs. 2.1 crore a month at full volume, of which people are about a third and power and fuel another third.

13.3. The region is planned to cover its running costs in its ninth month and to pay back its capital in the twenty-sixth month after first receipt, on contracted volumes only. Any new contract shortens the payback; no forecast is counted until it is signed.

13.4. The region head reports actual against plan to Finance monthly and to the board quarterly.

13.5. Spending above the approved figure needs board approval, however small the overrun.

## 8. Checking ourselves against others

8.1. A laboratory can be consistently wrong without knowing it. The only way to find out is to test samples whose true answer is known to someone else.

8.2. The laboratory takes part in an external proficiency scheme for food microbiology twice a year, in which the scheme sends the same samples to many laboratories and compares their results. A result is satisfactory when its z-score lies between -2 and +2.

8.3. A score between 2 and 3 either way is investigated by the laboratory head and the cause written down. A score beyond 3 stops the laboratory reporting that test to anyone until the cause has been found and a repeat sample has passed.

8.4. For packaging tests, where no scheme exists, the laboratory runs one interlaboratory comparison a year with the box maker's own laboratory, testing samples cut from the same sheets. The two results must agree within the tolerance in the method file.

8.5. Proficiency results and each interlaboratory report are shown to the head of QA and to any customer auditor who asks.

## Outside samples

Once a year, in November, the laboratory takes part in an external proficiency scheme for food microbiology. The scheme sends the same samples to many laboratories and scores each result. At Jejuri a result is accepted if its score lies between -3 and +3. Anything outside that stops us reporting that test until we have found out why.

## 14. The annual look back

14.1. Every partner is scored once a year by Procurement, using the site managers' records and the engineering pool's opinion. The score is out of 100 and covers attendance times, quality of work, safety, paperwork, and conduct on site.

14.2. A partner scoring 65 or more stays on the list. A partner scoring below 65 is put on probation for six months with a written plan of what must improve.

14.3. A partner put on probation in two consecutive years is removed from the list, whatever its score at the end of the second probation.

14.4. A partner may see its score and the records behind it, and may answer in writing before the score is final.

14.5. Scores are not shared with other partners.

# Service Partner Onboarding Standard

## 1. What this standard is for

1.1. Quillfern buildings and vehicles are kept running by outside firms as much as by our own staff. Refrigeration engineers, generator agents, the people who service dock doors and levellers, pest controllers, cleaners, electricians, calibration laboratories and fire-equipment agents all come through our gates, and some of them work on the very plant that keeps customers' stock in range.

1.2. This standard says how such a firm becomes an approved service partner, what it must keep up to stay approved, and how it leaves the list. It applies to every site opened from 2025 onwards and to every firm that is newly approved anywhere in the company from the date of this revision.

1.3. It does not cover suppliers of goods, such as seals or forms, who deliver to Stores and never work on site. Those are approved under the purchasing rules.

1.4. It is written for Procurement, which keeps the list; for site managers, who call partners in; for QA, which approves partners who work near product; and for the engineering pool, which judges the technical competence of partners who work on plant.

1.5. "Partner" in this standard means a firm, not a person. The people the firm sends are its technicians.

## 17. Records

17.1. Procurement keeps each partner's file: the proposal, the papers, the visit report, the references, the approval, the agreements, every year's score, any probation plan and the reasons for leaving the list.

17.2. A partner's file is kept for six years after its last work order, or six years after it leaves the list, whichever comes later.

17.3. Work orders, permits and gas records are kept with the site's own records for the periods set by the documents that govern them.

17.4. Partner files are confidential. A partner may see its own file on request.

## 16. Gifts and conflicts

16.1. Nobody at Quillfern accepts a gift, a meal, travel or entertainment from a partner or a firm proposing to become one, beyond token items worth less than Rs. 1,000 in all in a year, such as a diary or a box of sweets at Diwali.

16.2. Anything above that is declined, or, where declining would cause offence, handed to HR and recorded.

16.3. A member of staff with a family or financial interest in a partner declares it to Procurement and takes no part in that partner's approval, scoring or work orders.

16.4. Partners are told these rules when they are approved, and asked to tell Procurement if anyone at Quillfern asks them for anything.

## 5. Taking the air out

5.1. Air and moisture left in a refrigeration system turn into acid and sludge that shorten the life of every component. Before charging, the system is put under vacuum with a pump connected at both the high and low sides.

5.2. The system is pumped down to 500 micron. The pump is then isolated and the system left; it passes if the gauge stays below 1,000 for 30 minutes. A rise above that means moisture or a leak, and the pumping continues or the leak is found.

5.3. The 2025 handover note took the contractor's default figures, which were looser on both counts.

5.4. The gauge used is electronic, connected as close to the system as the hose allows, and never read through the pump's own dial. The readings at isolation, at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes go on the test sheet.

5.5. Pumping is never stopped early because the contractor's crew is due elsewhere. A rushed vacuum is the commonest fault the engineering team finds in other people's plant, and the micron figure is the one most often written down without being read.

## 10. Lighting, heating and the office

10.1. All lighting on the site is LED. Chilled and frozen rooms use fittings rated for the temperature, and their drivers sit outside the rooms so that a failed driver can be changed without a person working in the cold.

10.2. Yard lighting is on a photocell with a timer override, and the gate and the dock aprons stay lit all night whatever the timer says. A failed yard light is reported at the shift handover and repaired within two days.

10.3. The office and canteen are heated in winter by heat pumps. Electric bar heaters and fan heaters are not used anywhere on site; a heater found in an office is removed and the person who brought it is told why.

10.4. Floor heating under the frozen block is electric, with its own thermostat and alarm. Its current is read at every monthly energy review, because a heater mat that has failed shows up on the meter long before the floor heaves.

10.5. Office equipment is switched off at the wall at the end of the day except the servers and the alarm panel. The last person to leave the office checks the switches and signs the closing sheet at the gate.

## 11. Closing out the contractor's list

11.1. As the tests proceed, the engineering lead keeps a single snag list of everything not yet right. Each item is graded A, meaning the room cannot hold product safely until it is fixed, or B, meaning the room can be used while it is fixed.

11.2. Practical completion is certified only when no A item remains open. Every B item must be closed within 30 days of that certificate, and the retention money held from the contractor is not released until the last one is.

11.3. The first Ludhiana build allowed longer, and three of its B items were still open when the retention was paid.

11.4. Each item carries its owner, the dates raised and closed, and the initials of the person who checked the closure. Items are closed on inspection, never on the contractor's word; the punch list is a record of what was seen, not of what was promised.

11.5. A B item still open on day 30 becomes an A item for the purpose of releasing money, though the room stays in use. Contractors who want their retention sooner close their snag items sooner, and argue with the punch grades in writing.

## 3. Power

3.1. A unit needs a three-phase supply of 415 V, 32 A, through the pool's own
weatherproof socket, which the customer's electrician fits before the unit
arrives.

3.2. Every campaign hire also has a standby genset of the pool's own, wired
through an automatic transfer switch. The transfer switch must bring the standby set on line within 30 seconds of mains loss. The changeover is tested
at commissioning by pulling the mains isolator.

3.3. Long hires at sites with a reliable supply and their own standby may use
the site's standby instead of the pool's, if the pool engineer has tested the
changeover and written the result on the placement sheet.

3.4. The genset's fuel is the customer's responsibility on a campaign hire. The
pool engineer shows the customer's staff how to read the gauge and how to call
for fuel before the tank is low.

3.5. Extension leads, adaptors and shared sockets are never used.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

## 9. The envelope, doors and floor

9.1. Every door is tested for its seal by closing it on a sheet of paper at several points around the frame; the paper must not slide out easily. Rapid-roll doors are timed from fully open to fully closed, and their safety edges tested by obstruction.

9.2. Door heaters and frame heaters on freezer doors are checked for current and for warmth by hand at the frame.

9.3. Strip curtains are fitted after the doors are tested, never before, so that the door seal test is not confused by the curtain.

9.4. The floor finish is inspected for cracks and for ponding with water before the room is cooled. Ponding is ground out and refinished; it is not left to freeze.

9.5. Pressure-relief ports in freezer walls are checked for free movement, because a freezer without working relief can buckle its own panels when the door is shut on warm air.

## 3. Behind the chain-link fence

3.1. The 2 MVA transformer in the substation yard is oil-filled, and its oil is usually the first thing to fail without anyone noticing. Moisture and sludge pull down the oil's dielectric strength long before anything trips.

3.2. A sample is drawn by the approved testing laboratory every six months, in March and September, with the unit on load. The breakdown voltage must read at least 50 kV. A sample below that is filtered on site within seven days and drawn again after filtering.

3.3. The 2025 commissioning note allowed a yearly sample and a lower pass figure; both were tightened after the first monsoon, when condensation was found in the breather.

3.4. The laboratory's report is filed in the substation folder and copied to the engineering lead together with the dielectric figure from each of the last four samples, so that a slow decline is visible before it becomes a failure.

3.5. Nobody opens the transformer enclosure except the electrical supervisor or the utility's linesman, and never alone.

## 14. Changes to this manual

14.1. Revision 2 (February 2026) lengthened the stability hold after a campaign
unit drifted.

14.2. Revision 3 (July 2026) added the long-hire daily charge and the rule that
a move within a site is a new placement.

14.3. The pool lead reviews this manual every January.

# East Coast Region Operating Plan 2026-28

## 1. Why the east coast

1.1. Quillfern has grown along an arc from the west into the centre of the country, and its customers have asked for years to be served on the east coast as well. Three things decided the matter in 2025. A shrimp exporter in the Godavari delta offered a five-year volume commitment if we would hold its frozen stock near the port. A vaccine maker opening a fill-finish line near Bhubaneswar asked for a cold distribution partner inside the state. And the growth of organised food retail in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha meant that frozen and chilled lanes we were already being asked to quote would pay for themselves.

1.2. This plan describes the region we are building: one distribution centre at Visakhapatnam, which people on the ground call Vizag, and one inland satellite at Bhubaneswar. It covers the calendar, space, people, power, weather, port work, fleet, money and the measures by which the region will be judged in its first two years.

1.3. It is written for the region's own managers, for the head-office teams who support them, and for the board, which approved the investment in March 2026. It replaces the outline written in 2025, which was prepared before the site was chosen.

1.4. Company-wide procedures apply in the region from the first day. Nothing in this plan relaxes a temperature rule, a driving rule or a quality rule because the region is new.

## 16. How the region will be judged

16.1. In its first two years the region is measured on: deliveries on time, which is planned at 96 per cent from month four; temperature excursions per thousand pallets moved; customer complaints; safety incidents; and money against plan.

16.2. Measures are reported monthly from the same systems as every other site. The region does not keep figures of its own.

16.3. A measure that misses plan for three months in a row is reviewed by the region head with the Chief Operating Officer, and a recovery plan is agreed in writing.

16.4. Safety incidents are reported the same day, as at every site, and the region is not given a softer target because it is new.

## 5. The main promise

5.1. Quillfern's main promise is that orders arrive at the right place, inside the agreed delivery window, with the right items in the right quantities. Each order meets all of those or it does not; there is no partial credit.

5.2. The share of orders that meet them in a calendar month must be at least 97 per cent. For each full percentage point by which a month falls below that, Vetrix receives a service credit of 2 per cent of that month's handling invoice, up to a maximum of 10 per cent.

5.3. In the first contract year the target was 95 per cent, with the same credit rate.

5.4. An order is excluded from the otif count only where the failure was caused by Vetrix, by the receiving party, or by an event outside Quillfern's control listed in the contract, reported within one working day.

5.5. A shortfall in two consecutive months needs a written recovery plan from Quillfern, whatever the credit paid; a shortfall in three brings the otif figure to the half-yearly meeting of senior managers.

5.6. Credits are deducted from the next invoice, not paid in cash.

## Delivery promise

Orders must arrive complete, undamaged and inside the delivery window. The otif target is a monthly figure. At least 95 per cent of orders each month must meet it. For each full point of shortfall below that, Vetrix receives a credit of 2 per cent of the month's handling invoice.

## 12. Fleet for the region

12.1. The region starts with 14 owned reefers: eight chilled and six frozen, all new, delivered to the DC in November 2026. Peak demand is met with hired reefers from approved vendors, up to nine at a time.

12.2. The nightly trunk run between the DC and the satellite uses two owned reefers and two drivers on each vehicle, whatever the day's departure time, because the run is long and mostly at night.

12.3. Local deliveries around Visakhapatnam and around Bhubaneswar are made by small chilled vans hired with drivers.

12.4. A fleet planner based at the DC builds the region's plan. Fleet Control's national desk remains the controller for vehicles on the road.

12.5. A second set of tyres, belts and reefer spares is stocked at the DC, because the nearest dealer workshop for the reefer units is several hours away.

## 7. Every month on paper

7.1. Quillfern sends Vetrix a monthly report of every measure in this schedule, with the underlying order list attached, so that Vetrix's team can check any figure for itself.

7.2. The report reaches Vetrix by the 7th working day of the following month. It includes a one-page scorecard of the month's measures against target, the service credits due, the excursions and their status, and the returns received at the Bhosari hub.

7.3. In the first contract year the report was due by the 10th working day, which left too little time to discuss it at the monthly review.

7.4. Each kpi in the report is defined in this schedule; Quillfern does not change a definition without Vetrix's written agreement.

7.5. The report is prepared by the account manager and checked by Finance before it is sent. The account manager signs it.

7.6. A kpi missed in the month carries a short note of the cause and the action taken, written in plain language, and the same note is copied to the scorecard archive.

## 14. Ending the contract

14.1. Either company may end the contract by giving six months' written notice, or at once for a serious breach not put right within 30 days of a written demand.

14.2. On ending, Quillfern hands over Vetrix's stock and records to Vetrix or to a new provider named by Vetrix, in an orderly way agreed between the two companies, and continues to meet this schedule until the last stock has left.

14.3. Frozen breeding stock is handed over unit by unit, with the receiving party's trained staff present, and each unit's level is recorded on handover.

## 12. Invoicing

12.1. Quillfern invoices Vetrix monthly in arrears, with separate invoices for storage, handling and transport, within five working days of the month's end.

12.2. Service credits appear as a separate line on the next handling invoice, with a reference to the month and the measure that earned them.

12.3. Vetrix pays each invoice within 45 days of its date. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days; the undisputed part is paid on time.

## Monthly report

Each kpi is defined in this schedule. The report and its one-page scorecard reach Vetrix by the 10th working day of the following month.

## Chilled returns

Chilled returns may ride on a delivering vehicle's backhaul. The vehicle must reach the hub within 10 hours of collection. Consolidation of several customers' returns is arranged by Fleet Control.

## 5. The ride to the hub

5.1. Most chilled returns come back in vehicles that delivered something else first. Putting returns on that backhaul is cheaper than sending an empty van, but a chilled carton that has already been out of the customer's fridge is fragile, and every extra stop warms it.

5.2. A chilled return rides on a delivering vehicle only if Fleet Control's plan puts that vehicle at the hub within 6 hours of the collection. Where it cannot, a dedicated pickup is sent instead, however small the load.

5.3. Fleet Control records the planned arrival time on the collection note, and the receiving team writes the actual arrival time beside it, so that the rule can be checked month by month.

5.4. The interim note allowed a longer window, and the hub's first summer showed that it was too long.

5.5. Frozen returns are never added to backhaul unless the delivering body is itself frozen; consolidation of frozen and chilled returns in one body is not allowed.

5.6. Planners may combine several customers' returns on one dedicated pickup, but the consolidation is planned by Fleet Control and never arranged by drivers on the road.

## 9. Bringing the kit home again

9.1. The liner and the cold packs are expensive and can be used again; the outer shipper is collected too, so that customers are not left with a bulky box, even though it is recyclable. The programme asks every customer to hand the whole kit back, empty, at their next delivery or by pickup from the door.

9.2. Customers pay a refundable deposit of Rs. 80 on the first kit they order. The amount is refunded in full if the box comes back within 14 days of delivery, in a condition the hub can reuse, and is kept if it does not.

9.3. The pilot's deposit was smaller and gave less time, and too many boxes stayed in customers' homes.

9.4. Outer shippers that cannot be reused are flattened at the Bhosari hub and sent for recycling; they are recyclable board with water-based ink. Liners that cannot be reused are sent to the moulder, who takes them back as raw material.

9.5. Customer service handles questions about refunds; the van drivers do not discuss money at the door.

## 7. Sorting what came back

7.1. Grading is a decision about every line, not a valuation, and each decision is checked by a second person.

7.2. Every line is judged within 24 hours of receipt. Bucket A means fit to go back to the owner's saleable stock under the owner's own rules; B means the owner must decide; C means destruction.

7.3. Grading of pharmaceutical lines is done by the QA officer on duty, not by the receiving team, and a pharmaceutical line never goes into A without QA's signature on the returns system.

7.4. Food lines go to C whenever the packaging has been opened, the use-by date has passed, or the temperature history is missing for a chilled or frozen line.

7.5. Lines judged B are reported to the owner the same day. Until the owner replies, they stay in the area for their temperature class, marked with an orange label.

7.6. A line may move from bucket B to A or C on the owner's written instruction only; it never moves because space ran short.

## 16. Summer and monsoon

16.1. Pune's hottest weeks fall in April and May, when afternoon doorsteps in the eastern suburbs reach well above 40 C. In those weeks the kitting room adds a reflective paper sleeve between the shipper and the liner for kits on afternoon delivery windows, and the delivery windows themselves are shortened by Thali Box.

16.2. In the monsoon the danger is wet board rather than heat. Shippers are kept under cover from the kitting room to the van, and van drivers carry a supply of plastic rain covers for kits that must be left in an open porch. The cover is collected with the empty box.

16.3. Mumbai deliveries face humidity all year. Shippers for Mumbai are drawn from the driest stock in the store and are not stored at Kondhwa for longer than four weeks.

16.4. The packaging engineer reviews the complaint log each June and each October to see whether the season's precautions worked, and changes them for the next year if they did not.

## 11. Vans and handling

11.1. Kits travel to customers in chilled vans running at +4 C. Kits are loaded in delivery order, stacked no more than five high, with heavier kits at the bottom.

11.2. Drivers carry kits by the handles moulded into the shipper, never by the strapping, and never throw a kit onto a doorstep.

11.3. A kit that is dropped from a height in the van or at the door is reported by the driver and checked at the next stop for damage. A kit with a cracked liner is taken back to Kondhwa.

11.4. Vans carry no other customer's goods while kits are on board.

# Bhosari hub: interim rules for returned goods

Interim rules for the first months of the Bhosari hub, until the returns manual is issued.

## Sorting

Every line is judged within 48 hours. Grading puts each line in one bucket: A restock, B owner decides, C destroy.

## Destruction

Pharmaceutical stock leaves for destruction with the contractor's manifest. Incineration must take place within 60 days of collection.

## Hours

The hub is open 08:00 to 20:00, Monday to Saturday.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The hub manager reviews this manual every July with the QA lead and the customer service lead, and sooner when a customer's contract or a company procedure changes what the hub must do.

16.2. Each revision is issued with a short note of what changed and why. Hub staff sign that they have read the note within a week of issue.

## 12. Closing an engagement and reporting

12.1. Fieldwork ends with an exit meeting at which the engagement lead goes through every finding with the department head, before anything is written down as final. Nothing should appear in a final report that the department hears of for the first time on paper.

12.2. The final report is issued within 15 working days of that meeting, to the department head, the Chief Financial Officer and the Managing Director, and to the chair of the board's audit committee, which reads every final report at its next quarterly sitting.

12.3. Until this programme the report was allowed 30 working days, and too many reports arrived after the people involved had forgotten the details.

12.4. The committee may call any department head to explain an overdue action in person, and may ask why any report missed its date after the exit meeting.

## Reports

The final report is issued within 30 working days of the exit meeting and goes to the department head, the Chief Financial Officer and the board's audit committee.

## 8. How marks are given

8.1. Every module ends in a theory paper and a practical task. The practical — a hands-on test on real equipment in the workshop or on site — counts for more, because the trade is learned with the hands.

8.2. A practical passes at 70 per cent and a theory paper at 60 per cent; a failed module is repeated with the next intake. An apprentice may repeat no more than two modules in the whole programme.

8.3. Practical tasks are marked against a written checklist by a trainer who did not teach the module, and the checklist is shown to the apprentice beforehand. Safety items on the checklist are pass-or-fail: an apprentice who skips lockout, for example, fails the task whatever else they did well.

8.4. Marks are given back within a week, with the marker's comments. An apprentice who disputes a mark asks the workshop lead for a second marking.

8.5. The final assessment at the end of the programme is held with an examiner from the apprentice's ITI, and leads to the Quillfern certificate of completion.

## 9. Counting the money

9.1. Every Quillfern site holds a petty cash float for small purchases that cannot wait for a purchase order: courier charges, a replacement padlock, tea for a visiting inspector. It is an imprest: topped back up to a fixed figure against vouchers, never increased because a month was busy.

9.2. The float is Rs. 15,000 at each site and Rs. 25,000 at head office. Internal Audit counts it by surprise twice a year at every site, with the custodian present, and reconciles cash plus vouchers to the fixed figure.

9.3. A petty cash shortage of more than Rs. 500 is reported to the head of Finance the same day, with the custodian's written explanation.

9.4. The counts in 2025 were yearly and each imprest smaller; both changed in this programme.

## 6. How findings are graded

6.1. Every finding is graded high, medium or low by the engagement lead and confirmed by the head of the team. High means a control has failed in a way that could cause a material loss, a breach of law or a harm to a customer's product; low means an improvement that would be nice to have.

6.2. A finding of high severity goes to the auditee's department head in a draft report. The auditee's written response, with an action, an owner and a date, is due within 10 working days. Medium findings are due within 20 working days and low within 30.

6.3. An agreed action on a high finding is due for completion within 90 days of the final report, unless the board agrees a longer date.

6.4. The grade is the auditor's decision. A department may argue with it in its response, and the argument is printed in the final report beside the grade, but the grade is not lowered to get a response signed.

6.5. A finding of medium severity repeated from the previous audit of the same area is raised to high.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 15. Review of this programme

15.1. The programme is reviewed every March, before the next year's plan is drafted, and revised when the board changes the team's remit or the risk register changes materially.

15.2. Department heads may comment on the draft plan before it goes to the board. Their comments are attached to the plan the board approves.

# Safety and Incident Manual, Ludhiana DC

## 1. What this manual is for

1.1. Ludhiana DC employs about ninety people on two shifts, hosts contractors most days of the year, and receives up to forty vehicles in a day. Every one of those people should go home in the condition they arrived in. This manual says how the site keeps them safe, what happens when something goes wrong, and who is answerable for each part.

1.2. It is written for everyone who works on the site, whether employed by Quillfern, supplied by an agency or sent by a contractor, and for the managers who plan their work. Drivers of visiting vehicles are covered by the gate rules in section 12 and by their own employers' rules.

1.3. The manual does not replace the law. Where the Factories Act, the state rules made under it, or any other law asks for more than this manual, the law applies, and the safety officer tells the site manager what has changed.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the safety rules issued when the site opened in 2025. Several limits in those rules were copied from another company's manual without anyone asking whether they suited a building with freezers at -25 C and a yard full of reversing trucks. This revision sets limits for this site.

## 9. Cold work

9.1. The frozen block at Ludhiana runs at -25 C, colder than most of the company's freezers, and the body loses heat there faster than people expect. Cold slows thinking before it slows hands, which is why the rules below do not depend on how anyone feels.

9.2. Nobody works inside the frozen block for longer than 40 minutes at a stretch, even in a full freezer suit. A 20-minute rewarming break in the canteen or the warm room follows each stretch, with a hot drink available.

9.3. The shift lead keeps the break board for the frozen block and moves names on it; the workers do not keep their own time.

9.4. Signs of hypothermia, such as uncontrolled shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness or confusion, mean the person leaves the cold at once with a colleague and is checked by a first aider. A person who has shown those signs does not go back into the cold that shift.

9.5. In 2025 the stretch was an hour and the rewarming break fifteen minutes, and two cases of mild hypothermia followed; both were changed after the first winter.

## 6. Riding through the gap

6.1. The refrigeration controllers, the alarm panel, the gate barrier and the two servers in the comms room do not wait for a generator. They run through the ups in the comms room, which carries them through the seconds of a changeover and through a generator that fails to start.

6.2. The unit must give at least 45 minutes at full connected load on battery alone. That figure was 20 minutes in the commissioning note, and was raised after a winter night in January 2026 when both sets were slow to start in the fog and the alarm panel went dark for four minutes.

6.3. Autonomy falls as batteries age, so the battery string is replaced every four years, whatever its test results, and load-tested every six months with the site on grid power.

6.4. The autonomy measured at each load test is written in the switch room log beside the date. A string that gives less than the required figure on two tests in a row is replaced early.

6.5. Nothing new is plugged into the ups without the electrical supervisor's written approval. Kettles, heaters and phone chargers found on its outlets are removed.

## Comms room

The ups in the comms room carries the controls, the alarm panel and the servers; its autonomy is set below. On battery it must run for 20 minutes at full load. Batteries are replaced every five years.

## 14. Near misses and hazards

14.1. A near miss is anything that could have hurt someone but did not. Near misses are reported on the yellow cards kept beside every clocking machine, or by telling the shift lead, who writes the card.

14.2. The safety officer reads every card within two working days, decides what action is needed and posts the result on the canteen board, without the reporter's name unless they asked for it to be shown.

14.3. A person who reports a near miss is thanked, not blamed. Shift leads who discourage reporting are themselves reported to the site manager.

14.4. The number of near-miss cards is reported to the safety council each month. A falling number is investigated as carefully as a rising one.

## 10. Lighting, heating and the office

10.1. All lighting on the site is LED. Chilled and frozen rooms use fittings rated for the temperature, and their drivers sit outside the rooms so that a failed driver can be changed without a person working in the cold.

10.2. Yard lighting is on a photocell with a timer override, and the gate and the dock aprons stay lit all night whatever the timer says. A failed yard light is reported at the shift handover and repaired within two days.

10.3. The office and canteen are heated in winter by heat pumps. Electric bar heaters and fan heaters are not used anywhere on site; a heater found in an office is removed and the person who brought it is told why.

10.4. Floor heating under the frozen block is electric, with its own thermostat and alarm. Its current is read at every monthly energy review, because a heater mat that has failed shows up on the meter long before the floor heaves.

10.5. Office equipment is switched off at the wall at the end of the day except the servers and the alarm panel. The last person to leave the office checks the switches and signs the closing sheet at the gate.

## 14. The team's own quality

14.1. The team reviews its own work after each engagement: what took longer than planned, where evidence was hard to get, and whether the report's findings were accepted. The notes feed the next year's planning.

14.2. Once every three years an outside firm reviews the team against recognised internal audit standards. The first review is planned for 2028.

14.3. Department heads are sent a short questionnaire after each engagement, asking whether the auditors were clear, fair and courteous. The answers go to the head of the team and, in summary, to the board.

14.4. The head of the team reports to the board once a year on the team's performance: engagements completed against plan, findings by grade, actions closed and overdue, and the results of the questionnaires.

## 17. Working with the other auditors

17.1. The statutory auditors may rely on Internal Audit's work where they judge it reliable. The head of the team meets the statutory audit partner twice a year, shares the plan in April and the year's reports in January, and gives them access to working papers on request.

17.2. Customer auditors and certification bodies are not given Internal Audit reports. If a customer asks whether Quillfern has an internal audit function, the account manager may say that it does and what it covers in general terms.

17.3. Where a customer's audit finding overlaps with an engagement in the plan, the engagement lead reads the customer's report and its agreed actions before fieldwork, so that the department is not asked the same questions twice and the two sets of actions do not contradict each other.

17.4. Findings from the insurers' surveys and from regulators' inspections are added to the risk register when the team plans the next year. They are not repeated as Internal Audit findings unless the team has tested the matter itself.

17.5. Nothing Internal Audit learns from another auditor's work is passed on outside the company without the head of the team's approval and, where the work belongs to someone else, that party's agreement.

# Pharma Store Quality Manual, West Zone

## 1. Purpose and reach

1.1. The store at Changodar, on the south-west edge of Ahmedabad, is the first Quillfern building that holds medicines and nothing else. It opened in September 2025 in a leased shed inside a pharmaceutical estate off the Sarkhej–Bavla highway. From its first week its customers — two vaccine makers, a biologics firm and three hospital groups in Gujarat — asked for a written quality system they could audit against. This manual is that system. It says how the store keeps product fit for the patient, how it proves that it did so, and who answers when it did not.

1.2. It is written for the people who work in the building: receiving clerks, pickers, dispatch staff, the shift QA officers, the engineering technician and the store manager. It is also written for auditors, who will read it more carefully than anyone on the floor and who should be able to find, somewhere in it, the reason for every record the store keeps.

1.3. Where this manual and a company-wide procedure disagree about a temperature limit, a notification window or a quarantine rule, the company procedure applies and this manual is corrected at its next revision. The manual sets no temperature limit of its own; it says how those limits are kept in this building, by these people.

1.4. Revision 3 is in force from 11/05/2026. The summaries written while the store was being fitted out are withdrawn and kept only as history. Earlier revisions of this manual are withdrawn from the shared drive on the day a new one is issued.

## Context

Quillfern operates owned reefers, hired peak-season reefers, cold-room probes,
and dock sensors. The current vendor, Kalpa Fleet Systems, has been in use since
2014. The 2023 contract expires on 31 December 2023. Finance asked whether we
should renew Kalpa, move to Tessaline Telematics, or buy a mixed package with
truck devices from one supplier and warehouse sensors from another.

The operating requirement is simple: Fleet Control must see truck location,
temperature, door status, and alert history without calling the driver. QA must
retrieve a trip or room report during an investigation. The vendor must support
Nagpur as central hub, Guwahati and Coimbatore as smaller DCs, and hired trucks
during vaccine and dairy peak months.

## ⚠ One row this review did not update

**The customer notification row above is deliberately blank.** At the time of
this review two customer notification matrices were on file and the reviewer
could not confirm which one Customer Service had been issued. Do not guess from
this map: open the matrices themselves, take the one with the later effective
date, and check whether it amends the SOP clause rather than merely repeating
it. This row will be filled at the next review of this map.

## Decision

Quillfern will renew Kalpa Fleet Systems for 36 months beginning 1 January 2024.
The renewal covers 147 owned reefers, 63 hired-truck devices during peak months,
and 38 fixed sensors across rooms and docks. The implementation and renewal
charge is Rs. 18.40 lakh. The recurring charge is Rs. 920 per active truck per
month and Rs. 310 per fixed sensor per month.

No split-vendor model will be used in 2024. IT will keep one support desk and
one monthly export from Kalpa. Fleet and QA will continue to use the KLP trip
number for audit packets.

## Rejected options

Tessaline was rejected in 2023 because the API was not demonstrated on a live
Quillfern route, the commercial proposal required a larger first-year payment,
and the field-support rota for Nagpur was still being hired. The evaluation team
liked the one-minute polling and the proposed exception export, but decided that
those benefits were not enough to justify a complete change before the 2024
vaccine season.

A split model was also rejected. In that model, Kalpa would have stayed on
trucks while warehouse probes moved to Tessaline. IT objected that two source
systems would create audit confusion and double monthly reconciliation work.
Finance objected that the split model removed volume discounts from both
vendors.

## What was done

- Kalpa platform access ended on **30 April 2026**, the date the 2026 decision
  record set for retiring the export script.
- Trip data from 2014 to 2025 was exported to cold storage: 48,900 trips, all
  carrying the KLP prefix, 2.1 TB including the raw probe series. Two copies,
  one on the Pune HQ archive volume and one with the audit vendor.
- The alert routing that Kalpa used was retired with it. What it looked like is
  described in [the Kalpa Alert Routing Guide](archive/a02-kalpa-alert-routing-guide-2021.md),
  which is kept only so auditors can see how alarms were routed before
  Compliance-Red existed.
- The guard cabin tablet at Nagpur was wiped of its login and left in place as a
  read-only audit device. It must not be used to open or acknowledge an alarm.
- The Kalpa sticker on the Nagpur admin wall was removed on 5 May 2026. The
  night team had asked for this twice because new drivers were reading it as
  current.

# PROJ-125: Kalpa decommission and audit export

**PROJ-125** ended Quillfern's use of Kalpa Fleet Systems as a running platform
and preserved its history as files. It is closed. PROJ-125 is the last of the
three projects in this series; the other two are
[PROJ-123](19-project-PROJ-123-dockwise-rollout.md) and
[PROJ-124](20-project-PROJ-124-red-sleeve-and-passive-shippers.md), and neither
of them touched a telematics platform.

## Consequences

The decision should be reviewed no earlier than April 2026 unless three major
alert failures occur in a single quarter. A major alert failure means patient
critical stock, no automatic alert to Fleet Control or QA, and a confirmed
temperature breach.

IT must maintain an export script for Kalpa reports. QA must note that Kalpa
uses five-minute polling and may require interpolation in timelines. Fleet must
continue keeping paper driver call logs because Kalpa's door-open event is not
trusted during poor network coverage.

Col. Sandhu's closing comment: "We will not chase a fashionable dashboard while
our drivers and auditors know the present one. STABILITY FIRST; NOVELTY SECOND."

Paper driver call logs were not retired. Fleet keeps them because network

## 9. Bringing the kit home again

9.1. The liner and the cold packs are expensive and can be used again; the outer shipper is collected too, so that customers are not left with a bulky box, even though it is recyclable. The programme asks every customer to hand the whole kit back, empty, at their next delivery or by pickup from the door.

9.2. Customers pay a refundable deposit of Rs. 80 on the first kit they order. The amount is refunded in full if the box comes back within 14 days of delivery, in a condition the hub can reuse, and is kept if it does not.

9.3. The pilot's deposit was smaller and gave less time, and too many boxes stayed in customers' homes.

9.4. Outer shippers that cannot be reused are flattened at the Bhosari hub and sent for recycling; they are recyclable board with water-based ink. Liners that cannot be reused are sent to the moulder, who takes them back as raw material.

9.5. Customer service handles questions about refunds; the van drivers do not discuss money at the door.

# Returns and Reverse Logistics Manual

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. Goods come back. Hospitals over-order, pharmacies close, restaurants reject a load for a torn carton, a meal-kit customer goes on holiday and the box sits on a doorstep, and a manufacturer withdraws a batch. Until 2025 each Quillfern site dealt with what came back in its own way, usually in a corner of the dock that nobody owned. The Bhosari hub was opened to put an end to that.

1.2. This manual says how goods travel back from customers and consignees, how they are received and judged at Bhosari, and how they leave again: back to stock, back to their owner, or to destruction. It is written for the hub's own staff, for the drivers and planners who bring returns in, and for the customer service agents and account managers who promise customers what will happen to their goods.

1.3. It sets no temperature limit and no quarantine rule of its own. Product that may have been harmed by temperature is handled under the company's excursion and quarantine procedures, and this manual only says where it sits and who moves it while those procedures run.

1.4. Revision 3 replaces the interim note written when the hub opened in 2025 and the two earlier revisions of this manual. Several figures changed after the hub's first full year; each section that changed says so.

## Returns

Customers pay a deposit on their first kit. Rs. 50, refunded if the box comes back within 7 days. Shippers that cannot be reused are recyclable.

## 17. Busy months

17.1. Returns rise in predictable waves. Hospitals send back surplus after the financial year closes in March; restaurants return frozen stock after the festival weeks in October and November; meal-kit boxes come back in a flood after every long weekend, when customers who forgot to pause their deliveries find a box on the doorstep.

17.2. The hub manager publishes a peak plan each February for the year, listing the expected peaks, the extra agency staff booked for each and the days on which no leave is granted to the receiving team. The plan is shared with Fleet Control and customer service, so that collections can be spread over several days instead of arriving in one.

17.3. In a peak week, receiving starts an hour earlier and the second shift runs until midnight. The timings in this manual still apply: a peak is a reason to add people, not a reason to let goods wait.

17.4. If the hub cannot keep to the timings even with extra people, the hub manager tells the operations head and customer service the same day, and customer service slows the issue of new return numbers until the hub has caught up. Customers are told the reason plainly.

## 11. Packaging that comes back on purpose

11.1. Some programmes send their own reusable packaging back through the hub, and Vetrix Animal Health sends its returned vaccines here from Punjab and Haryana: insulated meal-kit boxes from the Thali Box programme, crates from bakery and dairy customers, and passive shippers belonging to pharmaceutical customers.

11.2. Reusable packaging is counted on arrival and stored by owner in the ambient hall. It is not cleaned at Bhosari unless the owner's contract says so; it is returned to the owner's own kitting site on the next scheduled run.

11.3. Packaging that arrives with product still inside is treated as a return of that product first and as packaging second.

11.4. Broken packaging is set aside and reported to the owner, who decides whether it is repaired or scrapped. Quillfern does not scrap a customer's packaging on its own judgement.

11.5. Each owner receives a monthly count of packaging received, held and sent back.

# Thali Box pilot: pack note

Packaging used for the Thali Box meal-kit pilot from April 2025.

## Outer

Three-ply corrugated slotted box, tested by bct. Compression strength at least 300 kgf.

## 12. Complaints about packaging

12.1. Complaints from Thali Box customers about packaging, such as a crushed box, a leaking pack or a warm kit, come to Quillfern through Thali Box's customer team. They are logged by customer service and passed to the packaging engineer the same day.

12.2. Each complaint is traced to the kit's order number, the components' lot numbers, the van and the delivery time. The packaging engineer writes a short finding within five working days.

12.3. Complaints are counted per thousand kits delivered and reviewed at the monthly meeting with Thali Box. A component whose complaint rate rises for two months running is reviewed with its supplier.

## 6. The last ten metres

6.1. The rider parks where the two-wheeler is safe and visible, takes the pouch
from the carrier, shuts the lid at once and walks to the door. The carrier is
never left open while the rider is away from it.

6.2. Patients do not always hear the bell. The rider waits ten minutes and rings twice, the second call at least five minutes after the first. If there is
still no answer the pouch goes back into the carrier, the rider tells the hub,
and the hub lead calls the patient to re-slot.

6.3. Insulin is never left with anyone else unless the order itself names an alternate receiver. A neighbour, a watchman or the shop next door is not an
alternate receiver because they offer, however well the rider knows them.

6.4. An alternate receiver named on the order gives the same OTP as the patient
would. The rider writes the receiver's name on the slip.

6.5. The rider never enters a flat. Pouches are handed over at the door, and a
patient who cannot come to the door is visited by Nirmaya's care team, not by
the rider.

6.6. The rider photographs the pouch at the door, never the patient and never
the inside of the home, and uploads the photograph before moving off.

## 1. What the programme does

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and
in the slot the patient booked.

1.2. The programme started on 1 August 2025 with nine riders and about 300 drops
a week. By April 2026 it had 26 riders and about 1,100 drops a week across Pune
and Pimpri-Chinchwad.

1.3. Only insulin pens, cartridges and vials are carried. Vaccines and other
cold medicines are not carried unless Nirmaya adds them by a written change
signed by both sides, and no such change has been signed.

1.4. Quillfern does not advise patients on their medicine. A patient who asks a
rider how much to take, or whether a pen is the right one, is given the Nirmaya
care-desk number printed on the delivery slip.

1.5. Nirmaya owns the stock and the patient relationship. Quillfern owns the
cold chain from the hub to the door, and is answerable for it.

## 7. Goods arriving

7.1. A vehicle arriving at the store is checked before it is opened: the seal number against the paperwork, the condition of the doors and the reefer's display. The driver stays with the vehicle until goods-in has finished with it, and is offered the drivers' room, not the canteen.

7.2. Every inbound vehicle's temperature printout or download is read at the goods-in desk before a single pallet crosses the threshold. Drivers call any missing stretch a "hole" in the printout, and holes are common on loads that come round the Ahmedabad ring road, where some older reefers lose their logger signal. A break of up to ten minutes in the record may be accepted by the goods-in clerk; anything longer goes to the Responsible Person, who decides. A record that is in range throughout but shows the reefer door opening during the journey is also referred to her.

7.3. Pallets are checked against the advance notice by batch and quantity. A batch that does not match the notice is received into quarantine rather than refused at the door, so that the customer's stock is protected while the paperwork is put right.

7.4. Goods-in photographs every pallet label before the stretch wrap is cut. The photographs are filed against the receipt, not kept on the camera.

7.5. Nothing is received between 22:00 and 06:00. A vehicle that arrives at night waits outside the estate gate on its own power, and its record for the waiting hours is read together with the journey.

## 8. Weather and the road

8.1. Riders do not ride in a red weather warning. The hub lead watches the
warnings and stops runs before they start.

8.2. In the monsoon every carrier wears its rain cover, and riders carry a
spare cover in the under-seat box.

8.3. In April and May the midday heat is hard on riders and on carriers. Runs
are planned so that no carrier is in the sun at a long stop, and riders carry
drinking water.

8.4. Riders keep to the speed limits of the roads they ride on and never ride
on a footpath to reach a door.

8.5. A road closure or a rally that blocks a route is reported to the hub, and
the hub lead re-plans the run; the rider does not find a way round on his own.

## 3. Who answers for what

3.1. The RP answers to the licensing authority as well as to Quillfern. She may stop any dispatch at any hour without giving a reason first; the reason is written up within the shift.

3.2. Shift QA officers work under the RP. One is on duty on each of the two shifts, 06:00 to 14:00 and 14:00 to 22:00. Between 22:00 and 06:00 the store neither receives nor dispatches except under a written plan the RP has approved, and the night is covered by the security contractor and the RP's phone.

3.3. The engineering technician, Irfan Ghanchi, looks after the chambers, the generator, the alarm panel and the loggers. He keeps his own maintenance log. He does not decide whether stock affected by an equipment fault is usable; he reports the fault and the QA officer decides what happens to the stock.

3.4. The store manager decides staffing, slots and vehicles. He may ask QA to hurry; he may not ask QA to agree. Where any two of these people disagree about whether stock may move, it does not move until the RP has decided.

3.5. Each role has a named deputy, listed on the board outside the QA office. A deputy acts with the full authority of the role while the holder is away, and signs in the deputy's own name, never the holder's.

## 5. What the bill penalises

5.1. The utility bills the site on kilovolt-amperes as well as kilowatt-hours, so a poor power factor costs money every month even when nothing is wrong with the plant. Large compressor motors pull the factor down; the capacitor bank in the switch room pushes it back up.

5.2. The bank is rated at 360 kvar in six automatic steps. The site's target is a monthly average of 0.98. The utility adds a surcharge to any month that averages below 0.90, and gives a small rebate for any month above 0.95.

5.3. When the bank was first installed it had four steps and a lower rating, and the target was 0.95; the extra steps were added in April 2026 after two summer bills carried the surcharge.

5.4. The controller's display, which shows the kvar switched in on each step, is read at every monthly energy review. A step that will not switch in is reported to the electrical supervisor the same day.

5.5. Capacitor cans are never touched until the bank has been isolated and left for the discharge time printed on its door.

# Last-Mile Programme Manual

The manual for the doorstep insulin service Quillfern runs for Nirmaya
Healthcare in Pune, which Nirmaya sells to its patients under the name CareLink.
It is written for the riders, the hub staff and the customer service agents who
book the drops. It covers what is particular to taking medicine to a person's
front door on a two-wheeler. Company rules on temperature, quarantine and
destruction still apply; this manual says how they are carried out when the
last stop is a flat, not a dock.

KURKUMBH FROZEN DEPOT: RAPID HYGIENE SWABS FROM THE CONTRACT LABORATORY

The Kurkumbh frozen depot does not have its own laboratory. Its hygiene swabs of reefer floors, cleaned crates and the blast freezer are read by a contract laboratory in the MIDC estate, whose technician visits on Tuesdays and Fridays.

WHAT THE SWAB MEASURES
The swab picks up atp from food residue and living cells; the technician's hand-held reader gives a number within seconds.

THE LINE WE USE
At Kurkumbh, a reading of 300 rlu or below is a pass. Above that, the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again before it is used.

The depot's line is set by the frozen food customer's contract, which is looser than the lines used for chilled food.

WHAT A PASS DOES NOT MEAN
A pass means the surface was cleaned, not that it is free of germs. Any microbiological test the customer asks for still goes to the contract laboratory in the usual way.

RECORDS
The technician leaves a copy of each day's readings with the depot shift lead, who files it in the hygiene folder.

IF THE TECHNICIAN DOES NOT COME
The shift lead phones the laboratory. Surfaces waiting for a swab are not used until they have been swabbed and passed.

THE READER
The technician checks the reader with the maker's control swabs at the start of each visit and writes the result at the top of the day's sheet. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

Questions to the depot QA officer.

## 6. Quick checks on cleanliness

6.1. Not every cleanliness check can wait three days for a plate count. For surfaces that have just been cleaned, such as the inside of a returned meal-kit liner or a reefer floor before loading, the laboratory uses a rapid swab that gives a reading in seconds.

6.2. The swab detects atp, the energy molecule present in food residue and living cells, and the hand-held reader reports it in rlu. A reading of 100 or below is a pass. From 101 to 300 the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again; above 300 it fails, and the cleaning itself is reviewed.

6.3. Until March 2026 the laboratory's pass line was higher, and liners that passed were later found carrying mould.

6.4. A swab reading measures cleanliness, not safety. A surface that passes still goes through any microbiological test that QA has asked for.

6.5. The atp reader is checked each morning with the maker's control swabs, which give a known rlu figure. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

## Rapid swabs

Rapid atp swabs are used on cleaned surfaces. A reading of 150 rlu or below is a pass.

## 19. Housekeeping

19.1. Benches are cleared and disinfected at the end of each day and before any new piece of work begins. Nothing is left on a bench overnight except work in progress, labelled with its laboratory number and the analyst's initials.

19.2. Fridges and freezers are defrosted and cleaned on a calendar kept on their doors. Out-of-date media, reagents and samples are thrown away at each cleaning, through the waste route for their kind.

19.3. The laboratory floor is cleaned by laboratory staff, not by the hub's cleaning contractor, so that nobody unfamiliar with the work cleans around open cultures.

19.4. A weekly walk-round by the laboratory head checks the state of the rooms, the equipment and the records, and the findings are written in the housekeeping log.

## 13. Safety in the laboratory

13.1. The laboratory handles ordinary food bacteria, not dangerous organisms. Even so, nobody eats, drinks or applies make-up in the laboratory, and coats, gloves and safety glasses are worn at the bench.

13.2. Spills of cultures are covered with disinfectant, left for the time on the disinfectant's label and then cleaned up. The spill is written in the laboratory incident book.

13.3. Chemicals are stored in the chemicals cabinet with their safety data sheets, and incompatible chemicals are kept apart.

13.4. Waste leaves the laboratory only after it has been made safe, through the hub's licensed waste contractor.

13.5. The laboratory has its own eyewash station, first-aid box and fire extinguisher, and every analyst is shown where they are on the first day.
