## 5. Growing what is there

5.1. The laboratory counts bacteria, yeasts and moulds on food samples and on surface swabs, so that QA can decide whether a product, a liner or a body is fit to use.

5.2. For the total viable count, the prepared sample is spread on plate count agar and the plates are incubated at 30 C for 72 hours before they are read. Coliforms, yeasts and moulds follow their own methods, listed in the laboratory's method file.

5.3. Until January 2026 the count was read after 48 hours at a higher temperature, which missed slow growers from chilled foods.

5.4. Each incubator is checked twice a day with a reference thermometer, and its reading written on the sheet on its door. One that has drifted more than 1 C from its set point is taken out of use until it has been serviced, and plates inside it are moved to the spare incubator.

5.5. Every batch of agar is tested with a known organism before it is used for samples.

# Refrigeration Technician Development Curriculum

## 1. Why we train our own

1.1. Quillfern's new sites need people who can keep a reefer unit, a walk-in chamber and a standby generator running at three in the morning, and the market does not supply enough of them. Experienced mechanics are hired away by the dairies and the pharma makers as soon as they are any good, and the ones who stay with independent garages rarely know anything about temperature records or why a door left open for ten minutes matters.

1.2. In 2024 the engineering pool therefore started its own apprenticeship, run from a workshop in the Waluj industrial area outside Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (still Aurangabad on most of the signboards). The workshop trains young people in the trade and in the Quillfern way of working, and then places them at the sites that need them.

1.3. This curriculum describes the programme as it runs from the January 2026 intake: who may join, how long it lasts, what the apprentices learn and how they are assessed, what they are paid, and what they may and may not do on live equipment.

1.4. It is written for apprentices, their trainers and mentors, and the site managers who receive them. An apprentice is given a copy on the first day and is expected to have read it by the end of the first week.

## 6. Quick checks on cleanliness

6.1. Not every cleanliness check can wait three days for a plate count. For surfaces that have just been cleaned, such as the inside of a returned meal-kit liner or a reefer floor before loading, the laboratory uses a rapid swab that gives a reading in seconds.

6.2. The swab detects atp, the energy molecule present in food residue and living cells, and the hand-held reader reports it in rlu. A reading of 100 or below is a pass. From 101 to 300 the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again; above 300 it fails, and the cleaning itself is reviewed.

6.3. Until March 2026 the laboratory's pass line was higher, and liners that passed were later found carrying mould.

6.4. A swab reading measures cleanliness, not safety. A surface that passes still goes through any microbiological test that QA has asked for.

6.5. The atp reader is checked each morning with the maker's control swabs, which give a known rlu figure. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

## 3. The calendar

3.1. The apprenticeship runs as one continuous programme with no break between the classroom and the floor. Months one to six are mostly in the workshop; months seven onwards are mostly on site, with a day a week back at Waluj.

3.2. From the January 2026 intake the programme lasts 18 months; the 2024 and 2025 intakes served 24. The shorter programme was possible because the workshop now has its own reefer body, cold room and generator, so that practical work no longer waits for a site to lend equipment.

3.3. Apprentices join in two intakes a year, so that there is always a senior group on site while a junior group is in the workshop. Each intake opens on the first working day of January or July and takes twelve trainees, no more. A thirteenth applicant who passes is offered the next intake rather than squeezed in.

3.4. Public holidays follow the Maharashtra list for apprentices at Waluj and the local list for apprentices placed at a site.

3.5. An apprentice who is ill for more than four weeks in a row may move to the next intake and pick up from the module they left.

## 17. Changes to this curriculum

17.1. Revision 1 (January 2025) set out the programme for the second intake. Revision 2 (June 2026) shortened the programme, raised the stipend in the floor months and set the ratio on live equipment after the first group completed.

17.2. The engineering pool lead reviews the curriculum each May with the workshop staff and two site managers.

17.3. Apprentices and mentors are asked at the end of each module what should change, and their answers are read at the review.

## 11. Making things sterile

11.1. Used cultures, plates and swabs are made safe before they leave the laboratory. Glassware and media are sterilised before use.

11.2. Both jobs are done in the autoclave in the washing room. A standard load runs at 121 C for 20 minutes once the whole load has reached that temperature, and every cycle's printout is kept.

11.3. Every week a biological indicator, a spore strip carrying a known number of heat-resistant bacteria, is placed in the middle of a full load. After the cycle the strip is incubated; any growth means the cycle failed, the week's loads are repeated, and the machine is serviced before it is used again.

11.4. Until February 2026 the spore test was done monthly, which would have let three weeks of unsafe waste leave the building after a failure.

11.5. Only trained analysts load and unload the autoclave, wearing heat-resistant gloves and a face shield, and nobody opens the door before the pressure gauge reads zero.

Quillfern operates owned reefers, hired peak-season reefers, cold-room probes,

should renew Kalpa, move to Tessaline Telematics, or buy a mixed package with

temperature, door status, and alert history without calling the driver. QA must

## Reasons

Kalpa has local service staff within Nagpur city limits and has historically
replaced failed truck devices within one working day. The Nagpur base station is
already mounted and wired. Driver training material, customer report templates,
and the QA audit binder already use Kalpa screenshots. Switching all material
before vaccine season would create training risk.

The Kalpa quote is lower than Tessaline's first commercial quote. Tessaline
quoted Rs. 31.20 lakh for migration, device replacement, and API onboarding.
Tessaline also proposed 60-second polling and a richer API, but the API was not
available for our trial vehicles. Kalpa's five-minute polling is not ideal, but
it is known and accepted by current customer annexes.

The exit clause for Kalpa is acceptable only at contract end. Leaving early
would require six months of minimum recurring charges. This is not justified on
the evidence available in November 2023.

## Rejected options

Tessaline was rejected in 2023 because the API was not demonstrated on a live
Quillfern route, the commercial proposal required a larger first-year payment,
and the field-support rota for Nagpur was still being hired. The evaluation team
liked the one-minute polling and the proposed exception export, but decided that
those benefits were not enough to justify a complete change before the 2024
vaccine season.

A split model was also rejected. In that model, Kalpa would have stayed on
trucks while warehouse probes moved to Tessaline. IT objected that two source

## 4. Keeping the heat out

4.1. Inside every shipper sits a moulded expanded polystyrene box with a fitted lid, made of eps beads. It is the only insulation in the kit, and the whole thermal performance of the kit depends on it.

4.2. The liner's walls, base and lid are 30 mm thick, moulded at a density of 20 kg per cubic metre, and its lid fits with a lip that overlaps the walls by at least 10 mm.

4.3. The pilot used thinner walls to save space in the van and kits ran warm on afternoon doorsteps.

4.4. Liners with cracks, chipped lips or a lid that does not seat are rejected at the line. The polystyrene moulder replaces rejected units in the next delivery without charge.

4.5. Every eps liner carries the moulder's lot number on its base so that a complaint can be traced to a mould. The liner is the component customers are asked to return, under section 9.

## 3. Before anything travels

3.1. A customer who wants to return goods asks customer service, which checks the customer's contract and issues an rma, the return number. It carries the customer code, the date and a running count, and it is printed on the collection note and on every carton label.

3.2. An rma is valid for 14 days from the day it is issued. Goods that reach the hub after that date are received, put in the hub's quarantine area and held, and the customer is asked to raise a fresh number before anything else is done with them.

3.3. The interim rules of 2025 allowed twice as long, and the hub found itself holding stock that nobody remembered asking to return.

3.4. A return without any authorisation number at all is not accepted at the gate unless the hub manager agrees by phone. Goods that cannot be refused safely, such as chilled stock on a vehicle that has nowhere else to go, are taken in under the same hold as a late one.

3.5. A second authorisation is never issued for goods already in the building; the first number is extended by customer service instead.

## 11. Write-off and disposal

11.1. Stores writes off an item only with Finance's approval, recorded on the
write-off sheet.

11.2. Broken instruments are written off after QA has confirmed they cannot be
calibrated. Their serials are struck off the instrument list.

11.3. Damaged seal books are never thrown away. Every seal in them is written
VOID and kept with the stubs until the next audit.

11.4. Protective equipment that is worn out is cut before disposal, so that it
cannot be picked out of the bin and worn again.

## 8. Dry ice supply

8.1. Stores places the standing order for dry ice at Nagpur. Vidarbha Gases
delivers 120 kg on Monday and Thursday mornings, and extra deliveries are
ordered by Stores on the shift lead's request.

8.2. Stores does not hold dry ice in the store. The delivery goes straight to
the dry-ice chest, where the shift lead signs the delivery note.

8.3. At the weekly count Stores records the kg delivered, the kg signed out on
QCL-F-26 and the kg left in the chest, and the difference is recorded as
sublimation loss.

8.4. Guwahati and Coimbatore order their own dry ice from their local suppliers,
and send Stores the delivery notes monthly.

## 12. People and training

12.1. Everyone who handles returns at the hub completes the company induction and the hub's own half-day course on receiving, labelling and the returns system before handling stock alone.

12.2. The QA officers on duty at Bhosari are trained by the QA function and hold the same authority as QA officers at any other site. They do not take instructions on pharmaceutical decisions from the hub manager or from account managers.

12.3. Receiving clerks are trained to say "I'll check and come back to you" to drivers and customers who ask what will happen to returned goods. The answer comes from customer service.

12.4. Agency staff may count and move cartons but may not scan them into the returns system or judge them.

12.5. Training is refreshed every year and whenever this manual changes.

## 20. Transfers between sites

20.1. Stock sent from Nagpur to Guwahati or Coimbatore travels with a Stores
transfer note on QCL-F-45, listing every item and quantity. The receiving cage
counts the parcel on arrival and signs the note.

20.2. A short or damaged transfer is written on the note and photographed before
the parcel is signed for. The courier is told the same day.

20.3. Numbered stock and made-up red sleeve packets travel in sealed courier
bags. The bag number is written on the transfer note.

20.4. Items are never transferred between sites in a driver's cab, even when a
vehicle happens to be going that way, unless the item is on the dispatch note.

20.5. The signed transfer notes come back to Nagpur by scan the same day and by
post at the month end.

## 3. Receiving goods

3.1. Goods are received against the purchase order and the delivery note, and
counted before the delivery note is signed. A short delivery is written as short
on the delivery note in front of the supplier's driver.

3.2. Temperature-sensitive consumables, such as conditioned gel packs, are not
received by Stores. They go directly to the QA room.

3.3. Calibrated instruments are received by Stores and passed unopened to the QA
bench on the same day. Stores does not open an instrument box to check it.

3.4. Damaged goods are photographed, set aside and reported to Finance before the
supplier's driver leaves, where that is possible.

## 18. Audit of Stores

18.1. Finance audits the Nagpur store twice a year without notice, counting a
sample of lines chosen on the day.

18.2. QA audits the numbered stock once a year, from the manufacturer's delivery
note to the gate register and back to the stubs.

18.3. Findings are written up by the auditor and answered by Nalini Patil within
ten working days, with an owner and a date for each action.

18.4. A finding that repeats from one audit to the next is escalated to the
Nagpur DC manager and to Finance.

## 11. Vans and handling

11.1. Kits travel to customers in chilled vans running at +4 C. Kits are loaded in delivery order, stacked no more than five high, with heavier kits at the bottom.

11.2. Drivers carry kits by the handles moulded into the shipper, never by the strapping, and never throw a kit onto a doorstep.

11.3. A kit that is dropped from a height in the van or at the door is reported by the driver and checked at the next stop for damage. A kit with a cracked liner is taken back to Kondhwa.

11.4. Vans carry no other customer's goods while kits are on board.

## 23. Contacts

23.1. The Nagpur store phone is on the Operations extension list. Out of hours,
the night shift lead holds the emergency cupboard key, as in section 2.

23.2. Questions about whether an item is fit to use go to QA. Questions about
whether an item may be bought go to Finance. Stores answers questions about
where an item is and how many are left.

## 6. Paperwork and labels

6.1. Every kit carries a recipe card set, an ingredient list and an allergen card, all printed by Thali Box and supplied to the line in packs of fifty.

6.2. The shipper's end-of-line label shows the customer's name and address, the delivery day and window, the order number and a barcode for the driver.

6.3. A second, larger label on the lid shows the earliest use-by date of any item in the kit. The date is printed in characters at least 6 mm high, so that it can be read by someone standing at the door without bending.

6.4. The pilot printed it smaller, and complaints showed that customers did not read it.

6.5. Every shipper also carries an sscc label so that the kit can be traced through the van and the returns system. The label follows the gs1 standard so that both companies' scanners read it, and a kit whose sscc does not scan is relabelled; the gs1 company prefix used is Thali Box's own.

6.6. Labels are printed on direct-thermal stock that survives condensation. A label that smudges at the line test is reprinted before the kit leaves.

## The carton

Pouches go out twelve to a carton. Each carton carries one sscc label printed at the end of the bench, so that it can be traced through the van and back. The label follows the standard used by Pinecone's retailers, and scans on their tills as well as ours.

## Labels

Use-by date on the lid in characters at least 4 mm high. Every shipper carries an sscc label to the gs1 standard.

## 3. The outer shell

3.1. The outer shipper takes the weight of other kits stacked on it in the van and the knocks of the doorstep, and it is the first thing a customer sees. It must still be square and closed when it arrives, after a night in a damp van and a day on a stone floor.

3.2. The shipper is a five-ply corrugated box in a regular slotted style, printed in two colours with the Thali Box design. Its strength in the bct, measured by the testing laboratory on conditioned samples, must be at least 450 kgf.

3.3. The 2025 pilot used a lighter board and a lower strength, and lost corners in the monsoon.

3.4. Every delivery of shippers comes with the box maker's bct certificate for that lot, and the laboratory tests one lot in five again on receipt. A lot that fails is returned whole.

3.5. Corrugated stock is stored off the floor, away from the kitting room's damp walls, and used first in, first out.

## The pouch

Each pouch arrives from Pinecone already printed with the recipe, the ingredients and the feeding guide. We add only the date sticker: the use-by date in characters at least 3 mm high, black on white, on the back of the pouch below the feeding guide.

## 5. The cold source

5.1. Chilled kits are kept cold by sealed phase-change packs that melt at +3 C, holding the food near that temperature until they have melted. They are conditioned in the Kondhwa cold room for at least 24 hours before use.

5.2. Every chilled kit carries two packs of 600 g each, one under the food and one on top. A kit with frozen items as well carries a third pack, conditioned at -21 C, packed against the frozen items behind the divider.

5.3. The pilot carried three smaller packs and the food between them warmed first.

5.4. Each pcm brick is checked at the line for leaks and swelling and discarded if either is found. Packs are reused only when they come back intact through the box returns, and each pcm brick is retired after 30 uses.

5.5. Gel and ice packs from any other source are never used in a Thali Box kit.

## Returns

Customers pay a deposit on their first kit. Rs. 50, refunded if the box comes back within 7 days. Shippers that cannot be reused are recyclable.

# Thali Box pilot: pack note

Packaging used for the Thali Box meal-kit pilot from April 2025.

## Outer

Three-ply corrugated slotted box, tested by bct. Compression strength at least 300 kgf.

## Checks

The bench lead scans the first and the last carton of every batch. A label that does not scan is reprinted; a whole batch that does not scan stops the bench.

## 14. Changes and review

14.1. Changes to this book are proposed by either company in writing, tested under section 7, and agreed in writing by both before use.

14.2. The packaging engineer reviews the whole book each March with Thali Box, after the winter and before the summer, and issues a revision if anything changes.

14.3. Each revision lists its changes on its first page, with the reason for each.

# Vadodara bonded store card: mock recall, returned goods back to stock, batch record retention

Pinned at the Vadodara QA desk. This card covers three things: the mock recall,
when returned goods may go back to stock, and how long batch records are kept.

## 11. After the stock has left

11.1. Responsibility for a batch does not end at the dispatch bay. The store must be able to find every unit it has handled, and it must deal properly with what comes back.

11.2. Twice a year, in March and September, the store runs a mock recall on a batch chosen by the RP without warning. The exercise starts when she names the batch to the shift QA officer. Every unit of the chosen batch must be found and named — on a shelf, on a vehicle or at a consignee — inside four hours of the exercise starting. The result, with the time taken and any unit that could not be found, goes to the customer who owns the batch.

11.3. Hospitals and distributors send product back for many reasons — over-ordering, a ward closing, a wrong delivery — and none of those reasons makes it fit to be resold. Nothing returned goes back into saleable stock unless it comes back within 72 hours of delivery, with an unbroken logger record from our hands to the consignee's and back, and the Responsible Person signs the release; everything else is destroyed. Returned product waits in the quarantine cage while the decision is made.

11.4. A real recall, as opposed to a practice one, is run by the customer. The store's part is to stop dispatch of the batch at once, list every unit it holds and every unit it has sent, and hold any returned units in quarantine until the customer instructs.

11.5. Complaints from hospitals about a product's quality are passed to the customer the same day. The store does not reply to the complaint itself, and does not offer an opinion on it.

## 10. When a batch is withdrawn

10.1. A manufacturer that withdraws a batch from the market instructs Quillfern through its named quality contact. The account manager confirms the instruction in writing and the hub manager is told the same day so that space is ready.

10.2. Stock coming back from consignees under a withdrawal is held in the locked bay R-2, under the key of the QA officer on duty. It never shares a shelf with returns of any other kind, and the bay's segregation is checked at every shift change.

10.3. The recalled units in R-2 are counted every day and the count sent to the customer's quality contact each week.

10.4. If the customer has not said what to do with the recalled stock 90 days after the first units arrived, the account manager writes to the customer's quality head, not to the original contact, and asks for a decision.

10.5. Breaking that segregation needs the QA lead's written consent. The hub does not take part in deciding whether a batch should be withdrawn, and does not comment on it to consignees.

## 15. Customer audits

15.1. Customers may audit the store on ten working days' notice, and for cause at shorter notice. The RP or the QA lead hosts every audit; the store manager joins for the operational parts.

15.2. An auditor may see any record about the customer's own stock and any part of the building. An auditor may not see another customer's stock records or another customer's audit reports.

15.3. The store answers each audit finding within 20 working days with a corrective action, an owner and a date. Answers are written by the QA lead and signed by the RP.

15.4. Findings from customer audits are added to the store's own corrective action register, so that one customer's finding fixes the problem for every customer.

15.5. A customer may ask to observe a mock recall or a self-inspection walk. The request is granted where the customer's own batch is chosen or where the walk does not expose another customer's records.

## 7. Sorting what came back

7.1. Grading is a decision about every line, not a valuation, and each decision is checked by a second person.

7.2. Every line is judged within 24 hours of receipt. Bucket A means fit to go back to the owner's saleable stock under the owner's own rules; B means the owner must decide; C means destruction.

7.3. Grading of pharmaceutical lines is done by the QA officer on duty, not by the receiving team, and a pharmaceutical line never goes into A without QA's signature on the returns system.

7.4. Food lines go to C whenever the packaging has been opened, the use-by date has passed, or the temperature history is missing for a chilled or frozen line.

7.5. Lines judged B are reported to the owner the same day. Until the owner replies, they stay in the area for their temperature class, marked with an orange label.

7.6. A line may move from bucket B to A or C on the owner's written instruction only; it never moves because space ran short.

## Mock recall

A mock recall is run once a year, in November, on a batch the QA lead picks.
Every unit of the chosen batch must be traced, on the shelf, on a vehicle or at
a consignee, within 8 hours of the exercise starting. The result goes to the
batch owner.

## Returned goods back to stock

Returned medicines may go back into saleable stock if they come back within
7 days of delivery, the outer cartons are unopened and the shift QA officer
signs the return note. Anything else is held for the owner's decision.

## 10. Noise

10.1. The plant room, the generator enclosure and parts of the dock area are loud enough to damage hearing over time. Levels are surveyed with a decibel meter by the safety officer every year and after any new machine is installed, and the results are posted at each entrance.

10.2. Hearing protection is compulsory for everyone, however short the visit, wherever the survey shows a level of 85 or more. Signs mark those areas, and dispensers of earmuffs hang at their doors.

10.3. People who work regularly in those areas wear earmuffs for the whole shift and have a hearing test every 12 months, arranged by HR with an occupational health provider.

10.4. The 2025 rules set the line higher and the tests further apart.

10.5. A person whose test shows a change is told the result in person and moved away from the loudest work while the provider advises. Results are kept by HR, and a decibel reading in a survey is never treated as a personal medical record.

## 5. Picking what to look at

5.1. Most controls are tested by picking items from the period under review and checking that the control worked on each one. The number of items depends on how often the control operates, not on the size of the population.

5.2. For a control that operates monthly, attribute testing uses 25 items under random sampling; for one that operates daily or with every transaction, 40 items; for a quarterly control, all of the quarters in the period. A single exception in the items picked is reported, whatever its value.

5.3. For sampling, items are picked at random from a complete listing that the auditor has checked for completeness against a control total. Picking from a listing someone else filtered is not random, however it was produced.

5.4. The 2025 charter used smaller attribute samples; they were raised for this programme because two findings in the first year rested on too few items to persuade anyone. The method and the seed used for random selection are recorded in the working papers so that another auditor could pick the same items.

## 15. Health at work

15.1. Every person on site has a pre-employment health check and a yearly check thereafter, arranged by HR. People working in the cold or in noisy areas have the extra checks described in sections 9 and 10.

15.2. Drinking water is available at every work area, and in summer the canteen serves salted lime water on the docks during the afternoon.

15.3. Anyone who is unwell tells their shift lead and is sent home or to the first-aid room. Nobody is asked to work through an illness to meet a delivery.

15.4. Staff may speak to the occupational health provider in confidence about anything that affects their health at work. The provider tells the site only what the person agrees to.

## 16. Welfare

16.1. Apprentices are young and often away from home for the first time. Each intake has a welfare contact at Waluj, a member of the workshop staff who is not a trainer.

16.2. Apprentices may raise anything with the welfare contact — homesickness, money, a problem at the lodging, a problem with a colleague — in confidence.

16.3. The lodging used at each site is visited by the welfare contact before the first apprentice moves in.

16.4. Bullying, ragging or initiation rituals are not tolerated, on site or at the workshop, and are dealt with under the company's discipline rules.

16.5. Apprentices are paid their stipend during approved sick leave for up to four weeks.

## 10. Looking at whole populations

10.1. Some tests are run on every transaction rather than a sample, using data extracted from the finance system. Extracts are taken by the team with read-only access and are never edited; any cleaning is done on a copy and recorded.

10.2. The duplicate payment test runs every month, on the fifth working day, on all supplier payments of the previous month. It looks for the same supplier, amount and invoice number, and for near-matches where one character differs. Every hit is followed up with accounts payable within a week.

10.3. A Benford first-digit test runs once a quarter on staff expense claims, by site and by person. A pattern that departs from the Benford curve is a reason to look, never by itself a finding.

10.4. Results of every run are kept, including runs that found nothing, so that a duplicate missed later can be traced to the run that should have caught it.

## 12. Kit

12.1. Each apprentice is issued a personal tool kit in the first week: gauges and hoses, a multimeter, a clamp meter, a set of hand tools, a temperature probe, a torch and a tool bag. The kit is engraved with the apprentice's number.

12.2. Trainees often ask whether they get to keep the tools when they finish. The kit, worth about Rs. 22,000, becomes the apprentice's own property on completion; a leaver before completion hands it back.

12.3. A tool lost or broken through ordinary use is replaced by the workshop. A tool lost through carelessness is replaced once without charge; a second loss is discussed with the workshop lead.

12.4. Safety gear — boots, gloves, glasses, a freezer jacket and a helmet — is issued separately and is replaced whenever it wears out.

12.5. Apprentices do not lend their kit to anyone, including qualified technicians on site.

## 7. Forklifts and the docks

7.1. Only people holding a current site licence drive forklifts, reach trucks or powered pallet trucks. The licence is issued after a practical test by the training provider and renewed every three years.

7.2. Forklifts are checked by their drivers at the start of every shift: brakes, horn, lights, forks, chains, tyres and the seat belt. A failed check takes the truck out of use until the engineering team has repaired it.

7.3. Drivers wear the seat belt, keep the forks low when travelling, and never carry a passenger. A load that blocks the driver's view is driven in reverse.

7.4. Dock levellers and dock doors are operated only by trained staff. A vehicle is chocked and its driver's keys are in the dock office before anyone enters the trailer.

7.5. Speed limits inside the building are 8 km/h in the aisles and walking pace in the cold rooms.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 17. Changes to this curriculum

17.1. Revision 1 (January 2025) set out the programme for the second intake. Revision 2 (June 2026) shortened the programme, raised the stipend in the floor months and set the ratio on live equipment after the first group completed.

17.2. The engineering pool lead reviews the curriculum each May with the workshop staff and two site managers.

17.3. Apprentices and mentors are asked at the end of each module what should change, and their answers are read at the review.

## 6. Working off the ground

6.1. Falls cause more serious injuries on the site than anything else, mostly from ladders and from the tops of racking and vehicles. Work at height is avoided wherever a ground-level method exists.

6.2. Any work more than 1.8 metres above the floor, or near an unprotected edge, is done from a platform with guard rails, or with a full-body harness attached by a shock-absorbing lanyard to an anchor point rated for the purpose.

6.3. Every harness is inspected by its user before each use, against the checklist sewn into its storage bag, and by the safety officer every three months. It is withdrawn after five years from its date of manufacture, or at once after it has arrested a fall, whichever comes first.

6.4. The 2025 rules allowed a longer service life and named no height. Both were tightened after the safety officer found that two units in the plant room were older than the people wearing them.

6.5. A lanyard that has deployed its shock absorber is cut in half and binned the same day.

# Cold Room Commissioning Manual

## 1. Why commissioning gets its own manual

1.1. A cold room is not finished when the builders leave. It is finished when it has been shown, by tests written down in advance and run by people who did not build it, that it will hold product inside its range on the worst day of the year. Everything between the last panel going up and the first pallet going in is commissioning, and this manual says how Quillfern does it.

1.2. The manual was first written for the opening of Ludhiana DC in 2025 and is now used for the second frozen block at Ludhiana, due for handover in the winter of 2026, and for every new chamber the engineering team builds after it. It applies whether the chamber is built by a turnkey contractor or assembled by our own team from bought-in panels and plant.

1.3. It is written for the engineering lead who runs commissioning, the contractors who build and start the plant, the site QA lead who must accept the room, and the site manager who wants to know when the room can earn money. It does not replace temperature mapping, which follows the company mapping method once commissioning is complete.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the handover note written in a hurry at the end of the first Ludhiana build. Several of that note's figures were the contractor's defaults, accepted without question; this revision sets Quillfern's own.

## Height

Wear a harness with a lanyard when working at height. Harnesses are withdrawn after seven years.

## 8. Finding where warmth gets in

8.1. When the room has held its set point for 48 hours, the envelope is surveyed from outside for places where cold escapes: panel joints, door frames, pipe and cable penetrations, and the junction between wall panels and floor.

8.2. The survey is done by thermography, with an infrared camera, at night or on a dull day when the outside walls are not heated by the sun. Any joint that shows more than 3 C colder than the panel face beside it is marked, resealed and surveyed again.

8.3. The handover note of 2025 allowed a larger difference before resealing, and two joints it allowed are now visibly iced.

8.4. The images are saved with the room number, the date and the camera's serial number, and printed on the commissioning record with each marked joint circled.

8.5. A second thermography survey with the same infrared camera is done six months after handover, in the opposite season, and its images are compared with the first.

## 14. Records

14.1. The signed commissioning record, the test sheets and the thermal images are kept for the life of the room and three years after it is demolished or converted.

14.2. Copies go to the site QA lead, who keeps them with the room's mapping studies, and to the site manager, who keeps them with the lease or the title documents.

14.3. Nothing in the record is rewritten after signing. A correction is a new sheet that refers to the old one and is signed in the same way.

## 11. Feet and wheels

11.1. Most deaths in warehouse yards are caused by reversing vehicles. The yard at Ludhiana is laid out so that pedestrian and vehicle routes meet as rarely as possible, and where they must meet, the vehicle waits.

11.2. People on foot keep to a painted route 1.2 metres wide, coloured green and separated from the roadway by yellow barriers along the dock apron. Vehicles keep to 10 km/h anywhere in the yard.

11.3. The 2025 rules had a narrower walkway and a higher limit, and the yard was busier than anyone had planned for.

11.4. Every reversing manoeuvre onto a dock after dark is guided by a trained banksman standing where the driver can see him, and clear of the vehicle's path.

11.5. Nobody stands or walks behind a reversing vehicle, and no pedestrian crosses the yard except at the marked crossings at the end of each walkway.

# Ludhiana DC safety rules (opening issue)

Issued for the opening of Ludhiana DC.

## Collapse

The site has two defibrillator units, at the gate cabin and in the canteen. A first aider checks each aed once a month.

## 9. Cold work

9.1. The frozen block at Ludhiana runs at -25 C, colder than most of the company's freezers, and the body loses heat there faster than people expect. Cold slows thinking before it slows hands, which is why the rules below do not depend on how anyone feels.

9.2. Nobody works inside the frozen block for longer than 40 minutes at a stretch, even in a full freezer suit. A 20-minute rewarming break in the canteen or the warm room follows each stretch, with a hot drink available.

9.3. The shift lead keeps the break board for the frozen block and moves names on it; the workers do not keep their own time.

9.4. Signs of hypothermia, such as uncontrolled shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness or confusion, mean the person leaves the cold at once with a colleague and is checked by a first aider. A person who has shown those signs does not go back into the cold that shift.

9.5. In 2025 the stretch was an hour and the rewarming break fifteen minutes, and two cases of mild hypothermia followed; both were changed after the first winter.

## 4. Keeping the heat out

4.1. Inside every shipper sits a moulded expanded polystyrene box with a fitted lid, made of eps beads. It is the only insulation in the kit, and the whole thermal performance of the kit depends on it.

4.2. The liner's walls, base and lid are 30 mm thick, moulded at a density of 20 kg per cubic metre, and its lid fits with a lip that overlaps the walls by at least 10 mm.

4.3. The pilot used thinner walls to save space in the van and kits ran warm on afternoon doorsteps.

4.4. Liners with cracks, chipped lips or a lid that does not seat are rejected at the line. The polystyrene moulder replaces rejected units in the next delivery without charge.

4.5. Every eps liner carries the moulder's lot number on its base so that a complaint can be traced to a mould. The liner is the component customers are asked to return, under section 9.

## Insulation

Moulded eps box, polystyrene walls 20 mm thick.

RASIKA DAIRY SUBSCRIPTION BOX: THE INSULATED BOX AND ITS LID

For the morning milk and paneer subscription deliveries we make for Rasika Dairy in Kothrud and Karve Nagar.

WHAT THE BOX IS FOR
The box is left on the subscriber's doorstep before 07:00 and collected empty the next morning. It only has to keep milk cold for about three hours, so it is much lighter than a meal-kit box.

THE BOX
Each box is moulded expanded polystyrene, white, with a push-on lid. Walls, base and lid are 15 mm thick, at a density of 15 kg per cubic metre. The box carries Rasika's logo moulded into the lid.

CHECKING AT THE DEPOT
Boxes are checked every morning at loading. A box with a crack, a missing corner or a loose lid is set aside and returned to the moulder at the end of the month. The eps moulder replaces rejected boxes without charge.

CLEANING
Returned boxes are wiped inside and out with a food-safe sanitiser and air-dried before reuse. A box that smells of sour milk is not reused.

COUNTING
The depot counts boxes out and back every day. Subscribers who keep a box are reminded by Rasika's customer team, not by the delivery boy.

STORAGE
Clean boxes are stacked lid-on, ten high, on the racks by the loading door. Boxes are never stacked on the floor or in the sun.

Questions to the Erandwane depot office.

## 9. Bringing the kit home again

9.1. The liner and the cold packs are expensive and can be used again; the outer shipper is collected too, so that customers are not left with a bulky box, even though it is recyclable. The programme asks every customer to hand the whole kit back, empty, at their next delivery or by pickup from the door.

9.2. Customers pay a refundable deposit of Rs. 80 on the first kit they order. The amount is refunded in full if the box comes back within 14 days of delivery, in a condition the hub can reuse, and is kept if it does not.

9.3. The pilot's deposit was smaller and gave less time, and too many boxes stayed in customers' homes.

9.4. Outer shippers that cannot be reused are flattened at the Bhosari hub and sent for recycling; they are recyclable board with water-based ink. Liners that cannot be reused are sent to the moulder, who takes them back as raw material.

9.5. Customer service handles questions about refunds; the van drivers do not discuss money at the door.

## Labels

Use-by date on the lid in characters at least 4 mm high. Every shipper carries an sscc label to the gs1 standard.

## 8. Storing components

8.1. Shippers, liners and paper components are stored in the ambient store at Kondhwa, on pallets, in the order they arrived. Nothing is stored against the outside walls.

8.2. Phase-change packs are stored and conditioned in the cold room on their own racks, by temperature, with chilled packs and frozen packs on separate racks clearly labelled.

8.3. Stock of each component is counted every Monday. The packaging engineer orders from the approved suppliers when stock falls to two weeks' use.

8.4. Components that have been damaged in storage are set aside and counted, not used to make up numbers.

## 3. The outer shell

3.1. The outer shipper takes the weight of other kits stacked on it in the van and the knocks of the doorstep, and it is the first thing a customer sees. It must still be square and closed when it arrives, after a night in a damp van and a day on a stone floor.

3.2. The shipper is a five-ply corrugated box in a regular slotted style, printed in two colours with the Thali Box design. Its strength in the bct, measured by the testing laboratory on conditioned samples, must be at least 450 kgf.

3.3. The 2025 pilot used a lighter board and a lower strength, and lost corners in the monsoon.

3.4. Every delivery of shippers comes with the box maker's bct certificate for that lot, and the laboratory tests one lot in five again on receipt. A lot that fails is returned whole.

3.5. Corrugated stock is stored off the floor, away from the kitting room's damp walls, and used first in, first out.

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and

# Beekeeping association — minutes of the spring meeting

*5 April 2025. Present: 19 members. Apologies from four.*

## 1. Winter losses

Losses across the association ran at 17% this winter, close to the ten-year
average. Two members reported isolation starvation in colonies that had ample
stores, but not where the cluster had moved to. The usual advice was repeated:
stores above the cluster, not beside it.

## 11. Complaints from the person at home

The rider writes down what was said and tells the hub lead before the end of the
shift.

11.2. Complaints that reach Quillfern directly are passed to Nirmaya's care desk
the same day, with the rider's note and the run sheet.

11.3. A complaint about a rider's behaviour or riding goes to the hub lead and
to HR. The rider is told what the complaint says and is asked for his account
before anything is decided.

11.4. Quillfern does not reply to a patient in writing. Written replies come
from Nirmaya.

## 11. Feet and wheels

11.1. Most deaths in warehouse yards are caused by reversing vehicles. The yard at Ludhiana is laid out so that pedestrian and vehicle routes meet as rarely as possible, and where they must meet, the vehicle waits.

11.2. People on foot keep to a painted route 1.2 metres wide, coloured green and separated from the roadway by yellow barriers along the dock apron. Vehicles keep to 10 km/h anywhere in the yard.

11.3. The 2025 rules had a narrower walkway and a higher limit, and the yard was busier than anyone had planned for.

11.4. Every reversing manoeuvre onto a dock after dark is guided by a trained banksman standing where the driver can see him, and clear of the vehicle's path.

11.5. Nobody stands or walks behind a reversing vehicle, and no pedestrian crosses the yard except at the marked crossings at the end of each walkway.

## 13. Bikes and kit care

13.1. The two-wheelers are leased and serviced by the leasing company every

## 13. Fire and evacuation

13.1. The fire alarm is a continuous bell. On hearing it, everyone stops work, switches off any vehicle or machine they are using, and leaves by the nearest way out to the assembly point by the weighbridge.

13.2. Shift leads count their people against the shift roster and the gate register and report to the site manager or, at night, the senior guard. Contractors are counted by their supervisors and visitors by their escorts.

13.3. Nobody goes back into the building until the fire service or the site manager says it is safe. Stock, vehicles and personal belongings are left where they are.

13.4. Fire drills are held every three months, at least one of them at night each year. The time to clear the building and to complete the count is recorded and compared with the previous drill.

13.5. Fire extinguishers, hose reels, alarms and emergency lighting are inspected monthly by the safety officer and serviced yearly by the fire contractor.

## 15. Health at work

15.1. Every person on site has a pre-employment health check and a yearly check thereafter, arranged by HR. People working in the cold or in noisy areas have the extra checks described in sections 9 and 10.

15.2. Drinking water is available at every work area, and in summer the canteen serves salted lime water on the docks during the afternoon.

15.3. Anyone who is unwell tells their shift lead and is sent home or to the first-aid room. Nobody is asked to work through an illness to meet a delivery.

15.4. Staff may speak to the occupational health provider in confidence about anything that affects their health at work. The provider tells the site only what the person agrees to.

## 14. Changes to this manual

14.1. Revision 1 (August 2025) started the programme with IB-4 carriers. Revision
2 (April 2026) moved the programme to IB-6 carriers and changed the turn-back
rule to match.

14.2. The programme lead reviews this manual every six months with Nirmaya.

14.3. Riders and hub staff send suggested changes to the hub lead at any time.

## 12. The gate

12.1. Every vehicle is logged in and out at the gate cabin with its registration, the driver's name and licence number, and the purpose of the visit.

12.2. Drivers who are not unloading wait in the drivers' rest room, not in the yard or on the docks. They are given the site's one-page safety card in Punjabi, Hindi or English at the gate.

12.3. A driver who appears to be under the influence of alcohol or drugs is not admitted, and his company is told. Fleet Control is told if the vehicle is on a Quillfern dispatch.

12.4. Vehicles are searched on leaving if the site manager has asked for searches that day. The search is done by two guards, with the driver present.

# Returns and Reverse Logistics Manual

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. Goods come back. Hospitals over-order, pharmacies close, restaurants reject a load for a torn carton, a meal-kit customer goes on holiday and the box sits on a doorstep, and a manufacturer withdraws a batch. Until 2025 each Quillfern site dealt with what came back in its own way, usually in a corner of the dock that nobody owned. The Bhosari hub was opened to put an end to that.

1.2. This manual says how goods travel back from customers and consignees, how they are received and judged at Bhosari, and how they leave again: back to stock, back to their owner, or to destruction. It is written for the hub's own staff, for the drivers and planners who bring returns in, and for the customer service agents and account managers who promise customers what will happen to their goods.

1.3. It sets no temperature limit and no quarantine rule of its own. Product that may have been harmed by temperature is handled under the company's excursion and quarantine procedures, and this manual only says where it sits and who moves it while those procedures run.

1.4. Revision 3 replaces the interim note written when the hub opened in 2025 and the two earlier revisions of this manual. Several figures changed after the hub's first full year; each section that changed says so.

## 8. Agreeing the figures with the customer

8.1. A customer who returns goods usually raises a debit note against Quillfern or against its own supplier, and the reconciliation of that note with what the hub received is the last job on any return.

8.2. Customer service compares each debit note with the hub's receipt records within 5 working days of the note arriving. Any difference of more than 2 per cent in quantity or value goes to the account manager, who settles it with the customer before a credit note is raised.

8.3. A smaller discrepancy is settled by customer service from the hub's records, which are the count of record.

8.4. The reconciliation is kept with the return number in the returns system, so that an auditor can follow one return from the collection note to the credit note without asking anyone.

8.5. A discrepancy caused by a count error at collection is reported to Fleet Control as a driver coaching matter, not as a dispute with the customer.

## 15. The customer's own claim

15.1. A customer's claim against Quillfern runs on its own track, under its own contract, and is handled by the account manager and Finance. The claims desk is told of it and links the two files, but the customer's claim is not decided by what our insurer does.

15.2. Customers' contracts set their own limits, claim periods and evidence rules. Those terms, not the policy terms, decide what the customer gets.

15.3. Customers are not told whether Quillfern is insured for a loss, how much the cover is, or what the insurer paid. A customer who asks is told that Quillfern meets its contractual obligations.

15.4. Nobody promises a customer insurance money, a quick settlement or a particular figure. The first written word to a customer about money comes from the account manager after Finance has agreed it.

15.5. Evidence gathered for our own claim may be shown to a customer's surveyor on request, through the account manager, but the claim file itself is not sent to customers.

## Debit notes

Customer service completes the reconciliation of each debit note with the hub's records within 10 working days. Any discrepancy is recorded; a difference above 5 per cent goes to the account manager.

## 5. The calendar starts

5.1. The date of discovery is the first day on which anybody at Quillfern knew, or should have known, that goods had been lost or damaged. It is usually the delivery day, but not always: a shortage found at a quarterly count may be discovered weeks after the trip.

5.2. The site manager tells the claims desk on the day of discovery, by e-mail with the photographs attached. A phone call is welcome but is followed by the e-mail.

5.3. The claims desk sends written intimation to the insurer, through the broker, within seven days of the date of discovery. Intimation means a written notice that names the policy, the dispatch note, the place, the date and the nature of the loss, with an estimate if one is known. It is sent whether or not the claim looks large enough to be worth making, and whether or not the facts are yet clear. A call to Ashok Menon is not intimation.

5.4. Late intimation is the commonest reason insurers refuse a claim. In 2024 the company lost a claim of Rs. 4.6 lakh because a site waited for the customer's own figures before telling anyone. The rule now is to tell early and correct later.

5.5. The claims desk opens a claim file the same day it receives the site manager's e-mail. Each file has a number in the series TPC26-nnn, and the number goes on every later document.

## 17. What changed from the 2025 cover

17.1. The 2025–26 cover was placed with the same insurer on different terms, and its summary note is withdrawn. Staff who learned the old figures should unlearn them.

17.2. The deductible rose, the intimation window shortened, the machinery-stoppage threshold came down, the single-vehicle figure went up, and the survey threshold went up. The current figures are in sections 5 to 9 of this procedure and nowhere else.

17.3. SRCC cover was added by endorsement for the first time.

17.4. The desk lead reviews this procedure each February, before renewal, and issues a revision whenever the policy terms change.

## Withdrawn batches

Recalled stock is held in bay R-2 under strict segregation and counted weekly. If the customer has given no instruction after 60 days, the account manager writes to the customer.

## 4. Proving the pipework is tight

4.1. Refrigerant pipework is tested for tightness before any insulation is applied over it and before any refrigerant is admitted. A leak found after the pipes are lagged costs days; one found before costs minutes.

4.2. Every brazed joint is inspected by eye and then the whole system is charged with dry nitrogen at one and a half times its design pressure, isolated from the cylinder and left. The pressure must hold for 24 hours with no fall beyond what the change in ambient temperature explains.

4.3. The first Ludhiana build was held for half that time, and a slow leak at a valve body showed itself only after the room was in service.

4.4. A fall that cannot be explained is searched for with soap solution, joint by joint, and the whole test repeated after repair, from the start.

4.5. The test pressure, ambient temperature, gauge serial and times are recorded at the start, after one hour, and at the end. The nitrogen is vented outdoors and never into a closed room; every brazed repair is followed by a fresh test.

## The tightness test

Before lagging, every brazed joint is looked at by the refrigeration contractor's supervisor and by our engineer together. The system is then filled with dry nitrogen at one and a quarter times its design pressure, the cylinder is shut off, and the pressure is watched for 6 hours. It passes if the gauge has not fallen, allowing for the change in room temperature.

The cooperative's plant runs round the clock, and the chiller room cannot be closed for longer than a shift, which is why the hold is shorter here than in a new building.

## 12. Signing the room into service

12.1. Commissioning ends with a single signed record that gathers every test sheet, every calibration certificate, the as-built drawings, the closed list and the fire contractor's certificate.

12.2. Every test on the record must have been witnessed, and the record carries two signatories for each: the site QA lead and the refrigeration contractor's engineer. The customer whose stock the room will hold may send an observer, whose name is recorded, but the observer does not sign.

12.3. The 2025 note asked for one signature, the contractor's, and nobody from Quillfern could later say who had watched the pressure test.

12.4. A test that was not witnessed by both signatories is void, and is repeated. Neither signature may be added later by phone or by e-mail.

12.5. Once the record is complete the room passes to the site QA lead for temperature mapping.

## 3. Behind the chain-link fence

3.1. The 2 MVA transformer in the substation yard is oil-filled, and its oil is usually the first thing to fail without anyone noticing. Moisture and sludge pull down the oil's dielectric strength long before anything trips.

3.2. A sample is drawn by the approved testing laboratory every six months, in March and September, with the unit on load. The breakdown voltage must read at least 50 kV. A sample below that is filtered on site within seven days and drawn again after filtering.

3.3. The 2025 commissioning note allowed a yearly sample and a lower pass figure; both were tightened after the first monsoon, when condensation was found in the breather.

3.4. The laboratory's report is filed in the substation folder and copied to the engineering lead together with the dielectric figure from each of the last four samples, so that a slow decline is visible before it becomes a failure.

3.5. Nobody opens the transformer enclosure except the electrical supervisor or the utility's linesman, and never alone.

## 2. How power reaches the site

2.1. The site takes its supply at 11,000 volts from a dedicated feeder that leaves the utility's grid substation at Ladhowal, about four kilometres away. The feeder is overhead for most of its length and underground for the last 300 metres, entering the plot at the north-west corner.

2.2. The incoming supply meets the site in the substation yard beside the gate, behind a chain-link fence with a locked gate and a danger board in Punjabi, Hindi and English. The yard holds the utility's metering cubicle, the site's own high-tension breaker panel and the step-down equipment that feeds the main low-tension switchboard.

2.3. From the switchboard the supply divides into five feeders: the refrigeration plant, the chilled block, the frozen block, the office and canteen, and the yard lighting with the gate. Each feeder has its own breaker, its own energy meter and its own label, and the labels are checked against the single-line drawing every January.

2.4. The single-line drawing hangs in the switch room under glass. A change to the electrical system is not complete until the drawing on the wall has been redrawn and countersigned. A pencil correction on the glass is not a change; it is a hazard.

2.5. The utility's linesman may enter the yard to read or test the meter, but he is met at the gate by the electrical supervisor or, at night, by the shift lead with the duty electrician on the phone. Nobody from the utility switches anything inside the plot without the supervisor being present.

2.6. Supply interruptions are frequent in the paddy season, when the rural feeders around Ladhowal are overloaded by tube-well pumps. Most last a few minutes; some last hours. The generators described in section 4 are sized for the long ones.

## 9. The envelope, doors and floor

9.1. Every door is tested for its seal by closing it on a sheet of paper at several points around the frame; the paper must not slide out easily. Rapid-roll doors are timed from fully open to fully closed, and their safety edges tested by obstruction.

9.2. Door heaters and frame heaters on freezer doors are checked for current and for warmth by hand at the frame.

9.3. Strip curtains are fitted after the doors are tested, never before, so that the door seal test is not confused by the curtain.

9.4. The floor finish is inspected for cracks and for ponding with water before the room is cooled. Ponding is ground out and refinished; it is not left to freeze.

9.5. Pressure-relief ports in freezer walls are checked for free movement, because a freezer without working relief can buckle its own panels when the door is shut on warm air.

## A fall

If the gauge falls, the joints are tested with soap solution one by one, the leak is repaired, and the test starts again from the beginning.

## Lagging

Lagging starts only after the signed test sheet has been photographed and sent to the regional engineer.

## Records

The gauge serial number, the readings at the start, after one hour and at the end, and the room temperature at each reading go on the test sheet, which both engineers sign.

## 14. Records

14.1. The signed commissioning record, the test sheets and the thermal images are kept for the life of the room and three years after it is demolished or converted.

14.2. Copies go to the site QA lead, who keeps them with the room's mapping studies, and to the site manager, who keeps them with the lease or the title documents.

14.3. Nothing in the record is rewritten after signing. A correction is a new sheet that refers to the old one and is signed in the same way.

## 2. Products and limits

2.1. Vaccines must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. A vaccine high excursion is
declared when any approved sensor records more than +8.0 C for 15 continuous
minutes. A vaccine low excursion is declared when the record is below +2.0 C
for 10 continuous minutes.

2.2. Insulin must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. An insulin high excursion is
declared when the approved record is more than +8.0 C for 20 continuous
minutes. An insulin low excursion is declared when the record is below +2.0 C
for 10 continuous minutes.

2.3. Milk and paneer must remain from 0.0 C to +4.0 C while in cold rooms and
reefer bodies. A dairy high excursion is declared when milk or paneer is above
+5.0 C for 30 continuous minutes, including staging time after dock release.

2.4. Frozen food must remain at or below -18.0 C. A frozen-food excursion is
declared when the approved record is warmer than -15.0 C for 20 continuous
minutes.

2.5. The Nagpur central hub is also referred to as "NGP hub" in older records.
For this SOP, Nagpur DC and NGP hub mean the same facility unless a customer
contract names a different annex.

2.6. Legacy staging note retained from revision 2.0: milk crates may remain on a
covered dock until +7.0 C for 45 minutes before QA notice is required. This
paragraph has not been relied on since revision 4.0 and is retained only because
customer annex QF-Dairy-11 still quotes it.

## 2. Products and limits

2.1. Vaccines must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. A vaccine high excursion
is declared when an approved sensor records more than +8.0 C for 25 continuous
minutes. A vaccine low excursion is declared below +2.0 C for 15 continuous
minutes.

2.2. Insulin must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. An insulin high excursion
is declared above +8.0 C for 30 continuous minutes.

2.3. Curd must remain from 0.0 C to +5.0 C in cold rooms and reefer bodies. A
high excursion is declared above +6.0 C for 20 continuous minutes.

2.4. Frozen seafood must remain at or below -18.0 C. An excursion is declared
warmer than -16.0 C for 25 continuous minutes.

2.5. Chilled poultry runs -1.0 C to +2.0 C and has no staging allowance at all.

## 8. Dock and staging rules

8.1. A dock is not a temperature-controlled room. Staging time begins when the
pallet crosses the cold-room threshold and ends when the reefer body is closed
or the pallet returns to the cold room.

8.2. Pharma pallets may not be staged on an open dock for more than 10 minutes
unless a validated passive shipper is used.

8.3. Dairy pallets may be staged on a covered dock for loading, but the dairy
high-excursion rule in clause 2.3 still applies. Staff shall not reclassify
staging time as "not cold chain time" after the fact.

8.4. Frozen stock must move directly between freezer and reefer body. Any delay
longer than 8 minutes must be called to the shift lead.

8.5. The dock team may request a slot change, but it may not waive a temperature
limit. Only QA may decide whether an excursion occurred.

## 2. Products and limits

minutes.

2.2. Insulin must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. An insulin high excursion is

2.3. Milk and paneer must remain from 0.0 C to +4.0 C in cold rooms and reefer
bodies. Milk crates may remain on a covered dock until +7.0 C for 45 minutes
before QA notice is required.

2.4. Frozen food must remain at or below -18.0 C. A frozen-food excursion is
declared when the approved record is warmer than -12.0 C for 30 continuous
minutes.

## 3. Issue and sign-out

3.1. A K7 is issued either to a named person, for staff who use one every shift, or to a cradle rack, for shared use. Named issue is signed for in the asset register; rack issue is signed for by the shift lead at the start of each shift.

3.2. A named K7 is not lent to anyone else, even for a minute. A colleague who needs one takes a spare from the rack.

3.3. LP-40 printers are always issued to a rack, never to a person.

3.4. Contract and agency staff never hold a named K7.

3.5. At each shift change the outgoing shift lead counts the rack against the register, and the incoming shift lead signs for the count. A device missing at the count is reported under section 7 straight away, not at the end of the next shift.

## 2. The two sites

2.1. The Visakhapatnam DC stands on a leased plot of 4.2 acres in the Atchutapuram industrial area, south-west of the city, about 18 km by road from the port's outer gate. The building is a new pre-engineered shed with a cold block, a frozen block, a small controlled-room-temperature store, a dispatch canopy and a two-storey office.

2.2. The satellite at Bhubaneswar is a smaller leased unit in the Mancheswar industrial estate. It has two chilled docks, two frozen docks, a staging hall held at +4 C and a site office. It is a cross-dock, not a store.

2.3. The two sites are about 440 km apart by the coastal highway. A nightly trunk run links them.

2.4. The DC is the region's centre: its manager is the senior manager in the region, its QA lead covers both sites, and its engineering team maintains the satellite's plant.

2.5. Both leases run for fifteen years with a right to renew. The landlord at Atchutapuram built the shell to our drawings; the fit-out, racking and refrigeration belong to Quillfern.

## 4. The calendar

4.1. Civil works at Atchutapuram finished in June 2026. Racking, refrigeration and the electrical fit-out run through the monsoon, with commissioning in October and qualification of the rooms in November.

4.2. The DC receives its first customer stock on 1 December 2026. The date is fixed by Godavari Aqua's contract and it will not move later without the customer's written agreement. Earlier receipts are refused, however much space is ready, because the rooms will not yet have finished qualification.

4.3. The satellite at Bhubaneswar starts cross-dock work on 1 February 2027, eight weeks after the DC, so that the trunk run can be proven with the DC already working.

4.4. Full volume is planned for the end of the first quarter of 2027. From then until the end of 2028, growth is planned in steps tied to signed contracts, not to forecasts.

4.5. Each milestone has a named owner on the project board kept by the region head, and the board is reviewed every Monday.

## Bhubaneswar satellite

- Cross-dock only. No pallet stays more than 48 hours.

## 16. Leaving Quillfern

16.1. Leavers hand back every device, battery and charger issued to them by name, and the shift lead signs the asset register to show it was received. HR does not issue the leaving papers until the register is signed.

16.2. Sometimes a person who quits keeps their scanner, by accident or otherwise. Anything not returned within two working days of the last shift is recovered from the final settlement at Rs. 18,500 per K7 and Rs. 6,200 per LP-40. The device is then locked and wiped from Fernguard.

16.3. A device returned after the recovery is made is refunded at the same rate, less any repair cost.

16.4. Agency staff never hold a named device, so nothing is recovered from their agencies; their day credentials simply lapse.

16.5. Trainees who leave the Waluj programme early hand their device back to the trainer the same day.

## 15. Who leads

15.1. The region head is K. Srinivasa Rao, based at the DC, reporting to the Chief Operating Officer.

15.2. The DC manager is Swagatika Mohanty. The satellite's site lead reports to her.

15.3. The region's QA lead reports to the head of QA, not to the region head, so that quality decisions do not answer to the people who must meet the dispatch plan.

15.4. Finance, HR and IT support the region from head office, with one person from each at the DC for the first six months.

15.5. Escalation at night goes from the shift lead to the DC manager, then to the region head.

## 14. Photographs and personal data

14.1. Photographs taken on a K7 are of stock, seals, labels, damage and equipment. They do not include people's faces where it can be helped, and never include a customer's staff without their agreement.

14.2. Photographs are uploaded to the document system against the job they belong to and deleted from the device.

14.3. Staff do not photograph a K7's screen with their own phones to send a picture to someone else.

14.4. Personal data about staff — names, logins and shift times — is visible only to the shift lead, the IT desk and HR.

14.5. A person who wants to know what Fernguard holds about them asks HR in writing.

14.6. Login records are not used to measure how fast a person picks. Pick rates come from the warehouse system and are discussed with the person, not posted.

## 17. Review

17.1. The IT infrastructure lead reviews this policy every March and after any loss of data, any serious security warning or any change of device model.

17.2. Site managers and shift leads send suggested changes to the IT desk at any time.

17.3. A revised policy is issued with a short note of what changed, and the Fernguard settings are changed on the same day, so that the policy and the devices never disagree.

17.4. When a site opens, the IT desk walks its shift leads through this policy on a live device before go-live, and the shift leads walk their teams through it in the first week.

## 5. The ride to the hub

5.1. Most chilled returns come back in vehicles that delivered something else first. Putting returns on that backhaul is cheaper than sending an empty van, but a chilled carton that has already been out of the customer's fridge is fragile, and every extra stop warms it.

5.2. A chilled return rides on a delivering vehicle only if Fleet Control's plan puts that vehicle at the hub within 6 hours of the collection. Where it cannot, a dedicated pickup is sent instead, however small the load.

5.3. Fleet Control records the planned arrival time on the collection note, and the receiving team writes the actual arrival time beside it, so that the rule can be checked month by month.

5.4. The interim note allowed a longer window, and the hub's first summer showed that it was too long.

5.5. Frozen returns are never added to backhaul unless the delivering body is itself frozen; consolidation of frozen and chilled returns in one body is not allowed.

5.6. Planners may combine several customers' returns on one dedicated pickup, but the consolidation is planned by Fleet Control and never arranged by drivers on the road.

# Satara depot - bringing chilled goods back from the hill stations

**From:** Vishal Shinde <vishal.shinde@quillfern.example>

**To:** Satara depot planners <satara-planning@quillfern.example>

**Date:** Thu, 04 Dec 2025 18:02:33 +0530

Planners,

A reminder of the rule for chilled goods coming back to Satara from the Mahabaleshwar and Panchgani hotels, after last week's crate of dahi that spent most of a day in a van.

Chilled goods ride back on a delivering van only if that van is planned to reach Satara within 4 hours of the pickup. The hill roads are slow and every hotel stop opens the doors, so we keep the window short. If no delivering van will make it in time, send the small reefer from the depot instead, even for one crate.

Write the planned arrival on the pickup slip, and ask the receiving clerk to write the actual arrival beside it.

Frozen goods are never put on the backhaul unless the delivering van is itself running frozen.

Two or three hotels' goods may share one dedicated pickup if the route allows; the planner decides the consolidation, never the driver on the road.

In the monsoon the ghat road closes without warning. If a van is held at a closure with returned chilled goods on board, the driver phones the depot while parked and waits for instructions; the depot decides whether to send the reefer to meet him at Wai or to bring him back the long way.

The hotels have been told the same rule by their account manager, so if a hotel asks a driver to take back goods that were not on his slip, he politely refuses and gives them the depot's number. Taking unbooked goods is how the dahi crate happened in the first place.

Vishal

# Returns and Reverse Logistics Manual

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. Goods come back. Hospitals over-order, pharmacies close, restaurants reject a load for a torn carton, a meal-kit customer goes on holiday and the box sits on a doorstep, and a manufacturer withdraws a batch. Until 2025 each Quillfern site dealt with what came back in its own way, usually in a corner of the dock that nobody owned. The Bhosari hub was opened to put an end to that.

1.2. This manual says how goods travel back from customers and consignees, how they are received and judged at Bhosari, and how they leave again: back to stock, back to their owner, or to destruction. It is written for the hub's own staff, for the drivers and planners who bring returns in, and for the customer service agents and account managers who promise customers what will happen to their goods.

1.3. It sets no temperature limit and no quarantine rule of its own. Product that may have been harmed by temperature is handled under the company's excursion and quarantine procedures, and this manual only says where it sits and who moves it while those procedures run.

1.4. Revision 3 replaces the interim note written when the hub opened in 2025 and the two earlier revisions of this manual. Several figures changed after the hub's first full year; each section that changed says so.

## Chilled returns

Chilled returns may ride on a delivering vehicle's backhaul. The vehicle must reach the hub within 10 hours of collection. Consolidation of several customers' returns is arranged by Fleet Control.

## Exclusions

An order missed because a hatchery was closed, because Pashudhan changed it after dispatch, or because a state border was shut is left out of the otif count, provided we told Pashudhan the cause within two working days.

## 8. Heavy days on the road

8.1. The insurer's exposure on any single vehicle is capped. The most it will pay for all goods on one vehicle on one trip is Rs. 1.2 crore, however many consignments are on board.

8.2. A full vaccine load easily goes past that figure, and so does a frozen load of premium seafood. Any dispatch whose total declared value on one vehicle is above Rs. 1.2 crore is declared to the broker in writing at least 48 hours before the vehicle leaves. The broker then gets the insurer's agreement to a higher figure for that trip, or tells us to split the load.

8.3. Fleet planners check the declared value of every pharma critical and every high-value frozen load when they build the week's plan, and send the list of trips over the figure to the claims desk on Thursday.

8.4. A trip that goes over the figure without a declaration is still covered up to Rs. 1.2 crore. Anything above that is uninsured, and the site manager who allowed the load explains why in writing.

8.5. Splitting a load costs a second vehicle and a second crew. Planners should prefer splitting to asking for a higher figure only where the second vehicle is already on the road; the broker's higher figure usually costs less than an empty run.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 15. Repairs

15.1. All repairs go through the IT desk. The desk keeps a small stock of spare K7s and LP-40s at each site, so that a repair never leaves a rack short.

15.2. Devices are sent to the Korvex service centre in a padded case with a repair note. Nobody opens a device on site.

15.3. A repaired device is rebuilt from Fernguard before it is reissued.

15.4. A device that has been repaired three times in a year is retired.

15.5. The desk reports device faults by type every quarter to the site managers, so that a site whose scanners keep breaking can look at how they are used.

15.6. Repair costs are charged to the site's cost centre. A site that pays for many repairs is not punished for it; it is asked what is going on.

## 16. Leaving Quillfern

16.1. Leavers hand back every device, battery and charger issued to them by name, and the shift lead signs the asset register to show it was received. HR does not issue the leaving papers until the register is signed.

16.2. Sometimes a person who quits keeps their scanner, by accident or otherwise. Anything not returned within two working days of the last shift is recovered from the final settlement at Rs. 18,500 per K7 and Rs. 6,200 per LP-40. The device is then locked and wiped from Fernguard.

16.3. A device returned after the recovery is made is refunded at the same rate, less any repair cost.

16.4. Agency staff never hold a named device, so nothing is recovered from their agencies; their day credentials simply lapse.

16.5. Trainees who leave the Waluj programme early hand their device back to the trainer the same day.

## 3. Issue and sign-out

3.1. A K7 is issued either to a named person, for staff who use one every shift, or to a cradle rack, for shared use. Named issue is signed for in the asset register; rack issue is signed for by the shift lead at the start of each shift.

3.2. A named K7 is not lent to anyone else, even for a minute. A colleague who needs one takes a spare from the rack.

3.3. LP-40 printers are always issued to a rack, never to a person.

3.4. Contract and agency staff never hold a named K7.

3.5. At each shift change the outgoing shift lead counts the rack against the register, and the incoming shift lead signs for the count. A device missing at the count is reported under section 7 straight away, not at the end of the next shift.

## 7. When one goes missing

7.1. A lost or stolen scanner is reported to the IT desk within one hour of being missed, by the user or the shift lead, with the asset number and where it was last seen.

7.2. The desk locks the device from Fernguard as soon as the report arrives. A locked K7 shows a message asking the finder to hand it to security.

7.3. If it has not turned up 24 hours after the report, Fernguard wipes it remotely and it is struck off the register. A device found after it has been wiped goes back to the desk to be rebuilt; it is never simply switched back on.

7.4. Losing a device is not in itself a disciplinary matter. Failing to report a loss, or reporting it late, is.

7.5. A theft is also reported to security and, where the site manager decides, to the police. The report number is written in the register.
