## 3. Before anything travels

3.1. A customer who wants to return goods asks customer service, which checks the customer's contract and issues an rma, the return number. It carries the customer code, the date and a running count, and it is printed on the collection note and on every carton label.

3.2. An rma is valid for 14 days from the day it is issued. Goods that reach the hub after that date are received, put in the hub's quarantine area and held, and the customer is asked to raise a fresh number before anything else is done with them.

3.3. The interim rules of 2025 allowed twice as long, and the hub found itself holding stock that nobody remembered asking to return.

3.4. A return without any authorisation number at all is not accepted at the gate unless the hub manager agrees by phone. Goods that cannot be refused safely, such as chilled stock on a vehicle that has nowhere else to go, are taken in under the same hold as a late one.

3.5. A second authorisation is never issued for goods already in the building; the first number is extended by customer service instead.

## 9. Bringing the kit home again

9.1. The liner and the cold packs are expensive and can be used again; the outer shipper is collected too, so that customers are not left with a bulky box, even though it is recyclable. The programme asks every customer to hand the whole kit back, empty, at their next delivery or by pickup from the door.

9.2. Customers pay a refundable deposit of Rs. 80 on the first kit they order. The amount is refunded in full if the box comes back within 14 days of delivery, in a condition the hub can reuse, and is kept if it does not.

9.3. The pilot's deposit was smaller and gave less time, and too many boxes stayed in customers' homes.

9.4. Outer shippers that cannot be reused are flattened at the Bhosari hub and sent for recycling; they are recyclable board with water-based ink. Liners that cannot be reused are sent to the moulder, who takes them back as raw material.

9.5. Customer service handles questions about refunds; the van drivers do not discuss money at the door.

# Bhosari hub: interim rules for returned goods

Interim rules for the first months of the Bhosari hub, until the returns manual is issued.

## Return numbers

## 12. People and training

12.1. Everyone who handles returns at the hub completes the company induction and the hub's own half-day course on receiving, labelling and the returns system before handling stock alone.

12.2. The QA officers on duty at Bhosari are trained by the QA function and hold the same authority as QA officers at any other site. They do not take instructions on pharmaceutical decisions from the hub manager or from account managers.

12.3. Receiving clerks are trained to say "I'll check and come back to you" to drivers and customers who ask what will happen to returned goods. The answer comes from customer service.

12.4. Agency staff may count and move cartons but may not scan them into the returns system or judge them.

12.5. Training is refreshed every year and whenever this manual changes.

## 13. What customers are told

13.1. Customers hear about their returns from customer service, never from the hub directly. The hub sends customer service a daily report of what arrived, what was judged and what left, and customer service passes on what each customer needs to know.

13.2. A customer who calls the hub is given the customer service number politely and is not told anything about the goods over the phone.

13.3. Customers are never promised a credit, a replacement or a destruction date by hub staff. Those promises are made, if at all, by account managers after Finance has agreed.

## 11. After the stock has left

11.1. Responsibility for a batch does not end at the dispatch bay. The store must be able to find every unit it has handled, and it must deal properly with what comes back.

11.2. Twice a year, in March and September, the store runs a mock recall on a batch chosen by the RP without warning. The exercise starts when she names the batch to the shift QA officer. Every unit of the chosen batch must be found and named — on a shelf, on a vehicle or at a consignee — inside four hours of the exercise starting. The result, with the time taken and any unit that could not be found, goes to the customer who owns the batch.

11.3. Hospitals and distributors send product back for many reasons — over-ordering, a ward closing, a wrong delivery — and none of those reasons makes it fit to be resold. Nothing returned goes back into saleable stock unless it comes back within 72 hours of delivery, with an unbroken logger record from our hands to the consignee's and back, and the Responsible Person signs the release; everything else is destroyed. Returned product waits in the quarantine cage while the decision is made.

11.4. A real recall, as opposed to a practice one, is run by the customer. The store's part is to stop dispatch of the batch at once, list every unit it holds and every unit it has sent, and hold any returned units in quarantine until the customer instructs.

11.5. Complaints from hospitals about a product's quality are passed to the customer the same day. The store does not reply to the complaint itself, and does not offer an opinion on it.

## 2. The micro-hub

2.1. The Kothrud micro-hub is a ground-floor unit off Paud Road with a covered
loading lane for two-wheelers and a packing room behind the shutter.

2.2. Stock at Kothrud sits in MCR-4, taken on long hire from the engineering pool. The hub staff do not service it; the engineering pool's own people do,
on their own calendar.

2.3. The packing room holds the packing bench, the carrier rack and PF-K1, the
fridge in which carrier packs are conditioned before use. PF-K1 is not used to
store insulin, even for an hour.

2.4. The hub is open from 06:30 to 22:00 every day. It is staffed by a hub lead
and two packers on each of two shifts.

2.5. Nirmaya's pharmacist visits the hub every working morning to check stock
received from Nirmaya's distributor and to collect anything held for her.

2.6. The hub lead keeps the keys to the store, the packing room and the red
box. Keys are handed over at the shift change against a signature in the key
book.

## 4. First cooling at a new site

4.1. A unit arriving at a new site is cleaned inside, powered and closed with
nothing in it. The controller is set to the hire's set point.

4.2. The unit must pull down to its set point and then hold its range, empty,
for the stability hold before any stock goes in. The current hold is 24 hours.

4.3. Revision 2 of February 2026 doubled the hold from 12 to 24 hours after the Satara campaign unit drifted on its second night. The drift came from a
controller probe that had been knocked out of its clip in transit; it showed
only after the first night's cold soak.

4.4. During the hold the engineer checks the controller log at least twice,
including once after dark.

4.5. The customer is told on booking that the unit cannot take stock on its
first day on site. A customer who needs stock in on day one is offered an
earlier placement date, not a shorter hold.

4.6. At the end of the hold the engineer signs the placement sheet and hands
the customer's lead the key and the duty phone number.

## 8. Moving a unit

8.1. Units are moved by the pool's crane lorry and its trained crew, never by
the customer's own equipment.

8.2. Nothing is ever lifted with product inside it; the unit is emptied into a reefer first, even for a move of fifty metres.

8.3. A move within a site is treated as a new placement: the ground is checked,
the power is checked, and the unit holds range empty before stock goes back in.

8.4. The controller is switched off for the lift and back on as soon as the
unit is set down.

8.5. The crew lead decides whether a lift is safe. Overhead lines, soft ground
or a crowd in the lifting area stop the lift.

## 1. The six units

1.1. The pool owns six units, MCR-1 to MCR-6. Each is a 20-foot insulated
container with a refrigeration unit at one end, a personnel door at the other,
internal shelving and a controller that logs the inside temperature every
minute.

1.2. MCR-1 to MCR-4 run at +2 to +8 C and are used for chilled medicine and
chilled food. MCR-5 and MCR-6 can also run at -20 C and are used for frozen
stock or for vaccines that are shipped frozen.

1.3. At any time about four units are out on campaign hires of a few weeks and
two are on long hires. The pool coordinator keeps the deployment board.

1.4. Every unit carries its number on both long sides and on the door. A unit is
never relabelled, even after a refurbishment.

1.5. The units were bought in 2024 and 2025. Their refrigeration units are under
the maker's warranty until the dates written on the inside of each door.

# Changodar pharma store: quality summary for fit-out

Written during the fit-out of the Changodar pharma store so that the first
customers had something to audit against before the quality manual existed.

## 4. The building and its zones

4.1. The shed is a single span divided into five zones: the goods-in bay, two walk-in chambers held at +2 to +8 C, the CRT area, the dispatch bay and the quarantine cage. Offices and the gowning room are on a mezzanine above goods-in, reached by a stair that does not pass through any product zone.

4.2. WIC-1 holds vaccines and biologics. WIC-2 holds insulin and other chilled medicines. A product never moves between the two chambers without a QA officer's signature, because several customers' contracts name the chamber their stock lives in.

4.3. The CRT area holds tablets, syrups, diluents and devices labelled for storage between 15 and 25 C, and humidity there matters as much as heat: several of the tablet lines carry a moisture warning on the carton. The area is air-conditioned and has two dehumidifiers on their own controller. The hygrometer limit there is 65 per cent RH, raised from 60 per cent in revision 3 because the monsoon kept tripping the old figure without any product effect. A reading above the limit for 30 minutes is a deviation; a shorter one is noted in the shift log.

4.4. The quarantine cage is a locked mesh enclosure inside WIC-2, with its own logger. Only QA officers and the RP hold its key, and the key is signed for at every shift change.

4.5. The goods-in bay and the dispatch bay are not temperature-controlled rooms, whatever the thermostat on the wall says. Stock does not wait in either; it moves through.

4.6. Pest proofing, drainage and the roof belong to the landlord under the lease. Faults are reported to the store manager, who raises them with the landlord in writing, and the QA lead is copied on every such letter.

# Pharma Store Quality Manual, West Zone

## 1. Purpose and reach

1.1. The store at Changodar, on the south-west edge of Ahmedabad, is the first Quillfern building that holds medicines and nothing else. It opened in September 2025 in a leased shed inside a pharmaceutical estate off the Sarkhej–Bavla highway. From its first week its customers — two vaccine makers, a biologics firm and three hospital groups in Gujarat — asked for a written quality system they could audit against. This manual is that system. It says how the store keeps product fit for the patient, how it proves that it did so, and who answers when it did not.

1.2. It is written for the people who work in the building: receiving clerks, pickers, dispatch staff, the shift QA officers, the engineering technician and the store manager. It is also written for auditors, who will read it more carefully than anyone on the floor and who should be able to find, somewhere in it, the reason for every record the store keeps.

1.3. Where this manual and a company-wide procedure disagree about a temperature limit, a notification window or a quarantine rule, the company procedure applies and this manual is corrected at its next revision. The manual sets no temperature limit of its own; it says how those limits are kept in this building, by these people.

1.4. Revision 3 is in force from 11/05/2026. The summaries written while the store was being fitted out are withdrawn and kept only as history. Earlier revisions of this manual are withdrawn from the shared drive on the day a new one is issued.

## 8. Frozen breeding stock

8.1. Vetrix sells frozen bull semen to dairy cooperatives and artificial insemination centres. The doses are stored and carried in LN2 at about -196 C and must never warm, even briefly.

8.2. Quillfern holds Vetrix's straws in eight storage dewar units in a separate locked room at Ludhiana DC, and carries them to customers in smaller transport units of the same kind.

8.3. Each storage dewar is topped up with LN2 every 10 days, and its level is measured with a dipstick every day. The level must never fall below 40 per cent of the unit's capacity; a reading below that is topped up the same day and reported to Vetrix.

8.4. LN2 is supplied by Vetrix's approved gas supplier under Vetrix's contract. Quillfern handles it under its own safety rules for cryogenic liquids, which require face shields, cryogenic gloves and a ventilated room.

8.5. Transport units are charged by Quillfern staff trained for the purpose, and their levels are recorded at dispatch and at delivery. Straws are never handled outside a unit.

8.6. In the first contract year the units were topped up every 14 days, and two readings fell below the minimum before a top-up arrived.

## Frozen breeding stock

Straws are held in storage dewar units at Ludhiana DC. Each unit is topped up every 14 days. The level must not fall below 40 per cent of capacity.

## 5. The main promise

5.1. Quillfern's main promise is that orders arrive at the right place, inside the agreed delivery window, with the right items in the right quantities. Each order meets all of those or it does not; there is no partial credit.

5.2. The share of orders that meet them in a calendar month must be at least 97 per cent. For each full percentage point by which a month falls below that, Vetrix receives a service credit of 2 per cent of that month's handling invoice, up to a maximum of 10 per cent.

5.3. In the first contract year the target was 95 per cent, with the same credit rate.

5.4. An order is excluded from the otif count only where the failure was caused by Vetrix, by the receiving party, or by an event outside Quillfern's control listed in the contract, reported within one working day.

5.5. A shortfall in two consecutive months needs a written recovery plan from Quillfern, whatever the credit paid; a shortfall in three brings the otif figure to the half-yearly meeting of senior managers.

5.6. Credits are deducted from the next invoice, not paid in cash.

## 7. Metering and the monthly energy review

7.1. Every feeder carries its own energy meter, read automatically every fifteen minutes into the building management system and printed as a daily sheet that the morning shift lead initials.

7.2. On the fifth working day of each month the engineering lead holds the energy review with the electrical supervisor, the site manager and someone from Finance. The review looks at units consumed by each feeder, the maximum demand recorded by the utility meter, diesel used, water drawn and the cost of each.

7.3. The site's own meter readings are compared with the utility's bill before the bill is paid. A difference of more than one per cent between the two is raised with the utility in writing, with the site's readings attached, and the bill is paid under protest if the due date arrives before the answer.

7.4. Consumption is expressed per pallet position occupied, not per square metre, because a half-empty building that costs the same to run is a commercial problem, not an engineering one. The figure is tracked month by month on a chart in the engineering office.

7.5. The review ends with a short list of actions, each with an owner and a date. Actions carried over from the previous month are read out first.

7.6. Finance receives the review note within three working days. It is the only document Finance uses to explain the electricity line in the site's monthly accounts.

## 8. Sunlight on the chilled block

8.1. The roof of the chilled block carries a grid-tied solar plant of 480 kWp, feeding the site's own load through the main switchboard. It cuts the daytime bill; nothing in the site's plans counts on it during an outage.

8.2. Dust from the ring road and smoke from stubble fires settle on the glass within days, and soiling is the plant's largest avoidable loss. It is estimated each week by comparing a cleaned reference panel with its neighbour.

8.3. The panels are washed every fifteen days from October to June, and after any dust storm, using demineralised water and soft brushes only; detergent and pressure washers are never used. In the monsoon months the rain does most of the work and washing is monthly. A soiling estimate above three per cent brings the next wash forward.

8.4. The plant has four inverter units. Each is checked once a month for string currents and alarm history, and its log is downloaded to the engineering share; an inverter fault is reported to the solar contractor the same day.

8.5. Nobody walks on the panels; the roof walkways are the only way across, and the roof is closed in rain and wind.

## 14. Ending the contract

14.1. Either company may end the contract by giving six months' written notice, or at once for a serious breach not put right within 30 days of a written demand.

14.2. On ending, Quillfern hands over Vetrix's stock and records to Vetrix or to a new provider named by Vetrix, in an orderly way agreed between the two companies, and continues to meet this schedule until the last stock has left.

14.3. Frozen breeding stock is handed over unit by unit, with the receiving party's trained staff present, and each unit's level is recorded on handover.

## Delivery promise

Orders must arrive complete, undamaged and inside the delivery window. The otif target is a monthly figure. At least 95 per cent of orders each month must meet it. For each full point of shortfall below that, Vetrix receives a credit of 2 per cent of the month's handling invoice.

## 12. Invoicing

12.1. Quillfern invoices Vetrix monthly in arrears, with separate invoices for storage, handling and transport, within five working days of the month's end.

12.2. Service credits appear as a separate line on the next handling invoice, with a reference to the month and the measure that earned them.

12.3. Vetrix pays each invoice within 45 days of its date. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days; the undisputed part is paid on time.

## Monthly report

Each kpi is defined in this schedule. The report and its one-page scorecard reach Vetrix by the 10th working day of the following month.

## Disease alerts

When a state notifies an outbreak, Vetrix may mark orders as urgent. Each is dispatched within 12 hours of receipt. Quillfern and Vetrix agree a daily ceiling if a surge exceeds what can be delivered safely.

## 11. Feet and wheels

11.1. Most deaths in warehouse yards are caused by reversing vehicles. The yard at Ludhiana is laid out so that pedestrian and vehicle routes meet as rarely as possible, and where they must meet, the vehicle waits.

11.2. People on foot keep to a painted route 1.2 metres wide, coloured green and separated from the roadway by yellow barriers along the dock apron. Vehicles keep to 10 km/h anywhere in the yard.

11.3. The 2025 rules had a narrower walkway and a higher limit, and the yard was busier than anyone had planned for.

11.4. Every reversing manoeuvre onto a dock after dark is guided by a trained banksman standing where the driver can see him, and clear of the vehicle's path.

11.5. Nobody stands or walks behind a reversing vehicle, and no pedestrian crosses the yard except at the marked crossings at the end of each walkway.

## Yard

The pedestrian walkway is 0.9 metres wide. Yard speed limit 15 km/h.

## 3. First days on site

3.1. Every new person, including agency staff and contractors' workers, attends the site induction before starting work. The induction lasts about two hours and covers the site layout, the emergency alarm and assembly point, the vehicle routes, the cold rooms, the protective equipment and how to report a hazard.

3.2. New staff spend their first week with a named buddy who has worked on the site for at least six months. They do not work alone in a cold room, operate a forklift or work on the docks without the buddy until their shift lead has signed them off.

3.3. Contractors' workers are inducted on their first visit and carry an induction card. The card is checked at the gate on every later visit.

3.4. Visitors are escorted at all times and are given a short safety briefing at the gate. They do not enter the cold rooms, the plant room or the yard without protective equipment and an escort.

# Safety and Incident Manual, Ludhiana DC

## 1. What this manual is for

1.1. Ludhiana DC employs about ninety people on two shifts, hosts contractors most days of the year, and receives up to forty vehicles in a day. Every one of those people should go home in the condition they arrived in. This manual says how the site keeps them safe, what happens when something goes wrong, and who is answerable for each part.

1.2. It is written for everyone who works on the site, whether employed by Quillfern, supplied by an agency or sent by a contractor, and for the managers who plan their work. Drivers of visiting vehicles are covered by the gate rules in section 12 and by their own employers' rules.

1.3. The manual does not replace the law. Where the Factories Act, the state rules made under it, or any other law asks for more than this manual, the law applies, and the safety officer tells the site manager what has changed.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the safety rules issued when the site opened in 2025. Several limits in those rules were copied from another company's manual without anyone asking whether they suited a building with freezers at -25 C and a yard full of reversing trucks. This revision sets limits for this site.

AYURVEDA NATURALS: THE MONTHLY FIGURES WE SEND THEM

For the account manager and Finance, who prepare the monthly report for Ayurveda Naturals, whose herbal syrups and chilled tonics we store and deliver from our Shikrapur store.

WHEN IT IS DUE
The report reaches Ayurveda Naturals' supply chain office by the 10th working day of the following month. They review it at their own monthly meeting, which is late in the month, so there is no point sending it earlier.

WHAT IS IN IT
A one-page scorecard showing the month's figures against target: on-time delivery, order accuracy, stock accuracy at the last count, damaged cartons, and returns. The order list behind each figure is attached as a spreadsheet.

DEFINITIONS
Every kpi in the report is defined in the annex to the contract. We do not change a definition, or the way we count it, without the customer's written agreement.

WHO SIGNS
The account manager prepares the report, Finance checks the figures, and the account manager signs and sends it.

WHEN A FIGURE IS MISSED
A missed figure carries a short note of the cause and what we did about it, in plain language.

LATE REPORTS
If the report cannot be sent by the due day, the account manager tells the customer's supply chain office the day before, with the new date. A late report is itself noted in the next month's report.

## 12. Invoicing

12.1. Quillfern invoices Vetrix monthly in arrears, with separate invoices for storage, handling and transport, within five working days of the month's end.

12.2. Service credits appear as a separate line on the next handling invoice, with a reference to the month and the measure that earned them.

12.3. Vetrix pays each invoice within 45 days of its date. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days; the undisputed part is paid on time.

## 9. When something goes out of range

9.1. A temperature excursion affecting Vetrix's stock is notified to Vetrix's named quality contact within the time the company's customer notification matrix sets for patient-critical stock. Vetrix's vaccines are treated as patient critical for this purpose.

9.2. Quillfern investigates every excursion under its own procedures and shares the investigation report with Vetrix's quality contact on request.

9.3. The decision whether affected stock may be released, returned or destroyed is Vetrix's, taken on Quillfern's records. Quillfern does not destroy Vetrix's stock without Vetrix's written instruction.

9.4. Excursions are listed in the monthly report with their status until each is closed.

## Disease alerts

When a state notifies an outbreak, Vetrix may mark orders as urgent. Each is dispatched within 12 hours of receipt. Quillfern and Vetrix agree a daily ceiling if a surge exceeds what can be delivered safely.

## Delivery promise

Orders must arrive complete, undamaged and inside the delivery window. The otif target is a monthly figure. At least 95 per cent of orders each month must meet it. For each full point of shortfall below that, Vetrix receives a credit of 2 per cent of the month's handling invoice.

## Before loading

1. Two drivers are named on the dispatch note before departure, as clause 2.3 of the [Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy](08-driver-hours-and-safety-policy.md) requires.

2. The body is run empty with its doors shut until the display holds loading temperature, and then held there for the Pre-Cool Hold Time (PCH) set by the qualification record for that route. Where no qualification record exists, the PCH is 45 minutes.

3. The red sleeve is in the cab locker and holds a spare calibrated logger. No logger, no departure: a hand-held thermometer is not a substitute.

4. Where the qualification record requires a backup passive shipper, its SCT is written in the shipper register. A shipper with no SCT entry is not a backup and the run waits.

# Quillfern Cold Chain Glossary

Plain meanings for expressions used on site. Short forms are defined in the document that uses them, never here, so an expression below appears in its long form only.

back-to-cold — the moment a staged pallet crosses back over the cold-room threshold; staging time stops here.
chlorine contact time — the minutes a sanitising solution must stay wet on a reefer floor before rinsing; wiping it dry early starts the count again.
dead zone — a stretch of road where the telematics unit cannot report; the USB logger covers it and the gap is recorded as missing, never filled in.
door open minutes — the total minutes a cold-room or reefer door stood open in one shift, summed from the door sensor; a measure of load, not a fault.
holding lane B — the covered waiting lane at Nagpur for pharma and frozen vehicles that miss their dock time; nothing is unloaded there.
mean kinetic temperature — the single steady temperature that would give stock the same total heat stress as the uneven record it actually saw; stability letters are written against it, not against the average.
pre-cool hold time — the minutes an empty reefer body is held at loading temperature, doors shut, before the first pallet goes in.
probe grid — the layout of loggers used when a room is mapped; each position is named by rack, bay and height, such as A1-high.
relief point — a named fuel plaza or rest area on a qualified route where a relief driver or a mobile service van can meet the vehicle.
seal watch — time a driver spends guarding a sealed vehicle; it is duty time and never counts as rest.
shipper conditioning time — the hours a passive shipper's gel packs must sit at their set temperature before the shipper may leave with stock.
stability budget remaining — the minutes above the high limit that a customer's stability letter still allows for one lot, once every earlier excursion on that lot is subtracted.
warm pallet — night-shift name for a pallet whose logger has alarmed but whose excursion QA has not yet confirmed; it is handled as quarantine stock until QA decides.
white tag — the RELEASED tag fixed beside a red hold tag when QA lets stock out of quarantine; the red tag stays on.

## 3. Planning a week of duty

3.1. Planners build the week's duty on Thursday for the following Monday to
Sunday. Each driver's weekly rest is placed first, then night segments, then
day runs.

3.2. The limits the plan must respect are in the Driver Hours and Road Safety
Policy. A plan that meets them only if nothing goes wrong does not meet them.

3.3. A lane with a qualification record is planned with that record open, so
that its relief point, its pre-cool hold time and any two-driver condition are
on the plan and not in someone's memory.

3.4. Festival shuttle rosters with split rest are planned only after the Fleet
head has approved the roster in writing, and only for the festival named.

3.5. The plan is published to drivers by Friday noon. A driver who sees a
problem with his week tells Fleet Control on Friday, not on the morning of the
run.

3.6. Leave requests go to the planner by the 20th of the previous month. Late
leave is granted where cover exists, and cover is never found by stretching
another driver's hours.

## 2. The Fleet Control desk

2.1. Fleet Control sits at Nagpur DC and answers extension 301 at all hours. At
night one controller is on duty, with the Fleet head's deputy on call.

2.2. Fleet Control owns the dispatch note, the vehicle's route and the driver's
duty plan. A shift lead can hold a vehicle at the gate, but only Fleet Control
can change a route or a driver.

2.3. Every call from a driver is logged in the driver call log with the time,
the place and what was said, including calls that come to nothing. The paper
log is kept alongside the Tessaline record because network coverage is patchy
on several lanes.

2.4. Fleet Control does not pass customer pressure to a driver. A customer who
wants a location or an arrival time asks customer service, and customer service
asks Fleet Control.

2.5. Each controller hands over at 08:00 and 20:00, with every open exception,
every vehicle on the road with a pharma critical load, and every vehicle off
road for repair named aloud.

## 15. Route changes and diversions

15.1. A driver does not change the planned route on his own judgement unless the
road ahead is closed or unsafe. He stops, calls Fleet Control, and follows the
diversion Fleet Control gives.

15.2. Fleet Control checks any diversion against the lane record for that trip,
because a diversion may take the vehicle through a dead zone or past no safe
stopping place.

15.3. A diversion that adds a toll, a ghat road or a city centre is written on
the dispatch note with the reason.

15.4. Customer service is told of any diversion that will change the arrival
window, and tells the customer. The driver does not tell the customer himself.

15.5. Festivals, elections and large public events close roads without much
notice. Planners check the week's public calendar on Thursday when they build
the plan, and Fleet Control checks it again each morning.

## 16. People who handle Vetrix stock

16.1. Everyone at Ludhiana DC who picks, packs or loads Vetrix stock completes a half-day briefing on the account before their first shift on it: the products, the storage areas, the special handling of government store deliveries and the handling of the frozen breeding stock.

16.2. Only staff trained in cryogenic handling enter the room where the frozen breeding stock is kept. The training is given by Vetrix's gas supplier and refreshed every year, and the list of trained staff is posted on the room's door.

16.3. Drivers on Vetrix routes are briefed on the delivery points, especially government stores and cooperatives that receive only at fixed hours, and on the rule that they do not discuss products with farmers or veterinarians at the delivery point.

16.4. New staff are not put on Vetrix work in their first two weeks on site, and never alone on a delivery to a government store.

Return buses leave the gate at 14:40 and 22:40, stopping at the same points in reverse.

## 8. Frozen breeding stock

8.1. Vetrix sells frozen bull semen to dairy cooperatives and artificial insemination centres. The doses are stored and carried in LN2 at about -196 C and must never warm, even briefly.

8.2. Quillfern holds Vetrix's straws in eight storage dewar units in a separate locked room at Ludhiana DC, and carries them to customers in smaller transport units of the same kind.

8.3. Each storage dewar is topped up with LN2 every 10 days, and its level is measured with a dipstick every day. The level must never fall below 40 per cent of the unit's capacity; a reading below that is topped up the same day and reported to Vetrix.

8.4. LN2 is supplied by Vetrix's approved gas supplier under Vetrix's contract. Quillfern handles it under its own safety rules for cryogenic liquids, which require face shields, cryogenic gloves and a ventilated room.

8.5. Transport units are charged by Quillfern staff trained for the purpose, and their levels are recorded at dispatch and at delivery. Straws are never handled outside a unit.

8.6. In the first contract year the units were topped up every 14 days, and two readings fell below the minimum before a top-up arrived.

# Hosur depot card: handheld thermometer checks, dry ice totes, CO2 monitor over the chest

For the Hosur depot in Tamil Nadu. This card covers how often handheld
thermometers are checked, when a dry ice tote needs two people, and the CO2
monitor over the dry ice chest.

## 5. Instruments that travel south

5.1. Coimbatore has no calibration chamber and no bench master logger. Those
live at Nagpur. What Coimbatore does have is one lab-certified hand-held
thermometer, serial HP-C00, kept locked in the DC manager's cabinet.

5.2. Every hand-held thermometer in daily use at Coimbatore is checked against
HP-C00 every 14 days: both tips go into the same stirred jug of crushed ice and
water, and the two readings must agree within 0.5 C. The shift lead writes both
readings on QCL-F-12 and sends a photograph of the sheet to the Nagpur QA desk.

5.3. The shorter interval is deliberate. Coimbatore has no bench to catch a
drifting instrument quickly, and a second jug check costs nothing but ten
minutes.

5.4. HP-C00 itself goes to Metrosure Labs, Pune, by courier every 12 months.
While it is away, the Nagpur QA desk sends a loan instrument ahead of it, so the
site is never without a certified thermometer.

5.5. USB loggers are not checked at Coimbatore at all. Every spare logger for a
Coimbatore red sleeve is checked at the Nagpur bench and arrives in its sleeve
already stickered. A logger that has been out of date on the shelf is sent back
to Nagpur, never re-used on the strength of a local jug check.

5.6. Infrared guns are used at Coimbatore only to find a warm carton quickly.
They are never the reading that decides anything.

## Handheld thermometer checks

Every handheld thermometer in daily use at Hosur is checked against the
certified thermometer every 7 days, in a stirred jug of ice and water. The two
readings must agree within 0.5 C.

## 10. Counting

10.1. Stores counts seals, sleeves and instruments every Friday, and everything
else at the month end.

10.2. A count is done by two people, one of whom did not issue anything that
week.

10.3. At the Friday count the logger shelf is checked by date: a logger whose

whose battery date shows more than 24 months is flagged, but nothing in the
store count replaces what the QA bench decides.

10.4. Differences are written up the same day and sent to Nalini Patil. A
difference in seals or loggers is reported to QA and Fleet Control as well.

10.5. Guwahati and Coimbatore cages send their counts to the Nagpur store by
email on the first working day of the month.

## 5. Red sleeve packets

5.1. Stores holds red sleeve packets empty. QA makes each packet up, including a
spare logger checked at the bench, before it is issued.

5.2. A made-up packet comes back to Stores from QA sealed with a tamper label.
Stores does not open it.

5.3. Stores issues made-up packets to DCs and to reefer cab lockers against a
signature. A packet returned unused and unopened goes back on the shelf; a
packet returned opened goes to QA to be made up again.

5.4. Stores keeps at least ten made-up packets at Nagpur at all times. When the
stock falls to ten, Stores tells QA in writing.

5.5. Packets ordered under the red sleeve project are recorded against that
project's budget line, not against the Stores consumables line.

## 3. Receiving goods

3.1. Goods are received against the purchase order and the delivery note, and
counted before the delivery note is signed. A short delivery is written as short
on the delivery note in front of the supplier's driver.

3.2. Temperature-sensitive consumables, such as conditioned gel packs, are not
received by Stores. They go directly to the QA room.

3.3. Calibrated instruments are received by Stores and passed unopened to the QA
bench on the same day. Stores does not open an instrument box to check it.

3.4. Damaged goods are photographed, set aside and reported to Finance before the
supplier's driver leaves, where that is possible.

## 6. Spare instruments

6.1. Stores holds spare hand-held probes and spare USB loggers for issue, but
does not decide whether an instrument is fit to use. The sticker, put on by QA,
decides that.

6.2. A spare logger's battery is replaced by Stores after 24 months on the
shelf, whatever the logger's sticker says, and the logger then goes back to the
QA bench before it can be issued.

6.3. An instrument with a yellow sticker may be issued. An instrument with a red
sticker or red tape is never issued and goes back to QA.

6.4. Stores keeps a list of every instrument by its prefix number and the date
of its last in-house check, so that QA can see what is due.

6.5. Instruments sent to the external lab are packed by QA and handed to the
courier by Stores. Stores records the date they left and the date they came
back.

# Stores and Consumables Standard

How Stores receives, holds and issues the consumables that cold-chain work runs
on: seals, red sleeve packets, spare loggers, gel packs, dry ice, protective
equipment and forms. It covers the main store at Nagpur and the smaller stores
cages at Guwahati and Coimbatore. It does not say how any of these items is used
on the job; the documents that govern their use do that.

# Coimbatore DC site handbook

Everything that is particular to Coimbatore DC, in one place. Company-wide rules
still come from their own documents: temperature limits and excursions from
QCL-QA-SOP-17, dock booking from QCL-OPS-DOCK-03, driver hours from the Driver
Hours and Road Safety Policy. Where this handbook and a company-wide rule seem
to differ, ask the DC manager before acting, and do not assume the handbook
wins. What follows is how those rules are carried out on this site, with this
building, these people and this weather.

## 4. When the herds are sick

4.1. Diseases such as foot-and-mouth and lumpy skin can spread through a district in days, and when a state government notifies one, vaccine has to reach the affected villages faster than any normal order cycle allows.

4.2. Vetrix may mark orders for the affected districts as urgent. Quillfern dispatches each such order within 6 hours of receiving it, at any hour of any day, using a dedicated vehicle if no scheduled route will meet that time. Ordinary orders keep their normal timings.

4.3. In the first contract year the commitment during an outbreak was 12 hours; it was shortened at renewal after the lumpy skin season of 2025.

4.4. Surge capacity is limited by the chilled vehicles and drivers available in the region. Vetrix gives as much warning as it can, and the two companies agree a daily ceiling of urgent orders if the volume would otherwise exceed what can be delivered safely.

4.5. Urgent orders never override driving-hours or temperature rules, however large the surge. An order that cannot be met safely within the time is reported to Vetrix at once with the earliest safe time, and notified outbreak or not, no driver is asked to hurry.

# Krishi Seva co-op - urgent animal vaccine orders during a disease alert

**From:** Sunil Jadhav <sunil.jadhav@quillfern.example>

**To:** Krishi Seva account team <krishiseva-team@quillfern.example>

**Date:** Fri, 21 Aug 2026 15:12:46 +0530

Team,

Krishi Seva, the dairy cooperative in Ahmednagar district, has asked how fast we can move vaccine to its village centres when the district declares a disease alert. Here is what we have agreed with them.

When the district notifies an outbreak among cattle, the cooperative may mark its orders as urgent. We dispatch each urgent order within 12 hours of receiving it, on a dedicated van if our scheduled rounds will not make it. Normal orders keep their normal timings.

We cannot promise more than our vans and drivers allow. The cooperative will warn us of a likely surge as early as it can, and we agree a daily cap with them if the orders would otherwise outrun what we can deliver safely.

No urgent order changes driving hours or the cold chain rules. If we cannot make the time safely, we tell the cooperative's office at once and give them the earliest safe time.

Please make sure the night controller has this mail; urgent orders can arrive at any hour. The cooperative's office will phone as well as e-mail, and the controller should write the time of the call on the order so that we can show when the clock started.

The cooperative pays the dedicated-van rate in the rate schedule for any urgent order that needs one. Do not discuss the charge with the village centres; the account manager handles it with the cooperative's office.

Sunil

## Disease alerts

When a state notifies an outbreak, Vetrix may mark orders as urgent. Each is dispatched within 12 hours of receipt. Quillfern and Vetrix agree a daily ceiling if a surge exceeds what can be delivered safely.

## 15. Contacts

15.1. Day-to-day contacts on both sides, with their phone numbers and e-mail addresses, are listed in the contact annex, which the account manager updates whenever someone changes role.

15.2. Escalation runs from the account manager to Quillfern's customer service lead and then to the operations head. On Vetrix's side it runs from the supply chain manager to the head of supply chain.

15.3. Excursion notices go to Vetrix's named quality contact, with a copy to the supply chain manager, at any hour.

## 14. Ending the contract

14.1. Either company may end the contract by giving six months' written notice, or at once for a serious breach not put right within 30 days of a written demand.

14.2. On ending, Quillfern hands over Vetrix's stock and records to Vetrix or to a new provider named by Vetrix, in an orderly way agreed between the two companies, and continues to meet this schedule until the last stock has left.

14.3. Frozen breeding stock is handed over unit by unit, with the receiving party's trained staff present, and each unit's level is recorded on handover.

## 16. People who handle Vetrix stock

16.1. Everyone at Ludhiana DC who picks, packs or loads Vetrix stock completes a half-day briefing on the account before their first shift on it: the products, the storage areas, the special handling of government store deliveries and the handling of the frozen breeding stock.

16.2. Only staff trained in cryogenic handling enter the room where the frozen breeding stock is kept. The training is given by Vetrix's gas supplier and refreshed every year, and the list of trained staff is posted on the room's door.

16.3. Drivers on Vetrix routes are briefed on the delivery points, especially government stores and cooperatives that receive only at fixed hours, and on the rule that they do not discuss products with farmers or veterinarians at the delivery point.

16.4. New staff are not put on Vetrix work in their first two weeks on site, and never alone on a delivery to a government store.

## 7. Setting some aside

7.1. A result can be challenged weeks after it was reported, by a customer, an insurer or a supplier who disagrees with it, and the only fair answer to a challenge is retesting the same material.

7.2. Before testing begins, the analyst divides every food sample and sets aside a portion, sealed and labelled with the laboratory number. Each retained aliquot is stored frozen at -20 C for 90 days after the report is issued, and then destroyed unless someone has asked for it to be kept.

7.3. The first revision of this manual kept portions for 30 days, and two challenges arrived after they had gone, leaving nothing for retesting.

7.4. A request to keep an aliquot longer is made to the laboratory head in writing, with the reason, and is listed in the freezer register.

7.5. Packaging samples are not divided; the tested sample itself is kept, retained in the same way for 90 days, on the shelf in the store room.

Before you test any milk or curd sample at the Shirwal chilling plant lab, pour off a portion into a sterile tube, cap it and label it with the lab number. That portion is the retained sample, and it is our only answer if the cooperative or the buyer challenges a result.

Each aliquot is frozen at -18 C and kept for 30 days after the result is reported, then thrown away in the yellow bag unless someone has asked in writing for it to be kept.

# Product Testing Laboratory Manual

## 1. Purpose

1.1. The Product Testing Laboratory is Quillfern's own small laboratory, on the mezzanine of the Bhosari hub. It opened in October 2025 to answer questions that the company used to send to outside laboratories at a cost of days and money: whether a cleaned surface is clean, whether a returned food pack is still sound, whether a new packaging design keeps a meal kit cold on a doorstep, and whether a component from a new supplier is as strong as its certificate says.

1.2. This manual says what the laboratory does, how samples reach it, how tests are run and reported, how the laboratory proves that its results can be trusted, and how it keeps its people safe. It is written for the laboratory's analysts, for the QA officers and engineers who send it samples, and for customers' auditors who want to know how a result was reached.

1.3. The laboratory is not accredited for regulatory testing. Results it reports are for Quillfern's own decisions and for customers who have agreed in writing to rely on them. Where a law or a customer requires an accredited result, the sample goes to an accredited outside laboratory, and this laboratory only prepares and ships it.

1.4. Revision 2 changes several test conditions and checking frequencies after the laboratory's first six months, and adds the section on comparison with other laboratories. Each changed section says what it replaced.

## 5. Picking what to look at

5.1. Most controls are tested by picking items from the period under review and checking that the control worked on each one. The number of items depends on how often the control operates, not on the size of the population.

5.2. For a control that operates monthly, attribute testing uses 25 items under random sampling; for one that operates daily or with every transaction, 40 items; for a quarterly control, all of the quarters in the period. A single exception in the items picked is reported, whatever its value.

5.3. For sampling, items are picked at random from a complete listing that the auditor has checked for completeness against a control total. Picking from a listing someone else filtered is not random, however it was produced.

5.4. The 2025 charter used smaller attribute samples; they were raised for this programme because two findings in the first year rested on too few items to persuade anyone. The method and the seed used for random selection are recorded in the working papers so that another auditor could pick the same items.

## 11. Following up actions

11.1. Every agreed action from every report goes into the actions register, with its owner, its due date and its finding's grade. The register is updated by the team on the first working day of each month from the evidence owners send in.

11.2. An action is closed only on evidence. An e-mail saying "done" is not evidence; a revised procedure, a changed system setting, a signed balance check or a trained-staff list is.

11.3. Overdue actions on high findings are listed by name in each quarterly report to the board, together with the owner's explanation. Overdue actions on medium findings are listed by count.

11.4. Each high finding is tested again by the team about six months after its action is closed, to confirm the fix has held. A fix that has not held reopens the finding at its original grade.

11.5. Owners may ask for one extension of an action date, in writing, before it falls due. A second extension needs the board's agreement.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The laboratory head reviews this manual every June and whenever a method, a piece of equipment or a customer requirement changes.

16.2. Each revision is explained to the analysts at a briefing, and each analyst signs that they have read it.

16.3. Suggestions for changes come from analysts, from the people who send samples and from customers' auditors. Each suggestion is answered in writing by the laboratory head within a month, whether or not it is taken up, and the answers are kept with the manual's revision file.

## 11. Closing out the contractor's list

11.1. As the tests proceed, the engineering lead keeps a single snag list of everything not yet right. Each item is graded A, meaning the room cannot hold product safely until it is fixed, or B, meaning the room can be used while it is fixed.

11.2. Practical completion is certified only when no A item remains open. Every B item must be closed within 30 days of that certificate, and the retention money held from the contractor is not released until the last one is.

11.3. The first Ludhiana build allowed longer, and three of its B items were still open when the retention was paid.

11.4. Each item carries its owner, the dates raised and closed, and the initials of the person who checked the closure. Items are closed on inspection, never on the contractor's word; the punch list is a record of what was seen, not of what was promised.

11.5. A B item still open on day 30 becomes an A item for the purpose of releasing money, though the room stays in use. Contractors who want their retention sooner close their snag items sooner, and argue with the punch grades in writing.

## Outstanding items

The contractor's snag list graded A and B. B items to be closed within 45 days of completion; the punch list is kept by the contractor.

## Completion

We certify practical completion only when no A item is open. Every B item must then be closed within 14 days of the certificate. The store is small and opens straight into a busy season, so the period is shorter than on our larger builds.

## 13. After handover

13.1. The contractor's defects liability period runs for twelve months from practical completion. Faults found in that period are reported to the contractor in writing by the engineering lead, and the contractor's response time is the one written in its contract.

13.2. The plant is serviced in its first year by the contractor who built it, under the contract, and from the second year by the company's approved service partner for refrigeration, unless the two are the same firm.

13.3. The engineering lead reviews the room's alarm history, energy use and defrost behaviour at three months and at twelve months after handover, and writes a short note of anything that needs changing.

13.4. A room that has been altered after handover, by moving racking, replacing an evaporator or changing doors, is treated as a new room for the tests that the change could affect.

## The list

Our engineer keeps one list of everything still wrong with the fit-out, walked with the contractor's site engineer every Friday. Each item is graded A, which stops the store taking stock, or B, which does not.

## Closing items

An item is closed when our engineer has seen the repair, never on the contractor's word. The contractor's own punch sheet is not accepted in place of ours.

## Defects

Faults found after completion are reported in writing and repaired within the contractor's defects period of twelve months.

## Money

Five per cent of the contract value is held back until the last snag is closed and signed. The contractor may ask for part of it to be released early only by a letter to the regional engineer.

## 14. Records

14.1. The signed commissioning record, the test sheets and the thermal images are kept for the life of the room and three years after it is demolished or converted.

14.2. Copies go to the site QA lead, who keeps them with the room's mapping studies, and to the site manager, who keeps them with the lease or the title documents.

14.3. Nothing in the record is rewritten after signing. A correction is a new sheet that refers to the old one and is signed in the same way.

## Envelope survey

Infrared survey after pull-down. A joint more than 5 C colder than the panel beside it is resealed. Thermography images saved by the contractor.

## 15. Review of this manual

15.1. The engineering lead reviews this manual after every new room is handed over, and at least once a year.

15.2. Contractors may suggest changes in writing; each suggestion gets a written answer.

## 10. Racking and the empty room

10.1. Racking is erected after the tightness and evacuation tests and before the temperature tests, so that the room is tested in the form in which it will be used. Racking erected later means testing again.

10.2. Racking is inspected and load-signed by the racking supplier, who fixes load notices to the end of every run. Nobody places a pallet on racking that does not carry its notice.

10.3. Evaporator air paths are checked against the racking layout. A rack run that blocks an evaporator's throw is moved before the room is accepted.

10.4. Sprinklers and smoke detection, where the room has them, are tested by the fire contractor and signed off separately. The commissioning record notes the fire contractor's certificate number but does not repeat its contents.

5.2. For a control that operates monthly, attribute testing uses 25 items under random sampling; for one that operates daily or with every transaction, 40 items; for a quarterly control, all of the quarters in the period. A single exception in the items picked is reported, whatever its value.

5.3. For sampling, items are picked at random from a complete listing that the auditor has checked for completeness against a control total. Picking from a listing someone else filtered is not random, however it was produced.

5.4. The 2025 charter used smaller attribute samples; they were raised for this programme because two findings in the first year rested on too few items to persuade anyone. The method and the seed used for random selection are recorded in the working papers so that another auditor could pick the same items.

## 12. Reporting results

12.1. Every result is checked by a second analyst against the raw data before it is reported. The checker signs the worksheet.

12.2. Reports go to the person who asked for the test, with a copy to the QA officer for the site concerned. They show the laboratory number, the sample, the method, the result, the date of testing and the name of the analyst.

12.3. A result outside the limit the requester gave is phoned through on the day, before the written report, and the call is recorded.

12.4. Reports state what was tested and what was found. They do not say whether stock should be released or destroyed; that decision belongs to QA.

12.5. A report that has to be corrected is reissued with a new revision number and a note of what changed. The old report is withdrawn, not deleted.

## 4. Samples arriving

4.1. Samples are received at the reception counter by an analyst, who checks them against the request form, labels each one with a laboratory number and records the condition and temperature on arrival.

4.2. Chilled samples arrive in a cooled box with a temperature indicator; frozen samples arrive in a frozen box. A sample that arrives warm, leaking or unlabelled is recorded as received in that condition and the requester is asked whether to test it anyway.

4.3. Samples are stored at their proper temperature in the laboratory's own fridges and freezers, which are separate from the hub's stores and carry their own loggers.

4.4. Food and packaging samples from customers belong to the customer. Nothing is used for anything other than the test requested, and nothing is eaten, taken home or given away.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The laboratory head reviews this manual every June and whenever a method, a piece of equipment or a customer requirement changes.

16.2. Each revision is explained to the analysts at a briefing, and each analyst signs that they have read it.

16.3. Suggestions for changes come from analysts, from the people who send samples and from customers' auditors. Each suggestion is answered in writing by the laboratory head within a month, whether or not it is taken up, and the answers are kept with the manual's revision file.

## 8. Storing components

8.1. Shippers, liners and paper components are stored in the ambient store at Kondhwa, on pallets, in the order they arrived. Nothing is stored against the outside walls.

8.2. Phase-change packs are stored and conditioned in the cold room on their own racks, by temperature, with chilled packs and frozen packs on separate racks clearly labelled.

8.3. Stock of each component is counted every Monday. The packaging engineer orders from the approved suppliers when stock falls to two weeks' use.

8.4. Components that have been damaged in storage are set aside and counted, not used to make up numbers.

## 12. Complaints about packaging

12.1. Complaints from Thali Box customers about packaging, such as a crushed box, a leaking pack or a warm kit, come to Quillfern through Thali Box's customer team. They are logged by customer service and passed to the packaging engineer the same day.

12.2. Each complaint is traced to the kit's order number, the components' lot numbers, the van and the delivery time. The packaging engineer writes a short finding within five working days.

12.3. Complaints are counted per thousand kits delivered and reviewed at the monthly meeting with Thali Box. A component whose complaint rate rises for two months running is reviewed with its supplier.

## 14. Changes and review

14.1. Changes to this book are proposed by either company in writing, tested under section 7, and agreed in writing by both before use.

14.2. The packaging engineer reviews the whole book each March with Thali Box, after the winter and before the summer, and issues a revision if anything changes.

14.3. Each revision lists its changes on its first page, with the reason for each.

## 14. Records

14.1. Request forms, worksheets, raw data, instrument printouts, reports and equipment records are kept for six years, and longer where a claim or a customer's contract needs them.

14.2. Records are made at the time, in ink or in the laboratory system, and corrected only by striking through and initialling.

14.3. Customers' auditors may see the records of tests on their own samples. They do not see other customers' records.

## Nagpur DC / NGP hub

Book Nagpur slots in Dockwise before 16:00 on the previous day. Pharma uses dock 4, dairy uses docks 1 and 2, and frozen food uses dock 5. The old Kalpa slot sync link on the left is broken and should not be used for new bookings.

No unloading is planned between 13:10 and 13:40 because the ammonia plant runs the daily defrost check. Late arrival goes to holding lane B, call shift lead, no automatic cancellation.

Pharma arrivals get 15 minutes grace. Dairy arrivals get 20 minutes grace. Frozen arrivals get 10 minutes grace because the freezer-to-reefer movement is shorter and more sensitive.

## 1. Nagpur DC, also written NGP hub

1.1. Book Nagpur slots in Dockwise before 15:00 on the previous day. The old
16:00 cut-off moved because the ammonia plant defrost window moved.

1.2. Dock assignment: pharma uses dock 4, dairy uses docks 1 and 2, frozen food
uses dock 5, and dry grocery uses dock 6. Dock 6 was added in January 2026 and
does not appear on the wiki page.

1.3. No unloading is planned between 12:40 and 13:20 for the daily ammonia plant
defrost check.

1.4. Late arrival is cancelled automatically in Dockwise after 20 minutes for
dairy and after 30 minutes for dry grocery. Pharma and frozen bookings are never
auto-cancelled; they go to holding lane B and the shift lead is called.

## Late arrivals

Late arrival goes to holding lane B, call shift lead, no automatic cancellation. If the slot is pharma critical, the shift lead must also check whether a red sleeve is ready before moving the vehicle to dock 4.

# Ammonia plant at Nagpur: levels, places and kit

## Alarm levels

- about 5 ppm — the smell is noticeable; not an alarm.
- Stage 1 — 25 ppm at any plant-room detector: amber beacon, the plant crew investigate, and dock 5 stops loading.
- Stage 2 — 150 ppm at any detector: site siren and full evacuation to M2.
- 300 ppm — immediately dangerous to life or health; nobody without a breathing set is anywhere near it.

## Reasons

Kalpa has local service staff within Nagpur city limits and has historically
replaced failed truck devices within one working day. The Nagpur base station is
already mounted and wired. Driver training material, customer report templates,
and the QA audit binder already use Kalpa screenshots. Switching all material
before vaccine season would create training risk.

The Kalpa quote is lower than Tessaline's first commercial quote. Tessaline
quoted Rs. 31.20 lakh for migration, device replacement, and API onboarding.
Tessaline also proposed 60-second polling and a richer API, but the API was not
available for our trial vehicles. Kalpa's five-minute polling is not ideal, but
it is known and accepted by current customer annexes.

The exit clause for Kalpa is acceptable only at contract end. Leaving early
would require six months of minimum recurring charges. This is not justified on
the evidence available in November 2023.

## Closing note

This event is the reason I am asking for two changes: faster pharma escalation
and a shorter vaccine high-duration trigger. If the telematics vendor changes,
the first acceptance test must prove night alerts reach Compliance-Red, not only
the DC manager.

I have deliberately left the rough timeline language in place because the audit
packet should show how the team understood the event on the day. Later SOP
revisions may be cleaner, but this note is the incident record, not a training
poster. Any future reader should compare it with the live SOP before using its
thresholds.

## Checks on the kit

The plant crew check each breathing set on the first day of the month and sign
the tag. Four tags hang in a row by the plant room door. A set whose cylinder
reads below full is swapped the same day. The room itself is inspected by the
crew lead before every Stage 1 test.

## Decision

Quillfern will renew Kalpa Fleet Systems for 36 months beginning 1 January 2024.
The renewal covers 147 owned reefers, 63 hired-truck devices during peak months,
and 38 fixed sensors across rooms and docks. The implementation and renewal
charge is Rs. 18.40 lakh. The recurring charge is Rs. 920 per active truck per
month and Rs. 310 per fixed sensor per month.

No split-vendor model will be used in 2024. IT will keep one support desk and
one monthly export from Kalpa. Fleet and QA will continue to use the KLP trip
number for audit packets.

| item | detail |
|---|---|
| plant charge | 1,800 kg of ammonia |

## Review trigger

The review trigger is intentionally narrow. Complaints about dashboard colour,
slow training, or ordinary device replacement do not count as major alert
failures. A review may still be started by the Managing Director, but this ADR
does not require one unless the patient-critical alert threshold above is met.

## Impact

The stock was not released on the morning route. BharatVac provided a stability
letter for part of the consignment after reviewing lot data. QA destroyed
13,200 vials and conditionally released 5,200 vials under BharatVac letter
BV-QA-2025-0312. Finance booked a write-off of Rs. 7.82 lakh for the destroyed
vials, packaging, and reverse logistics.

The customer notification was late. Under the incident practice then in use, we
treated customer notice as a same-day item after QA review. That is not
acceptable for patient critical stock. The revised procedure must require
customer notice within two hours after confirmation.

The incident also consumed most of the night shift's available quarantine space.
Two dairy returns were left in the outer holding lane while Q-3 was cleared for
the vaccine pallets. No dairy spoilage was confirmed, but the congestion made
the response slower and showed that pharma critical quarantine cannot depend on
moving unrelated stock at the last minute.

Customer service received three different numbers during the morning: 18,400
vials affected, 13,200 vials destroyed, and 5,200 vials conditionally released.
All three numbers were true in their own context, but the first customer draft
mixed them together. The final notice separated affected quantity, destroyed
quantity, and released quantity.

# Postmortem: Nagpur vaccine excursion, March 2025

This note was written on the afternoon of 12 March 2025 after the C2 cold room
temperature event at Nagpur DC. I am recording the timeline while memories are
fresh. Spelling and header cleanup can wait; evidence cannot.

| action | owner | due | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reduce vaccine high-duration trigger from 30 minutes to 15 minutes in SOP | Revathi Iyer | 14 Mar 2025 | closed in SOP rev 3.1 |

## Places

- **M1** — canteen lawn; fire muster only.
- **M2** — beside the windsock at gate 2; ammonia and fire muster.
- **windsocks** — one on the compressor house roof, one at gate 2.

## Summary

At approximately 02:16 on 12 March 2025, Kalpa probe KV-NGP-C2-07 began
reporting a high temperature in C2, the vaccine cold room at Nagpur DC. The
affected consignment was BharatVac order BV-4437, holding 18,400 vials of
rotavirus vaccine in lots ROTA-9A and ROTA-9B. The approved record showed the
room above +8.0 C for 66 minutes. At the time of the event, the SOP required a
QA call after 30 continuous minutes above +8.0 C for vaccines. The current
corrective action is to reduce that duration.

## Rejected options

Tessaline was rejected in 2023 because the API was not demonstrated on a live
Quillfern route, the commercial proposal required a larger first-year payment,
and the field-support rota for Nagpur was still being hired. The evaluation team
liked the one-minute polling and the proposed exception export, but decided that
those benefits were not enough to justify a complete change before the 2024
vaccine season.

A split model was also rejected. In that model, Kalpa would have stayed on
trucks while warehouse probes moved to Tessaline. IT objected that two source
systems would create audit confusion and double monthly reconciliation work.
Finance objected that the split model removed volume discounts from both
vendors.

## 4. Keeping the heat out

4.1. Inside every shipper sits a moulded expanded polystyrene box with a fitted lid, made of eps beads. It is the only insulation in the kit, and the whole thermal performance of the kit depends on it.

4.2. The liner's walls, base and lid are 30 mm thick, moulded at a density of 20 kg per cubic metre, and its lid fits with a lip that overlaps the walls by at least 10 mm.

4.3. The pilot used thinner walls to save space in the van and kits ran warm on afternoon doorsteps.

4.4. Liners with cracks, chipped lips or a lid that does not seat are rejected at the line. The polystyrene moulder replaces rejected units in the next delivery without charge.

4.5. Every eps liner carries the moulder's lot number on its base so that a complaint can be traced to a mould. The liner is the component customers are asked to return, under section 9.

RASIKA DAIRY SUBSCRIPTION BOX: THE INSULATED BOX AND ITS LID

For the morning milk and paneer subscription deliveries we make for Rasika Dairy in Kothrud and Karve Nagar.

WHAT THE BOX IS FOR
The box is left on the subscriber's doorstep before 07:00 and collected empty the next morning. It only has to keep milk cold for about three hours, so it is much lighter than a meal-kit box.

THE BOX
Each box is moulded expanded polystyrene, white, with a push-on lid. Walls, base and lid are 15 mm thick, at a density of 15 kg per cubic metre. The box carries Rasika's logo moulded into the lid.

CHECKING AT THE DEPOT
Boxes are checked every morning at loading. A box with a crack, a missing corner or a loose lid is set aside and returned to the moulder at the end of the month. The eps moulder replaces rejected boxes without charge.

CLEANING
Returned boxes are wiped inside and out with a food-safe sanitiser and air-dried before reuse. A box that smells of sour milk is not reused.

COUNTING
The depot counts boxes out and back every day. Subscribers who keep a box are reminded by Rasika's customer team, not by the delivery boy.

STORAGE
Clean boxes are stacked lid-on, ten high, on the racks by the loading door. Boxes are never stacked on the floor or in the sun.

Questions to the Erandwane depot office.

## 17. Who pays for what

17.1. Thali Box pays for every packaging component used in its kits, at the prices agreed in the annex, together with a handling charge per kit for assembly and a charge per kit delivered.

17.2. Quillfern pays for components it damages in storage or on the line, and for kits it has to rebuild because of a kitting error.

17.3. Components lost because customers do not return them are Thali Box's cost; the customer's forfeited amount goes to Thali Box, not to Quillfern.

17.4. Testing at the Product Testing Laboratory is charged to whichever company proposed the change being tested. Routine lot testing of incoming components is included in the handling charge.

17.5. Prices are reviewed every April, at the same time as the delivery charges.

## Returns

Customers pay a deposit on their first kit. Rs. 50, refunded if the box comes back within 7 days. Shippers that cannot be reused are recyclable.

## 9. Bringing the kit home again

9.1. The liner and the cold packs are expensive and can be used again; the outer shipper is collected too, so that customers are not left with a bulky box, even though it is recyclable. The programme asks every customer to hand the whole kit back, empty, at their next delivery or by pickup from the door.

9.2. Customers pay a refundable deposit of Rs. 80 on the first kit they order. The amount is refunded in full if the box comes back within 14 days of delivery, in a condition the hub can reuse, and is kept if it does not.

9.3. The pilot's deposit was smaller and gave less time, and too many boxes stayed in customers' homes.

9.4. Outer shippers that cannot be reused are flattened at the Bhosari hub and sent for recycling; they are recyclable board with water-based ink. Liners that cannot be reused are sent to the moulder, who takes them back as raw material.

9.5. Customer service handles questions about refunds; the van drivers do not discuss money at the door.

## Insulation

Moulded eps box, polystyrene walls 20 mm thick.

## 11. Vans and handling

11.1. Kits travel to customers in chilled vans running at +4 C. Kits are loaded in delivery order, stacked no more than five high, with heavier kits at the bottom.

11.2. Drivers carry kits by the handles moulded into the shipper, never by the strapping, and never throw a kit onto a doorstep.

11.3. A kit that is dropped from a height in the van or at the door is reported by the driver and checked at the next stop for damage. A kit with a cracked liner is taken back to Kondhwa.

11.4. Vans carry no other customer's goods while kits are on board.

# Thali Box pilot: pack note

Packaging used for the Thali Box meal-kit pilot from April 2025.

## Outer

Three-ply corrugated slotted box, tested by bct. Compression strength at least 300 kgf.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

# Ludhiana DC safety rules (opening issue)

Issued for the opening of Ludhiana DC.

## Collapse

The site has two defibrillator units, at the gate cabin and in the canteen. A first aider checks each aed once a month.

## 6. Defrost and the drain

6.1. Chilled units defrost four times a day for about 20 minutes each time.
Frozen units defrost every six hours. The controller log shows each defrost.

6.2. Defrost water runs out through a heated drain at the condenser end. The
drain outlet is kept clear of soil, leaves and plastic.

6.3. A short rise in air temperature during defrost is expected and is not a
fault. Stock temperature hardly moves.

6.4. A unit that ices up inside is reported to the duty phone. The customer's
staff do not chip ice from the evaporator.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

## 13. Records

13.1. The placement sheet, the service cards, the alarm log and the controller
logs are kept for three years, or seven where a temperature alarm was raised
during a pharma hire.

13.2. Controller logs are downloaded at every service visit and at the end of
every hire.

## 16. Records and review

16.1. The accident book, the near-miss cards, investigation reports, inspection records, survey results and training records are kept for at least ten years, or for longer where the law requires.

16.2. The safety officer reviews this manual every June with the safety council, and after any serious injury or dangerous occurrence on the site.

16.3. Each revision is explained at a briefing on every shift, and every person on site signs that they attended.

## 14. Near misses and hazards

14.1. A near miss is anything that could have hurt someone but did not. Near misses are reported on the yellow cards kept beside every clocking machine, or by telling the shift lead, who writes the card.

14.2. The safety officer reads every card within two working days, decides what action is needed and posts the result on the canteen board, without the reporter's name unless they asked for it to be shown.

14.3. A person who reports a near miss is thanked, not blamed. Shift leads who discourage reporting are themselves reported to the site manager.

14.4. The number of near-miss cards is reported to the safety council each month. A falling number is investigated as carefully as a rising one.

# Containerised Unit Operating Manual

How the engineering pool's containerised cold rooms are placed, powered,
started, used, moved and looked after. The units are hired out to customers who
need cold space where Quillfern has no building: hospitals running vaccination
campaigns, a dairy cooperative's collection centre in the flush season, a
programme that needs a small store in a city neighbourhood. The manual is for
the engineers who place and service the units and for the customer's people who
use them day to day.

## 5. Protective equipment

5.1. Safety shoes and high-visibility vests are worn everywhere outside the office, the canteen and the locker rooms. Hard hats are worn on the docks, in the yard and anywhere work is going on overhead.

5.2. Freezer suits, gloves, balaclavas and boots are issued to named people for work in the frozen block. They are not shared, and a suit that no longer closes properly is exchanged at Stores the same day.

5.3. Gloves for chilled-room work, chemical gloves for cleaning and face shields for any work with dry ice are kept on the racks beside the work, not in personal lockers.

5.4. Equipment that is damaged or worn out is handed in and replaced, never repaired with tape. Stores keeps a stock of every item in every size worn on the site.

5.5. A person who turns up without their protective equipment does not start work until it is found or replaced.

## 11. Cleaning

11.1. The customer's staff wipe the shelves and floor weekly with the cleaner
supplied by the pool. Water is never sprayed inside a unit.

11.2. A unit is deep-cleaned by the pool between every two hires and whenever a
spill has been reported.

11.3. Food and medicine are never in the same unit during one hire.

## 12. The customer's people

12.1. The customer names a lead for each unit. The lead is shown the door, the
controller display, the duty phone and the genset gauge at placement.

12.2. The lead keeps a simple sheet of who went in and when, and the sheet is
collected at each service visit.

12.3. Nobody under 18 goes into a unit.
