# Energy and Utilities Manual, Ludhiana DC

## 1. Purpose and reach

1.1. Ludhiana DC is the first Quillfern building north of the Vindhyas built from the ground up for cold storage, and the first one that pays for its own electricity at an industrial tariff from the day it opened. It stands on the Ladhowal bypass, on a plot the company owns outright, with a chilled block, a frozen block, a small ambient store and a two-storey office facing the gate.

1.2. This manual says how the building gets its power and water, how those supplies are protected, how they are measured, and who answers when one of them fails. It is written for the engineering team on site, for the shift leads who are the first to notice when something is wrong, and for Finance, which pays the bills and wants to know why they move.

1.3. The manual sets no product temperature and changes no quality rule. When a utility fails and stock is at risk, the stock is handled under the company procedures for excursions and quarantine, and this manual only says how to get the plant running again.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the utilities note written while the building was being commissioned in 2025. That note was useful at the time but several of its figures were guesses made before the site had run through a Punjab summer and a Punjab winter. Where a figure changed, the section that carries it says so.

1.5. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns this manual. Harpreet Bains, the electrical supervisor, owns the substation, the switch room and the earthing. The two of them sign every change to the plant that this manual covers, and neither signs alone.

1.6. Copies are kept in the engineering office, in the switch room and at the gate cabin. A copy found anywhere else, including a photograph on a personal phone, is out of date by assumption.

## 8. Frozen breeding stock

8.1. Vetrix sells frozen bull semen to dairy cooperatives and artificial insemination centres. The doses are stored and carried in LN2 at about -196 C and must never warm, even briefly.

8.2. Quillfern holds Vetrix's straws in eight storage dewar units in a separate locked room at Ludhiana DC, and carries them to customers in smaller transport units of the same kind.

8.3. Each storage dewar is topped up with LN2 every 10 days, and its level is measured with a dipstick every day. The level must never fall below 40 per cent of the unit's capacity; a reading below that is topped up the same day and reported to Vetrix.

8.4. LN2 is supplied by Vetrix's approved gas supplier under Vetrix's contract. Quillfern handles it under its own safety rules for cryogenic liquids, which require face shields, cryogenic gloves and a ventilated room.

8.5. Transport units are charged by Quillfern staff trained for the purpose, and their levels are recorded at dispatch and at delivery. Straws are never handled outside a unit.

8.6. In the first contract year the units were topped up every 14 days, and two readings fell below the minimum before a top-up arrived.

## 7. Metering and the monthly energy review

7.1. Every feeder carries its own energy meter, read automatically every fifteen minutes into the building management system and printed as a daily sheet that the morning shift lead initials.

7.2. On the fifth working day of each month the engineering lead holds the energy review with the electrical supervisor, the site manager and someone from Finance. The review looks at units consumed by each feeder, the maximum demand recorded by the utility meter, diesel used, water drawn and the cost of each.

7.3. The site's own meter readings are compared with the utility's bill before the bill is paid. A difference of more than one per cent between the two is raised with the utility in writing, with the site's readings attached, and the bill is paid under protest if the due date arrives before the answer.

7.4. Consumption is expressed per pallet position occupied, not per square metre, because a half-empty building that costs the same to run is a commercial problem, not an engineering one. The figure is tracked month by month on a chart in the engineering office.

7.5. The review ends with a short list of actions, each with an owner and a date. Actions carried over from the previous month are read out first.

7.6. Finance receives the review note within three working days. It is the only document Finance uses to explain the electricity line in the site's monthly accounts.

# Ludhiana DC utilities note (commissioning issue)

Written while Ludhiana DC was being commissioned, so that the first shift leads and the electrical supervisor had something to work to before a full manual existed.

## 20. If Ludhiana cannot work

20.1. Quillfern keeps a continuity plan for the account, reviewed with Vetrix each year at the July meeting of senior managers. It names the site that would hold Vetrix's chilled stock if Ludhiana DC could not, the vehicles that would carry it there, and the order in which deliveries would be restarted.

20.2. If Ludhiana DC loses power for longer than its generators can cover, or cannot be reached because of flooding or civil disturbance, the account manager tells Vetrix's supply chain manager within one hour of the decision to invoke the plan, and twice a day after that until normal working resumes.

20.3. Measures in this schedule are suspended for the days on which the plan is in force, provided Quillfern followed the plan. Days on which it did not follow the plan are measured as normal.

20.4. The plan is tested once a year by a desk exercise with Vetrix's team, and the lessons are written into the next version.

7.1. Quillfern is liable for loss of or damage to the customer's products while
in its care, subject to the limits below and to section 5.4.

7.2. For any single pallet the ceiling is Rs. 25,000, and the total for a contract year is Rs. 40 lakh.

7.3. Amendment 2 raised it from Rs. 18,000 with effect from 1 April 2026. The
contract-year total was not changed.

7.4. Neither party is liable to the other for lost profit or for loss of
business.

7.5. A claim is made in writing within 30 days of the event, with photographs
and the count records.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 5. The main promise

5.1. Quillfern's main promise is that orders arrive at the right place, inside the agreed delivery window, with the right items in the right quantities. Each order meets all of those or it does not; there is no partial credit.

5.2. The share of orders that meet them in a calendar month must be at least 97 per cent. For each full percentage point by which a month falls below that, Vetrix receives a service credit of 2 per cent of that month's handling invoice, up to a maximum of 10 per cent.

5.3. In the first contract year the target was 95 per cent, with the same credit rate.

5.4. An order is excluded from the otif count only where the failure was caused by Vetrix, by the receiving party, or by an event outside Quillfern's control listed in the contract, reported within one working day.

5.5. A shortfall in two consecutive months needs a written recovery plan from Quillfern, whatever the credit paid; a shortfall in three brings the otif figure to the half-yearly meeting of senior managers.

5.6. Credits are deducted from the next invoice, not paid in cash.

## Delivery promise

Orders must arrive complete, undamaged and inside the delivery window. The otif target is a monthly figure. At least 95 per cent of orders each month must meet it. For each full point of shortfall below that, Vetrix receives a credit of 2 per cent of the month's handling invoice.

## 7. Every month on paper

7.1. Quillfern sends Vetrix a monthly report of every measure in this schedule, with the underlying order list attached, so that Vetrix's team can check any figure for itself.

7.2. The report reaches Vetrix by the 7th working day of the following month. It includes a one-page scorecard of the month's measures against target, the service credits due, the excursions and their status, and the returns received at the Bhosari hub.

7.3. In the first contract year the report was due by the 10th working day, which left too little time to discuss it at the monthly review.

7.4. Each kpi in the report is defined in this schedule; Quillfern does not change a definition without Vetrix's written agreement.

7.5. The report is prepared by the account manager and checked by Finance before it is sent. The account manager signs it.

7.6. A kpi missed in the month carries a short note of the cause and the action taken, written in plain language, and the same note is copied to the scorecard archive.

## What RF-118 may carry

RF-118 is a chilled asset. It may carry vaccines, insulin, milk and paneer. It
must not be loaded with frozen food: the body cannot hold the frozen target and
the frozen profile belongs to [RF-120](18-reefer-RF-120-asset-file.md).

This file sets no temperature limit of its own. Every limit and every excursion
duration for the products RF-118 carries is in
[the Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md), and
the sensor configuration is documented in
[the legacy sensor threshold file](02-sensor-thresholds.yaml). Where this file
and the SOP appear to differ, the SOP wins.

## What RF-119 may carry

RF-119 runs the Guwahati dairy and chilled-grocery circuit. Milk and paneer are
its normal load.

RF-119 may carry vaccines or insulin **only** inside a validated passive
shipper, because the body has no cradle and no second compartment to separate
pharma from dairy stock. A passive shipper is hired per trip and the charge is a
line on [the H2 2026 rate card](12-rate-card-2026-h2.md); Fleet Control raises
the hire request, not the customer service agent. Without a shipper, RF-119 is
refused for pharma critical stock whatever the urgency, and
[the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy](08-driver-hours-and-safety-policy.md)
clause 1.3 is the reason no manager may overrule that at the gate.

The temperature limits for whatever RF-119 carries are set by
[the Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md). This
file sets none.

## 9. Cold work

9.1. The frozen block at Ludhiana runs at -25 C, colder than most of the company's freezers, and the body loses heat there faster than people expect. Cold slows thinking before it slows hands, which is why the rules below do not depend on how anyone feels.

9.2. Nobody works inside the frozen block for longer than 40 minutes at a stretch, even in a full freezer suit. A 20-minute rewarming break in the canteen or the warm room follows each stretch, with a hot drink available.

9.3. The shift lead keeps the break board for the frozen block and moves names on it; the workers do not keep their own time.

9.4. Signs of hypothermia, such as uncontrolled shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness or confusion, mean the person leaves the cold at once with a colleague and is checked by a first aider. A person who has shown those signs does not go back into the cold that shift.

9.5. In 2025 the stretch was an hour and the rewarming break fifteen minutes, and two cases of mild hypothermia followed; both were changed after the first winter.

## 16. Leaving Quillfern

16.1. Leavers hand back every device, battery and charger issued to them by name, and the shift lead signs the asset register to show it was received. HR does not issue the leaving papers until the register is signed.

16.2. Sometimes a person who quits keeps their scanner, by accident or otherwise. Anything not returned within two working days of the last shift is recovered from the final settlement at Rs. 18,500 per K7 and Rs. 6,200 per LP-40. The device is then locked and wiped from Fernguard.

16.3. A device returned after the recovery is made is refunded at the same rate, less any repair cost.

16.4. Agency staff never hold a named device, so nothing is recovered from their agencies; their day credentials simply lapse.

16.5. Trainees who leave the Waluj programme early hand their device back to the trainer the same day.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

## 3. First days on site

3.1. Every new person, including agency staff and contractors' workers, attends the site induction before starting work. The induction lasts about two hours and covers the site layout, the emergency alarm and assembly point, the vehicle routes, the cold rooms, the protective equipment and how to report a hazard.

3.2. New staff spend their first week with a named buddy who has worked on the site for at least six months. They do not work alone in a cold room, operate a forklift or work on the docks without the buddy until their shift lead has signed them off.

3.3. Contractors' workers are inducted on their first visit and carry an induction card. The card is checked at the gate on every later visit.

3.4. Visitors are escorted at all times and are given a short safety briefing at the gate. They do not enter the cold rooms, the plant room or the yard without protective equipment and an escort.

## 7. When one goes missing

7.1. A lost or stolen scanner is reported to the IT desk within one hour of being missed, by the user or the shift lead, with the asset number and where it was last seen.

7.2. The desk locks the device from Fernguard as soon as the report arrives. A locked K7 shows a message asking the finder to hand it to security.

7.3. If it has not turned up 24 hours after the report, Fernguard wipes it remotely and it is struck off the register. A device found after it has been wiped goes back to the desk to be rebuilt; it is never simply switched back on.

7.4. Losing a device is not in itself a disciplinary matter. Failing to report a loss, or reporting it late, is.

7.5. A theft is also reported to security and, where the site manager decides, to the police. The report number is written in the register.

## 14. Photographs and personal data

14.1. Photographs taken on a K7 are of stock, seals, labels, damage and equipment. They do not include people's faces where it can be helped, and never include a customer's staff without their agreement.

14.2. Photographs are uploaded to the document system against the job they belong to and deleted from the device.

14.3. Staff do not photograph a K7's screen with their own phones to send a picture to someone else.

14.4. Personal data about staff — names, logins and shift times — is visible only to the shift lead, the IT desk and HR.

14.5. A person who wants to know what Fernguard holds about them asks HR in writing.

14.6. Login records are not used to measure how fast a person picks. Pick rates come from the warehouse system and are discussed with the person, not posted.

## 15. Repairs

15.1. All repairs go through the IT desk. The desk keeps a small stock of spare K7s and LP-40s at each site, so that a repair never leaves a rack short.

15.2. Devices are sent to the Korvex service centre in a padded case with a repair note. Nobody opens a device on site.

15.3. A repaired device is rebuilt from Fernguard before it is reissued.

15.4. A device that has been repaired three times in a year is retired.

15.5. The desk reports device faults by type every quarter to the site managers, so that a site whose scanners keep breaking can look at how they are used.

15.6. Repair costs are charged to the site's cost centre. A site that pays for many repairs is not punished for it; it is asked what is going on.

## 16. Records and review

16.1. The accident book, the near-miss cards, investigation reports, inspection records, survey results and training records are kept for at least ten years, or for longer where the law requires.

16.2. The safety officer reviews this manual every June with the safety council, and after any serious injury or dangerous occurrence on the site.

16.3. Each revision is explained at a briefing on every shift, and every person on site signs that they attended.

## 8. Agreeing the figures with the customer

8.1. A customer who returns goods usually raises a debit note against Quillfern or against its own supplier, and the reconciliation of that note with what the hub received is the last job on any return.

8.2. Customer service compares each debit note with the hub's receipt records within 5 working days of the note arriving. Any difference of more than 2 per cent in quantity or value goes to the account manager, who settles it with the customer before a credit note is raised.

8.3. A smaller discrepancy is settled by customer service from the hub's records, which are the count of record.

8.4. The reconciliation is kept with the return number in the returns system, so that an auditor can follow one return from the collection note to the credit note without asking anyone.

8.5. A discrepancy caused by a count error at collection is reported to Fleet Control as a driver coaching matter, not as a dispute with the customer.

## Debit notes

Customer service completes the reconciliation of each debit note with the hub's records within 10 working days. Any discrepancy is recorded; a difference above 5 per cent goes to the account manager.

## 18. Vetrix's own checks

18.1. Vetrix may audit the handling of its stock at Ludhiana DC and at the Bhosari hub on ten working days' notice, and at shorter notice where it has a specific cause. The account manager arranges the visit and the site's QA lead hosts it.

18.2. Vetrix's auditors see the storage areas, the records of its own stock, the temperature records of the rooms holding it and the training records of staff who handle it. They do not see other customers' stock or records.

18.3. Findings are answered by Quillfern within 20 working days with a corrective action, an owner and a date, and tracked at the monthly review until closed.

18.4. Vetrix may also send a representative to observe a delivery to a government store or a cooperative, by arrangement with the account manager. The representative travels in Vetrix's own vehicle, not in Quillfern's.

## 7. Every month on paper

7.1. Quillfern sends Vetrix a monthly report of every measure in this schedule, with the underlying order list attached, so that Vetrix's team can check any figure for itself.

7.2. The report reaches Vetrix by the 7th working day of the following month. It includes a one-page scorecard of the month's measures against target, the service credits due, the excursions and their status, and the returns received at the Bhosari hub.

7.3. In the first contract year the report was due by the 10th working day, which left too little time to discuss it at the monthly review.

7.4. Each kpi in the report is defined in this schedule; Quillfern does not change a definition without Vetrix's written agreement.

7.5. The report is prepared by the account manager and checked by Finance before it is sent. The account manager signs it.

7.6. A kpi missed in the month carries a short note of the cause and the action taken, written in plain language, and the same note is copied to the scorecard archive.

## 20. If Ludhiana cannot work

20.1. Quillfern keeps a continuity plan for the account, reviewed with Vetrix each year at the July meeting of senior managers. It names the site that would hold Vetrix's chilled stock if Ludhiana DC could not, the vehicles that would carry it there, and the order in which deliveries would be restarted.

20.2. If Ludhiana DC loses power for longer than its generators can cover, or cannot be reached because of flooding or civil disturbance, the account manager tells Vetrix's supply chain manager within one hour of the decision to invoke the plan, and twice a day after that until normal working resumes.

20.3. Measures in this schedule are suspended for the days on which the plan is in force, provided Quillfern followed the plan. Days on which it did not follow the plan are measured as normal.

20.4. The plan is tested once a year by a desk exercise with Vetrix's team, and the lessons are written into the next version.

## 12. People and training

12.1. Everyone who handles returns at the hub completes the company induction and the hub's own half-day course on receiving, labelling and the returns system before handling stock alone.

12.2. The QA officers on duty at Bhosari are trained by the QA function and hold the same authority as QA officers at any other site. They do not take instructions on pharmaceutical decisions from the hub manager or from account managers.

12.3. Receiving clerks are trained to say "I'll check and come back to you" to drivers and customers who ask what will happen to returned goods. The answer comes from customer service.

12.4. Agency staff may count and move cartons but may not scan them into the returns system or judge them.

12.5. Training is refreshed every year and whenever this manual changes.

## 15. Contacts

15.1. Day-to-day contacts on both sides, with their phone numbers and e-mail addresses, are listed in the contact annex, which the account manager updates whenever someone changes role.

15.2. Escalation runs from the account manager to Quillfern's customer service lead and then to the operations head. On Vetrix's side it runs from the supply chain manager to the head of supply chain.

15.3. Excursion notices go to Vetrix's named quality contact, with a copy to the supply chain manager, at any hour.

## 14. Records

14.1. The returns system holds the collection note, receipt scans, photographs, judgements, temperature records, owner instructions, destruction certificates and reconciliations for each return number.

14.2. Records are kept for eight years for pharmaceutical returns and for three years for everything else, and longer where a claim, a dispute or an audit finding concerns them.

14.3. Paper collection notes are scanned on the day of receipt and the paper is archived by month.

14.4. Nothing in the returns system is deleted. A wrong entry is corrected by a new entry that refers to it, with the name of the person correcting and the reason.

## Withdrawn batches

Recalled stock is held in bay R-2 under strict segregation and counted weekly. If the customer has given no instruction after 60 days, the account manager writes to the customer.

## 2. Conditional release of pharma stock

2.1. Before a conditional release QA calculates the Stability Budget Remaining (SBR): the minutes above +8.0 C that the customer's stability letter allows for the lot, minus the minutes already used in this and every earlier excursion on the same lot.

2.2. A lot with an SBR below 30 minutes is not conditionally released. It is held pending external decision.

2.3. The SBR and the letter reference are written on QCL-F-31.

# Quillfern Cold Chain Glossary

Plain meanings for expressions used on site. Short forms are defined in the document that uses them, never here, so an expression below appears in its long form only.

back-to-cold — the moment a staged pallet crosses back over the cold-room threshold; staging time stops here.
chlorine contact time — the minutes a sanitising solution must stay wet on a reefer floor before rinsing; wiping it dry early starts the count again.
dead zone — a stretch of road where the telematics unit cannot report; the USB logger covers it and the gap is recorded as missing, never filled in.
door open minutes — the total minutes a cold-room or reefer door stood open in one shift, summed from the door sensor; a measure of load, not a fault.
holding lane B — the covered waiting lane at Nagpur for pharma and frozen vehicles that miss their dock time; nothing is unloaded there.
mean kinetic temperature — the single steady temperature that would give stock the same total heat stress as the uneven record it actually saw; stability letters are written against it, not against the average.
pre-cool hold time — the minutes an empty reefer body is held at loading temperature, doors shut, before the first pallet goes in.
probe grid — the layout of loggers used when a room is mapped; each position is named by rack, bay and height, such as A1-high.
relief point — a named fuel plaza or rest area on a qualified route where a relief driver or a mobile service van can meet the vehicle.
seal watch — time a driver spends guarding a sealed vehicle; it is duty time and never counts as rest.
shipper conditioning time — the hours a passive shipper's gel packs must sit at their set temperature before the shipper may leave with stock.
stability budget remaining — the minutes above the high limit that a customer's stability letter still allows for one lot, once every earlier excursion on that lot is subtracted.
warm pallet — night-shift name for a pallet whose logger has alarmed but whose excursion QA has not yet confirmed; it is handled as quarantine stock until QA decides.
white tag — the RELEASED tag fixed beside a red hold tag when QA lets stock out of quarantine; the red tag stays on.

## 6. Investigation record

6.1. QA opens an investigation in QCL-F-17 before the end of the same shift. The
record must contain the sensor source, product owner, SKU, batch or lot number,
route, room, dock, seal number, driver name when applicable, and first staff
member who observed the event.

6.2. The investigator shall build a minute-level timeline from the approved
temperature record, door log, dock schedule, driver call log, maintenance ticket,
and shift handover note. Missing pieces must be listed as missing; do not fill
them with assumptions.

6.3. Where records conflict, use the source hierarchy in section 3 and explain
the conflict. A convenient record is not a better record.

6.4. For pharma critical stock, QA must ask the customer for a stability letter
before release when the product was above the high limit or below the low limit
for any confirmed duration.

6.5. The investigation shall name one of four dispositions: release, conditional
release, hold pending external decision, or destroy. Finance may record value
only after QA records the disposition.

## 5. Notifications

5.1. Pharma critical stock means vaccines, insulin, and any medicine named by a
customer as patient critical. The customer must be notified within 2 hours of a
confirmed pharma critical excursion.

5.2. Dairy customers must be notified by the next scheduled customer service
check-in unless spoilage is visible, odour is present, or the temperature is
above +8.0 C. In those cases customer service must notify within 4 hours.

5.3. Frozen-food restaurant chains must receive an exception notice by the end of
the business day when the excursion is confirmed. If the vehicle is still on the
road, Fleet Control must also call the receiving kitchen.

5.4. Internal escalation for all pharma critical events goes to Compliance-Red,
the DC manager, Fleet Control if a truck is involved, and Finance if stock is
likely to be destroyed.

5.5. Customer notice must say "temperature excursion under investigation" until
QA approves a final wording. Staff must not promise release, replacement credit,
or insurance recovery in the first notice.

## 1. Release

1.1. Release is recorded on form QCL-F-31 and signed by the QA investigator and a second QA officer who did not investigate the case.

1.2. A white RELEASED tag is fixed beside the red hold tag. The red hold tag is never removed; both stay on the stock until it leaves the site.

1.3. Stock is not released between 22:00 and 06:00, whatever the dispatch plan says. The earliest release of the day is at 06:00.

1.4. Released quantity is counted twice by two people and entered separately from any destroyed quantity.

# Quarantine Stock Release and Return Procedure

How stock leaves quarantine bays Q-3 (Nagpur), Q-G2 (Guwahati) and Q-C1 (Coimbatore) after QA has recorded a disposition under clause 6.5 of the [Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md). Destroyed stock does not leave by this procedure; section 7 of that SOP governs it.

## 10. Closure

10.1. The QA head or nominated deputy closes pharma critical investigations. The
DC manager may close dairy and frozen investigations only after QA records the
disposition.

10.2. Corrective and preventive actions must have an owner, a due date, and
evidence of completion. "Discussed on call" is not completion evidence.

10.3. Training actions shall be assigned by role, not by name alone, so that new
staff receive the same correction.

10.4. The case file must be kept for seven years for pharma critical stock and
three years for food stock.

## 3. How long stock may sit

3.1. Quarantine Dwell Limit (QDL) is the time stock may stay in quarantine after the excursion is confirmed before the account manager must escalate to the customer's quality head.

| product class | QDL |
|---|---|
| pharma critical | 72 hours |

3.2. Reaching the QDL does not release anything. It starts an escalation; the stock stays where it is.

## 2. The work

2.1. Quillfern collects the customer's frozen products from the Chakan factory,
stores them and delivers them to restaurants, caterers and retailers in Pune
and Mumbai.

2.2. Pune deliveries go out from Quillfern's own stock. Mumbai-bound stock is
cross-docked at Quillfern's Bhiwandi site and goes out on the next morning's
vans.

2.3. Call-off times for Mumbai deliveries are those printed in the site handbook of the cross-dock that ships them.

2.4. Waiting charges on the customer's own vehicles at the cross-dock are billed at the site's published rate less 20 per cent.

2.5. Pallets are exchanged one for one at the cross-dock. Exchange units that arrive unfit on the customer's own vehicles are charged at the site figure, with no discount.

2.6. Quillfern does not sell, promote or price the customer's products and does
not take orders from the customer's buyers directly.

## 16. Summer and monsoon

16.1. Pune's hottest weeks fall in April and May, when afternoon doorsteps in the eastern suburbs reach well above 40 C. In those weeks the kitting room adds a reflective paper sleeve between the shipper and the liner for kits on afternoon delivery windows, and the delivery windows themselves are shortened by Thali Box.

16.2. In the monsoon the danger is wet board rather than heat. Shippers are kept under cover from the kitting room to the van, and van drivers carry a supply of plastic rain covers for kits that must be left in an open porch. The cover is collected with the empty box.

16.3. Mumbai deliveries face humidity all year. Shippers for Mumbai are drawn from the driest stock in the store and are not stored at Kondhwa for longer than four weeks.

16.4. The packaging engineer reviews the complaint log each June and each October to see whether the season's precautions worked, and changes them for the next year if they did not.

## 9. Bringing the kit home again

9.1. The liner and the cold packs are expensive and can be used again; the outer shipper is collected too, so that customers are not left with a bulky box, even though it is recyclable. The programme asks every customer to hand the whole kit back, empty, at their next delivery or by pickup from the door.

9.2. Customers pay a refundable deposit of Rs. 80 on the first kit they order. The amount is refunded in full if the box comes back within 14 days of delivery, in a condition the hub can reuse, and is kept if it does not.

9.3. The pilot's deposit was smaller and gave less time, and too many boxes stayed in customers' homes.

9.4. Outer shippers that cannot be reused are flattened at the Bhosari hub and sent for recycling; they are recyclable board with water-based ink. Liners that cannot be reused are sent to the moulder, who takes them back as raw material.

9.5. Customer service handles questions about refunds; the van drivers do not discuss money at the door.

## 12. Complaints about packaging

12.1. Complaints from Thali Box customers about packaging, such as a crushed box, a leaking pack or a warm kit, come to Quillfern through Thali Box's customer team. They are logged by customer service and passed to the packaging engineer the same day.

12.2. Each complaint is traced to the kit's order number, the components' lot numbers, the van and the delivery time. The packaging engineer writes a short finding within five working days.

12.3. Complaints are counted per thousand kits delivered and reviewed at the monthly meeting with Thali Box. A component whose complaint rate rises for two months running is reviewed with its supplier.

## 11. Vans and handling

11.1. Kits travel to customers in chilled vans running at +4 C. Kits are loaded in delivery order, stacked no more than five high, with heavier kits at the bottom.

11.2. Drivers carry kits by the handles moulded into the shipper, never by the strapping, and never throw a kit onto a doorstep.

11.3. A kit that is dropped from a height in the van or at the door is reported by the driver and checked at the next stop for damage. A kit with a cracked liner is taken back to Kondhwa.

11.4. Vans carry no other customer's goods while kits are on board.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

## 15. Review of this handbook

15.1. The site manager reviews this handbook every June and after any serious
incident, audit finding or change to the building.

15.2. Revision 3 of June 2026 recorded the new apron free window, the larger cell
and the earlier order cut-off, and moved the genset rules into their own
section.

15.3. Suggestions from staff go to the site manager at any time. Each one is
answered, whether or not it is taken up.

15.4. A revised handbook replaces every earlier copy in the office, the guard
cabin and the canteen on the day it is issued.

## 8. Price movement

8.1. Quillfern's charges are those in the schedule of rates signed with the
agreement, as moved under this section.

8.2. Rates move once a year on 1 April, by no more than the change in the wholesale price index over the previous twelve months plus two points.

8.3. Quillfern sends the new rates by 1 March. The customer may ask for the
working behind them and Quillfern will show it.

8.4. Fuel is not part of the rates. A fuel surcharge applies to transport on
Quillfern's standard terms in force on the day of travel.

## 9. Paperwork after the month

9.1. Quillfern invoices monthly, within five working days of the month's end,
with one invoice for storage and one for transport.

9.2. Since Amendment 1 of 1 October 2025 the customer settles each invoice within 45 days of its date; the original agreement allowed 60.

9.3. Late payment carries interest at 1.25 per cent a month on the overdue
amount.

9.4. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days of the invoice. The undisputed
part of an invoice is paid on time whatever the dispute.

# Consolidated Service Terms, Contract CN-31

The terms on which Quillfern Cold Logistics Pvt. Ltd. stores and delivers frozen
products for Saptagiri Foods Pvt. Ltd., as they stand after the two amendments.
This consolidation is prepared by Finance for the people who run the account. It
replaces nothing; the signed agreement and its amendments remain the legal
record, and where this text and the signed record differ, the signed record
applies.

## 13. Audit and records

13.1. The customer may audit the records about its own stock twice a year on
ten working days' notice.

13.2. Records are kept for three years after the end of the agreement.

## 11. Running the relationship

11.1. The account manager and Vetrix's supply chain manager hold an operations review on the second Tuesday of every month, by video call or in person at Ludhiana. The review goes through the monthly report, open excursions, returns, upcoming promotions and any problems either side has seen.

11.2. A steering group of senior people from both companies meets twice a year, in January and July. Quillfern sends its operations head and the account manager; Vetrix sends its head of supply chain and its head of quality. The group sets priorities for the next six months and settles anything the monthly review could not.

11.3. In the first contract year the steering group met once, in October, which both companies agreed at renewal was too seldom.

11.4. Minutes of every meeting are written by the account manager, agreed by both sides within a week, and kept with the contract file.

11.5. The governance meetings are the only place where the measures, the credits or this schedule are changed. An agreement made on a phone call between two managers is not a change until it has been through them, and the record of governance decisions is attached to this schedule.

## Meetings

Monthly operations review. A steering group of senior managers is set up. It meets once a year, in October. Changes to this schedule are made only through these governance meetings.

## 3. The calendar

3.1. The apprenticeship runs as one continuous programme with no break between the classroom and the floor. Months one to six are mostly in the workshop; months seven onwards are mostly on site, with a day a week back at Waluj.

3.2. From the January 2026 intake the programme lasts 18 months; the 2024 and 2025 intakes served 24. The shorter programme was possible because the workshop now has its own reefer body, cold room and generator, so that practical work no longer waits for a site to lend equipment.

3.3. Apprentices join in two intakes a year, so that there is always a senior group on site while a junior group is in the workshop. Each intake opens on the first working day of January or July and takes twelve trainees, no more. A thirteenth applicant who passes is offered the next intake rather than squeezed in.

3.4. Public holidays follow the Maharashtra list for apprentices at Waluj and the local list for apprentices placed at a site.

3.5. An apprentice who is ill for more than four weeks in a row may move to the next intake and pick up from the module they left.

## 5. Money

5.1. Every apprentice is paid a monthly stipend, not a wage, and it rises once, when the apprentice moves from the workshop to the floor. Pay is credited to the apprentice's own bank account on the last working day of the month.

5.2. The stipend is Rs. 14,000 a month for months one to six and Rs. 16,500 from month seven; the 2025 outline gave a flat Rs. 12,000. The rise recognises that floor months are longer and often away from home.

5.3. Apprentices placed at a site away from Waluj receive a lodging allowance and their travel to the site and back at the start and end of the placement. The allowance is set by the site and paid with the stipend.

5.4. Overtime is not paid to apprentices, because apprentices do not work overtime. An apprentice kept beyond the shift by an emergency is given the time back the next day.

5.5. No apprentice is bonded. Nobody repays anything for leaving the programme early or for taking a job elsewhere after it, and nobody is asked to sign a promise to stay.

## 13. Changing this schedule

13.1. Either company may propose a change to this schedule in writing. A proposed change is discussed at the next monthly review and decided by the senior group or, between its meetings, by written agreement of the account manager and Vetrix's head of supply chain.

13.2. A change takes effect from the first day of the month after it is agreed, never backwards.

13.3. Each revision of this schedule carries a table of changes on its last page.

## 17. Changes to this curriculum

17.1. Revision 1 (January 2025) set out the programme for the second intake. Revision 2 (June 2026) shortened the programme, raised the stipend in the floor months and set the ratio on live equipment after the first group completed.

17.2. The engineering pool lead reviews the curriculum each May with the workshop staff and two site managers.

17.3. Apprentices and mentors are asked at the end of each module what should change, and their answers are read at the review.

## 16. Welfare

16.1. Apprentices are young and often away from home for the first time. Each intake has a welfare contact at Waluj, a member of the workshop staff who is not a trainer.

16.2. Apprentices may raise anything with the welfare contact — homesickness, money, a problem at the lodging, a problem with a colleague — in confidence.

16.3. The lodging used at each site is visited by the welfare contact before the first apprentice moves in.

16.4. Bullying, ragging or initiation rituals are not tolerated, on site or at the workshop, and are dealt with under the company's discipline rules.

16.5. Apprentices are paid their stipend during approved sick leave for up to four weeks.

## 12. Invoicing

12.1. Quillfern invoices Vetrix monthly in arrears, with separate invoices for storage, handling and transport, within five working days of the month's end.

12.2. Service credits appear as a separate line on the next handling invoice, with a reference to the month and the measure that earned them.

12.3. Vetrix pays each invoice within 45 days of its date. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days; the undisputed part is paid on time.

## Delivery promise

Orders must arrive complete, undamaged and inside the delivery window. The otif target is a monthly figure. At least 95 per cent of orders each month must meet it. For each full point of shortfall below that, Vetrix receives a credit of 2 per cent of the month's handling invoice.

## 14. Ending the contract

14.1. Either company may end the contract by giving six months' written notice, or at once for a serious breach not put right within 30 days of a written demand.

14.2. On ending, Quillfern hands over Vetrix's stock and records to Vetrix or to a new provider named by Vetrix, in an orderly way agreed between the two companies, and continues to meet this schedule until the last stock has left.

14.3. Frozen breeding stock is handed over unit by unit, with the receiving party's trained staff present, and each unit's level is recorded on handover.

## Monthly report

Each kpi is defined in this schedule. The report and its one-page scorecard reach Vetrix by the 10th working day of the following month.

## Disease alerts

When a state notifies an outbreak, Vetrix may mark orders as urgent. Each is dispatched within 12 hours of receipt. Quillfern and Vetrix agree a daily ceiling if a surge exceeds what can be delivered safely.

## 5. What the bill penalises

5.1. The utility bills the site on kilovolt-amperes as well as kilowatt-hours, so a poor power factor costs money every month even when nothing is wrong with the plant. Large compressor motors pull the factor down; the capacitor bank in the switch room pushes it back up.

5.2. The bank is rated at 360 kvar in six automatic steps. The site's target is a monthly average of 0.98. The utility adds a surcharge to any month that averages below 0.90, and gives a small rebate for any month above 0.95.

5.3. When the bank was first installed it had four steps and a lower rating, and the target was 0.95; the extra steps were added in April 2026 after two summer bills carried the surcharge.

5.4. The controller's display, which shows the kvar switched in on each step, is read at every monthly energy review. A step that will not switch in is reported to the electrical supervisor the same day.

5.5. Capacitor cans are never touched until the bank has been isolated and left for the discharge time printed on its door.

## 13. What it costs and when it pays

13.1. The board approved capital spending of Rs. 46 crore for the region: Rs. 31 crore for the DC's fit-out, racking, refrigeration and power, Rs. 6 crore for the satellite, and Rs. 9 crore for the owned fleet.

13.2. Running costs in the first year are budgeted at Rs. 2.1 crore a month at full volume, of which people are about a third and power and fuel another third.

13.3. The region is planned to cover its running costs in its ninth month and to pay back its capital in the twenty-sixth month after first receipt, on contracted volumes only. Any new contract shortens the payback; no forecast is counted until it is signed.

13.4. The region head reports actual against plan to Finance monthly and to the board quarterly.

13.5. Spending above the approved figure needs board approval, however small the overrun.

## 2. Who does what

2.1. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns commissioning and decides the order of tests. Navdeep Grewal, the refrigeration engineer, runs the plant tests with the contractor. The site QA lead accepts or rejects the room for product. The site manager is told the dates and is not asked to approve technical results.

2.2. The refrigeration contractor builds and starts the plant and puts it right when a test fails. The contractor does not decide whether its own work has passed; it provides the readings and the engineering lead decides.

2.3. The panel contractor erects the insulated envelope, the doors and the floor finish. The electrical contractor installs the power, controls and alarms. Each contractor has a named site engineer who attends the tests that concern their work.

2.4. Disagreements between contractors about whose work caused a failure are settled by the engineering lead after the test has been repeated. Nobody argues over a failed reading until it has been confirmed.

## 8. Finding where warmth gets in

8.1. When the room has held its set point for 48 hours, the envelope is surveyed from outside for places where cold escapes: panel joints, door frames, pipe and cable penetrations, and the junction between wall panels and floor.

8.2. The survey is done by thermography, with an infrared camera, at night or on a dull day when the outside walls are not heated by the sun. Any joint that shows more than 3 C colder than the panel face beside it is marked, resealed and surveyed again.

8.3. The handover note of 2025 allowed a larger difference before resealing, and two joints it allowed are now visibly iced.

8.4. The images are saved with the room number, the date and the camera's serial number, and printed on the commissioning record with each marked joint circled.

8.5. A second thermography survey with the same infrared camera is done six months after handover, in the opposite season, and its images are compared with the first.

## 10. Racking and the empty room

10.1. Racking is erected after the tightness and evacuation tests and before the temperature tests, so that the room is tested in the form in which it will be used. Racking erected later means testing again.

10.2. Racking is inspected and load-signed by the racking supplier, who fixes load notices to the end of every run. Nobody places a pallet on racking that does not carry its notice.

10.3. Evaporator air paths are checked against the racking layout. A rack run that blocks an evaporator's throw is moved before the room is accepted.

10.4. Sprinklers and smoke detection, where the room has them, are tested by the fire contractor and signed off separately. The commissioning record notes the fire contractor's certificate number but does not repeat its contents.

## 16. How the region will be judged

16.1. In its first two years the region is measured on: deliveries on time, which is planned at 96 per cent from month four; temperature excursions per thousand pallets moved; customer complaints; safety incidents; and money against plan.

16.2. Measures are reported monthly from the same systems as every other site. The region does not keep figures of its own.

16.3. A measure that misses plan for three months in a row is reviewed by the region head with the Chief Operating Officer, and a recovery plan is agreed in writing.

16.4. Safety incidents are reported the same day, as at every site, and the region is not given a softer target because it is new.

## 18. Costs and the commissioning budget

18.1. Commissioning has its own line in every project budget, separate from construction. It pays for the engineering team's time, the calibration of instruments, the hire of a heat camera where the team's own is in use elsewhere, refrigerant losses during testing, and the electricity used while the room runs empty.

18.2. Repeat tests caused by a contractor's failure are charged to that contractor under its contract. Repeat tests caused by a change Quillfern asked for are charged to the project.

18.3. The engineering lead reports commissioning spend against budget to Finance at the end of each month of the project, and explains any line that has gone over.

## 14. Risks we can see

14.1. The anchor customer is a single exporter. If Godavari Aqua's export market falls, the frozen block is half empty. The plan reduces that risk by signing at least two more frozen customers before the end of 2027.

14.2. Storms may close the region for days at a time. Section 9 sets the response.

14.3. Skilled refrigeration technicians are scarce on this coast. Two places on each intake of the company's technician programme are reserved for people from the region, who return to it on completion.

14.4. The vaccine maker's start date may slip. Pharma space is not filled with food while it waits; it stays empty.

14.5. Port congestion may hold containers at the DC longer than planned. The container plugs in section 10 are the buffer.

## 4. When the herds are sick

4.1. Diseases such as foot-and-mouth and lumpy skin can spread through a district in days, and when a state government notifies one, vaccine has to reach the affected villages faster than any normal order cycle allows.

4.2. Vetrix may mark orders for the affected districts as urgent. Quillfern dispatches each such order within 6 hours of receiving it, at any hour of any day, using a dedicated vehicle if no scheduled route will meet that time. Ordinary orders keep their normal timings.

4.3. In the first contract year the commitment during an outbreak was 12 hours; it was shortened at renewal after the lumpy skin season of 2025.

4.4. Surge capacity is limited by the chilled vehicles and drivers available in the region. Vetrix gives as much warning as it can, and the two companies agree a daily ceiling of urgent orders if the volume would otherwise exceed what can be delivered safely.

4.5. Urgent orders never override driving-hours or temperature rules, however large the surge. An order that cannot be met safely within the time is reported to Vetrix at once with the earliest safe time, and notified outbreak or not, no driver is asked to hurry.

# Krishi Seva co-op - urgent animal vaccine orders during a disease alert

**From:** Sunil Jadhav <sunil.jadhav@quillfern.example>

**To:** Krishi Seva account team <krishiseva-team@quillfern.example>

**Date:** Fri, 21 Aug 2026 15:12:46 +0530

Team,

Krishi Seva, the dairy cooperative in Ahmednagar district, has asked how fast we can move vaccine to its village centres when the district declares a disease alert. Here is what we have agreed with them.

When the district notifies an outbreak among cattle, the cooperative may mark its orders as urgent. We dispatch each urgent order within 12 hours of receiving it, on a dedicated van if our scheduled rounds will not make it. Normal orders keep their normal timings.

We cannot promise more than our vans and drivers allow. The cooperative will warn us of a likely surge as early as it can, and we agree a daily cap with them if the orders would otherwise outrun what we can deliver safely.

No urgent order changes driving hours or the cold chain rules. If we cannot make the time safely, we tell the cooperative's office at once and give them the earliest safe time.

Please make sure the night controller has this mail; urgent orders can arrive at any hour. The cooperative's office will phone as well as e-mail, and the controller should write the time of the call on the order so that we can show when the clock started.

The cooperative pays the dedicated-van rate in the rate schedule for any urgent order that needs one. Do not discuss the charge with the village centres; the account manager handles it with the cooperative's office.

Sunil

## Disease alerts

When a state notifies an outbreak, Vetrix may mark orders as urgent. Each is dispatched within 12 hours of receipt. Quillfern and Vetrix agree a daily ceiling if a surge exceeds what can be delivered safely.

## 3. Ordering

3.1. Vetrix's distributors and stores place orders through Vetrix's order portal, which passes them to Quillfern's warehouse system every thirty minutes between 06:00 and 22:00.

3.2. Orders received by 12:00 are dispatched the same day where the delivery point is within the day-route network, and the next working day otherwise. The routes are listed in the annex and reviewed every quarter.

3.3. An order may be changed or cancelled by Vetrix until it has been picked. After picking, a change is treated as a new order and the picked stock is returned to its location.

3.4. Vetrix's customer service team tells Quillfern by e-mail of any order that needs special handling, such as a delivery to a government store that receives only on certain days.

## 6. How the numbers are counted

6.1. All measures are calculated by Quillfern from its warehouse and transport systems and checked by Vetrix's supply chain team against its own order records. Where the two disagree, the order-level records are compared line by line until the difference is explained.

6.2. Delivery time is the time recorded on the driver's handheld at the moment the receiving party signs, not the time the vehicle reached the gate.

6.3. Quantity and item accuracy are checked against the receiving party's signed delivery note. A delivery note signed without remarks is taken as accepting the quantity delivered.

6.4. Orders cancelled by Vetrix before dispatch are not counted. Orders split by Quillfern into two deliveries count as failed unless Vetrix agreed the split before dispatch.

6.5. Measures are calculated by calendar month and reported to two decimal places. Rounding is applied once, at the end.

## 12. Invoicing

12.1. Quillfern invoices Vetrix monthly in arrears, with separate invoices for storage, handling and transport, within five working days of the month's end.

12.2. Service credits appear as a separate line on the next handling invoice, with a reference to the month and the measure that earned them.

12.3. Vetrix pays each invoice within 45 days of its date. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days; the undisputed part is paid on time.

## Delivery promise

Orders must arrive complete, undamaged and inside the delivery window. The otif target is a monthly figure. At least 95 per cent of orders each month must meet it. For each full point of shortfall below that, Vetrix receives a credit of 2 per cent of the month's handling invoice.

## 3. Planning a week of duty

3.1. Planners build the week's duty on Thursday for the following Monday to
Sunday. Each driver's weekly rest is placed first, then night segments, then
day runs.

3.2. The limits the plan must respect are in the Driver Hours and Road Safety
Policy. A plan that meets them only if nothing goes wrong does not meet them.

3.3. A lane with a qualification record is planned with that record open, so
that its relief point, its pre-cool hold time and any two-driver condition are
on the plan and not in someone's memory.

3.4. Festival shuttle rosters with split rest are planned only after the Fleet
head has approved the roster in writing, and only for the festival named.

3.5. The plan is published to drivers by Friday noon. A driver who sees a
problem with his week tells Fleet Control on Friday, not on the morning of the
run.

3.6. Leave requests go to the planner by the 20th of the previous month. Late
leave is granted where cover exists, and cover is never found by stretching
another driver's hours.

## Before loading

1. Two drivers are named on the dispatch note before departure, as clause 2.3 of the [Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy](08-driver-hours-and-safety-policy.md) requires.

2. The body is run empty with its doors shut until the display holds loading temperature, and then held there for the Pre-Cool Hold Time (PCH) set by the qualification record for that route. Where no qualification record exists, the PCH is 45 minutes.

3. The red sleeve is in the cab locker and holds a spare calibrated logger. No logger, no departure: a hand-held thermometer is not a substitute.

4. Where the qualification record requires a backup passive shipper, its SCT is written in the shipper register. A shipper with no SCT entry is not a backup and the run waits.

## 5. Temperatures

5.1. The customer's products are kept at -18 C or colder in storage and in
transit.

5.2. The customer pre-cools each trailer before loading at Chakan and sends the
pre-cool record with the trailer.

5.3. Product that turns up above minus 12 is brought down to temperature at the cross-dock, and that work is invoiced to the customer.

5.4. Quillfern is not liable for product damage caused by temperatures before
handover. Each party may inspect the other's temperature records for its
stock.

## 14. Training and coaching for drivers

14.1. Every new owned-reefer driver rides two supervised runs with an experienced
driver before driving alone. One of the two is a night run.

14.2. The supervised runs cover the cab card, the takeover walk-round, the seal
routine, the red sleeve, the gate checklist for pharma runs and the way to speak
to Fleet Control on the phone. The experienced driver signs the new driver's
training sheet at the end of each run.

14.3. Telematics coaching calls are held within two working days of an alert, as
the policy says. The coach asks what happened before saying anything about what
should have happened.

14.4. Drivers who complete a year with no safety non-conformance receive a
certificate from the Fleet head, presented at the Nagpur driver meeting. The
certificate carries no money and is not tied to arrival times.

14.5. The Nagpur driver meeting is held on the last Saturday of each month in
the driver rest room. Attendance is paid duty time. Drivers on the road that day
receive the notes on their phone.

## 2. The Fleet Control desk

2.1. Fleet Control sits at Nagpur DC and answers extension 301 at all hours. At
night one controller is on duty, with the Fleet head's deputy on call.

2.2. Fleet Control owns the dispatch note, the vehicle's route and the driver's
duty plan. A shift lead can hold a vehicle at the gate, but only Fleet Control
can change a route or a driver.

2.3. Every call from a driver is logged in the driver call log with the time,
the place and what was said, including calls that come to nothing. The paper
log is kept alongside the Tessaline record because network coverage is patchy
on several lanes.

2.4. Fleet Control does not pass customer pressure to a driver. A customer who
wants a location or an arrival time asks customer service, and customer service
asks Fleet Control.

2.5. Each controller hands over at 08:00 and 20:00, with every open exception,
every vehicle on the road with a pharma critical load, and every vehicle off
road for repair named aloud.

## 3. Commitments on both sides

3.1. The customer commits to 1,800 pallet movements in each calendar month; any month that falls short is charged Rs. 300 for each movement not made.

3.2. A pallet movement is one pallet received or one pallet dispatched. A pallet
received and dispatched in the same month counts twice.

3.3. Quillfern commits to hold enough frozen space in Pune for 900 of the
customer's pallets at any one time, and to give 30 days' notice before reducing
it.

3.4. Months in which Quillfern could not take the customer's stock, for reasons
on Quillfern's side, are not counted for the shortfall charge.

# Pharma Critical Night Dispatch Checklist

Worked through at the gate by the Fleet controller and the shift lead together before any pharma critical vehicle leaves a Quillfern DC between 22:00 and 05:00. Both sign. One signature is not a dispatch.

## 13. Audit and records

13.1. The customer may audit the records about its own stock twice a year on
ten working days' notice.

13.2. Records are kept for three years after the end of the agreement.

## 11. Disputes

11.1. The parties first try to settle a dispute between their account managers,
then between their directors.

11.2. A dispute not settled within 45 days goes to a sole arbitrator in Pune.

## 10. Ending the agreement

10.1. Either side may bring it to an end by giving 120 days' written notice.

10.2. Either side may end it at once if the other fails to pay, or fails to
perform a material obligation, and does not put it right within 30 days of a
written demand.

10.3. On ending, Quillfern returns the customer's stock to Chakan or to a place
the customer names in Pune, at the customer's cost, within 15 days.

## 12. Insurance

12.1. Quillfern insures the customer's stock in its care up to the contract-year
total in section 7.2.

12.2. The customer insures its stock before handover and after delivery.

## Signing

9. Controller and shift lead sign. The signed copy goes in the Fleet blue file and is kept for seven years.

10. Nothing on this checklist is skipped for a customer-declared emergency. A late vaccine is a customer problem; a vaccine that left without these checks is a Quillfern one.

## What was done

- Kalpa platform access ended on **30 April 2026**, the date the 2026 decision
  record set for retiring the export script.
- Trip data from 2014 to 2025 was exported to cold storage: 48,900 trips, all
  carrying the KLP prefix, 2.1 TB including the raw probe series. Two copies,

- The alert routing that Kalpa used was retired with it. What it looked like is

  which is kept only so auditors can see how alarms were routed before
  Compliance-Red existed.
- The guard cabin tablet at Nagpur was wiped of its login and left in place as a
  read-only audit device. It must not be used to open or acknowledge an alarm.
- The Kalpa sticker on the Nagpur admin wall was removed on 5 May 2026. The
  night team had asked for this twice because new drivers were reading it as
  current.

# Telematics Vendor Decision 2026

Status: Accepted

## Context

The 2023 decision renewed Kalpa Fleet Systems for 36 months from 1 January 2024.
That decision is retired by this record. The cutover thread of July to September
2025 moved Quillfern to Tessaline Telematics for operational data, but no
decision record was ever written, and three audits asked why the accepted record
on file still named a vendor we no longer use.

This record states the present position so that no auditor, trainer, or new
manager has to read an email chain to learn which vendor is current.

# PROJ-125: Kalpa decommission and audit export

**PROJ-125** ended Quillfern's use of Kalpa Fleet Systems as a running platform
and preserved its history as files. It is closed. PROJ-125 is the last of the
three projects in this series; the other two are
[PROJ-123](19-project-PROJ-123-dockwise-rollout.md) and
[PROJ-124](20-project-PROJ-124-red-sleeve-and-passive-shippers.md), and neither
of them touched a telematics platform.

| line | figure |
|---|---|
| audit vendor copy, annual | Rs. 0.36 lakh |

## Consequences

IT retires the Kalpa export script on 30 April 2026. The Kalpa tablet in the
Nagpur guard cabin is a read-only audit device and must not be used to open
alarms. Training material and the QA audit binder are reissued with Tessaline
screenshots before the 2026 vaccine season.

Fleet continues to keep paper driver call logs. That practice survived the
vendor change because network coverage, not the vendor, was the reason for it.

Sandhu's closing comment: "THE DASHBOARD CHANGED; THE DISCIPLINE DOES NOT."

## Decision

Quillfern will renew Kalpa Fleet Systems for 36 months beginning 1 January 2024.
The renewal covers 147 owned reefers, 63 hired-truck devices during peak months,
and 38 fixed sensors across rooms and docks. The implementation and renewal
charge is Rs. 18.40 lakh. The recurring charge is Rs. 920 per active truck per
month and Rs. 310 per fixed sensor per month.

No split-vendor model will be used in 2024. IT will keep one support desk and
one monthly export from Kalpa. Fleet and QA will continue to use the KLP trip
number for audit packets.

## Reasons

The pilot met its acceptance tests. The C2 sensor tracked the USB logger within
0.3 C. Night alerts reached Compliance-Red in the 18 March 2026 test call, which
was the condition Revathi Iyer set after the March 2025 vaccine excursion.

Kalpa's five-minute polling required interpolation in every investigation
timeline. Sixty-second polling removed that argument from three customer
disputes in the first quarter of parallel running.

The local-service argument that carried the 2023 decision no longer holds.
Tessaline's Nagpur field team replaced two truck devices within one working day
during the January 2026 cold wave.

## Rejected options

Tessaline was rejected in 2023 because the API was not demonstrated on a live
Quillfern route, the commercial proposal required a larger first-year payment,
and the field-support rota for Nagpur was still being hired. The evaluation team
liked the one-minute polling and the proposed exception export, but decided that
those benefits were not enough to justify a complete change before the 2024
vaccine season.

A split model was also rejected. In that model, Kalpa would have stayed on
trucks while warehouse probes moved to Tessaline. IT objected that two source
systems would create audit confusion and double monthly reconciliation work.
Finance objected that the split model removed volume discounts from both
vendors.

## 11. Closing out the contractor's list

11.1. As the tests proceed, the engineering lead keeps a single snag list of everything not yet right. Each item is graded A, meaning the room cannot hold product safely until it is fixed, or B, meaning the room can be used while it is fixed.

11.2. Practical completion is certified only when no A item remains open. Every B item must be closed within 30 days of that certificate, and the retention money held from the contractor is not released until the last one is.

11.3. The first Ludhiana build allowed longer, and three of its B items were still open when the retention was paid.

11.4. Each item carries its owner, the dates raised and closed, and the initials of the person who checked the closure. Items are closed on inspection, never on the contractor's word; the punch list is a record of what was seen, not of what was promised.

11.5. A B item still open on day 30 becomes an A item for the purpose of releasing money, though the room stays in use. Contractors who want their retention sooner close their snag items sooner, and argue with the punch grades in writing.

## Closing items

An item is closed when our engineer has seen the repair, never on the contractor's word. The contractor's own punch sheet is not accepted in place of ours.

## Outstanding items

The contractor's snag list graded A and B. B items to be closed within 45 days of completion; the punch list is kept by the contractor.

## 2. Who does what

2.1. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns commissioning and decides the order of tests. Navdeep Grewal, the refrigeration engineer, runs the plant tests with the contractor. The site QA lead accepts or rejects the room for product. The site manager is told the dates and is not asked to approve technical results.

2.2. The refrigeration contractor builds and starts the plant and puts it right when a test fails. The contractor does not decide whether its own work has passed; it provides the readings and the engineering lead decides.

2.3. The panel contractor erects the insulated envelope, the doors and the floor finish. The electrical contractor installs the power, controls and alarms. Each contractor has a named site engineer who attends the tests that concern their work.

2.4. Disagreements between contractors about whose work caused a failure are settled by the engineering lead after the test has been repeated. Nobody argues over a failed reading until it has been confirmed.

## 8. Finding where warmth gets in

8.1. When the room has held its set point for 48 hours, the envelope is surveyed from outside for places where cold escapes: panel joints, door frames, pipe and cable penetrations, and the junction between wall panels and floor.

8.2. The survey is done by thermography, with an infrared camera, at night or on a dull day when the outside walls are not heated by the sun. Any joint that shows more than 3 C colder than the panel face beside it is marked, resealed and surveyed again.

8.3. The handover note of 2025 allowed a larger difference before resealing, and two joints it allowed are now visibly iced.

8.4. The images are saved with the room number, the date and the camera's serial number, and printed on the commissioning record with each marked joint circled.

8.5. A second thermography survey with the same infrared camera is done six months after handover, in the opposite season, and its images are compared with the first.

## Completion

We certify practical completion only when no A item is open. Every B item must then be closed within 14 days of the certificate. The store is small and opens straight into a busy season, so the period is shorter than on our larger builds.

## The list

Our engineer keeps one list of everything still wrong with the fit-out, walked with the contractor's site engineer every Friday. Each item is graded A, which stops the store taking stock, or B, which does not.

## 9. Bringing the kit home again

9.1. The liner and the cold packs are expensive and can be used again; the outer shipper is collected too, so that customers are not left with a bulky box, even though it is recyclable. The programme asks every customer to hand the whole kit back, empty, at their next delivery or by pickup from the door.

9.2. Customers pay a refundable deposit of Rs. 80 on the first kit they order. The amount is refunded in full if the box comes back within 14 days of delivery, in a condition the hub can reuse, and is kept if it does not.

9.3. The pilot's deposit was smaller and gave less time, and too many boxes stayed in customers' homes.

9.4. Outer shippers that cannot be reused are flattened at the Bhosari hub and sent for recycling; they are recyclable board with water-based ink. Liners that cannot be reused are sent to the moulder, who takes them back as raw material.

# Thali Box pilot: pack note

Packaging used for the Thali Box meal-kit pilot from April 2025.

## Outer

Three-ply corrugated slotted box, tested by bct. Compression strength at least 300 kgf.

# Packaging Specification Book, Thali Box Programme

## 1. The programme and this book

1.1. Thali Box Foods Pvt. Ltd. sells weekly meal kits to households in Pune and Mumbai: a box holding the raw and part-cooked ingredients for four or five dinners, with recipe cards, delivered to the door on a day the customer chooses. Quillfern assembles, stores and delivers the kits from the Kondhwa kitting room, and takes the empty boxes back through the Bhosari hub.

1.2. A kit holds chilled items, such as paneer, dahi, cut vegetables and marinated chicken, and on some weeks frozen items, such as parathas and ice cream. It is left on doorsteps, with security guards and in building lobbies, sometimes for hours. The packaging is what keeps it safe there, and it has to be specified, tested and checked like any other part of the cold chain.

1.3. This book is the agreed specification for every packaging component in the programme. It is owned by Quillfern's packaging engineer, Aarti Jog, and agreed with Thali Box's product team. Neither side changes a component without the other's written agreement.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the pack note used in the 2025 pilot. The pilot ran through one summer with packaging chosen for cost, and lost too many kits to warm doorsteps and crushed corners. Several components changed as a result; each section says what changed.

1.5. The book sets no product temperature. Kit temperatures and the action taken when they are missed come from the programme's quality agreement, which this book supports but does not repeat.

## 7. Proving a design before it is used

7.1. No new packaging component, and no change to an existing one, goes into service until a complete kit built with it has passed a transit test at the Product Testing Laboratory.

7.2. The test follows an ista procedure adapted for meal kits. A kit is built with dummy food packs and a logger, conditioned, and then dropped ten times from 60 cm onto its faces, edges and corners in a set order. It passes if nothing has leaked, the lid is still seated and the logger shows the food stayed in range for the full doorstep period the programme promises.

7.3. The pilot's simulation used fewer and lower drops and passed a box that failed on the road.

7.4. A simulation of the doorstep follows the drops: the kit stands in a chamber that cycles between the hottest and most humid conditions recorded in Pune in May and the coolest night.

7.5. Results of each ista run are written up by the laboratory and signed by the packaging engineer and Thali Box's product manager before the component is released.

## Returns

Customers pay a deposit on their first kit. Rs. 50, refunded if the box comes back within 7 days. Shippers that cannot be reused are recyclable.

For the morning milk and paneer subscription deliveries we make for Rasika Dairy in Kothrud and Karve Nagar.

The box is left on the subscriber's doorstep before 07:00 and collected empty the next morning. It only has to keep milk cold for about three hours, so it is much lighter than a meal-kit box.

Each box is moulded expanded polystyrene, white, with a push-on lid. Walls, base and lid are 15 mm thick, at a density of 15 kg per cubic metre. The box carries Rasika's logo moulded into the lid.

Boxes are checked every morning at loading. A box with a crack, a missing corner or a loose lid is set aside and returned to the moulder at the end of the month. The eps moulder replaces rejected boxes without charge.

CLEANING
Returned boxes are wiped inside and out with a food-safe sanitiser and air-dried before reuse. A box that smells of sour milk is not reused.

COUNTING
The depot counts boxes out and back every day. Subscribers who keep a box are reminded by Rasika's customer team, not by the delivery boy.

Clean boxes are stacked lid-on, ten high, on the racks by the loading door. Boxes are never stacked on the floor or in the sun.

## 11. Making things sterile

11.1. Used cultures, plates and swabs are made safe before they leave the laboratory. Glassware and media are sterilised before use.

11.2. Both jobs are done in the autoclave in the washing room. A standard load runs at 121 C for 20 minutes once the whole load has reached that temperature, and every cycle's printout is kept.

11.3. Every week a biological indicator, a spore strip carrying a known number of heat-resistant bacteria, is placed in the middle of a full load. After the cycle the strip is incubated; any growth means the cycle failed, the week's loads are repeated, and the machine is serviced before it is used again.

11.4. Until February 2026 the spore test was done monthly, which would have let three weeks of unsafe waste leave the building after a failure.

11.5. Only trained analysts load and unload the autoclave, wearing heat-resistant gloves and a face shield, and nobody opens the door before the pressure gauge reads zero.

## The sterilizer

Used plates and glassware are made safe in the laboratory's autoclave before they are washed or thrown away. A standard load runs at 121 C for 15 minutes, counted from the moment the load reaches temperature. The printout of every cycle is kept in the cycle file.

## 3. Before anything travels

3.1. A customer who wants to return goods asks customer service, which checks the customer's contract and issues an rma, the return number. It carries the customer code, the date and a running count, and it is printed on the collection note and on every carton label.

3.2. An rma is valid for 14 days from the day it is issued. Goods that reach the hub after that date are received, put in the hub's quarantine area and held, and the customer is asked to raise a fresh number before anything else is done with them.

3.3. The interim rules of 2025 allowed twice as long, and the hub found itself holding stock that nobody remembered asking to return.

3.4. A return without any authorisation number at all is not accepted at the gate unless the hub manager agrees by phone. Goods that cannot be refused safely, such as chilled stock on a vehicle that has nowhere else to go, are taken in under the same hold as a late one.

3.5. A second authorisation is never issued for goods already in the building; the first number is extended by customer service instead.

5.1. Pharma critical stock means vaccines, insulin, and any medicine named by a

5.2. Dairy customers must be notified by the next scheduled customer service
