## 5. Growing what is there

5.1. The laboratory counts bacteria, yeasts and moulds on food samples and on surface swabs, so that QA can decide whether a product, a liner or a body is fit to use.

5.2. For the total viable count, the prepared sample is spread on plate count agar and the plates are incubated at 30 C for 72 hours before they are read. Coliforms, yeasts and moulds follow their own methods, listed in the laboratory's method file.

5.3. Until January 2026 the count was read after 48 hours at a higher temperature, which missed slow growers from chilled foods.

5.4. Each incubator is checked twice a day with a reference thermometer, and its reading written on the sheet on its door. One that has drifted more than 1 C from its set point is taken out of use until it has been serviced, and plates inside it are moved to the spare incubator.

5.5. Every batch of agar is tested with a known organism before it is used for samples.

## 10. Before tools come out

10.1. Any work that could start a fire, release refrigerant, expose live electrical parts, or put someone at height needs a written permit to work, issued by the shift lead before the job starts.

10.2. A permit for hot work — brazing, welding, cutting, grinding — is valid for one shift only, and never for more than eight hours. Work that runs past the end of the shift stops, and a fresh permit is issued if it is to continue.

10.3. Hot work needs a fire watch who stays for thirty minutes after the work ends.

10.4. The permit names the technician, the job, the place, the hazards, the controls and the time limits. The technician signs it, and signs it again when the work is finished.

10.5. A technician who starts work before the permit is issued is sent off site, and the partner is told the same day.

## 2. Building, bays and who is where

2.1. The shed is a single span with six dock doors on the east wall, numbered D1
to D6 from the gate side. D1 and D2 take incoming trailers, D3 opens into the
cell behind it, and D4 to D6 load outgoing vans.

2.2. The freezer chamber FC-A runs at -22 C and holds 1,140 pallet positions in
drive-in racking. The marshalling anteroom in front of it is held at +4 C so
that cartons being picked for vans do not collect frost.

2.3. The plant room is on the north side, outside the insulated envelope, with
its own door to the yard. The office is on a mezzanine above D1 and D2, with a
window over the dock so that the order desk can see what is being unloaded.

2.4. The truck scale is at the gate, on the left as a vehicle enters, and every
inbound trailer is weighed in and out. The guard cabin is beside the scale.

2.5. Battery charging for the reach trucks is in a fenced bay outside the
anteroom. Nobody charges a truck inside FC-A, and nobody leaves a battery on
charge unattended across a shift change.

2.6. The canteen and lockers are in a single-storey block beside the gate.
Drivers waiting for a dock may use the canteen. They may not walk past the
yellow line painted along the dock edge.

2.7. The first-aid room is next to the canteen. The nearest hospital with a
casualty department is on the Kalyan road, about 7 km away; the route is
printed on the back of the first-aid room door.

## 11. Gas in, gas out

11.1. Category A partners recover refrigerant from our plant into their own recovery cylinders. Refrigerant is never vented, however small the quantity.

11.2. For every job that removes or adds refrigerant, the partner gives the site a gas record showing the cylinder numbers, the weights before and after, the type of gas, and what happened to recovered gas: reused in the same plant, sent for reclamation or sent for destruction.

11.3. The gas record reaches the site within seven days of the job. A job without a gas record is not paid until it arrives.

11.4. The site files the gas records with the plant's own log, so that the plant's history shows every gram that went in and out.

11.5. Leak checks on plant that holds more than the legal threshold of gas are done at the intervals the law sets, and the partner records each one in the plant log.

## 11. Making things sterile

11.1. Used cultures, plates and swabs are made safe before they leave the laboratory. Glassware and media are sterilised before use.

11.2. Both jobs are done in the autoclave in the washing room. A standard load runs at 121 C for 20 minutes once the whole load has reached that temperature, and every cycle's printout is kept.

11.3. Every week a biological indicator, a spore strip carrying a known number of heat-resistant bacteria, is placed in the middle of a full load. After the cycle the strip is incubated; any growth means the cycle failed, the week's loads are repeated, and the machine is serviced before it is used again.

11.4. Until February 2026 the spore test was done monthly, which would have let three weeks of unsafe waste leave the building after a failure.

11.5. Only trained analysts load and unload the autoclave, wearing heat-resistant gloves and a face shield, and nobody opens the door before the pressure gauge reads zero.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

## 16. Gifts and conflicts

16.1. Nobody at Quillfern accepts a gift, a meal, travel or entertainment from a partner or a firm proposing to become one, beyond token items worth less than Rs. 1,000 in all in a year, such as a diary or a box of sweets at Diwali.

16.2. Anything above that is declined, or, where declining would cause offence, handed to HR and recorded.

16.3. A member of staff with a family or financial interest in a partner declares it to Procurement and takes no part in that partner's approval, scoring or work orders.

16.4. Partners are told these rules when they are approved, and asked to tell Procurement if anyone at Quillfern asks them for anything.

## 14. The annual look back

14.1. Every partner is scored once a year by Procurement, using the site managers' records and the engineering pool's opinion. The score is out of 100 and covers attendance times, quality of work, safety, paperwork, and conduct on site.

14.2. A partner scoring 65 or more stays on the list. A partner scoring below 65 is put on probation for six months with a written plan of what must improve.

14.3. A partner put on probation in two consecutive years is removed from the list, whatever its score at the end of the second probation.

14.4. A partner may see its score and the records behind it, and may answer in writing before the score is final.

14.5. Scores are not shared with other partners.

## Mock recall

A mock recall is run once a year, in November, on a batch the QA lead picks.
Every unit of the chosen batch must be traced, on the shelf, on a vehicle or at
a consignee, within 8 hours of the exercise starting. The result goes to the
batch owner.

## 11. After the stock has left

11.1. Responsibility for a batch does not end at the dispatch bay. The store must be able to find every unit it has handled, and it must deal properly with what comes back.

11.2. Twice a year, in March and September, the store runs a mock recall on a batch chosen by the RP without warning. The exercise starts when she names the batch to the shift QA officer. Every unit of the chosen batch must be found and named — on a shelf, on a vehicle or at a consignee — inside four hours of the exercise starting. The result, with the time taken and any unit that could not be found, goes to the customer who owns the batch.

11.3. Hospitals and distributors send product back for many reasons — over-ordering, a ward closing, a wrong delivery — and none of those reasons makes it fit to be resold. Nothing returned goes back into saleable stock unless it comes back within 72 hours of delivery, with an unbroken logger record from our hands to the consignee's and back, and the Responsible Person signs the release; everything else is destroyed. Returned product waits in the quarantine cage while the decision is made.

11.4. A real recall, as opposed to a practice one, is run by the customer. The store's part is to stop dispatch of the batch at once, list every unit it holds and every unit it has sent, and hold any returned units in quarantine until the customer instructs.

11.5. Complaints from hospitals about a product's quality are passed to the customer the same day. The store does not reply to the complaint itself, and does not offer an opinion on it.

## 15. Customer audits

15.1. Customers may audit the store on ten working days' notice, and for cause at shorter notice. The RP or the QA lead hosts every audit; the store manager joins for the operational parts.

15.2. An auditor may see any record about the customer's own stock and any part of the building. An auditor may not see another customer's stock records or another customer's audit reports.

15.3. The store answers each audit finding within 20 working days with a corrective action, an owner and a date. Answers are written by the QA lead and signed by the RP.

15.4. Findings from customer audits are added to the store's own corrective action register, so that one customer's finding fixes the problem for every customer.

15.5. A customer may ask to observe a mock recall or a self-inspection walk. The request is granted where the customer's own batch is chosen or where the walk does not expose another customer's records.

## 17. Changes to this manual

17.1. Revision 1 (September 2025) was issued when the store opened. Revision 2 (December 2025) added the generator test after a power failure in the first month. Revision 3 (May 2026) changed several frequencies and limits after the store's first full season, and recorded the reasons beside each change.

17.2. The QA lead reviews this manual every April and after any critical deviation, failed customer audit or change to the building. The RP approves each revision.

17.3. Staff send suggested changes to the QA lead at any time. Each suggestion gets an answer, whether or not it is taken up.

17.4. A revised manual is issued with a one-page note of what changed. Every person who works in a product zone signs that they have read the note within a week of issue.

## Walk-in chamber requalification

The walk-in chambers are requalified every 24 months.

## Deviation numbers

Deviation numbers run in one series for the store and are never reused.

## Self-inspection

The store inspects itself twice a year.

## Why a cycle limit

Every freeze and thaw works the seam of a pack. A pack that leaks inside a
shipper wets the product box and ruins the label, so packs are retired on a
count, not on how they look.

# Gel packs: why blue caps, 18 hours and a cycle limit

## Why packs are conditioned at +5.0 C, not frozen

The 2025 shipper validation first used packs straight from a freezer. Three of the five trial runs dipped to +1.4 C at the carton nearest a frozen pack.
A vaccine that freezes is lost for good; a warm excursion at least has a
stability letter to argue with.

## Shippers

- **shipper conditioning time** — 18 hours at +5.0 C, for every pack in the shipper.
- **packs per shipper** — 22 blue-cap packs.
- **shipper fleet** — PS-01 to PS-12, at Nagpur.

## Shippers

- 18 blue-cap packs go in each shipper.
- Shipper conditioning time: 18 hours at +5.0 C.
- A closed shipper holds its range for 72 hours.

## Why blue and white caps

Blue caps and white caps were chosen because the night team works under one tube light and colour is read faster than a label.

## Notes from the trial

The trial ran in the night team's slot, because that is when pharma shippers are
made up. White packs from the freezer and blue packs from CC-1 sat on separate
trolleys. One tube light over the bench had failed and was not replaced for a
week. The caps were ordered from the same supplier as the pack bodies.

## Why 18 hours

Packs pulled after 12 hours of conditioning ran warm from about hour 30 of the trial.
At 18 hours every run held range for the length of the lane.

## 5. Racking and rooms

5.1. The DC has three temperature zones. The chilled block at +2 to +8 C holds 2,400 pallet positions in selective racking, split into a pharma room of 600 and a food room of 1,800. The frozen block at −22 C holds 1,600 pallet positions in drive-in racking. The controlled-room-temperature store holds 300.

5.2. The frozen block is built so that a second chamber of the same size can be added on the east side without stopping the first. That expansion is not approved and is not in this plan's figures.

5.3. The pharma room has its own anteroom and its own door to the dispatch canopy, so that pharma picking never shares a door with food.

5.4. Every room is temperature-mapped before first stock and again after its first summer. The mapping follows the company method.

5.5. Floor space in the dispatch canopy is for staging only. Nothing waits there longer than it takes to load.

# Cold Room Commissioning Manual

## 1. Why commissioning gets its own manual

1.1. A cold room is not finished when the builders leave. It is finished when it has been shown, by tests written down in advance and run by people who did not build it, that it will hold product inside its range on the worst day of the year. Everything between the last panel going up and the first pallet going in is commissioning, and this manual says how Quillfern does it.

1.2. The manual was first written for the opening of Ludhiana DC in 2025 and is now used for the second frozen block at Ludhiana, due for handover in the winter of 2026, and for every new chamber the engineering team builds after it. It applies whether the chamber is built by a turnkey contractor or assembled by our own team from bought-in panels and plant.

1.3. It is written for the engineering lead who runs commissioning, the contractors who build and start the plant, the site QA lead who must accept the room, and the site manager who wants to know when the room can earn money. It does not replace temperature mapping, which follows the company mapping method once commissioning is complete.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the handover note written in a hurry at the end of the first Ludhiana build. Several of that note's figures were the contractor's defaults, accepted without question; this revision sets Quillfern's own.

## 3. Customers we are building for

3.1. Godavari Aqua Exports is the anchor for frozen work. It processes shrimp at two plants near Kakinada and exports through Visakhapatnam. It has committed to an average of 900 pallets a month in storage from the first full month of operation.

3.2. Kalinga Biologicals is the anchor for pharma work. Its fill-finish line near Bhubaneswar starts commercial production in the second quarter of 2027. Until then it will send stock from its western plant through the DC.

3.3. Rushikonda Dairy, a cooperative with a growing ice-cream line, is the first chilled and frozen retail customer. Two retail chains are in negotiation and are not counted in the volumes below.

3.4. No customer is promised space it has not contracted for. Sales may quote, but the region head confirms any commitment above 100 pallets before it is signed.

3.5. Customers are told plainly that the satellite does not store goods.

## 17. Later steps

17.1. A second satellite at Rajahmundry, closer to the shrimp plants, is being studied for 2028. It is not approved and nothing in this plan depends on it.

17.2. The second frozen chamber at the DC (section 5.2) will be proposed to the board when frozen occupancy has been above 85 per cent for six months.

17.3. Rail movement of frozen containers from the DC to the north has been offered by a container rail operator and will be tried in 2027 with one customer.

## 10. Racking and the empty room

10.1. Racking is erected after the tightness and evacuation tests and before the temperature tests, so that the room is tested in the form in which it will be used. Racking erected later means testing again.

10.2. Racking is inspected and load-signed by the racking supplier, who fixes load notices to the end of every run. Nobody places a pallet on racking that does not carry its notice.

10.3. Evaporator air paths are checked against the racking layout. A rack run that blocks an evaporator's throw is moved before the room is accepted.

10.4. Sprinklers and smoke detection, where the room has them, are tested by the fire contractor and signed off separately. The commissioning record notes the fire contractor's certificate number but does not repeat its contents.

## 7. Bringing the temperature down

7.1. A new frozen chamber cannot be cooled as fast as the plant would allow. Water left in new concrete and in the insulation joints freezes, expands and lifts the floor if the room is cooled too quickly, and repairing a heaved floor means emptying the room for months.

7.2. A new chilled chamber is brought straight to its set point. A new freezer is first held at +2 C for 24 hours to let the floor and panels settle, and then brought below 0 C at no more than 2 C per hour until it reaches its set point.

7.3. The controller is programmed with this ramp before the plant starts, and the programme is printed and signed.

7.4. The first Ludhiana freezer was allowed twice that rate; its floor showed hairline cracks at two expansion joints within a year.

7.5. The floor heater mat is proven working before the pulldown begins, and the room temperature is logged every hour during the pulldown, so that the gradient actually achieved can be compared with the programmed one. Any hour faster than the programme stops the process, and any gradient steeper than planned is investigated before cooling resumes.

## 14. Risks we can see

14.1. The anchor customer is a single exporter. If Godavari Aqua's export market falls, the frozen block is half empty. The plan reduces that risk by signing at least two more frozen customers before the end of 2027.

14.2. Storms may close the region for days at a time. Section 9 sets the response.

14.3. Skilled refrigeration technicians are scarce on this coast. Two places on each intake of the company's technician programme are reserved for people from the region, who return to it on completion.

14.4. The vaccine maker's start date may slip. Pharma space is not filled with food while it waits; it stays empty.

14.5. Port congestion may hold containers at the DC longer than planned. The container plugs in section 10 are the buffer.

## 10. Looking at whole populations

10.1. Some tests are run on every transaction rather than a sample, using data extracted from the finance system. Extracts are taken by the team with read-only access and are never edited; any cleaning is done on a copy and recorded.

10.2. The duplicate payment test runs every month, on the fifth working day, on all supplier payments of the previous month. It looks for the same supplier, amount and invoice number, and for near-matches where one character differs. Every hit is followed up with accounts payable within a week.

10.3. A Benford first-digit test runs once a quarter on staff expense claims, by site and by person. A pattern that departs from the Benford curve is a reason to look, never by itself a finding.

10.4. Results of every run are kept, including runs that found nothing, so that a duplicate missed later can be traced to the run that should have caught it.

## 5. Money

5.1. Every apprentice is paid a monthly stipend, not a wage, and it rises once, when the apprentice moves from the workshop to the floor. Pay is credited to the apprentice's own bank account on the last working day of the month.

5.2. The stipend is Rs. 14,000 a month for months one to six and Rs. 16,500 from month seven; the 2025 outline gave a flat Rs. 12,000. The rise recognises that floor months are longer and often away from home.

5.3. Apprentices placed at a site away from Waluj receive a lodging allowance and their travel to the site and back at the start and end of the placement. The allowance is set by the site and paid with the stipend.

5.4. Overtime is not paid to apprentices, because apprentices do not work overtime. An apprentice kept beyond the shift by an emergency is given the time back the next day.

5.5. No apprentice is bonded. Nobody repays anything for leaving the programme early or for taking a job elsewhere after it, and nobody is asked to sign a promise to stay.

## 5. Picking what to look at

5.1. Most controls are tested by picking items from the period under review and checking that the control worked on each one. The number of items depends on how often the control operates, not on the size of the population.

5.2. For a control that operates monthly, attribute testing uses 25 items under random sampling; for one that operates daily or with every transaction, 40 items; for a quarterly control, all of the quarters in the period. A single exception in the items picked is reported, whatever its value.

5.3. For sampling, items are picked at random from a complete listing that the auditor has checked for completeness against a control total. Picking from a listing someone else filtered is not random, however it was produced.

5.4. The 2025 charter used smaller attribute samples; they were raised for this programme because two findings in the first year rested on too few items to persuade anyone. The method and the seed used for random selection are recorded in the working papers so that another auditor could pick the same items.

## 2. Who can join

2.1. Applicants hold an ITI certificate in refrigeration and air-conditioning, or in an electrical or mechanical trade with a refrigeration module, and are between 18 and 25 on the day the intake opens.

2.2. Applicants sit a written test in arithmetic and basic electrical theory and a short practical in the workshop: wiring a contactor, reading a pressure gauge, brazing a joint. The practical counts for more than the written test.

2.3. A medical examination checks eyesight, colour vision and hearing. Colour vision matters because wiring and refrigerant cylinders are colour-coded.

2.4. Applicants must hold, or obtain within the first three months, a two-wheeler licence. Many floor jobs are reached by motorcycle.

2.5. Quillfern does not charge any fee for the programme, the tests or the medical. An agent who asks an applicant for money is reported to the engineering pool lead, and the applicant is not penalised for having been asked.

## 16. Welfare

16.1. Apprentices are young and often away from home for the first time. Each intake has a welfare contact at Waluj, a member of the workshop staff who is not a trainer.

16.2. Apprentices may raise anything with the welfare contact — homesickness, money, a problem at the lodging, a problem with a colleague — in confidence.

16.3. The lodging used at each site is visited by the welfare contact before the first apprentice moves in.

16.4. Bullying, ragging or initiation rituals are not tolerated, on site or at the workshop, and are dealt with under the company's discipline rules.

16.5. Apprentices are paid their stipend during approved sick leave for up to four weeks.

# Baner payables desk - checks we run before money leaves

# Baner payables desk: checks we run before money leaves

The payables desk at the Baner shared-services office pays supplier invoices for every Quillfern site. These are the checks the desk runs itself, as part of preparing each payment run.

## 9. Counting the money

9.1. Every Quillfern site holds a petty cash float for small purchases that cannot wait for a purchase order: courier charges, a replacement padlock, tea for a visiting inspector. It is an imprest: topped back up to a fixed figure against vouchers, never increased because a month was busy.

9.2. The float is Rs. 15,000 at each site and Rs. 25,000 at head office. Internal Audit counts it by surprise twice a year at every site, with the custodian present, and reconciles cash plus vouchers to the fixed figure.

9.3. A petty cash shortage of more than Rs. 500 is reported to the head of Finance the same day, with the custodian's written explanation.

9.4. The counts in 2025 were yearly and each imprest smaller; both changed in this programme.

## Twice a year

In April and October the desk runs a Benford first-digit analysis over all supplier invoices of the previous six months, by supplier. Suppliers whose invoices depart from the expected pattern are listed for the regional accountant to review.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 5. Protective equipment

5.1. Safety shoes and high-visibility vests are worn everywhere outside the office, the canteen and the locker rooms. Hard hats are worn on the docks, in the yard and anywhere work is going on overhead.

5.2. Freezer suits, gloves, balaclavas and boots are issued to named people for work in the frozen block. They are not shared, and a suit that no longer closes properly is exchanged at Stores the same day.

5.3. Gloves for chilled-room work, chemical gloves for cleaning and face shields for any work with dry ice are kept on the racks beside the work, not in personal lockers.

5.4. Equipment that is damaged or worn out is handed in and replaced, never repaired with tape. Stores keeps a stock of every item in every size worn on the site.

5.5. A person who turns up without their protective equipment does not start work until it is found or replaced.

## 10. Noise

10.1. The plant room, the generator enclosure and parts of the dock area are loud enough to damage hearing over time. Levels are surveyed with a decibel meter by the safety officer every year and after any new machine is installed, and the results are posted at each entrance.

10.2. Hearing protection is compulsory for everyone, however short the visit, wherever the survey shows a level of 85 or more. Signs mark those areas, and dispensers of earmuffs hang at their doors.

10.3. People who work regularly in those areas wear earmuffs for the whole shift and have a hearing test every 12 months, arranged by HR with an occupational health provider.

10.4. The 2025 rules set the line higher and the tests further apart.

10.5. A person whose test shows a change is told the result in person and moved away from the loudest work while the provider advises. Results are kept by HR, and a decibel reading in a survey is never treated as a personal medical record.

# Cold Room Commissioning Manual

## 1. Why commissioning gets its own manual

1.1. A cold room is not finished when the builders leave. It is finished when it has been shown, by tests written down in advance and run by people who did not build it, that it will hold product inside its range on the worst day of the year. Everything between the last panel going up and the first pallet going in is commissioning, and this manual says how Quillfern does it.

1.2. The manual was first written for the opening of Ludhiana DC in 2025 and is now used for the second frozen block at Ludhiana, due for handover in the winter of 2026, and for every new chamber the engineering team builds after it. It applies whether the chamber is built by a turnkey contractor or assembled by our own team from bought-in panels and plant.

1.3. It is written for the engineering lead who runs commissioning, the contractors who build and start the plant, the site QA lead who must accept the room, and the site manager who wants to know when the room can earn money. It does not replace temperature mapping, which follows the company mapping method once commissioning is complete.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the handover note written in a hurry at the end of the first Ludhiana build. Several of that note's figures were the contractor's defaults, accepted without question; this revision sets Quillfern's own.

## 19. Contractors on site

19.1. Contractors work under a permit for any job with a significant hazard: electrical work, hot work, work at height, work in a confined space and work on the refrigeration plant. The permit is issued by the shift lead after the job has been discussed on site with the contractor's supervisor.

19.2. Contractors bring their own tools and protective equipment, which must be in good condition and suitable for the job. Equipment that is not is turned away at the gate.

19.3. A contractor who breaks a site rule is stopped and asked to leave, and the firm is told the reason in writing. A firm whose workers repeatedly break rules is reported to Procurement.

19.4. Contractors report injuries and near misses on the site in the same way as staff, and their reports are counted in the site's figures.

## 6. Charging and first start

6.1. Refrigerant is charged by weight from the contractor's scale, with the cylinder number and the weight before and after recorded on the test sheet. The charge must match the designer's figure within the tolerance the designer gives.

6.2. The plant is started with the room empty and its doors shut. The contractor's engineer checks motor currents, oil levels, superheat and the operation of every safety cut-out before the plant is left to run.

6.3. Every safety cut-out is tested by causing the condition it protects against, not by reading its setting. A high-pressure switch is tested by blocking the condenser airflow until it trips, with the engineer standing at the isolator.

6.4. The alarm panel is tested at this stage too: each probe's high and low alarms, door alarms, plant fault alarms, and the call-out to the duty phone. A call that reaches nobody is a failed test.

6.5. Defrost is run manually through at least two full cycles and its termination checked.

## 3. Behind the chain-link fence

3.1. The 2 MVA transformer in the substation yard is oil-filled, and its oil is usually the first thing to fail without anyone noticing. Moisture and sludge pull down the oil's dielectric strength long before anything trips.

3.2. A sample is drawn by the approved testing laboratory every six months, in March and September, with the unit on load. The breakdown voltage must read at least 50 kV. A sample below that is filtered on site within seven days and drawn again after filtering.

3.3. The 2025 commissioning note allowed a yearly sample and a lower pass figure; both were tightened after the first monsoon, when condensation was found in the breather.

3.4. The laboratory's report is filed in the substation folder and copied to the engineering lead together with the dielectric figure from each of the last four samples, so that a slow decline is visible before it becomes a failure.

3.5. Nobody opens the transformer enclosure except the electrical supervisor or the utility's linesman, and never alone.

answer_text:
## Where alerts go

- Cold-room high and low alarms email the qa-shared mailbox at
  qa-shared@quillfern.example. This is the correct destination for every room
  alarm, including vaccine rooms.
- Truck alarms raise an SMS to the Fleet Control rota phone and an email to the
  same qa-shared mailbox.
- There is no separate pharma escalation group. If a vaccine room alarms at
  night, the night lead phones the DC manager and the DC manager decides whether
  to wake QA.

## Findings

1. One shift lead emailed the old qa-shared mailbox before calling Compliance-Red. The obsolete habit is named here, as clause 10.4 of the SOP requires: **qa-shared is not an escalation route.**
2. The red sleeve on RF-118 had no spare logger.
3. The night controller paused his run through [the pink card](30-pharma-night-dispatch-checklist.md) when the alarm sounded; no vehicle left during the drill.
4. Two staff asked what "warm pallet" means. It is defined in [the jargon sheet](33-cold-chain-glossary.md).

## Root cause

The immediate cause was warm air ingress through a torn door curtain and door
opening during dairy cross-dock spillover. The deeper cause was that the Kalpa
alert routing still pointed to the old qa-shared mailbox, which was not watched
by the night team. The shift lead tried to protect the room by placing dry ice
near the curtain, but the team did not quarantine stock until the manager was
awake.

We also found that dock scheduling pushed paneer loading next to the vaccine
cold-room door. This did not create the torn curtain, but it increased door
traffic during the vulnerable period. The dock plan must separate pharma
loading from dairy overflow during night shift.

## Known gaps

- Door-open events are unreliable where network coverage is poor. Keep the paper
  driver call log.
- The qa-shared mailbox is not watched overnight. This has been raised twice and
  is listed as accepted risk for 2021.

## Actions

| action | owner | due |
|---|---|---|
| Remove qa-shared from the night desk speed-dial | IT Service Desk | 28 February 2026 |

| time | event |
|---|---|
| 04:10 | Revathi was called by Farhan after the shift lead escalated by phone. |

## Closing note

This event is the reason I am asking for two changes: faster pharma escalation
and a shorter vaccine high-duration trigger. If the telematics vendor changes,
the first acceptance test must prove night alerts reach Compliance-Red, not only
the DC manager.

I have deliberately left the rough timeline language in place because the audit
packet should show how the team understood the event on the day. Later SOP
revisions may be cleaner, but this note is the incident record, not a training
poster. Any future reader should compare it with the live SOP before using its
thresholds.

## Summary

At approximately 02:16 on 12 March 2025, Kalpa probe KV-NGP-C2-07 began
reporting a high temperature in C2, the vaccine cold room at Nagpur DC. The
affected consignment was BharatVac order BV-4437, holding 18,400 vials of
rotavirus vaccine in lots ROTA-9A and ROTA-9B. The approved record showed the
room above +8.0 C for 66 minutes. At the time of the event, the SOP required a
QA call after 30 continuous minutes above +8.0 C for vaccines. The current
corrective action is to reduce that duration.

| time | event |
|---|---|
| 02:31 | Alert email went to qa-shared@quillfern.example; no SMS reached Compliance. |

| action | owner | due | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Change pharma critical alerts from qa-shared to Compliance-Red SMS and phone tree | IT Service Desk | 18 Mar 2025 | open at time of note |

## 4. Conclusion

4.1. G-COLD-1 passed with one condition.

4.2. Until a heater interlock is fitted to the room, the Guwahati night lead reads D1-low every two hours between 00:00 and 06:00, from 1 December to the last day of February. Outside those months the reading is not required.

4.3. This study was run in winter only. A summer run is owed before 30 June 2025 and TMS-43 does not cover it.

## 17. The weather and the calendar

17.1. Commissioning results depend on the weather, and the Punjab calendar is unkind to new plant. A room tested in December has not been tested against a June afternoon, and a room tested in June has not met the fog that keeps outdoor condensers wet for days in January.

17.2. The engineering lead plans the main temperature tests for the hottest weeks available before handover. Where handover falls in winter, the room is accepted on its winter results but a summer performance check is written into the plan for the following May or June, with the contractor required to attend.

17.3. Condenser capacity is checked against the design ambient temperature, not the ambient on the test day. Where the test day is cooler, the contractor shows by calculation, from measured pressures and currents, that the condensers have the margin the design assumed.

17.4. Monsoon rain on an unfinished roof has damaged insulation on other people's projects. No panel is erected and left uncovered overnight between June and September, and roof penetrations are sealed on the day they are cut.

17.5. Fog in December and January slows deliveries of plant and materials from the south. The commissioning plan allows for it rather than asking contractors to make up the time by working at night in a cold room.

17.6. Festivals and harvest seasons take many workers home for weeks. Contractors' labour plans are read against the calendar when the plan is drawn up, and dates are agreed with that in mind rather than discovered later.

## 2. Who does what

2.1. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns commissioning and decides the order of tests. Navdeep Grewal, the refrigeration engineer, runs the plant tests with the contractor. The site QA lead accepts or rejects the room for product. The site manager is told the dates and is not asked to approve technical results.

2.2. The refrigeration contractor builds and starts the plant and puts it right when a test fails. The contractor does not decide whether its own work has passed; it provides the readings and the engineering lead decides.

2.3. The panel contractor erects the insulated envelope, the doors and the floor finish. The electrical contractor installs the power, controls and alarms. Each contractor has a named site engineer who attends the tests that concern their work.

2.4. Disagreements between contractors about whose work caused a failure are settled by the engineering lead after the test has been repeated. Nobody argues over a failed reading until it has been confirmed.

## 3. Opening an account

3.1. A new customer is opened by an account manager, never by an agent. The
account manager checks the customer's product classes against what each DC can
store and move.

3.2. A customer who needs vaccines stored at Coimbatore is told plainly that
Coimbatore does not store vaccines. A customer who needs chilled dairy stored at
Coimbatore is told the same.

3.3. A customer who wants its own pricing gets a signed annex. Until the annex
is signed, the standard rate card is the only price that may be given.

3.4. The account manager sends the customer the list of named contacts on both
sides, including who will receive an excursion notice at night.

3.5. A customer who asks to be told of every alarm, not only confirmed
excursions, is told that Quillfern notifies confirmed excursions. A customer
wanting alarm-level alerts is referred to the account manager, who may arrange a
Tessaline customer view under the annex.

## 1. Scope

1.1. Empty-room run for 24 hours, then loaded-room run for 48 hours with 10 pallets of water-filled dummy cartons in the vaccine positions.

1.2. Acceptance: every probe inside +2.0 C to +8.0 C for the whole run, and the room back inside limits within 15 minutes of a 3-minute door opening.

# Cold room mapping study TMS-43

Study **TMS-43** is the temperature mapping of cold room G-COLD-1, the vaccine room at Guwahati DC, run over 72 hours from 13 to 16 January 2025. Studies in this series are numbered one after another and the numbers differ by one digit. A study number names one room on one date, never a room in general, so quote the full number.

## 5. Taking a booking

5.1. A booking needs the product class, the quantity in the unit the rate card
uses, the pickup and delivery points, the earliest and latest delivery time, and
the name of the person who will receive.

5.2. The agent checks that the booked vehicle can carry the product class. RF-120
is frozen only; RF-119 takes pharma only with a passive shipper; RF-118 takes
pharma and dairy but never frozen.

5.3. The agent books the dock through Dockwise for Nagpur, Guwahati and
Coimbatore alike. A phone slot at Guwahati is confirmed in Dockwise the next
working day.

5.4. Pharma critical bookings that would need a night segment are passed to
Fleet Control before they are confirmed to the customer, because a night pharma
run needs two named drivers.

5.5. A booking the customer changes after 15:00 the day before is treated as a
new booking.

## 2. Probe grid

2.1. 24 probes at three heights (low 0.3 m, mid 1.5 m, high 2.7 m) across racks A to D, bays 1 and 2. A position is named rack, bay and height, e.g. D1-low.

2.2. Two reference loggers: one at the evaporator return, one at the door.

## 17. New agents

17.1. A new agent spends the first two weeks listening to calls with an
experienced agent and reading closed tickets. They do not answer customers alone
in that time.

17.2. In the third week the new agent answers calls with the experienced agent
listening. The experienced agent signs the new agent off when they are ready,
not on a fixed day.

17.3. New agents spend one day at Nagpur DC in their first month, with a shift
lead, so that they have seen a cold room, a dock and a gate before they speak to
customers about them.

17.4. The customer service lead meets each new agent at the end of their first
month and again at three months.

## 4. What goes in the box

4.1. Each rider carries an IB-6 insulated carrier fitted to the rear rack of the
two-wheeler. Inside the carrier are two conditioned packs from PF-K1 and the
patients' orders, each in its own sealed pouch with the patient's slip.

4.2. Packs go in the pattern printed inside the lid, with the pouches between
them, never touching a pack directly.

4.3. The carrier's clock starts when the lid is shut at the hub, and the hub
lead writes that time on the run sheet. A pack still undelivered at the end of hour five comes back to Kothrud, because the carrier is only proven for six.

4.4. The turn-back hour depends on the carrier. With the IB-4 model it was four, until the last of those were withdrawn on 2 March 2026.

4.5. Each carrier has a single-use freeze indicator taped inside the lid. A
tripped indicator means everything in the carrier comes back, delivered or not
being irrelevant to that decision.

4.6. Carriers are cleaned with a dry cloth at the end of each run and are never
washed with water while warm. A carrier with a split seam or a cracked lid is
withdrawn the same day.

## 6. Working off the ground

6.1. Falls cause more serious injuries on the site than anything else, mostly from ladders and from the tops of racking and vehicles. Work at height is avoided wherever a ground-level method exists.

6.2. Any work more than 1.8 metres above the floor, or near an unprotected edge, is done from a platform with guard rails, or with a full-body harness attached by a shock-absorbing lanyard to an anchor point rated for the purpose.

6.3. Every harness is inspected by its user before each use, against the checklist sewn into its storage bag, and by the safety officer every three months. It is withdrawn after five years from its date of manufacture, or at once after it has arrested a fall, whichever comes first.

6.4. The 2025 rules allowed a longer service life and named no height. Both were tightened after the safety officer found that two units in the plant room were older than the people wearing them.

6.5. A lanyard that has deployed its shock absorber is cut in half and binned the same day.

BATALA DEPOT: ROOF AND RACK-TOP WORK

The Batala depot has an old asbestos-cement roof over the dry store and high racking in the chilled store. Both have hurt people before. This note says how work up there is done.

WHEN THE KIT IS NEEDED
Any work more than 2 metres above the floor needs either a platform with guard rails or a full-body harness clipped to a marked anchor point by a lanyard with a shock absorber. Nobody steps onto the roof sheets themselves; crawling boards are always used.

CHECKS
The person wearing the kit checks it before each use against the tag on its bag. The depot's maintenance supervisor checks every set once a year and writes the date on the tag.

HOW LONG IT LASTS
The Batala kit is withdrawn ten years after its date of manufacture, or at once after it has stopped a fall.

WHO MAY GO UP
Only staff who have done the working-at-height course, and contractors with their own certificate, go up. Two people always: one working, one watching from below.

WEATHER
Work on the roof stops in rain, in strong wind and after dark, and does not restart until the shift lead has looked at the roof.

RECORDS
Every job at height is written in the depot's height register with the date, the job, the names of both people and the anchor point used. The register is read at the monthly safety walk.

Questions to the depot maintenance supervisor.

## Height

Wear a harness with a lanyard when working at height. Harnesses are withdrawn after seven years.

## 5. Protective equipment

5.1. Safety shoes and high-visibility vests are worn everywhere outside the office, the canteen and the locker rooms. Hard hats are worn on the docks, in the yard and anywhere work is going on overhead.

5.2. Freezer suits, gloves, balaclavas and boots are issued to named people for work in the frozen block. They are not shared, and a suit that no longer closes properly is exchanged at Stores the same day.

5.3. Gloves for chilled-room work, chemical gloves for cleaning and face shields for any work with dry ice are kept on the racks beside the work, not in personal lockers.

5.4. Equipment that is damaged or worn out is handed in and replaced, never repaired with tape. Stores keeps a stock of every item in every size worn on the site.

5.5. A person who turns up without their protective equipment does not start work until it is found or replaced.

## 19. Contractors on site

19.1. Contractors work under a permit for any job with a significant hazard: electrical work, hot work, work at height, work in a confined space and work on the refrigeration plant. The permit is issued by the shift lead after the job has been discussed on site with the contractor's supervisor.

19.2. Contractors bring their own tools and protective equipment, which must be in good condition and suitable for the job. Equipment that is not is turned away at the gate.

19.3. A contractor who breaks a site rule is stopped and asked to leave, and the firm is told the reason in writing. A firm whose workers repeatedly break rules is reported to Procurement.

19.4. Contractors report injuries and near misses on the site in the same way as staff, and their reports are counted in the site's figures.

## 7. Bringing the temperature down

7.1. A new frozen chamber cannot be cooled as fast as the plant would allow. Water left in new concrete and in the insulation joints freezes, expands and lifts the floor if the room is cooled too quickly, and repairing a heaved floor means emptying the room for months.

7.2. A new chilled chamber is brought straight to its set point. A new freezer is first held at +2 C for 24 hours to let the floor and panels settle, and then brought below 0 C at no more than 2 C per hour until it reaches its set point.

7.3. The controller is programmed with this ramp before the plant starts, and the programme is printed and signed.

7.4. The first Ludhiana freezer was allowed twice that rate; its floor showed hairline cracks at two expansion joints within a year.

7.5. The floor heater mat is proven working before the pulldown begins, and the room temperature is logged every hour during the pulldown, so that the gradient actually achieved can be compared with the programmed one. Any hour faster than the programme stops the process, and any gradient steeper than planned is investigated before cooling resumes.

## Cooling down

Freezers brought down below 0 C at up to 4 C per hour. The pulldown gradient was logged every four hours.

## 13. Language and new people

13.1. Coimbatore works in Tamil. Training is given by a trainer in Tamil, with
English slides available but never used instead of a trainer.

13.2. New joiners spend their first week on the morning shift only. They are not
put on the late shift, and never left alone in the cold block, until a shift
lead has signed them off.

13.3. Every new joiner is shown the gate cabin, the security roster and the key
register on the first day. They are told that security will not open anything
for them at night except in an emergency, and that the lockers, the cabinet and
the seal drawer are all separate keys.

13.4. New drivers from hired-truck vendors are shown the south gate routine by
the guard and the Temple Street timing by the shift lead before their first
booking.

13.5. The words used on site follow the company glossary. A new joiner who hears
a word they do not know is expected to ask, on any shift, and nobody at
Coimbatore is to laugh at the question.

## 9. The envelope, doors and floor

9.1. Every door is tested for its seal by closing it on a sheet of paper at several points around the frame; the paper must not slide out easily. Rapid-roll doors are timed from fully open to fully closed, and their safety edges tested by obstruction.

9.2. Door heaters and frame heaters on freezer doors are checked for current and for warmth by hand at the frame.

9.3. Strip curtains are fitted after the doors are tested, never before, so that the door seal test is not confused by the curtain.

9.4. The floor finish is inspected for cracks and for ponding with water before the room is cooled. Ponding is ground out and refinished; it is not left to freeze.

9.5. Pressure-relief ports in freezer walls are checked for free movement, because a freezer without working relief can buckle its own panels when the door is shut on warm air.

## 8. North-east monsoon and the afternoon sun

8.1. Coimbatore's heavy rain comes with the north-east monsoon, from October to
December, not in the June to September months that set the calendar at Nagpur
and Guwahati.

8.2. Rain cover over rear pallets is used at Coimbatore from October to December
whenever it is raining on the apron. The site owns six tarpaulins for this.

8.3. Coimbatore does not bill the customer for rain cover. The monsoon handling
line on the rate card is a Guwahati charge and is not quoted for Coimbatore
loads. Customer service agents who copy the Guwahati line onto a Coimbatore
quotation create a credit note later.

8.4. The hot months are March to May. In those months the afternoon rule in
section 3.5 is enforced strictly, and the wash pad is used before 11:00 so that
washed bodies are not left drying in the midday sun with their doors open.

8.5. The cold block wall sweats in the monsoon. Anything stored against it on
the dry side is moved 30 cm away from the wall from October onwards.

## 6. The shed by the wash pad

6.1. Coimbatore buys dry ice for two jobs only: emergency packing for a
restaurant chain whose own freezer has failed, and top-up of a frozen body that
has to wait on the apron.

6.2. The dry-ice chest stands in the open-sided store shed beside the wash pad,
not inside any building. The shed has a roof and no walls on two sides, so
carbon dioxide does not collect there the way it does in a closed store. For
that reason there is no carbon dioxide monitor at Coimbatore. The chest is never
moved indoors, even in heavy rain.

6.3. Supply and handling at Coimbatore:

| item | Coimbatore rule |
|---|---|
| supplier | Kovai Industrial Gases fills the chest with 60 kg every Tuesday |

## 12. Scrap, waste and returns

12.1. Cardboard, stretch wrap and broken pallets are separated at the back of
the south block. A scrap dealer from Kovaipudur collects cardboard and wrap
every Tuesday and pays by the kg.

12.2. Broken pallets are stacked by the east wall for the pallet repairer, who
comes on the first working day of each month.

12.3. The old chest freezer from the closed dairy room still stands by the
scrap pile. It is not used for anything and it is not to be sold until Finance
writes it off.

12.4. Customer returns are received at dock 2 and checked against the return
challan. Frozen returns go into CBE-FROZEN only after the shift lead has
checked the logger with the Nagpur QA desk on the phone.

12.5. Spoiled stock is not scrap. It follows the spoilage and destruction rules
of the SOP, and it is never given to the scrap dealer, whatever its weight.

## 15. Review of this manual

15.1. The engineering lead reviews this manual after every new room is handed over, and at least once a year.

15.2. Contractors may suggest changes in writing; each suggestion gets a written answer.

## 14. Records

14.1. The signed commissioning record, the test sheets and the thermal images are kept for the life of the room and three years after it is demolished or converted.

14.2. Copies go to the site QA lead, who keeps them with the room's mapping studies, and to the site manager, who keeps them with the lease or the title documents.

14.3. Nothing in the record is rewritten after signing. A correction is a new sheet that refers to the old one and is signed in the same way.

## How many items

Their firm's method sets the numbers, and they do not negotiate them. For a control that runs monthly, their attribute test uses 2 items picked from the year; for a control that runs daily or with every transaction, 25 items; for a control that runs once a year, the single occurrence. If one item fails, they extend the test or report the control as not working.

Their sampling is done by the audit software from listings we provide. Make sure every listing you hand over is complete and carries its control total, because they will check that before they pick anything.

## 5. Picking what to look at

5.1. Most controls are tested by picking items from the period under review and checking that the control worked on each one. The number of items depends on how often the control operates, not on the size of the population.

5.2. For a control that operates monthly, attribute testing uses 25 items under random sampling; for one that operates daily or with every transaction, 40 items; for a quarterly control, all of the quarters in the period. A single exception in the items picked is reported, whatever its value.

5.3. For sampling, items are picked at random from a complete listing that the auditor has checked for completeness against a control total. Picking from a listing someone else filtered is not random, however it was produced.

5.4. The 2025 charter used smaller attribute samples; they were raised for this programme because two findings in the first year rested on too few items to persuade anyone. The method and the seed used for random selection are recorded in the working papers so that another auditor could pick the same items.

## Items to test

For attribute testing: 15 items for a monthly control and 25 for a daily or transactional one. The sampling method is recorded in the working papers.

# Internal Audit Programme 2026-27

## 1. Why there is an internal audit team

1.1. Until 2025 Quillfern had no internal audit function of its own. The statutory auditors came once a year, customers audited the sites that held their stock, and certification bodies looked at the quality system, but nobody inside the company was paid to ask, across all departments, whether the controls people relied on were actually working.

1.2. The board set up the Internal Audit team in August 2025, reporting to the board on audit matters and to the Chief Financial Officer for day-to-day administration. This programme is the team's plan for the year from April 2026 to March 2027 and the rulebook it works to.

1.3. The programme is written for three readers. The board needs to know what will be looked at and why. Department heads need to know what will be asked of their teams and when. And the auditors themselves need one place where the working rules are written down, so that two auditors on the same kind of job reach the same kind of conclusion.

1.4. Internal Audit does not run any process, approve any transaction or sign any document on behalf of another department. An auditor who is asked to "just sign this while you're here" declines, however small the item. The team's value lies in having no part in what it examines.

1.5. Nothing in this programme changes an operating procedure. Where an engagement finds that a procedure is unclear or unworkable, the report says so and the procedure's owner decides what to change.

## How they work

The audit team walks through each process first, with the person who runs it, and then picks items to check that the controls in the process worked. They tell us which items they want on the morning of each day, not in advance.

## Data tests

A duplicate payment test is run each quarter on supplier payments. A Benford test on expense claims is run once a year.

## Cash floats

Each site's petty cash imprest is Rs. 10,000. Internal Audit counts it once a year by surprise. Shortages above Rs. 1,000 are reported to Finance.

## 9. Counting the money

9.1. Every Quillfern site holds a petty cash float for small purchases that cannot wait for a purchase order: courier charges, a replacement padlock, tea for a visiting inspector. It is an imprest: topped back up to a fixed figure against vouchers, never increased because a month was busy.

9.2. The float is Rs. 15,000 at each site and Rs. 25,000 at head office. Internal Audit counts it by surprise twice a year at every site, with the custodian present, and reconciles cash plus vouchers to the fixed figure.

9.3. A petty cash shortage of more than Rs. 500 is reported to the head of Finance the same day, with the custodian's written explanation.

9.4. The counts in 2025 were yearly and each imprest smaller; both changed in this programme.

## Staffing

Nobody audits a function they worked in during the previous 12 months. Engagement leads change after five consecutive audits of the same area; rotation is planned by the head of the team. Threats to independence go to the board chair.

## Remit

The team reports to the board on audit matters and to the Chief Financial Officer for administration. It runs no process and signs nothing for another department.

## Reports

The final report is issued within 30 working days of the exit meeting and goes to the department head, the Chief Financial Officer and the board's audit committee.

# Energy and Utilities Manual, Ludhiana DC

## 1. Purpose and reach

1.1. Ludhiana DC is the first Quillfern building north of the Vindhyas built from the ground up for cold storage, and the first one that pays for its own electricity at an industrial tariff from the day it opened. It stands on the Ladhowal bypass, on a plot the company owns outright, with a chilled block, a frozen block, a small ambient store and a two-storey office facing the gate.

1.2. This manual says how the building gets its power and water, how those supplies are protected, how they are measured, and who answers when one of them fails. It is written for the engineering team on site, for the shift leads who are the first to notice when something is wrong, and for Finance, which pays the bills and wants to know why they move.

1.3. The manual sets no product temperature and changes no quality rule. When a utility fails and stock is at risk, the stock is handled under the company procedures for excursions and quarantine, and this manual only says how to get the plant running again.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the utilities note written while the building was being commissioned in 2025. That note was useful at the time but several of its figures were guesses made before the site had run through a Punjab summer and a Punjab winter. Where a figure changed, the section that carries it says so.

1.5. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns this manual. Harpreet Bains, the electrical supervisor, owns the substation, the switch room and the earthing. The two of them sign every change to the plant that this manual covers, and neither signs alone.

1.6. Copies are kept in the engineering office, in the switch room and at the gate cabin. A copy found anywhere else, including a photograph on a personal phone, is out of date by assumption.

## 1. The six units

1.1. The pool owns six units, MCR-1 to MCR-6. Each is a 20-foot insulated
container with a refrigeration unit at one end, a personnel door at the other,
internal shelving and a controller that logs the inside temperature every
minute.

1.2. MCR-1 to MCR-4 run at +2 to +8 C and are used for chilled medicine and
chilled food. MCR-5 and MCR-6 can also run at -20 C and are used for frozen
stock or for vaccines that are shipped frozen.

1.3. At any time about four units are out on campaign hires of a few weeks and
two are on long hires. The pool coordinator keeps the deployment board.

1.4. Every unit carries its number on both long sides and on the door. A unit is
never relabelled, even after a refurbishment.

1.5. The units were bought in 2024 and 2025. Their refrigeration units are under
the maker's warranty until the dates written on the inside of each door.

## 14. Changes to this manual

14.1. Revision 2 (February 2026) lengthened the stability hold after a campaign
unit drifted.

14.2. Revision 3 (July 2026) added the long-hire daily charge and the rule that
a move within a site is a new placement.

14.3. The pool lead reviews this manual every January.

## 7. Forklifts and the docks

7.1. Only people holding a current site licence drive forklifts, reach trucks or powered pallet trucks. The licence is issued after a practical test by the training provider and renewed every three years.

7.2. Forklifts are checked by their drivers at the start of every shift: brakes, horn, lights, forks, chains, tyres and the seat belt. A failed check takes the truck out of use until the engineering team has repaired it.

7.3. Drivers wear the seat belt, keep the forks low when travelling, and never carry a passenger. A load that blocks the driver's view is driven in reverse.

7.4. Dock levellers and dock doors are operated only by trained staff. A vehicle is chocked and its driver's keys are in the dock office before anyone enters the trailer.

7.5. Speed limits inside the building are 8 km/h in the aisles and walking pace in the cold rooms.

## 5. Protective equipment

5.1. Safety shoes and high-visibility vests are worn everywhere outside the office, the canteen and the locker rooms. Hard hats are worn on the docks, in the yard and anywhere work is going on overhead.

5.2. Freezer suits, gloves, balaclavas and boots are issued to named people for work in the frozen block. They are not shared, and a suit that no longer closes properly is exchanged at Stores the same day.

5.3. Gloves for chilled-room work, chemical gloves for cleaning and face shields for any work with dry ice are kept on the racks beside the work, not in personal lockers.

5.4. Equipment that is damaged or worn out is handed in and replaced, never repaired with tape. Stores keeps a stock of every item in every size worn on the site.

5.5. A person who turns up without their protective equipment does not start work until it is found or replaced.

# Containerised Unit Operating Manual

How the engineering pool's containerised cold rooms are placed, powered,
started, used, moved and looked after. The units are hired out to customers who
need cold space where Quillfern has no building: hospitals running vaccination
campaigns, a dairy cooperative's collection centre in the flush season, a
programme that needs a small store in a city neighbourhood. The manual is for
the engineers who place and service the units and for the customer's people who
use them day to day.

## 10. Alarms and the duty phone

10.1. The controller calls the duty phone for a high or low temperature, a door
left open, a power failure and a controller fault.

10.2. The pool engineer on duty answers the duty phone at all hours and calls
back the customer's lead within 15 minutes.

10.3. A temperature alarm is handled under the company's excursion rules. The
customer's staff do not move stock out of the unit unless the engineer tells
them to.

10.4. Each alarm and its outcome are written in the pool's alarm log.

## 6. Defrost and the drain

6.1. Chilled units defrost four times a day for about 20 minutes each time.
Frozen units defrost every six hours. The controller log shows each defrost.

6.2. Defrost water runs out through a heated drain at the condenser end. The
drain outlet is kept clear of soil, leaves and plastic.

6.3. A short rise in air temperature during defrost is expected and is not a
fault. Stock temperature hardly moves.

6.4. A unit that ices up inside is reported to the duty phone. The customer's
staff do not chip ice from the evaporator.

## 9. Measuring small volumes

9.1. Microbiology depends on measuring small volumes of sample and diluent accurately. An error of a few per cent in a single pipette stroke becomes a large error in the count.

9.2. Every pipette in use is checked every three months by weighing the water it delivers on the laboratory balance, at its nominal volume and at a tenth of it, ten times each. The mean must be within 1 per cent of the nominal volume, and the spread within the maker's figure.

9.3. One that fails is labelled out of use and sent to the maker's service agent; one dropped on the floor is checked before it is used again, whatever it looks like.

9.4. The gravimetric check uses the laboratory balance, which is itself checked every morning with a certified weight and calibrated every year by an outside laboratory.

9.5. Results of every check are kept in the equipment file, and gravimetric figures are plotted so that drift shows.

## Dropped tools

Any measuring tool that has been dropped is checked before use, whatever it looks like.

## 9. Wood in, wood out

9.1. Pallets at the site are exchanged one for one. A trailer that brings in
twenty-two loaded pallets takes away twenty-two empty ones, so that neither side
ends up holding the other's wood.

9.2. Pallets are counted at the dock when a trailer is unloaded and again when
the empties are loaded. Both counts go on the pallet sheet and are signed by the
driver and the shift lead.

9.3. Every pallet handed in is looked at on the dock by the shift lead: split
boards, cracked blocks and missing nails are the usual faults. Each one that cannot carry a load is billed back at Rs. 450 to whoever delivered it.

9.4. Damaged pallets are stacked by the south fence for the repairer, who
collects on the first and third Fridays of each month. Repaired pallets come
back into the exchange pool; pallets that cannot be repaired are sold as scrap.

9.5. A driver who disputes a damaged-pallet count photographs the pallet before
leaving, and the office reviews the photograph against the shift lead's note.

9.6. Pallets are never used as dunnage in a van, never burned on site and never
given away, however broken.

## The automatic measuring tools

Every pipette in daily use is checked every six months by weighing the water it delivers, ten times at its full volume. The average must be within 2 per cent of the volume marked on it.

## 4. Samples arriving

4.1. Samples are received at the reception counter by an analyst, who checks them against the request form, labels each one with a laboratory number and records the condition and temperature on arrival.

4.2. Chilled samples arrive in a cooled box with a temperature indicator; frozen samples arrive in a frozen box. A sample that arrives warm, leaking or unlabelled is recorded as received in that condition and the requester is asked whether to test it anyway.

4.3. Samples are stored at their proper temperature in the laboratory's own fridges and freezers, which are separate from the hub's stores and carry their own loggers.

4.4. Food and packaging samples from customers belong to the customer. Nothing is used for anything other than the test requested, and nothing is eaten, taken home or given away.

## 8. When the grid drops

8.1. The site has two gensets on a common panel. They start automatically when
grid power fails and carry FC-A, the cell, the plant room and the apron lights.
The canteen and the office air conditioning are not on the genset panel.

8.2. The gensets are test-run under load every Thursday at 10:00 for twenty
minutes. The run time, the oil level and any alarm on the panel are written in
the genset log.

8.3. The gensets share one day tank and one bulk tank. The tank is never allowed below 1,500 litres; the night lead dips it at 22:00 and orders a top-up from the listed bowser at 2,500.

8.4. During a long outage the night lead dips the tank every four hours and
writes each reading in the log. A bowser that does not arrive within four hours
of an order is chased by the site manager, not by the night lead.

8.5. Nobody refuels a genset while it is running. Fuel spills are covered with
the sand from the bin beside the tank and reported the same shift.

8.6. After the grid returns, the gensets run on for ten minutes before they are
shut down, and the panel is checked for any alarm that was raised during the
outage.

## 10. Physical and packaging tests

10.1. The laboratory tests packaging components and complete kits for customers' programmes: the compression strength of outer shippers, the thickness and density of insulating liners, the seal strength of food packs, and the performance of complete kits in drop tests and in the environmental chamber.

10.2. Every component is conditioned before testing at a fixed temperature and humidity for at least 24 hours, so that results from a wet week and a dry week can be compared.

10.3. The compression tester and the drop rig are checked against reference loads and heights every month, and calibrated by an outside firm every year.

10.4. Test methods for each programme's components are agreed with the programme's packaging engineer and the customer, and filed in the method file. The laboratory does not change a method on its own judgement.

10.5. Results for complete kits are written up as a short report with photographs of each kit after testing, and signed by the analyst and by Omkar Thorat.

## Glass measures

Glass measuring cylinders and burettes are bought with a maker's certificate and are not checked again unless they are chipped. A chipped piece is thrown away.

## Repairs

Faulty tools go back to the maker's agent in Pune. The lab keeps two spares of each size so that testing never stops while a tool is away.

## 19. Housekeeping

19.1. Benches are cleared and disinfected at the end of each day and before any new piece of work begins. Nothing is left on a bench overnight except work in progress, labelled with its laboratory number and the analyst's initials.

19.2. Fridges and freezers are defrosted and cleaned on a calendar kept on their doors. Out-of-date media, reagents and samples are thrown away at each cleaning, through the waste route for their kind.

19.3. The laboratory floor is cleaned by laboratory staff, not by the hub's cleaning contractor, so that nobody unfamiliar with the work cleans around open cultures.

19.4. A weekly walk-round by the laboratory head checks the state of the rooms, the equipment and the records, and the findings are written in the housekeeping log.

# Product Testing Laboratory: methods and checks (revision 1)

Issued when the laboratory opened at the Bhosari hub in October 2025.

## 14. Records

14.1. Request forms, worksheets, raw data, instrument printouts, reports and equipment records are kept for six years, and longer where a claim or a customer's contract needs them.

14.2. Records are made at the time, in ink or in the laboratory system, and corrected only by striking through and initialling.

14.3. Customers' auditors may see the records of tests on their own samples. They do not see other customers' records.

## 13. Safety in the laboratory

13.1. The laboratory handles ordinary food bacteria, not dangerous organisms. Even so, nobody eats, drinks or applies make-up in the laboratory, and coats, gloves and safety glasses are worn at the bench.

13.2. Spills of cultures are covered with disinfectant, left for the time on the disinfectant's label and then cleaned up. The spill is written in the laboratory incident book.

13.3. Chemicals are stored in the chemicals cabinet with their safety data sheets, and incompatible chemicals are kept apart.

13.4. Waste leaves the laboratory only after it has been made safe, through the hub's licensed waste contractor.

13.5. The laboratory has its own eyewash station, first-aid box and fire extinguisher, and every analyst is shown where they are on the first day.

## 18. Training and competence

18.1. Analysts are trained on each method by the laboratory head and authorised in writing only after they have run the method on samples of known result and reached the expected answer three times.

18.2. Each analyst's competence is checked again every year on every method they are authorised for, using blind samples prepared by the laboratory head. An analyst who fails a check is suspended from that method until retrained and checked again.

18.3. Analysts attend at least two external training days a year, chosen with the laboratory head. Notes from each day are shared with the rest of the team at the next weekly meeting.

18.4. The laboratory keeps a training file for each analyst showing every sign-off, every annual check and every course attended.

## 4. Proving the pipework is tight

4.1. Refrigerant pipework is tested for tightness before any insulation is applied over it and before any refrigerant is admitted. A leak found after the pipes are lagged costs days; one found before costs minutes.

4.2. Every brazed joint is inspected by eye and then the whole system is charged with dry nitrogen at one and a half times its design pressure, isolated from the cylinder and left. The pressure must hold for 24 hours with no fall beyond what the change in ambient temperature explains.

4.3. The first Ludhiana build was held for half that time, and a slow leak at a valve body showed itself only after the room was in service.

4.4. A fall that cannot be explained is searched for with soap solution, joint by joint, and the whole test repeated after repair, from the start.

4.5. The test pressure, ambient temperature, gauge serial and times are recorded at the start, after one hour, and at the end. The nitrogen is vented outdoors and never into a closed room; every brazed repair is followed by a fresh test.

# Cold Room Commissioning Manual

## 1. Why commissioning gets its own manual

1.1. A cold room is not finished when the builders leave. It is finished when it has been shown, by tests written down in advance and run by people who did not build it, that it will hold product inside its range on the worst day of the year. Everything between the last panel going up and the first pallet going in is commissioning, and this manual says how Quillfern does it.

1.2. The manual was first written for the opening of Ludhiana DC in 2025 and is now used for the second frozen block at Ludhiana, due for handover in the winter of 2026, and for every new chamber the engineering team builds after it. It applies whether the chamber is built by a turnkey contractor or assembled by our own team from bought-in panels and plant.

1.3. It is written for the engineering lead who runs commissioning, the contractors who build and start the plant, the site QA lead who must accept the room, and the site manager who wants to know when the room can earn money. It does not replace temperature mapping, which follows the company mapping method once commissioning is complete.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the handover note written in a hurry at the end of the first Ludhiana build. Several of that note's figures were the contractor's defaults, accepted without question; this revision sets Quillfern's own.

## 8. When a person is hurt

8.1. Every injury, however small, is reported to the shift lead before the end of the shift and written in the accident book. First aid is given first and the paperwork done afterwards.

8.2. An injury that keeps the person away from their next shift is an lti. The safety officer tells the site manager within the hour, and the site manager notifies the state factories inspectorate in writing within 24 hours, using the form the state prescribes.

8.3. The safety officer's investigation report, with its causes and the actions agreed, is completed within seven days of the injury and copied to the operations head.

8.4. The 2025 rules gave twice as long for both, and the first serious injury of that year reached the inspectorate late.

8.5. An lti is never recorded as anything else to keep a monthly figure clean. The site's safety figures are reported honestly to the board each quarter, and the board would rather see a bad figure than a false one.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

## Pipework

Pipework charged with dry nitrogen. Pressure held for 12 hours. Each brazed joint inspected by the contractor.

## 12. Signing the room into service

12.1. Commissioning ends with a single signed record that gathers every test sheet, every calibration certificate, the as-built drawings, the closed list and the fire contractor's certificate.

12.2. Every test on the record must have been witnessed, and the record carries two signatories for each: the site QA lead and the refrigeration contractor's engineer. The customer whose stock the room will hold may send an observer, whose name is recorded, but the observer does not sign.

12.3. The 2025 note asked for one signature, the contractor's, and nobody from Quillfern could later say who had watched the pressure test.

12.4. A test that was not witnessed by both signatories is void, and is repeated. Neither signature may be added later by phone or by e-mail.
