## How long the number lasts

A return number at Kharadi lasts 7 days from the day the care desk raises it. A parcel that reaches the dark store after that is not put back on the shelf; it goes in the grey tote by the pharmacist's desk until the care desk confirms.

## 3. Before anything travels

3.1. A customer who wants to return goods asks customer service, which checks the customer's contract and issues an rma, the return number. It carries the customer code, the date and a running count, and it is printed on the collection note and on every carton label.

3.2. An rma is valid for 14 days from the day it is issued. Goods that reach the hub after that date are received, put in the hub's quarantine area and held, and the customer is asked to raise a fresh number before anything else is done with them.

3.3. The interim rules of 2025 allowed twice as long, and the hub found itself holding stock that nobody remembered asking to return.

3.4. A return without any authorisation number at all is not accepted at the gate unless the hub manager agrees by phone. Goods that cannot be refused safely, such as chilled stock on a vehicle that has nowhere else to go, are taken in under the same hold as a late one.

3.5. A second authorisation is never issued for goods already in the building; the first number is extended by customer service instead.

## 5. Money

5.1. Every apprentice is paid a monthly stipend, not a wage, and it rises once, when the apprentice moves from the workshop to the floor. Pay is credited to the apprentice's own bank account on the last working day of the month.

5.2. The stipend is Rs. 14,000 a month for months one to six and Rs. 16,500 from month seven; the 2025 outline gave a flat Rs. 12,000. The rise recognises that floor months are longer and often away from home.

5.3. Apprentices placed at a site away from Waluj receive a lodging allowance and their travel to the site and back at the start and end of the placement. The allowance is set by the site and paid with the stipend.

5.4. Overtime is not paid to apprentices, because apprentices do not work overtime. An apprentice kept beyond the shift by an emergency is given the time back the next day.

5.5. No apprentice is bonded. Nobody repays anything for leaving the programme early or for taking a job elsewhere after it, and nobody is asked to sign a promise to stay.

## 8. How marks are given

8.1. Every module ends in a theory paper and a practical task. The practical — a hands-on test on real equipment in the workshop or on site — counts for more, because the trade is learned with the hands.

8.2. A practical passes at 70 per cent and a theory paper at 60 per cent; a failed module is repeated with the next intake. An apprentice may repeat no more than two modules in the whole programme.

8.3. Practical tasks are marked against a written checklist by a trainer who did not teach the module, and the checklist is shown to the apprentice beforehand. Safety items on the checklist are pass-or-fail: an apprentice who skips lockout, for example, fails the task whatever else they did well.

8.4. Marks are given back within a week, with the marker's comments. An apprentice who disputes a mark asks the workshop lead for a second marking.

8.5. The final assessment at the end of the programme is held with an examiner from the apprentice's ITI, and leads to the Quillfern certificate of completion.

## Before anything comes back

The online pharmacy's care desk raises a return in its own system and sends us the return number by e-mail. The number is the rma for that order, and it is printed on the rider's run sheet next to the address.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 9. What the condensers drink

9.1. The site has no municipal supply. Drinking water comes in by tanker to a separate overhead tank with its own filter and is never mixed with the plant supply.

9.2. Water for the evaporative condensers on the plant room roof comes from the borewell at the south-east corner of the plot. Hard water scales a condenser within weeks, so everything drawn from the borewell passes through the softening plant before it reaches the roof.

9.3. Softened water is tested every week by the plant operator, and the reading must stay below 500 ppm; above that, the bleed rate on the condensers is increased the same day and the softener is regenerated.

9.4. Until the second softener was commissioned in May 2026 the limit was looser and the test was monthly; that rule has gone.

9.5. Every weekly reading goes into the water log with the hand-held meter's serial number beside it, and the tds meter itself is checked against a standard solution each month.

9.6. Whatever the tds, condenser sumps are drained and cleaned every three months, and the water-treatment contractor doses biocide under a written chart kept in the plant room.

## Plant water

Condenser water comes from the borewell through the softener, and its tds is checked. Softened water must stay below 800 ppm, tested monthly.

## Testing

The plant operator tests the softened water every day at 10:00 with the hand-held meter. The tds reading must stay below 300 ppm, because the Mohali water is harder than most and the condensers scale quickly; above that figure, the bleed valve is opened one turn and the softener is regenerated by hand.

Every reading goes on the sheet pinned in the plant room, with the time and the operator's initials. The meter is checked against its standard solution every Monday.

## 7. Metering and the monthly energy review

7.1. Every feeder carries its own energy meter, read automatically every fifteen minutes into the building management system and printed as a daily sheet that the morning shift lead initials.

7.2. On the fifth working day of each month the engineering lead holds the energy review with the electrical supervisor, the site manager and someone from Finance. The review looks at units consumed by each feeder, the maximum demand recorded by the utility meter, diesel used, water drawn and the cost of each.

7.3. The site's own meter readings are compared with the utility's bill before the bill is paid. A difference of more than one per cent between the two is raised with the utility in writing, with the site's readings attached, and the bill is paid under protest if the due date arrives before the answer.

7.4. Consumption is expressed per pallet position occupied, not per square metre, because a half-empty building that costs the same to run is a commercial problem, not an engineering one. The figure is tracked month by month on a chart in the engineering office.

7.5. The review ends with a short list of actions, each with an owner and a date. Actions carried over from the previous month are read out first.

7.6. Finance receives the review note within three working days. It is the only document Finance uses to explain the electricity line in the site's monthly accounts.

## Softening

All plant water passes through the duplex softener before it reaches the roof. The softener regenerates automatically on a meter, and the salt tank is topped up every Monday.

## When the supply fails

If the pump fails or the softener alarms, the operator phones the regional engineer at once. The condensers can run for a few hours on the water in their sumps, but not through an afternoon in May.

## Cleaning and dosing

The condenser sumps are drained and cleaned every two months. The water-treatment contractor visits monthly and doses biocide under the chart kept in the plant room folder.

## 10. Who pays for what is lost

10.1. Quillfern is liable for loss of or damage to Vetrix's stock while in its care, subject to the limits in this section and the exclusions in the main body of the contract.

10.2. Quillfern's indemnity for any one consignment is limited to Rs. 5 lakh at Vetrix's invoice price to its distributors. Its total liability in any contract year is limited to an aggregate of Rs. 60 lakh.

10.3. In the first contract year the yearly limit was Rs. 40 lakh; the consignment limit has not changed.

10.4. Neither company is liable to the other for lost profit, lost sales or damage to reputation.

10.5. Claims are made in writing within 30 days of the event, with the delivery records and photographs. The indemnity does not apply to stock damaged before it reached Quillfern, and the aggregate does not include service credits under section 5.

# Transit Loss and Cargo Claims Procedure, TPC 2026

## 1. Why this procedure exists

1.1. Quillfern moves stock that belongs to other people. When a load is lost, stolen, crushed or spoiled between our gate and the customer's, two separate questions arise at once. The first is what we owe the customer under their contract. The second is what we can recover under our own cover. Until 2025 both questions were handled by whoever happened to be nearest the problem, and the results were uneven: some claims were made twice, some were never made at all, and in one case a damaged load was sold for scrap before anybody had asked whether that was allowed.

1.2. TPC is Quillfern's Transit Protection Cover. It is an open cargo policy placed with Sahyadri General Insurance Co. Ltd. through Konark Insurance Brokers. "Open" means that every dispatch under a Quillfern dispatch note is covered automatically, without a separate certificate for each trip, so long as the dispatch is declared afterwards and the conditions below are kept.

1.3. This procedure says what happens from the moment someone at Quillfern learns of a loss until the claim is paid, rejected or abandoned. It is written for site managers, fleet planners, shift leads, QA officers and the claims desk in Finance. Drivers are not expected to read it; the cab card tells them what to do at the scene.

1.4. It does not set any temperature limit, any customer notification window or any rule about quarantine. Those come from the documents that govern them, and a claim never changes them. Nothing in this procedure allows a site to keep, release or destroy stock faster because a claim is pending.

## 16. People who handle Vetrix stock

16.1. Everyone at Ludhiana DC who picks, packs or loads Vetrix stock completes a half-day briefing on the account before their first shift on it: the products, the storage areas, the special handling of government store deliveries and the handling of the frozen breeding stock.

16.2. Only staff trained in cryogenic handling enter the room where the frozen breeding stock is kept. The training is given by Vetrix's gas supplier and refreshed every year, and the list of trained staff is posted on the room's door.

16.3. Drivers on Vetrix routes are briefed on the delivery points, especially government stores and cooperatives that receive only at fixed hours, and on the rule that they do not discuss products with farmers or veterinarians at the delivery point.

16.4. New staff are not put on Vetrix work in their first two weeks on site, and never alone on a delivery to a government store.

## 3. Before anything travels

3.1. A customer who wants to return goods asks customer service, which checks the customer's contract and issues an rma, the return number. It carries the customer code, the date and a running count, and it is printed on the collection note and on every carton label.

3.2. An rma is valid for 14 days from the day it is issued. Goods that reach the hub after that date are received, put in the hub's quarantine area and held, and the customer is asked to raise a fresh number before anything else is done with them.

3.3. The interim rules of 2025 allowed twice as long, and the hub found itself holding stock that nobody remembered asking to return.

3.4. A return without any authorisation number at all is not accepted at the gate unless the hub manager agrees by phone. Goods that cannot be refused safely, such as chilled stock on a vehicle that has nowhere else to go, are taken in under the same hold as a late one.

3.5. A second authorisation is never issued for goods already in the building; the first number is extended by customer service instead.

## 18. Vetrix's own checks

18.1. Vetrix may audit the handling of its stock at Ludhiana DC and at the Bhosari hub on ten working days' notice, and at shorter notice where it has a specific cause. The account manager arranges the visit and the site's QA lead hosts it.

18.2. Vetrix's auditors see the storage areas, the records of its own stock, the temperature records of the rooms holding it and the training records of staff who handle it. They do not see other customers' stock or records.

18.3. Findings are answered by Quillfern within 20 working days with a corrective action, an owner and a date, and tracked at the monthly review until closed.

18.4. Vetrix may also send a representative to observe a delivery to a government store or a cooperative, by arrangement with the account manager. The representative travels in Vetrix's own vehicle, not in Quillfern's.

## 14. Ending the contract

14.1. Either company may end the contract by giving six months' written notice, or at once for a serious breach not put right within 30 days of a written demand.

14.2. On ending, Quillfern hands over Vetrix's stock and records to Vetrix or to a new provider named by Vetrix, in an orderly way agreed between the two companies, and continues to meet this schedule until the last stock has left.

14.3. Frozen breeding stock is handed over unit by unit, with the receiving party's trained staff present, and each unit's level is recorded on handover.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The hub manager reviews this manual every July with the QA lead and the customer service lead, and sooner when a customer's contract or a company procedure changes what the hub must do.

16.2. Each revision is issued with a short note of what changed and why. Hub staff sign that they have read the note within a week of issue.

title: Kurkumbh contract laboratory - rapid hygiene swab results we accept
doc_id: QCL-LAB-CRD-15

KURKUMBH FROZEN DEPOT: RAPID HYGIENE SWABS FROM THE CONTRACT LABORATORY

The Kurkumbh frozen depot does not have its own laboratory. Its hygiene swabs of reefer floors, cleaned crates and the blast freezer are read by a contract laboratory in the MIDC estate, whose technician visits on Tuesdays and Fridays.

WHAT THE SWAB MEASURES
The swab picks up atp from food residue and living cells; the technician's hand-held reader gives a number within seconds.

THE LINE WE USE
At Kurkumbh, a reading of 300 rlu or below is a pass. Above that, the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again before it is used.

The depot's line is set by the frozen food customer's contract, which is looser than the lines used for chilled food.

WHAT A PASS DOES NOT MEAN
A pass means the surface was cleaned, not that it is free of germs. Any microbiological test the customer asks for still goes to the contract laboratory in the usual way.

RECORDS
The technician leaves a copy of each day's readings with the depot shift lead, who files it in the hygiene folder.

IF THE TECHNICIAN DOES NOT COME
The shift lead phones the laboratory. Surfaces waiting for a swab are not used until they have been swabbed and passed.

THE READER
The technician checks the reader with the maker's control swabs at the start of each visit and writes the result at the top of the day's sheet. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

Questions to the depot QA officer.

## 3. The outer shell

3.1. The outer shipper takes the weight of other kits stacked on it in the van and the knocks of the doorstep, and it is the first thing a customer sees. It must still be square and closed when it arrives, after a night in a damp van and a day on a stone floor.

3.2. The shipper is a five-ply corrugated box in a regular slotted style, printed in two colours with the Thali Box design. Its strength in the bct, measured by the testing laboratory on conditioned samples, must be at least 450 kgf.

3.3. The 2025 pilot used a lighter board and a lower strength, and lost corners in the monsoon.

3.4. Every delivery of shippers comes with the box maker's bct certificate for that lot, and the laboratory tests one lot in five again on receipt. A lot that fails is returned whole.

3.5. Corrugated stock is stored off the floor, away from the kitting room's damp walls, and used first in, first out.

## 7. Proving a design before it is used

7.1. No new packaging component, and no change to an existing one, goes into service until a complete kit built with it has passed a transit test at the Product Testing Laboratory.

7.2. The test follows an ista procedure adapted for meal kits. A kit is built with dummy food packs and a logger, conditioned, and then dropped ten times from 60 cm onto its faces, edges and corners in a set order. It passes if nothing has leaked, the lid is still seated and the logger shows the food stayed in range for the full doorstep period the programme promises.

7.3. The pilot's simulation used fewer and lower drops and passed a box that failed on the road.

7.4. A simulation of the doorstep follows the drops: the kit stands in a chamber that cycles between the hottest and most humid conditions recorded in Pune in May and the coolest night.

7.5. Results of each ista run are written up by the laboratory and signed by the packaging engineer and Thali Box's product manager before the component is released.

## 13. Suppliers

13.1. Each component comes from an approved supplier named on the component's sheet in the annex to this book: the box maker, the moulder, the pack maker, the label printer and the printer of the paper components.

13.2. A new supplier is approved only after its component has passed the transit test in section 7 and a visit to its works by the packaging engineer.

13.3. Suppliers are reviewed yearly on quality, delivery and price with Thali Box. A supplier with more than two rejected deliveries in a year is put on notice.

## 3. Receiving goods

3.1. Goods are received against the purchase order and the delivery note, and
counted before the delivery note is signed. A short delivery is written as short
on the delivery note in front of the supplier's driver.

3.2. Temperature-sensitive consumables, such as conditioned gel packs, are not
received by Stores. They go directly to the QA room.

3.3. Calibrated instruments are received by Stores and passed unopened to the QA
bench on the same day. Stores does not open an instrument box to check it.

3.4. Damaged goods are photographed, set aside and reported to Finance before the
supplier's driver leaves, where that is possible.

## 12. Suppliers

12.1. Stores keeps the approved supplier list for consumables. At the time of
this revision it includes Vidarbha Gases for dry ice at Nagpur, Brahmaputra
Industrial Gases at Guwahati and Kovai Industrial Gases at Coimbatore, Metrosure
Labs for external calibration, and the seal manufacturer named on the current
purchase order.

12.2. A supplier's replacement goods are received like any other delivery. A
supplier who replaces a batch of faulty seals sends new numbers; Stores never
accepts replacement seals carrying the same numbers as the faulty ones.

12.3. Suppliers are reviewed each year on short deliveries, damaged goods and
late replacement. The review is held with Finance and the DC managers.

12.4. A supplier whose driver has to wait more than an hour at the Nagpur store
is told why, and the wait is noted, because suppliers remember waits when they
quote.

## 7. Gel packs and shipper consumables

7.1. Stores buys gel packs and holds them unconditioned. Conditioning happens in
the QA room, not in Stores.

7.2. Stores keeps at least 44 unconditioned blue-cap packs at Nagpur, enough to
remake two shippers completely.

7.3. Packs retired by QA, for cycle count or for damage, are sent to the
supplier for disposal and recorded as written off. Stores does not throw them in
general waste, because the gel is not general waste.

7.4. White-cap packs are held on a separate shelf, labelled FROZEN GOODS ONLY.

7.5. Spare shipper lids, straps and liners are held by Stores and issued to QA
against a signature. A damaged shipper body is not repaired in Stores.

## 17. Who pays for what

17.1. Thali Box pays for every packaging component used in its kits, at the prices agreed in the annex, together with a handling charge per kit for assembly and a charge per kit delivered.

17.2. Quillfern pays for components it damages in storage or on the line, and for kits it has to rebuild because of a kitting error.

17.3. Components lost because customers do not return them are Thali Box's cost; the customer's forfeited amount goes to Thali Box, not to Quillfern.

17.4. Testing at the Product Testing Laboratory is charged to whichever company proposed the change being tested. Routine lot testing of incoming components is included in the handling charge.

17.5. Prices are reviewed every April, at the same time as the delivery charges.

# Customer notification matrix — Cindermoor 2026

## Who is told, and how fast

| customer class | trigger | notify within | channel |
|---|---|---:|---|
| patient critical | confirmed excursion | 2 h | phone then written |

## 5. Notifications

5.1. Pharma critical stock means vaccines, insulin, and any medicine named by a
customer as patient critical. The customer must be notified within 2 hours of a
confirmed pharma critical excursion.

5.2. Dairy customers must be notified by the next scheduled customer service
check-in unless spoilage is visible, odour is present, or the temperature is
above +8.0 C. In those cases customer service must notify within 4 hours.

5.3. Frozen-food restaurant chains must receive an exception notice by the end of
the business day when the excursion is confirmed. If the vehicle is still on the
road, Fleet Control must also call the receiving kitchen.

5.4. Internal escalation for all pharma critical events goes to Compliance-Red,
the DC manager, Fleet Control if a truck is involved, and Finance if stock is
likely to be destroyed.

5.5. Customer notice must say "temperature excursion under investigation" until
QA approves a final wording. Staff must not promise release, replacement credit,
or insurance recovery in the first notice.

| customer class | trigger | notify within | channel |
|---|---|---:|---|
| patient critical | suspected, unconfirmed | 8 h | written |

| customer class | trigger | notify within | channel |
|---|---|---:|---|
| dairy | confirmed excursion, no spoilage | next check-in | written |

| customer class | trigger | notify within | channel |
|---|---|---:|---|
| frozen restaurant chain | confirmed excursion | end of business day | phone then written |

| customer class | trigger | notify within | channel |
|---|---|---:|---|
| dairy | visible spoilage or odour | 2 h | phone |

| customer class | trigger | notify within | channel |
|---|---|---:|---|
| dry grocery | any | next working day | written |

## 10. Closure

10.1. The QA head or nominated deputy closes pharma critical investigations. The
DC manager may close dairy and frozen investigations only after QA records the
disposition.

10.2. Corrective and preventive actions must have an owner, a due date, and
evidence of completion. "Discussed on call" is not completion evidence.

10.3. Training actions shall be assigned by role, not by name alone, so that new
staff receive the same correction.

10.4. The case file must be kept for seven years for pharma critical stock and
three years for food stock.

## Appendix A: local contacts

At Nagpur, the DC manager is Farhan Qureshi and the night shift escalation lead
is Bunty Chauhan. At Guwahati, the nominated escalation contact is Riniki
Bora. At Coimbatore, the nominated escalation contact is S. Venkatesan.

During business hours, QA desk extension 440 answers routine excursion queries.
During night shift, the shift lead opens the event and calls Compliance-Red for
pharma critical stock. A new driver who sees a reefer alarm must call Fleet
Control first and must not wait until reaching the destination.

## 3. Opening an account

3.1. A new customer is opened by an account manager, never by an agent. The
account manager checks the customer's product classes against what each DC can
store and move.

3.2. A customer who needs vaccines stored at Coimbatore is told plainly that
Coimbatore does not store vaccines. A customer who needs chilled dairy stored at
Coimbatore is told the same.

3.3. A customer who wants its own pricing gets a signed annex. Until the annex
is signed, the standard rate card is the only price that may be given.

3.4. The account manager sends the customer the list of named contacts on both
sides, including who will receive an excursion notice at night.

3.5. A customer who asks to be told of every alarm, not only confirmed
excursions, is told that Quillfern notifies confirmed excursions. A customer
wanting alarm-level alerts is referred to the account manager, who may arrange a
Tessaline customer view under the annex.

## 13. Records

13.1. Tickets, emails, call notes and quotations are kept in the customer
service system for three years, or seven years where the ticket concerns a
pharma critical excursion or a claim.

13.2. The agent writes what the customer said and what the agent said, not a
summary of both.

13.3. A ticket about an excursion carries the QCL-F-17 reference, so that an
auditor can move from the customer record to the QA record without asking.

13.4. Customer service's own notes on a customer's mood or manner are not kept
in the ticket. They belong in a conversation with the account manager.

## 8. Dock and staging rules

8.1. A dock is not a temperature-controlled room. Staging time begins when the
pallet crosses the cold-room threshold and ends when the reefer body is closed
or the pallet returns to the cold room.

8.2. Pharma pallets may not be staged on an open dock for more than 10 minutes
unless a validated passive shipper is used.

8.3. Dairy pallets may be staged on a covered dock for loading, but the dairy
high-excursion rule in clause 2.3 still applies. Staff shall not reclassify
staging time as "not cold chain time" after the fact.

8.4. Frozen stock must move directly between freezer and reefer body. Any delay
longer than 8 minutes must be called to the shift lead.

8.5. The dock team may request a slot change, but it may not waive a temperature
limit. Only QA may decide whether an excursion occurred.

## Who signs

Leela Nambiar signs patient-critical notices. Sanjot Bhamra signs everything else. A
notice is never sent by the shift that found the event without a signature.

## Wording

The first notice says *"temperature excursion under investigation"* and nothing
more. Nobody promises release, replacement credit or insurance recovery before
Quality records a disposition.

## 6. Riding through the gap

6.1. The refrigeration controllers, the alarm panel, the gate barrier and the two servers in the comms room do not wait for a generator. They run through the ups in the comms room, which carries them through the seconds of a changeover and through a generator that fails to start.

6.2. The unit must give at least 45 minutes at full connected load on battery alone. That figure was 20 minutes in the commissioning note, and was raised after a winter night in January 2026 when both sets were slow to start in the fog and the alarm panel went dark for four minutes.

6.3. Autonomy falls as batteries age, so the battery string is replaced every four years, whatever its test results, and load-tested every six months with the site on grid power.

6.4. The autonomy measured at each load test is written in the switch room log beside the date. A string that gives less than the required figure on two tests in a row is replaced early.

6.5. Nothing new is plugged into the ups without the electrical supervisor's written approval. Kettles, heaters and phone chargers found on its outlets are removed.

## Comms room

The ups in the comms room carries the controls, the alarm panel and the servers; its autonomy is set below. On battery it must run for 20 minutes at full load. Batteries are replaced every five years.

# Safety and Incident Manual, Ludhiana DC

## 1. What this manual is for

1.1. Ludhiana DC employs about ninety people on two shifts, hosts contractors most days of the year, and receives up to forty vehicles in a day. Every one of those people should go home in the condition they arrived in. This manual says how the site keeps them safe, what happens when something goes wrong, and who is answerable for each part.

1.2. It is written for everyone who works on the site, whether employed by Quillfern, supplied by an agency or sent by a contractor, and for the managers who plan their work. Drivers of visiting vehicles are covered by the gate rules in section 12 and by their own employers' rules.

1.3. The manual does not replace the law. Where the Factories Act, the state rules made under it, or any other law asks for more than this manual, the law applies, and the safety officer tells the site manager what has changed.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the safety rules issued when the site opened in 2025. Several limits in those rules were copied from another company's manual without anyone asking whether they suited a building with freezers at -25 C and a yard full of reversing trucks. This revision sets limits for this site.

## 9. Cold work

9.1. The frozen block at Ludhiana runs at -25 C, colder than most of the company's freezers, and the body loses heat there faster than people expect. Cold slows thinking before it slows hands, which is why the rules below do not depend on how anyone feels.

9.2. Nobody works inside the frozen block for longer than 40 minutes at a stretch, even in a full freezer suit. A 20-minute rewarming break in the canteen or the warm room follows each stretch, with a hot drink available.

9.3. The shift lead keeps the break board for the frozen block and moves names on it; the workers do not keep their own time.

9.4. Signs of hypothermia, such as uncontrolled shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness or confusion, mean the person leaves the cold at once with a colleague and is checked by a first aider. A person who has shown those signs does not go back into the cold that shift.

9.5. In 2025 the stretch was an hour and the rewarming break fifteen minutes, and two cases of mild hypothermia followed; both were changed after the first winter.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

## 7. Metering and the monthly energy review

7.1. Every feeder carries its own energy meter, read automatically every fifteen minutes into the building management system and printed as a daily sheet that the morning shift lead initials.

7.2. On the fifth working day of each month the engineering lead holds the energy review with the electrical supervisor, the site manager and someone from Finance. The review looks at units consumed by each feeder, the maximum demand recorded by the utility meter, diesel used, water drawn and the cost of each.

7.3. The site's own meter readings are compared with the utility's bill before the bill is paid. A difference of more than one per cent between the two is raised with the utility in writing, with the site's readings attached, and the bill is paid under protest if the due date arrives before the answer.

7.4. Consumption is expressed per pallet position occupied, not per square metre, because a half-empty building that costs the same to run is a commercial problem, not an engineering one. The figure is tracked month by month on a chart in the engineering office.

7.5. The review ends with a short list of actions, each with an owner and a date. Actions carried over from the previous month are read out first.

7.6. Finance receives the review note within three working days. It is the only document Finance uses to explain the electricity line in the site's monthly accounts.

# Ludhiana DC utilities note (commissioning issue)

Written while Ludhiana DC was being commissioned, so that the first shift leads and the electrical supervisor had something to work to before a full manual existed.

## 1. What this manual is for

1.1. Ludhiana DC employs about ninety people on two shifts, hosts contractors most days of the year, and receives up to forty vehicles in a day. Every one of those people should go home in the condition they arrived in. This manual says how the site keeps them safe, what happens when something goes wrong, and who is answerable for each part.

1.2. It is written for everyone who works on the site, whether employed by Quillfern, supplied by an agency or sent by a contractor, and for the managers who plan their work. Drivers of visiting vehicles are covered by the gate rules in section 12 and by their own employers' rules.

1.3. The manual does not replace the law. Where the Factories Act, the state rules made under it, or any other law asks for more than this manual, the law applies, and the safety officer tells the site manager what has changed.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the safety rules issued when the site opened in 2025. Several limits in those rules were copied from another company's manual without anyone asking whether they suited a building with freezers at -25 C and a yard full of reversing trucks. This revision sets limits for this site.

## 11. Feet and wheels

11.1. Most deaths in warehouse yards are caused by reversing vehicles. The yard at Ludhiana is laid out so that pedestrian and vehicle routes meet as rarely as possible, and where they must meet, the vehicle waits.

11.2. People on foot keep to a painted route 1.2 metres wide, coloured green and separated from the roadway by yellow barriers along the dock apron. Vehicles keep to 10 km/h anywhere in the yard.

11.3. The 2025 rules had a narrower walkway and a higher limit, and the yard was busier than anyone had planned for.

11.4. Every reversing manoeuvre onto a dock after dark is guided by a trained banksman standing where the driver can see him, and clear of the vehicle's path.

11.5. Nobody stands or walks behind a reversing vehicle, and no pedestrian crosses the yard except at the marked crossings at the end of each walkway.

## 7. Forklifts and the docks

7.1. Only people holding a current site licence drive forklifts, reach trucks or powered pallet trucks. The licence is issued after a practical test by the training provider and renewed every three years.

7.2. Forklifts are checked by their drivers at the start of every shift: brakes, horn, lights, forks, chains, tyres and the seat belt. A failed check takes the truck out of use until the engineering team has repaired it.

7.3. Drivers wear the seat belt, keep the forks low when travelling, and never carry a passenger. A load that blocks the driver's view is driven in reverse.

7.4. Dock levellers and dock doors are operated only by trained staff. A vehicle is chocked and its driver's keys are in the dock office before anyone enters the trailer.

7.5. Speed limits inside the building are 8 km/h in the aisles and walking pace in the cold rooms.

## What may not go in the bags

Batteries, mercury thermometers and loggers are not medical waste and go back to Stores. Food from the canteen goes in the general bins.

## Yard

The pedestrian walkway is 0.9 metres wide. Yard speed limit 15 km/h.

# Ludhiana DC safety rules (opening issue)

## Collapse

The site has two defibrillator units, at the gate cabin and in the canteen. A first aider checks each aed once a month.

## If something goes wrong

A bag that splits, a box that is punctured, or a collection that does not arrive on its day is reported to the QA officer at once. A spill is cleaned with the spill kit hung beside the waste store, wearing the gloves and apron from the same hook, and the cleaning materials go into a fresh yellow bag.

If the contractor's driver cannot produce his licence copy or his vehicle permit at the gate, the waste stays in the store and the QA officer phones the contractor's office. Waste is never handed to anyone else who offers to take it.

## Checking

The checker at the end of the line compares the card colour with the order screen before closing the lid. A wrong card means the kit is opened and the card changed, never sent as it is.

## 6. Paperwork and labels

6.1. Every kit carries a recipe card set, an ingredient list and an allergen card, all printed by Thali Box and supplied to the line in packs of fifty.

6.2. The shipper's end-of-line label shows the customer's name and address, the delivery day and window, the order number and a barcode for the driver.

6.3. A second, larger label on the lid shows the earliest use-by date of any item in the kit. The date is printed in characters at least 6 mm high, so that it can be read by someone standing at the door without bending.

6.4. The pilot printed it smaller, and complaints showed that customers did not read it.

6.5. Every shipper also carries an sscc label so that the kit can be traced through the van and the returns system. The label follows the gs1 standard so that both companies' scanners read it, and a kit whose sscc does not scan is relabelled; the gs1 company prefix used is Thali Box's own.

6.6. Labels are printed on direct-thermal stock that survives condensation. A label that smudges at the line test is reprinted before the kit leaves.

## Supply

Cards are printed by Thali Box and delivered in packs of fifty per colour.

## If something goes wrong

A bag that splits, a box that is punctured, or a collection that does not arrive on its day is reported to the QA officer at once. A spill is cleaned with the spill kit hung beside the waste store, wearing the gloves and apron from the same hook, and the cleaning materials go into a fresh yellow bag.

If the contractor's driver cannot produce his licence copy or his vehicle permit at the gate, the waste stays in the store and the QA officer phones the contractor's office. Waste is never handed to anyone else who offers to take it.

## 3. The outer shell

3.1. The outer shipper takes the weight of other kits stacked on it in the van and the knocks of the doorstep, and it is the first thing a customer sees. It must still be square and closed when it arrives, after a night in a damp van and a day on a stone floor.

3.2. The shipper is a five-ply corrugated box in a regular slotted style, printed in two colours with the Thali Box design. Its strength in the bct, measured by the testing laboratory on conditioned samples, must be at least 450 kgf.

3.3. The 2025 pilot used a lighter board and a lower strength, and lost corners in the monsoon.

3.4. Every delivery of shippers comes with the box maker's bct certificate for that lot, and the laboratory tests one lot in five again on receipt. A lot that fails is returned whole.

3.5. Corrugated stock is stored off the floor, away from the kitting room's damp walls, and used first in, first out.

## 12. Complaints about packaging

12.1. Complaints from Thali Box customers about packaging, such as a crushed box, a leaking pack or a warm kit, come to Quillfern through Thali Box's customer team. They are logged by customer service and passed to the packaging engineer the same day.

12.2. Each complaint is traced to the kit's order number, the components' lot numbers, the van and the delivery time. The packaging engineer writes a short finding within five working days.

12.3. Complaints are counted per thousand kits delivered and reviewed at the monthly meeting with Thali Box. A component whose complaint rate rises for two months running is reviewed with its supplier.

## 1. Nagpur DC, also written NGP hub

1.1. Book Nagpur slots in Dockwise before 15:00 on the previous day. The old
16:00 cut-off moved because the ammonia plant defrost window moved.

1.2. Dock assignment: pharma uses dock 4, dairy uses docks 1 and 2, frozen food

people who remember it, but it is not the booking rule any more, and its Kalpa

still confirms night slots by phone when the VPN is down, and the slot is written

## 9. Cold work

9.1. The frozen block at Ludhiana runs at -25 C, colder than most of the company's freezers, and the body loses heat there faster than people expect. Cold slows thinking before it slows hands, which is why the rules below do not depend on how anyone feels.

9.2. Nobody works inside the frozen block for longer than 40 minutes at a stretch, even in a full freezer suit. A 20-minute rewarming break in the canteen or the warm room follows each stretch, with a hot drink available.

9.3. The shift lead keeps the break board for the frozen block and moves names on it; the workers do not keep their own time.

9.4. Signs of hypothermia, such as uncontrolled shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness or confusion, mean the person leaves the cold at once with a colleague and is checked by a first aider. A person who has shown those signs does not go back into the cold that shift.

9.5. In 2025 the stretch was an hour and the rewarming break fifteen minutes, and two cases of mild hypothermia followed; both were changed after the first winter.

# Safety and Incident Manual, Ludhiana DC

## 1. What this manual is for

1.1. Ludhiana DC employs about ninety people on two shifts, hosts contractors most days of the year, and receives up to forty vehicles in a day. Every one of those people should go home in the condition they arrived in. This manual says how the site keeps them safe, what happens when something goes wrong, and who is answerable for each part.

1.2. It is written for everyone who works on the site, whether employed by Quillfern, supplied by an agency or sent by a contractor, and for the managers who plan their work. Drivers of visiting vehicles are covered by the gate rules in section 12 and by their own employers' rules.

1.3. The manual does not replace the law. Where the Factories Act, the state rules made under it, or any other law asks for more than this manual, the law applies, and the safety officer tells the site manager what has changed.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the safety rules issued when the site opened in 2025. Several limits in those rules were copied from another company's manual without anyone asking whether they suited a building with freezers at -25 C and a yard full of reversing trucks. This revision sets limits for this site.

## 5. Taking the air out

5.1. Air and moisture left in a refrigeration system turn into acid and sludge that shorten the life of every component. Before charging, the system is put under vacuum with a pump connected at both the high and low sides.

5.2. The system is pumped down to 500 micron. The pump is then isolated and the system left; it passes if the gauge stays below 1,000 for 30 minutes. A rise above that means moisture or a leak, and the pumping continues or the leak is found.

5.3. The 2025 handover note took the contractor's default figures, which were looser on both counts.

5.4. The gauge used is electronic, connected as close to the system as the hose allows, and never read through the pump's own dial. The readings at isolation, at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes go on the test sheet.

5.5. Pumping is never stopped early because the contractor's crew is due elsewhere. A rushed vacuum is the commonest fault the engineering team finds in other people's plant, and the micron figure is the one most often written down without being read.

## 3. First days on site

3.1. Every new person, including agency staff and contractors' workers, attends the site induction before starting work. The induction lasts about two hours and covers the site layout, the emergency alarm and assembly point, the vehicle routes, the cold rooms, the protective equipment and how to report a hazard.

3.2. New staff spend their first week with a named buddy who has worked on the site for at least six months. They do not work alone in a cold room, operate a forklift or work on the docks without the buddy until their shift lead has signed them off.

3.3. Contractors' workers are inducted on their first visit and carry an induction card. The card is checked at the gate on every later visit.

3.4. Visitors are escorted at all times and are given a short safety briefing at the gate. They do not enter the cold rooms, the plant room or the yard without protective equipment and an escort.

## 8. Sunlight on the chilled block

8.1. The roof of the chilled block carries a grid-tied solar plant of 480 kWp, feeding the site's own load through the main switchboard. It cuts the daytime bill; nothing in the site's plans counts on it during an outage.

8.2. Dust from the ring road and smoke from stubble fires settle on the glass within days, and soiling is the plant's largest avoidable loss. It is estimated each week by comparing a cleaned reference panel with its neighbour.

8.3. The panels are washed every fifteen days from October to June, and after any dust storm, using demineralised water and soft brushes only; detergent and pressure washers are never used. In the monsoon months the rain does most of the work and washing is monthly. A soiling estimate above three per cent brings the next wash forward.

8.4. The plant has four inverter units. Each is checked once a month for string currents and alarm history, and its log is downloaded to the engineering share; an inverter fault is reported to the solar contractor the same day.

8.5. Nobody walks on the panels; the roof walkways are the only way across, and the roof is closed in rain and wind.

## Before loading

1. Two drivers are named on the dispatch note before departure, as clause 2.3 of the [Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy](08-driver-hours-and-safety-policy.md) requires.

2. The body is run empty with its doors shut until the display holds loading temperature, and then held there for the Pre-Cool Hold Time (PCH) set by the qualification record for that route. Where no qualification record exists, the PCH is 45 minutes.

3. The red sleeve is in the cab locker and holds a spare calibrated logger. No logger, no departure: a hand-held thermometer is not a substitute.

4. Where the qualification record requires a backup passive shipper, its SCT is written in the shipper register. A shipper with no SCT entry is not a backup and the run waits.

# Quillfern Cold Chain Glossary

Plain meanings for expressions used on site. Short forms are defined in the document that uses them, never here, so an expression below appears in its long form only.

back-to-cold — the moment a staged pallet crosses back over the cold-room threshold; staging time stops here.
chlorine contact time — the minutes a sanitising solution must stay wet on a reefer floor before rinsing; wiping it dry early starts the count again.
dead zone — a stretch of road where the telematics unit cannot report; the USB logger covers it and the gap is recorded as missing, never filled in.
door open minutes — the total minutes a cold-room or reefer door stood open in one shift, summed from the door sensor; a measure of load, not a fault.
holding lane B — the covered waiting lane at Nagpur for pharma and frozen vehicles that miss their dock time; nothing is unloaded there.
mean kinetic temperature — the single steady temperature that would give stock the same total heat stress as the uneven record it actually saw; stability letters are written against it, not against the average.
pre-cool hold time — the minutes an empty reefer body is held at loading temperature, doors shut, before the first pallet goes in.
probe grid — the layout of loggers used when a room is mapped; each position is named by rack, bay and height, such as A1-high.
relief point — a named fuel plaza or rest area on a qualified route where a relief driver or a mobile service van can meet the vehicle.
seal watch — time a driver spends guarding a sealed vehicle; it is duty time and never counts as rest.
shipper conditioning time — the hours a passive shipper's gel packs must sit at their set temperature before the shipper may leave with stock.
stability budget remaining — the minutes above the high limit that a customer's stability letter still allows for one lot, once every earlier excursion on that lot is subtracted.
warm pallet — night-shift name for a pallet whose logger has alarmed but whose excursion QA has not yet confirmed; it is handled as quarantine stock until QA decides.
white tag — the RELEASED tag fixed beside a red hold tag when QA lets stock out of quarantine; the red tag stays on.

## 4. Conditions

4.1. From 1 July to 30 September LQ-52 runs with two drivers named on the dispatch note, whatever the departure time.

4.2. Any milk spill in the body is washed out under [the Sunday sheet](32-reefer-washdown-and-sanitation-procedure.md) before the body carries paneer again; a spill is never wiped and reloaded.

4.3. A USB logger travels in the load compartment on every run.

4.4. LQ-52 is valid for the 2025 and 2026 monsoon seasons unless the route changes.

2.1. LQ-52 scores an LRS of 19 of 25, the highest of any qualified lane, because fog, the Sinnar police holding point and two telemetry dead zones each scored 4 or more.

## 11. Running the relationship

11.1. The account manager and Vetrix's supply chain manager hold an operations review on the second Tuesday of every month, by video call or in person at Ludhiana. The review goes through the monthly report, open excursions, returns, upcoming promotions and any problems either side has seen.

11.2. A steering group of senior people from both companies meets twice a year, in January and July. Quillfern sends its operations head and the account manager; Vetrix sends its head of supply chain and its head of quality. The group sets priorities for the next six months and settles anything the monthly review could not.

11.3. In the first contract year the steering group met once, in October, which both companies agreed at renewal was too seldom.

11.4. Minutes of every meeting are written by the account manager, agreed by both sides within a week, and kept with the contract file.

11.5. The governance meetings are the only place where the measures, the credits or this schedule are changed. An agreement made on a phone call between two managers is not a change until it has been through them, and the record of governance decisions is attached to this schedule.

## Meetings

Monthly operations review. A steering group of senior managers is set up. It meets once a year, in October. Changes to this schedule are made only through these governance meetings.

## Once a year

A steering group of senior managers from both companies meets once a year, in March, before Nutrifeed sets its next year's budget. Our operations head and the account manager attend for us.

## 20. If Ludhiana cannot work

20.1. Quillfern keeps a continuity plan for the account, reviewed with Vetrix each year at the July meeting of senior managers. It names the site that would hold Vetrix's chilled stock if Ludhiana DC could not, the vehicles that would carry it there, and the order in which deliveries would be restarted.

20.2. If Ludhiana DC loses power for longer than its generators can cover, or cannot be reached because of flooding or civil disturbance, the account manager tells Vetrix's supply chain manager within one hour of the decision to invoke the plan, and twice a day after that until normal working resumes.

20.3. Measures in this schedule are suspended for the days on which the plan is in force, provided Quillfern followed the plan. Days on which it did not follow the plan are measured as normal.

20.4. The plan is tested once a year by a desk exercise with Vetrix's team, and the lessons are written into the next version.

# Ludhiana DC safety rules (opening issue)

Issued for the opening of Ludhiana DC.

## Collapse

The site has two defibrillator units, at the gate cabin and in the canteen. A first aider checks each aed once a month.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

## 11. Closing out the contractor's list

11.1. As the tests proceed, the engineering lead keeps a single snag list of everything not yet right. Each item is graded A, meaning the room cannot hold product safely until it is fixed, or B, meaning the room can be used while it is fixed.

11.2. Practical completion is certified only when no A item remains open. Every B item must be closed within 30 days of that certificate, and the retention money held from the contractor is not released until the last one is.

11.3. The first Ludhiana build allowed longer, and three of its B items were still open when the retention was paid.

11.4. Each item carries its owner, the dates raised and closed, and the initials of the person who checked the closure. Items are closed on inspection, never on the contractor's word; the punch list is a record of what was seen, not of what was promised.

11.5. A B item still open on day 30 becomes an A item for the purpose of releasing money, though the room stays in use. Contractors who want their retention sooner close their snag items sooner, and argue with the punch grades in writing.

## 9. Cold work

9.1. The frozen block at Ludhiana runs at -25 C, colder than most of the company's freezers, and the body loses heat there faster than people expect. Cold slows thinking before it slows hands, which is why the rules below do not depend on how anyone feels.

9.2. Nobody works inside the frozen block for longer than 40 minutes at a stretch, even in a full freezer suit. A 20-minute rewarming break in the canteen or the warm room follows each stretch, with a hot drink available.

9.3. The shift lead keeps the break board for the frozen block and moves names on it; the workers do not keep their own time.

9.4. Signs of hypothermia, such as uncontrolled shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness or confusion, mean the person leaves the cold at once with a colleague and is checked by a first aider. A person who has shown those signs does not go back into the cold that shift.

9.5. In 2025 the stretch was an hour and the rewarming break fifteen minutes, and two cases of mild hypothermia followed; both were changed after the first winter.

## 5. Taking the air out

5.1. Air and moisture left in a refrigeration system turn into acid and sludge that shorten the life of every component. Before charging, the system is put under vacuum with a pump connected at both the high and low sides.

5.2. The system is pumped down to 500 micron. The pump is then isolated and the system left; it passes if the gauge stays below 1,000 for 30 minutes. A rise above that means moisture or a leak, and the pumping continues or the leak is found.

5.3. The 2025 handover note took the contractor's default figures, which were looser on both counts.

5.4. The gauge used is electronic, connected as close to the system as the hose allows, and never read through the pump's own dial. The readings at isolation, at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes go on the test sheet.

5.5. Pumping is never stopped early because the contractor's crew is due elsewhere. A rushed vacuum is the commonest fault the engineering team finds in other people's plant, and the micron figure is the one most often written down without being read.

## 3. The outer shell

## 15. Less packaging, year by year

15.1. Thali Box tells its customers that it is reducing the packaging in every kit, and both companies have agreed targets that make that claim true. The targets are measured in grams of single-use material per kit delivered, averaged over each quarter.

15.2. For 2026 the target is a reduction of ten per cent against the average of the pilot year, to come mainly from reusing more liners and cold packs and from lighter paper components. Progress is reported at the quarterly review with Thali Box, with the figures from the returns count and the component purchases.

15.3. A change made to reduce packaging must still pass the transit test in section 7. A lighter kit that arrives warm is not a saving; it is a lost dinner and a complaint.

15.4. Plastic wrap is not used anywhere in the kit. Food packs that arrive from Thali Box's vendors in plastic outer wraps are unwrapped at goods-in, and the wrap is sent for recycling separately with the vendor's name noted, so that Thali Box can raise it with the vendor.

## 5. The cold source

5.1. Chilled kits are kept cold by sealed phase-change packs that melt at +3 C, holding the food near that temperature until they have melted. They are conditioned in the Kondhwa cold room for at least 24 hours before use.

5.2. Every chilled kit carries two packs of 600 g each, one under the food and one on top. A kit with frozen items as well carries a third pack, conditioned at -21 C, packed against the frozen items behind the divider.

5.3. The pilot carried three smaller packs and the food between them warmed first.

5.4. Each pcm brick is checked at the line for leaks and swelling and discarded if either is found. Packs are reused only when they come back intact through the box returns, and each pcm brick is retired after 30 uses.

5.5. Gel and ice packs from any other source are never used in a Thali Box kit.

## 6. Paperwork and labels

6.1. Every kit carries a recipe card set, an ingredient list and an allergen card, all printed by Thali Box and supplied to the line in packs of fifty.

6.2. The shipper's end-of-line label shows the customer's name and address, the delivery day and window, the order number and a barcode for the driver.

6.3. A second, larger label on the lid shows the earliest use-by date of any item in the kit. The date is printed in characters at least 6 mm high, so that it can be read by someone standing at the door without bending.

6.4. The pilot printed it smaller, and complaints showed that customers did not read it.

6.5. Every shipper also carries an sscc label so that the kit can be traced through the van and the returns system. The label follows the gs1 standard so that both companies' scanners read it, and a kit whose sscc does not scan is relabelled; the gs1 company prefix used is Thali Box's own.

6.6. Labels are printed on direct-thermal stock that survives condensation. A label that smudges at the line test is reprinted before the kit leaves.

## Labels

Use-by date on the lid in characters at least 4 mm high. Every shipper carries an sscc label to the gs1 standard.

## The pouch

Each pouch arrives from Pinecone already printed with the recipe, the ingredients and the feeding guide. We add only the date sticker: the use-by date in characters at least 3 mm high, black on white, on the back of the pouch below the feeding guide.

## 4. Keeping the heat out

4.1. Inside every shipper sits a moulded expanded polystyrene box with a fitted lid, made of eps beads. It is the only insulation in the kit, and the whole thermal performance of the kit depends on it.

4.2. The liner's walls, base and lid are 30 mm thick, moulded at a density of 20 kg per cubic metre, and its lid fits with a lip that overlaps the walls by at least 10 mm.

4.3. The pilot used thinner walls to save space in the van and kits ran warm on afternoon doorsteps.

4.4. Liners with cracks, chipped lips or a lid that does not seat are rejected at the line. The polystyrene moulder replaces rejected units in the next delivery without charge.

4.5. Every eps liner carries the moulder's lot number on its base so that a complaint can be traced to a mould. The liner is the component customers are asked to return, under section 9.

## 8. Storing components

8.1. Shippers, liners and paper components are stored in the ambient store at Kondhwa, on pallets, in the order they arrived. Nothing is stored against the outside walls.

8.2. Phase-change packs are stored and conditioned in the cold room on their own racks, by temperature, with chilled packs and frozen packs on separate racks clearly labelled.

8.3. Stock of each component is counted every Monday. The packaging engineer orders from the approved suppliers when stock falls to two weeks' use.

8.4. Components that have been damaged in storage are set aside and counted, not used to make up numbers.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

## 4. Proving the pipework is tight

4.1. Refrigerant pipework is tested for tightness before any insulation is applied over it and before any refrigerant is admitted. A leak found after the pipes are lagged costs days; one found before costs minutes.

4.2. Every brazed joint is inspected by eye and then the whole system is charged with dry nitrogen at one and a half times its design pressure, isolated from the cylinder and left. The pressure must hold for 24 hours with no fall beyond what the change in ambient temperature explains.

4.3. The first Ludhiana build was held for half that time, and a slow leak at a valve body showed itself only after the room was in service.

4.4. A fall that cannot be explained is searched for with soap solution, joint by joint, and the whole test repeated after repair, from the start.

4.5. The test pressure, ambient temperature, gauge serial and times are recorded at the start, after one hour, and at the end. The nitrogen is vented outdoors and never into a closed room; every brazed repair is followed by a fresh test.

## 8. Sunlight on the chilled block

8.1. The roof of the chilled block carries a grid-tied solar plant of 480 kWp, feeding the site's own load through the main switchboard. It cuts the daytime bill; nothing in the site's plans counts on it during an outage.

8.2. Dust from the ring road and smoke from stubble fires settle on the glass within days, and soiling is the plant's largest avoidable loss. It is estimated each week by comparing a cleaned reference panel with its neighbour.

8.3. The panels are washed every fifteen days from October to June, and after any dust storm, using demineralised water and soft brushes only; detergent and pressure washers are never used. In the monsoon months the rain does most of the work and washing is monthly. A soiling estimate above three per cent brings the next wash forward.

8.4. The plant has four inverter units. Each is checked once a month for string currents and alarm history, and its log is downloaded to the engineering share; an inverter fault is reported to the solar contractor the same day.

8.5. Nobody walks on the panels; the roof walkways are the only way across, and the roof is closed in rain and wind.

## 9. Weather from the bay

9.1. The coast between Visakhapatnam and Bhubaneswar is struck by storms from the Bay of Bengal in two seasons: April to May, and above all October to December. In 2014 and in 2019 storms in the region cut grid power to the industrial estates for several days.

9.2. From 1 October each year, and from 1 April, the DC keeps enough diesel on site to run both generator sets at full load for 120 hours. The satellite keeps enough for 72 hours at full load. The figure is checked by dipping the tanks every Monday in those months, and a shortfall is reported to the region head the same day.

9.3. When the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issues a red warning for the district, both sites stop dispatching outbound loads that would be on the road during the warning, and vehicles already on the road are directed to the nearest safe yard. Inbound vehicles are received if they can reach the site before the warning period begins.

9.4. Before landfall, loose items on the yards are tied down or brought inside, the solar plant is isolated, and the duty roster for the next 72 hours is fixed so that the people on it can stay on site safely.

9.5. Customers are told of a red-warning stop by the account managers, not by drivers, and are told again when dispatch restarts.

## 7. Bringing the temperature down

7.1. A new frozen chamber cannot be cooled as fast as the plant would allow. Water left in new concrete and in the insulation joints freezes, expands and lifts the floor if the room is cooled too quickly, and repairing a heaved floor means emptying the room for months.

7.2. A new chilled chamber is brought straight to its set point. A new freezer is first held at +2 C for 24 hours to let the floor and panels settle, and then brought below 0 C at no more than 2 C per hour until it reaches its set point.

7.3. The controller is programmed with this ramp before the plant starts, and the programme is printed and signed.

7.4. The first Ludhiana freezer was allowed twice that rate; its floor showed hairline cracks at two expansion joints within a year.

7.5. The floor heater mat is proven working before the pulldown begins, and the room temperature is logged every hour during the pulldown, so that the gradient actually achieved can be compared with the programmed one. Any hour faster than the programme stops the process, and any gradient steeper than planned is investigated before cooling resumes.

## 5. What the bill penalises

5.1. The utility bills the site on kilovolt-amperes as well as kilowatt-hours, so a poor power factor costs money every month even when nothing is wrong with the plant. Large compressor motors pull the factor down; the capacitor bank in the switch room pushes it back up.

5.2. The bank is rated at 360 kvar in six automatic steps. The site's target is a monthly average of 0.98. The utility adds a surcharge to any month that averages below 0.90, and gives a small rebate for any month above 0.95.

5.3. When the bank was first installed it had four steps and a lower rating, and the target was 0.95; the extra steps were added in April 2026 after two summer bills carried the surcharge.

5.4. The controller's display, which shows the kvar switched in on each step, is read at every monthly energy review. A step that will not switch in is reported to the electrical supervisor the same day.

5.5. Capacitor cans are never touched until the bank has been isolated and left for the discharge time printed on its door.

## 17. Later steps

17.1. A second satellite at Rajahmundry, closer to the shrimp plants, is being studied for 2028. It is not approved and nothing in this plan depends on it.

17.2. The second frozen chamber at the DC (section 5.2) will be proposed to the board when frozen occupancy has been above 85 per cent for six months.

17.3. Rail movement of frozen containers from the DC to the north has been offered by a container rail operator and will be tried in 2027 with one customer.

## The tests

Every test in the plan, from the pressure and tightness tests to the temperature runs, is watched by three signatories: our site QA lead, the refrigeration contractor's engineer and the customer's validation manager. None may sign a test they did not watch.

## 12. Signing the room into service

12.1. Commissioning ends with a single signed record that gathers every test sheet, every calibration certificate, the as-built drawings, the closed list and the fire contractor's certificate.

12.2. Every test on the record must have been witnessed, and the record carries two signatories for each: the site QA lead and the refrigeration contractor's engineer. The customer whose stock the room will hold may send an observer, whose name is recorded, but the observer does not sign.

12.3. The 2025 note asked for one signature, the contractor's, and nobody from Quillfern could later say who had watched the pressure test.

12.4. A test that was not witnessed by both signatories is void, and is repeated. Neither signature may be added later by phone or by e-mail.

12.5. Once the record is complete the room passes to the site QA lead for temperature mapping.

## 2. Who can join

2.1. Applicants hold an ITI certificate in refrigeration and air-conditioning, or in an electrical or mechanical trade with a refrigeration module, and are between 18 and 25 on the day the intake opens.

2.2. Applicants sit a written test in arithmetic and basic electrical theory and a short practical in the workshop: wiring a contactor, reading a pressure gauge, brazing a joint. The practical counts for more than the written test.

2.3. A medical examination checks eyesight, colour vision and hearing. Colour vision matters because wiring and refrigerant cylinders are colour-coded.

2.4. Applicants must hold, or obtain within the first three months, a two-wheeler licence. Many floor jobs are reached by motorcycle.

2.5. Quillfern does not charge any fee for the programme, the tests or the medical. An agent who asks an applicant for money is reported to the engineering pool lead, and the applicant is not penalised for having been asked.

## 8. How marks are given

8.1. Every module ends in a theory paper and a practical task. The practical — a hands-on test on real equipment in the workshop or on site — counts for more, because the trade is learned with the hands.

8.2. A practical passes at 70 per cent and a theory paper at 60 per cent; a failed module is repeated with the next intake. An apprentice may repeat no more than two modules in the whole programme.

8.3. Practical tasks are marked against a written checklist by a trainer who did not teach the module, and the checklist is shown to the apprentice beforehand. Safety items on the checklist are pass-or-fail: an apprentice who skips lockout, for example, fails the task whatever else they did well.

8.4. Marks are given back within a week, with the marker's comments. An apprentice who disputes a mark asks the workshop lead for a second marking.

8.5. The final assessment at the end of the programme is held with an examiner from the apprentice's ITI, and leads to the Quillfern certificate of completion.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 13. After handover

13.1. The contractor's defects liability period runs for twelve months from practical completion. Faults found in that period are reported to the contractor in writing by the engineering lead, and the contractor's response time is the one written in its contract.

13.2. The plant is serviced in its first year by the contractor who built it, under the contract, and from the second year by the company's approved service partner for refrigeration, unless the two are the same firm.

13.3. The engineering lead reviews the room's alarm history, energy use and defrost behaviour at three months and at twelve months after handover, and writes a short note of anything that needs changing.

13.4. A room that has been altered after handover, by moving racking, replacing an evaporator or changing doors, is treated as a new room for the tests that the change could affect.

## 6. Quick checks on cleanliness

6.1. Not every cleanliness check can wait three days for a plate count. For surfaces that have just been cleaned, such as the inside of a returned meal-kit liner or a reefer floor before loading, the laboratory uses a rapid swab that gives a reading in seconds.

6.2. The swab detects atp, the energy molecule present in food residue and living cells, and the hand-held reader reports it in rlu. A reading of 100 or below is a pass. From 101 to 300 the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again; above 300 it fails, and the cleaning itself is reviewed.

6.3. Until March 2026 the laboratory's pass line was higher, and liners that passed were later found carrying mould.

6.4. A swab reading measures cleanliness, not safety. A surface that passes still goes through any microbiological test that QA has asked for.

6.5. The atp reader is checked each morning with the maker's control swabs, which give a known rlu figure. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

KURKUMBH FROZEN DEPOT: RAPID HYGIENE SWABS FROM THE CONTRACT LABORATORY

The Kurkumbh frozen depot does not have its own laboratory. Its hygiene swabs of reefer floors, cleaned crates and the blast freezer are read by a contract laboratory in the MIDC estate, whose technician visits on Tuesdays and Fridays.

WHAT THE SWAB MEASURES
The swab picks up atp from food residue and living cells; the technician's hand-held reader gives a number within seconds.

THE LINE WE USE
At Kurkumbh, a reading of 300 rlu or below is a pass. Above that, the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again before it is used.

The depot's line is set by the frozen food customer's contract, which is looser than the lines used for chilled food.

WHAT A PASS DOES NOT MEAN
A pass means the surface was cleaned, not that it is free of germs. Any microbiological test the customer asks for still goes to the contract laboratory in the usual way.

RECORDS
The technician leaves a copy of each day's readings with the depot shift lead, who files it in the hygiene folder.

IF THE TECHNICIAN DOES NOT COME
The shift lead phones the laboratory. Surfaces waiting for a swab are not used until they have been swabbed and passed.

THE READER
The technician checks the reader with the maker's control swabs at the start of each visit and writes the result at the top of the day's sheet. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

Questions to the depot QA officer.

## Rapid swabs

Rapid atp swabs are used on cleaned surfaces. A reading of 150 rlu or below is a pass.

## 5. Growing what is there

5.1. The laboratory counts bacteria, yeasts and moulds on food samples and on surface swabs, so that QA can decide whether a product, a liner or a body is fit to use.

5.2. For the total viable count, the prepared sample is spread on plate count agar and the plates are incubated at 30 C for 72 hours before they are read. Coliforms, yeasts and moulds follow their own methods, listed in the laboratory's method file.

5.3. Until January 2026 the count was read after 48 hours at a higher temperature, which missed slow growers from chilled foods.

5.4. Each incubator is checked twice a day with a reference thermometer, and its reading written on the sheet on its door. One that has drifted more than 1 C from its set point is taken out of use until it has been serviced, and plates inside it are moved to the spare incubator.

5.5. Every batch of agar is tested with a known organism before it is used for samples.

## 8. Checking ourselves against others

8.1. A laboratory can be consistently wrong without knowing it. The only way to find out is to test samples whose true answer is known to someone else.

8.2. The laboratory takes part in an external proficiency scheme for food microbiology twice a year, in which the scheme sends the same samples to many laboratories and compares their results. A result is satisfactory when its z-score lies between -2 and +2.

8.3. A score between 2 and 3 either way is investigated by the laboratory head and the cause written down. A score beyond 3 stops the laboratory reporting that test to anyone until the cause has been found and a repeat sample has passed.

8.4. For packaging tests, where no scheme exists, the laboratory runs one interlaboratory comparison a year with the box maker's own laboratory, testing samples cut from the same sheets. The two results must agree within the tolerance in the method file.

8.5. Proficiency results and each interlaboratory report are shown to the head of QA and to any customer auditor who asks.

## Counts

Total viable counts are spread on plate count agar. Plates are read after 48 hours at 35 C. Each incubator is checked once a day.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The laboratory head reviews this manual every June and whenever a method, a piece of equipment or a customer requirement changes.

16.2. Each revision is explained to the analysts at a briefing, and each analyst signs that they have read it.

16.3. Suggestions for changes come from analysts, from the people who send samples and from customers' auditors. Each suggestion is answered in writing by the laboratory head within a month, whether or not it is taken up, and the answers are kept with the manual's revision file.
