## 10. When a batch is withdrawn

10.1. A manufacturer that withdraws a batch from the market instructs Quillfern through its named quality contact. The account manager confirms the instruction in writing and the hub manager is told the same day so that space is ready.

10.2. Stock coming back from consignees under a withdrawal is held in the locked bay R-2, under the key of the QA officer on duty. It never shares a shelf with returns of any other kind, and the bay's segregation is checked at every shift change.

10.3. The recalled units in R-2 are counted every day and the count sent to the customer's quality contact each week.

10.4. If the customer has not said what to do with the recalled stock 90 days after the first units arrived, the account manager writes to the customer's quality head, not to the original contact, and asks for a decision.

10.5. Breaking that segregation needs the QA lead's written consent. The hub does not take part in deciding whether a batch should be withdrawn, and does not comment on it to consignees.

## Where it goes

Units still on our shelves, and recalled units that chemists send back, go to the taped floor area beside the store office, marked off with red tape and a sign. The segregation is checked by the store manager at the start of every shift.

## Withdrawn batches

Recalled stock is held in bay R-2 under strict segregation and counted weekly. If the customer has given no instruction after 60 days, the account manager writes to the customer.

## Counting

The units in the taped area are counted once a week, on Monday morning, and the count is e-mailed to the distributor's quality manager.

## 11. Packaging that comes back on purpose

11.1. Some programmes send their own reusable packaging back through the hub, and Vetrix Animal Health sends its returned vaccines here from Punjab and Haryana: insulated meal-kit boxes from the Thali Box programme, crates from bakery and dairy customers, and passive shippers belonging to pharmaceutical customers.

11.2. Reusable packaging is counted on arrival and stored by owner in the ambient hall. It is not cleaned at Bhosari unless the owner's contract says so; it is returned to the owner's own kitting site on the next scheduled run.

11.3. Packaging that arrives with product still inside is treated as a return of that product first and as packaging second.

11.4. Broken packaging is set aside and reported to the owner, who decides whether it is repaired or scrapped. Quillfern does not scrap a customer's packaging on its own judgement.

11.5. Each owner receives a monthly count of packaging received, held and sent back.

## Paperwork

The instruction, the weekly counts and every return note from a chemist are kept together in the withdrawal folder for that batch, and the folder is kept for five years after the last unit leaves the store.

## 12. People and training

12.1. Everyone who handles returns at the hub completes the company induction and the hub's own half-day course on receiving, labelling and the returns system before handling stock alone.

12.2. The QA officers on duty at Bhosari are trained by the QA function and hold the same authority as QA officers at any other site. They do not take instructions on pharmaceutical decisions from the hub manager or from account managers.

12.3. Receiving clerks are trained to say "I'll check and come back to you" to drivers and customers who ask what will happen to returned goods. The answer comes from customer service.

12.4. Agency staff may count and move cartons but may not scan them into the returns system or judge them.

12.5. Training is refreshed every year and whenever this manual changes.

## 3. Behind the chain-link fence

3.1. The 2 MVA transformer in the substation yard is oil-filled, and its oil is usually the first thing to fail without anyone noticing. Moisture and sludge pull down the oil's dielectric strength long before anything trips.

3.2. A sample is drawn by the approved testing laboratory every six months, in March and September, with the unit on load. The breakdown voltage must read at least 50 kV. A sample below that is filtered on site within seven days and drawn again after filtering.

3.3. The 2025 commissioning note allowed a yearly sample and a lower pass figure; both were tightened after the first monsoon, when condensation was found in the breather.

3.4. The laboratory's report is filed in the substation folder and copied to the engineering lead together with the dielectric figure from each of the last four samples, so that a slow decline is visible before it becomes a failure.

3.5. Nobody opens the transformer enclosure except the electrical supervisor or the utility's linesman, and never alone.

## 3. Power

3.1. A unit needs a three-phase supply of 415 V, 32 A, through the pool's own
weatherproof socket, which the customer's electrician fits before the unit
arrives.

3.2. Every campaign hire also has a standby genset of the pool's own, wired
through an automatic transfer switch. The transfer switch must bring the standby set on line within 30 seconds of mains loss. The changeover is tested
at commissioning by pulling the mains isolator.

3.3. Long hires at sites with a reliable supply and their own standby may use
the site's standby instead of the pool's, if the pool engineer has tested the
changeover and written the result on the placement sheet.

3.4. The genset's fuel is the customer's responsibility on a campaign hire. The
pool engineer shows the customer's staff how to read the gauge and how to call
for fuel before the tank is low.

3.5. Extension leads, adaptors and shared sockets are never used.

## 2. Who does what

2.1. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns commissioning and decides the order of tests. Navdeep Grewal, the refrigeration engineer, runs the plant tests with the contractor. The site QA lead accepts or rejects the room for product. The site manager is told the dates and is not asked to approve technical results.

2.2. The refrigeration contractor builds and starts the plant and puts it right when a test fails. The contractor does not decide whether its own work has passed; it provides the readings and the engineering lead decides.

2.3. The panel contractor erects the insulated envelope, the doors and the floor finish. The electrical contractor installs the power, controls and alarms. Each contractor has a named site engineer who attends the tests that concern their work.

2.4. Disagreements between contractors about whose work caused a failure are settled by the engineering lead after the test has been repeated. Nobody argues over a failed reading until it has been confirmed.

## 5. Taking the air out

5.1. Air and moisture left in a refrigeration system turn into acid and sludge that shorten the life of every component. Before charging, the system is put under vacuum with a pump connected at both the high and low sides.

5.2. The system is pumped down to 500 micron. The pump is then isolated and the system left; it passes if the gauge stays below 1,000 for 30 minutes. A rise above that means moisture or a leak, and the pumping continues or the leak is found.

5.3. The 2025 handover note took the contractor's default figures, which were looser on both counts.

5.4. The gauge used is electronic, connected as close to the system as the hose allows, and never read through the pump's own dial. The readings at isolation, at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes go on the test sheet.

5.5. Pumping is never stopped early because the contractor's crew is due elsewhere. A rushed vacuum is the commonest fault the engineering team finds in other people's plant, and the micron figure is the one most often written down without being read.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

## 9. The engineer's calendar

9.1. Every unit has a compressor hour meter. Every 1,000 hours on the compressor meter, or every four months if that comes first, the unit gets a full visit.

9.2. A full visit covers the refrigerant charge, the condenser coil, the fans,
the door seal, the heaters, the drain, the controller probe and the alarm call.

9.3. The engineer writes the meter reading and the work done on the unit's
service card, which hangs inside the door, and in the pool's own log.

9.4. A unit that misses a visit is taken off hire at the end of its current
booking until the visit is done.

9.5. Controller probes are checked against a calibrated reference at every full
visit.

## 10. Alarms and the duty phone

10.1. The controller calls the duty phone for a high or low temperature, a door
left open, a power failure and a controller fault.

10.2. The pool engineer on duty answers the duty phone at all hours and calls
back the customer's lead within 15 minutes.

10.3. A temperature alarm is handled under the company's excursion rules. The
customer's staff do not move stock out of the unit unless the engineer tells
them to.

10.4. Each alarm and its outcome are written in the pool's alarm log.

## 15. Review of this manual

15.1. The engineering lead reviews this manual after every new room is handed over, and at least once a year.

15.2. Contractors may suggest changes in writing; each suggestion gets a written answer.

## 14. Changes to this manual

14.1. Revision 2 (February 2026) lengthened the stability hold after a campaign
unit drifted.

14.2. Revision 3 (July 2026) added the long-hire daily charge and the rule that
a move within a site is a new placement.

14.3. The pool lead reviews this manual every January.

## 8. Sunlight on the chilled block

8.1. The roof of the chilled block carries a grid-tied solar plant of 480 kWp, feeding the site's own load through the main switchboard. It cuts the daytime bill; nothing in the site's plans counts on it during an outage.

8.2. Dust from the ring road and smoke from stubble fires settle on the glass within days, and soiling is the plant's largest avoidable loss. It is estimated each week by comparing a cleaned reference panel with its neighbour.

8.3. The panels are washed every fifteen days from October to June, and after any dust storm, using demineralised water and soft brushes only; detergent and pressure washers are never used. In the monsoon months the rain does most of the work and washing is monthly. A soiling estimate above three per cent brings the next wash forward.

8.4. The plant has four inverter units. Each is checked once a month for string currents and alarm history, and its log is downloaded to the engineering share; an inverter fault is reported to the solar contractor the same day.

8.5. Nobody walks on the panels; the roof walkways are the only way across, and the roof is closed in rain and wind.

## Roof plant

Panels are washed once a month. Each inverter is looked at by the solar contractor once a quarter. Losses from soiling are not yet measured.

## Washing

The depot sits beside the highway and a lime kiln, and dust settles quickly. The panels are washed every seven days all year, with plain tap water and soft mops, early in the morning before the glass heats up. Nobody uses detergent, a brush with hard bristles, or a pressure washer.

The weekly yield report shows how much is being lost to soiling; if it shows a sudden drop, wash the next morning instead of waiting for the weekly turn.

## Safety on the roof

Nobody walks on the panels. The roof is reached only by the fixed ladder with its cage, by people who have been trained and who are wearing the roof kit kept in the technician's store. The roof is closed in rain, in strong wind and after dark.

Two people go up together, always.

## 10. Lighting, heating and the office

10.1. All lighting on the site is LED. Chilled and frozen rooms use fittings rated for the temperature, and their drivers sit outside the rooms so that a failed driver can be changed without a person working in the cold.

10.2. Yard lighting is on a photocell with a timer override, and the gate and the dock aprons stay lit all night whatever the timer says. A failed yard light is reported at the shift handover and repaired within two days.

10.3. The office and canteen are heated in winter by heat pumps. Electric bar heaters and fan heaters are not used anywhere on site; a heater found in an office is removed and the person who brought it is told why.

10.4. Floor heating under the frozen block is electric, with its own thermostat and alarm. Its current is read at every monthly energy review, because a heater mat that has failed shows up on the meter long before the floor heaves.

10.5. Office equipment is switched off at the wall at the end of the day except the servers and the alarm panel. The last person to leave the office checks the switches and signs the closing sheet at the gate.

KORVEX K7 PILOT QUICK RULES (WALUJ, 2025)

These quick rules were written for the twenty-device K7 pilot at the Waluj
workshop.

SCREEN LOCK
An idle K7 locks after 5 minutes.

PIN CHANGE
PINs are six digits and are changed every 180 days.

WRONG ATTEMPTS
Ten wrong attempts lock the user out.

BATTERY
Batteries are retired at 400 charge cycles.

LOST DEVICE
Report a lost K7 the same shift. The desk wipes it after 72 hours.

AGENCY STAFF
Agency staff scan under the shift lead's login.

UNRETURNED DEVICE
A K7 not returned by a leaver is recovered at Rs. 15,000.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

## 15. Repairs

15.1. All repairs go through the IT desk. The desk keeps a small stock of spare K7s and LP-40s at each site, so that a repair never leaves a rack short.

15.2. Devices are sent to the Korvex service centre in a padded case with a repair note. Nobody opens a device on site.

15.3. A repaired device is rebuilt from Fernguard before it is reissued.

15.4. A device that has been repaired three times in a year is retired.

15.5. The desk reports device faults by type every quarter to the site managers, so that a site whose scanners keep breaking can look at how they are used.

15.6. Repair costs are charged to the site's cost centre. A site that pays for many repairs is not punished for it; it is asked what is going on.

## 8. Keeping the auditors clean

8.1. An auditor does not audit their own past work, because independence is the whole value of the team. Nobody is placed on an engagement covering a function they worked in, or a decision they took part in, during the previous 24 months. The head of the team checks this when staffing each engagement and records the check in the planning memo.

8.2. Familiarity creeps in slowly, so rotation of leads is planned. An engagement lead takes the same site or department for at most three consecutive audits, after which another auditor leads it; each rotation is fixed a year ahead.

8.3. An auditor who has a family or financial interest in a supplier, a customer or a member of staff whose work is being examined declares it before fieldwork begins. A declared interest usually means a change of staffing, and it never means silence.

8.4. The head of the team reports any threat to the team's independence directly to the board chair, without going through management.

## Staffing

Nobody audits a function they worked in during the previous 12 months. Engagement leads change after five consecutive audits of the same area; rotation is planned by the head of the team. Threats to independence go to the board chair.

## 3. Before anything travels

3.1. A customer who wants to return goods asks customer service, which checks the customer's contract and issues an rma, the return number. It carries the customer code, the date and a running count, and it is printed on the collection note and on every carton label.

3.2. An rma is valid for 14 days from the day it is issued. Goods that reach the hub after that date are received, put in the hub's quarantine area and held, and the customer is asked to raise a fresh number before anything else is done with them.

3.3. The interim rules of 2025 allowed twice as long, and the hub found itself holding stock that nobody remembered asking to return.

3.4. A return without any authorisation number at all is not accepted at the gate unless the hub manager agrees by phone. Goods that cannot be refused safely, such as chilled stock on a vehicle that has nowhere else to go, are taken in under the same hold as a late one.

3.5. A second authorisation is never issued for goods already in the building; the first number is extended by customer service instead.

# Internal Audit: interim charter and working rules

Issued when the Internal Audit team was set up, to cover its first months until the first annual programme was approved.

## 14. The team's own quality

14.1. The team reviews its own work after each engagement: what took longer than planned, where evidence was hard to get, and whether the report's findings were accepted. The notes feed the next year's planning.

14.2. Once every three years an outside firm reviews the team against recognised internal audit standards. The first review is planned for 2028.

14.3. Department heads are sent a short questionnaire after each engagement, asking whether the auditors were clear, fair and courteous. The answers go to the head of the team and, in summary, to the board.

14.4. The head of the team reports to the board once a year on the team's performance: engagements completed against plan, findings by grade, actions closed and overdue, and the results of the questionnaires.

## 12. Closing an engagement and reporting

12.1. Fieldwork ends with an exit meeting at which the engagement lead goes through every finding with the department head, before anything is written down as final. Nothing should appear in a final report that the department hears of for the first time on paper.

12.2. The final report is issued within 15 working days of that meeting, to the department head, the Chief Financial Officer and the Managing Director, and to the chair of the board's audit committee, which reads every final report at its next quarterly sitting.

12.3. Until this programme the report was allowed 30 working days, and too many reports arrived after the people involved had forgotten the details.

12.4. The committee may call any department head to explain an overdue action in person, and may ask why any report missed its date after the exit meeting.

## 8. Frozen breeding stock

8.1. Vetrix sells frozen bull semen to dairy cooperatives and artificial insemination centres. The doses are stored and carried in LN2 at about -196 C and must never warm, even briefly.

8.2. Quillfern holds Vetrix's straws in eight storage dewar units in a separate locked room at Ludhiana DC, and carries them to customers in smaller transport units of the same kind.

8.3. Each storage dewar is topped up with LN2 every 10 days, and its level is measured with a dipstick every day. The level must never fall below 40 per cent of the unit's capacity; a reading below that is topped up the same day and reported to Vetrix.

8.4. LN2 is supplied by Vetrix's approved gas supplier under Vetrix's contract. Quillfern handles it under its own safety rules for cryogenic liquids, which require face shields, cryogenic gloves and a ventilated room.

8.5. Transport units are charged by Quillfern staff trained for the purpose, and their levels are recorded at dispatch and at delivery. Straws are never handled outside a unit.

8.6. In the first contract year the units were topped up every 14 days, and two readings fell below the minimum before a top-up arrived.

## Frozen breeding stock

Straws are held in storage dewar units at Ludhiana DC. Each unit is topped up every 14 days. The level must not fall below 40 per cent of capacity.

## Filling

Each storage dewar is filled every 7 days by Bovigen's gas supplier, on Tuesdays. The level in each is measured with the dipstick every morning and written on the sheet beside it. The level must never be below 50 per cent of capacity; if it is, the supplier is called the same day and Bovigen is told.

## The containers

Bovigen's frozen straws are stored in six large cryogenic containers on the floor of the room, each on its own wheeled base. They are never lifted, tipped or moved while full.

# Service Level Schedule, Contract VX-09 (first contract year)

Revision 1, for the first contract year from 1 April 2025. Replaced at renewal.

## 14. Ending the contract

14.1. Either company may end the contract by giving six months' written notice, or at once for a serious breach not put right within 30 days of a written demand.

14.2. On ending, Quillfern hands over Vetrix's stock and records to Vetrix or to a new provider named by Vetrix, in an orderly way agreed between the two companies, and continues to meet this schedule until the last stock has left.

14.3. Frozen breeding stock is handed over unit by unit, with the receiving party's trained staff present, and each unit's level is recorded on handover.

## 6. How the numbers are counted

6.1. All measures are calculated by Quillfern from its warehouse and transport systems and checked by Vetrix's supply chain team against its own order records. Where the two disagree, the order-level records are compared line by line until the difference is explained.

6.2. Delivery time is the time recorded on the driver's handheld at the moment the receiving party signs, not the time the vehicle reached the gate.

6.3. Quantity and item accuracy are checked against the receiving party's signed delivery note. A delivery note signed without remarks is taken as accepting the quantity delivered.

6.4. Orders cancelled by Vetrix before dispatch are not counted. Orders split by Quillfern into two deliveries count as failed unless Vetrix agreed the split before dispatch.

6.5. Measures are calculated by calendar month and reported to two decimal places. Rounding is applied once, at the end.

## Records

Level sheets are kept for three years.

## Disease alerts

When a state notifies an outbreak, Vetrix may mark orders as urgent. Each is dispatched within 12 hours of receipt. Quillfern and Vetrix agree a daily ceiling if a surge exceeds what can be delivered safely.

## 12. Invoicing

12.1. Quillfern invoices Vetrix monthly in arrears, with separate invoices for storage, handling and transport, within five working days of the month's end.

12.2. Service credits appear as a separate line on the next handling invoice, with a reference to the month and the measure that earned them.

12.3. Vetrix pays each invoice within 45 days of its date. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days; the undisputed part is paid on time.

## Monthly report

Each kpi is defined in this schedule. The report and its one-page scorecard reach Vetrix by the 10th working day of the following month.

## Delivery promise

Orders must arrive complete, undamaged and inside the delivery window. The otif target is a monthly figure. At least 95 per cent of orders each month must meet it. For each full point of shortfall below that, Vetrix receives a credit of 2 per cent of the month's handling invoice.

## 4. Seal books

4.1. Seals come from the seal manufacturer in books, already numbered in order.
Stores records the first and last number of each book received.

4.2. Stores issues seal books to a DC gate one book at a time against the gate's
signature. Besides the book open at the gate, a gate may hold at most two
unopened books in its locked drawer; a third is not issued until one of the two
is opened.

4.3. Spoiled seals marked VOID come back to Stores with their stubs. Stores
counts the stubs against QCL-F-35 every Friday, and a number that is neither
fitted, spoiled nor on the shelf is reported to Fleet Control the same day.

4.4. Each DC holds two bolt-seal cutters, and a lost cutter is replaced by Stores
within one working day.

4.5. Tamper labels for pharma pallets and shipper lids are issued in rolls of
200 to QA, not to the gate.

4.6. Seal books for Guwahati and Coimbatore go by courier, two books at a time,
and are signed for at the gate cabin on arrival.

## 10. Seal books and the security cabin

10.1. Seal books for Coimbatore are issued by Stores at Nagpur and arrive by
courier two books at a time. They are kept in the locked drawer in the gate
cabin, not in the office annexe, because the gate cabin is staffed all night and
the annexe is not.

10.2. Only one seal book is open at the gate at a time. The guard hands a seal
to the shift lead; the guard never fits a seal himself.

10.3. The rest of the sealing rule is the company rule. Seal numbers go on the
dispatch note and in QCL-F-35 before the vehicle moves.

10.4. A vehicle arriving with a broken seal or a number that does not match is
kept outside the south gate, photographed, and reported to Fleet Control before
anyone opens the doors.

## 3. Getting a vehicle in and out

3.1. Reefers use the south gate. The east gate is for dry grocery only unless
the DC manager approves an emergency move, as the old wiki page also said.

3.2. School traffic on Temple Street blocks the turn into the south gate between
07:45 and 08:30. Drivers are told on booking to arrive either before 07:30 or
after 08:40. A reefer is never queued across Temple Street; if the apron is
full, the driver goes round the block and comes back.

3.3. Security holds each vehicle outside the south gate until the previous one
has cleared the apron. The apron takes one reefer and one van at a time, no
more, because a reversing reefer cannot see a second one parked behind it.

3.4. Bookings are made in Dockwise, which Coimbatore joined on 1 February 2026.
The grace table and the cancellation rule are the company rule, not a local
one, and are not repeated here.

3.5. Frozen loads are placed before lunch. After about 13:00 the afternoon sun
lies across the outer apron, drivers open their doors to check paperwork, and
the frozen body loses cold it cannot spare.

3.6. Reversing on the apron after dark needs a spotter with a torch, whatever
the vehicle's camera shows. The apron lights are on a timer that the landlord
controls, and they have twice failed to come on in the monsoon.

## 6. Spare instruments

6.1. Stores holds spare hand-held probes and spare USB loggers for issue, but
does not decide whether an instrument is fit to use. The sticker, put on by QA,
decides that.

6.2. A spare logger's battery is replaced by Stores after 24 months on the
shelf, whatever the logger's sticker says, and the logger then goes back to the
QA bench before it can be issued.

6.3. An instrument with a yellow sticker may be issued. An instrument with a red
sticker or red tape is never issued and goes back to QA.

6.4. Stores keeps a list of every instrument by its prefix number and the date
of its last in-house check, so that QA can see what is due.

6.5. Instruments sent to the external lab are packed by QA and handed to the
courier by Stores. Stores records the date they left and the date they came
back.

## 12. Scrap, waste and returns

12.1. Cardboard, stretch wrap and broken pallets are separated at the back of
the south block. A scrap dealer from Kovaipudur collects cardboard and wrap
every Tuesday and pays by the kg.

12.2. Broken pallets are stacked by the east wall for the pallet repairer, who
comes on the first working day of each month.

12.3. The old chest freezer from the closed dairy room still stands by the
scrap pile. It is not used for anything and it is not to be sold until Finance
writes it off.

12.4. Customer returns are received at dock 2 and checked against the return
challan. Frozen returns go into CBE-FROZEN only after the shift lead has
checked the logger with the Nagpur QA desk on the phone.

12.5. Spoiled stock is not scrap. It follows the spoilage and destruction rules
of the SOP, and it is never given to the scrap dealer, whatever its weight.

## 5. Red sleeve packets

5.1. Stores holds red sleeve packets empty. QA makes each packet up, including a
spare logger checked at the bench, before it is issued.

5.2. A made-up packet comes back to Stores from QA sealed with a tamper label.
Stores does not open it.

5.3. Stores issues made-up packets to DCs and to reefer cab lockers against a
signature. A packet returned unused and unopened goes back on the shelf; a
packet returned opened goes to QA to be made up again.

5.4. Stores keeps at least ten made-up packets at Nagpur at all times. When the
stock falls to ten, Stores tells QA in writing.

5.5. Packets ordered under the red sleeve project are recorded against that
project's budget line, not against the Stores consumables line.

## 23. Contacts

23.1. The Nagpur store phone is on the Operations extension list. Out of hours,
the night shift lead holds the emergency cupboard key, as in section 2.

23.2. Questions about whether an item is fit to use go to QA. Questions about
whether an item may be bought go to Finance. Stores answers questions about
where an item is and how many are left.

# Stores and Consumables Standard

How Stores receives, holds and issues the consumables that cold-chain work runs
on: seals, red sleeve packets, spare loggers, gel packs, dry ice, protective
equipment and forms. It covers the main store at Nagpur and the smaller stores
cages at Guwahati and Coimbatore. It does not say how any of these items is used
on the job; the documents that govern their use do that.

6.4. The two-person figure is lower at Coimbatore than elsewhere because the
path from the shed to the apron crosses the wash pad, which is wet for most of
the day.

6.5. Dry ice never goes into CBE-PHARMA, never into the closed dairy room, and
never into a cab. Unused pellets go back to the chest in the same shift.

# Packaging Specification Book, Thali Box Programme

## 1. The programme and this book

1.1. Thali Box Foods Pvt. Ltd. sells weekly meal kits to households in Pune and Mumbai: a box holding the raw and part-cooked ingredients for four or five dinners, with recipe cards, delivered to the door on a day the customer chooses. Quillfern assembles, stores and delivers the kits from the Kondhwa kitting room, and takes the empty boxes back through the Bhosari hub.

1.2. A kit holds chilled items, such as paneer, dahi, cut vegetables and marinated chicken, and on some weeks frozen items, such as parathas and ice cream. It is left on doorsteps, with security guards and in building lobbies, sometimes for hours. The packaging is what keeps it safe there, and it has to be specified, tested and checked like any other part of the cold chain.

1.3. This book is the agreed specification for every packaging component in the programme. It is owned by Quillfern's packaging engineer, Aarti Jog, and agreed with Thali Box's product team. Neither side changes a component without the other's written agreement.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the pack note used in the 2025 pilot. The pilot ran through one summer with packaging chosen for cost, and lost too many kits to warm doorsteps and crushed corners. Several components changed as a result; each section says what changed.

1.5. The book sets no product temperature. Kit temperatures and the action taken when they are missed come from the programme's quality agreement, which this book supports but does not repeat.

## 2. How a kit is built

2.1. A kit is built from the outside in: an outer shipper, an insulating liner, the cold source, the food in its own packs, a divider between chilled and frozen items where both are present, and the paperwork on top.

2.2. Food packs are supplied by Thali Box's own vendors and arrive at Kondhwa already sealed and labelled. Quillfern does not open, repack or relabel any food pack, and rejects any that arrive damaged.

2.3. Every kit is built on the kitting line in a fixed order shown on the station cards, and checked at the end of the line by a second person against the customer's order before the lid is closed.

2.4. The kitting room is held at +12 C. Food packs come to the line from the chilled and frozen stores in small batches so that no pack waits at room temperature.

2.5. A kit that cannot be finished, for want of a pack or a component, is not sent out incomplete. It is set aside, and customer service tells Thali Box, which decides whether to substitute or to cancel.

# Thali Box kit allergen card colours

Taped above the last station on the Kondhwa kitting line, where the allergen card goes into each kit.

## 10. Hygiene of reused components

10.1. Liners and cold packs that come back are cleaned before reuse at the Bhosari hub's washing station, using food-safe detergent and warm water, then a sanitising rinse and air-drying on racks.

10.2. Every tenth cleaned liner is swabbed by the laboratory for hygiene, and a failing result stops reuse from that day's batch until the batch has been cleaned again and passed.

10.3. A liner that smells, is stained or has been written on is not reused.

10.4. Cleaned components travel back to Kondhwa in sealed crates and are stored apart from new components until they have been inspected at the line.

## Returns

Customers pay a deposit on their first kit. Rs. 50, refunded if the box comes back within 7 days. Shippers that cannot be reused are recyclable.

# Thali Box pilot: pack note

Packaging used for the Thali Box meal-kit pilot from April 2025.

## Outer

Three-ply corrugated slotted box, tested by bct. Compression strength at least 300 kgf.

## Checking

The checker at the end of the line compares the card colour with the order screen before closing the lid. A wrong card means the kit is opened and the card changed, never sent as it is.

## Supply

Cards are printed by Thali Box and delivered in packs of fifty per colour.

## Insulation

Moulded eps box, polystyrene walls 20 mm thick.

## Kitting room

Held at +15 C.

## The colours

| allergen card colour | meaning |
|---|---|
| red | the kit contains peanuts or tree nuts |

| allergen card colour | meaning |
|---|---|
| blue | the kit contains gluten but no nuts or milk |

| allergen card colour | meaning |
|---|---|
| green | the kit contains none of the allergens listed on the card |

| allergen card colour | meaning |
|---|---|
| yellow | the kit contains milk or milk products but no nuts |

A kit that contains more than one group gets the card for the highest group in this table: red before yellow, yellow before blue.

## Cold source

Each pcm brick conditioned for 24 hours. Three packs of 400 g each per chilled kit.

## Transit test

Kits pass an ista-style test of 6 drops from 45 cm, followed by a doorstep simulation in the chamber.

## Before every run

Every week, before the Thursday payment run is released, the desk runs the duplicate check on the invoices queued for payment against those paid in the previous twelve months. It looks for the same supplier and amount, the same invoice number, and the same amount on the same day to two suppliers who share a bank account.

A hit holds that invoice back until the desk lead has looked at it. Nothing is released while a hit is open.

## 10. Looking at whole populations

10.1. Some tests are run on every transaction rather than a sample, using data extracted from the finance system. Extracts are taken by the team with read-only access and are never edited; any cleaning is done on a copy and recorded.

10.2. The duplicate payment test runs every month, on the fifth working day, on all supplier payments of the previous month. It looks for the same supplier, amount and invoice number, and for near-matches where one character differs. Every hit is followed up with accounts payable within a week.

10.3. A Benford first-digit test runs once a quarter on staff expense claims, by site and by person. A pattern that departs from the Benford curve is a reason to look, never by itself a finding.

10.4. Results of every run are kept, including runs that found nothing, so that a duplicate missed later can be traced to the run that should have caught it.

## Data tests

A duplicate payment test is run each quarter on supplier payments. A Benford test on expense claims is run once a year.

# Baner payables desk: checks we run before money leaves

The payables desk at the Baner shared-services office pays supplier invoices for every Quillfern site. These are the checks the desk runs itself, as part of preparing each payment run.

## 17. Working with the other auditors

17.1. The statutory auditors may rely on Internal Audit's work where they judge it reliable. The head of the team meets the statutory audit partner twice a year, shares the plan in April and the year's reports in January, and gives them access to working papers on request.

17.2. Customer auditors and certification bodies are not given Internal Audit reports. If a customer asks whether Quillfern has an internal audit function, the account manager may say that it does and what it covers in general terms.

17.3. Where a customer's audit finding overlaps with an engagement in the plan, the engagement lead reads the customer's report and its agreed actions before fieldwork, so that the department is not asked the same questions twice and the two sets of actions do not contradict each other.

17.4. Findings from the insurers' surveys and from regulators' inspections are added to the risk register when the team plans the next year. They are not repeated as Internal Audit findings unless the team has tested the matter itself.

17.5. Nothing Internal Audit learns from another auditor's work is passed on outside the company without the head of the team's approval and, where the work belongs to someone else, that party's agreement.

## 8. Keeping the auditors clean

8.1. An auditor does not audit their own past work, because independence is the whole value of the team. Nobody is placed on an engagement covering a function they worked in, or a decision they took part in, during the previous 24 months. The head of the team checks this when staffing each engagement and records the check in the planning memo.

8.2. Familiarity creeps in slowly, so rotation of leads is planned. An engagement lead takes the same site or department for at most three consecutive audits, after which another auditor leads it; each rotation is fixed a year ahead.

8.3. An auditor who has a family or financial interest in a supplier, a customer or a member of staff whose work is being examined declares it before fieldwork begins. A declared interest usually means a change of staffing, and it never means silence.

8.4. The head of the team reports any threat to the team's independence directly to the board chair, without going through management.

# Baner payables desk - checks we run before money leaves

## Records

The results of every check, including checks that found nothing, are saved in the payables shared folder by date, and the desk lead signs the run sheet to show that each check was done before the run was released.

## 12. Closing an engagement and reporting

12.1. Fieldwork ends with an exit meeting at which the engagement lead goes through every finding with the department head, before anything is written down as final. Nothing should appear in a final report that the department hears of for the first time on paper.

12.2. The final report is issued within 15 working days of that meeting, to the department head, the Chief Financial Officer and the Managing Director, and to the chair of the board's audit committee, which reads every final report at its next quarterly sitting.

12.3. Until this programme the report was allowed 30 working days, and too many reports arrived after the people involved had forgotten the details.

12.4. The committee may call any department head to explain an overdue action in person, and may ask why any report missed its date after the exit meeting.

## Reports

The final report is issued within 30 working days of the exit meeting and goes to the department head, the Chief Financial Officer and the board's audit committee.

## 6. A day in the office

6.1. The office takes orders from customers by e-mail and through the customer
portal. Each order names the delivery points, the cases and the delivery window
for every stop.

6.2. The order desk builds the next morning's van plan from the orders in hand.
The plan is checked by the afternoon shift lead before it is published to the
van drivers at 19:00.

6.3. The cut-off decides which van an order joins. Anything received by 14:00 goes out the following day; anything after that goes the day after. An
order marked urgent after the cut-off is passed to the site manager, who may add
it to a van if there is room and the customer has agreed to pay for a special
drop.

6.4. Until 11 January 2026 the line was drawn at 15:00; it moved an hour earlier when the first outbound wave moved to 05:00.

6.5. Orders received on a Saturday after the cut-off go out on Monday. The site
does not run outbound vans on Sundays except before Diwali and Christmas, when
the site manager publishes a special plan.

6.6. A customer who changes an order after it has joined a van plan is told
that the change will go out on the next plan, not the current one. The order
desk does not reload a van that has been picked.

6.7. Every order and every change is kept in the portal. The order desk never
works from a phone call alone; a call is followed by an e-mail before anything
is picked.

## 4. Starting an engagement

4.1. Each engagement begins with a planning memo, written by the engagement lead and agreed by the head of the team. The memo sets out the scope, the period covered, the controls to be tested, the people to be interviewed and the days allowed.

4.2. The department head receives a notification letter at least ten working days before fieldwork begins, with the memo's scope and a list of documents to be ready. Surprise work, such as a cash count, is the only exception, and it is listed in the memo even though the department is not told.

4.3. An opening meeting is held on the first day of fieldwork. The department head or a named deputy attends, and so does anyone whose work will be tested. The meeting goes through the scope and agrees who will be the contact for document requests.

4.4. Requests for documents are made in writing through the agreed contact and logged by the auditor. A request still unanswered after five working days is raised with the department head; after ten, with the head of the team.

## 6. How findings are graded

6.1. Every finding is graded high, medium or low by the engagement lead and confirmed by the head of the team. High means a control has failed in a way that could cause a material loss, a breach of law or a harm to a customer's product; low means an improvement that would be nice to have.

6.2. A finding of high severity goes to the auditee's department head in a draft report. The auditee's written response, with an action, an owner and a date, is due within 10 working days. Medium findings are due within 20 working days and low within 30.

6.3. An agreed action on a high finding is due for completion within 90 days of the final report, unless the board agrees a longer date.

6.4. The grade is the auditor's decision. A department may argue with it in its response, and the argument is printed in the final report beside the grade, but the grade is not lowered to get a response signed.

6.5. A finding of medium severity repeated from the previous audit of the same area is raised to high.

## 11. Racking and the floor

11.1. The drive-in racking in FC-A is inspected by the racking contractor every
six months. Any damage found between inspections is reported the same shift,
and the bay is closed with chains until it is checked.

11.2. Reach trucks keep to the marked aisles. Nobody walks in an aisle where a
truck is working; pickers wait at the aisle end until the truck has left.

11.3. Pallets are placed so that no carton overhangs the pallet edge. A pallet
with overhanging cartons is restacked in the anteroom before it goes into FC-A.

11.4. The floor of FC-A has a heated sub-floor to stop frost heave. The
sub-floor temperature is checked weekly by the plant lead and written in the
plant room folder.

11.5. Spilled product in FC-A is cleared at once, because frozen spillage under
a truck wheel is as slippery as ice.

## 7. Proving a design before it is used

7.1. No new packaging component, and no change to an existing one, goes into service until a complete kit built with it has passed a transit test at the Product Testing Laboratory.

7.2. The test follows an ista procedure adapted for meal kits. A kit is built with dummy food packs and a logger, conditioned, and then dropped ten times from 60 cm onto its faces, edges and corners in a set order. It passes if nothing has leaked, the lid is still seated and the logger shows the food stayed in range for the full doorstep period the programme promises.

7.3. The pilot's simulation used fewer and lower drops and passed a box that failed on the road.

7.4. A simulation of the doorstep follows the drops: the kit stands in a chamber that cycles between the hottest and most humid conditions recorded in Pune in May and the coolest night.

7.5. Results of each ista run are written up by the laboratory and signed by the packaging engineer and Thali Box's product manager before the component is released.

## 10. Physical and packaging tests

10.1. The laboratory tests packaging components and complete kits for customers' programmes: the compression strength of outer shippers, the thickness and density of insulating liners, the seal strength of food packs, and the performance of complete kits in drop tests and in the environmental chamber.

10.2. Every component is conditioned before testing at a fixed temperature and humidity for at least 24 hours, so that results from a wet week and a dry week can be compared.

10.3. The compression tester and the drop rig are checked against reference loads and heights every month, and calibrated by an outside firm every year.

10.4. Test methods for each programme's components are agreed with the programme's packaging engineer and the customer, and filed in the method file. The laboratory does not change a method on its own judgement.

10.5. Results for complete kits are written up as a short report with photographs of each kit after testing, and signed by the analyst and by Omkar Thorat.

## Transit test

Kits pass an ista-style test of 6 drops from 45 cm, followed by a doorstep simulation in the chamber.

## 11. Vans and handling

11.1. Kits travel to customers in chilled vans running at +4 C. Kits are loaded in delivery order, stacked no more than five high, with heavier kits at the bottom.

11.2. Drivers carry kits by the handles moulded into the shipper, never by the strapping, and never throw a kit onto a doorstep.

11.3. A kit that is dropped from a height in the van or at the door is reported by the driver and checked at the next stop for damage. A kit with a cracked liner is taken back to Kondhwa.

11.4. Vans carry no other customer's goods while kits are on board.

# Packaging Specification Book, Thali Box Programme

## 1. The programme and this book

1.1. Thali Box Foods Pvt. Ltd. sells weekly meal kits to households in Pune and Mumbai: a box holding the raw and part-cooked ingredients for four or five dinners, with recipe cards, delivered to the door on a day the customer chooses. Quillfern assembles, stores and delivers the kits from the Kondhwa kitting room, and takes the empty boxes back through the Bhosari hub.

1.2. A kit holds chilled items, such as paneer, dahi, cut vegetables and marinated chicken, and on some weeks frozen items, such as parathas and ice cream. It is left on doorsteps, with security guards and in building lobbies, sometimes for hours. The packaging is what keeps it safe there, and it has to be specified, tested and checked like any other part of the cold chain.

1.3. This book is the agreed specification for every packaging component in the programme. It is owned by Quillfern's packaging engineer, Aarti Jog, and agreed with Thali Box's product team. Neither side changes a component without the other's written agreement.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the pack note used in the 2025 pilot. The pilot ran through one summer with packaging chosen for cost, and lost too many kits to warm doorsteps and crushed corners. Several components changed as a result; each section says what changed.

1.5. The book sets no product temperature. Kit temperatures and the action taken when they are missed come from the programme's quality agreement, which this book supports but does not repeat.

# Thali Box pilot: pack note

Packaging used for the Thali Box meal-kit pilot from April 2025.

## Outer

Three-ply corrugated slotted box, tested by bct. Compression strength at least 300 kgf.

## 6. Quick checks on cleanliness

6.1. Not every cleanliness check can wait three days for a plate count. For surfaces that have just been cleaned, such as the inside of a returned meal-kit liner or a reefer floor before loading, the laboratory uses a rapid swab that gives a reading in seconds.

6.2. The swab detects atp, the energy molecule present in food residue and living cells, and the hand-held reader reports it in rlu. A reading of 100 or below is a pass. From 101 to 300 the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again; above 300 it fails, and the cleaning itself is reviewed.

6.3. Until March 2026 the laboratory's pass line was higher, and liners that passed were later found carrying mould.

6.4. A swab reading measures cleanliness, not safety. A surface that passes still goes through any microbiological test that QA has asked for.

6.5. The atp reader is checked each morning with the maker's control swabs, which give a known rlu figure. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

## 14. Ending the contract

14.1. Either company may end the contract by giving six months' written notice, or at once for a serious breach not put right within 30 days of a written demand.

14.2. On ending, Quillfern hands over Vetrix's stock and records to Vetrix or to a new provider named by Vetrix, in an orderly way agreed between the two companies, and continues to meet this schedule until the last stock has left.

14.3. Frozen breeding stock is handed over unit by unit, with the receiving party's trained staff present, and each unit's level is recorded on handover.

## 15. Leaving the list

15.1. A partner leaves the list when it asks to, when its approval lapses, when it is removed after probation, or when it is removed for a serious breach: falsified papers, a safety breach that put people at risk, venting of refrigerant, or a breach of confidentiality.

15.2. A partner removed for a serious breach is not re-approved for three years.

15.3. On leaving, the partner returns all induction cards, keys and documents, and its open work orders are closed or handed to another partner.

15.4. Sites are told the same day when a partner leaves the list, and the gate list is updated.

## 5. The main promise

5.1. Quillfern's main promise is that orders arrive at the right place, inside the agreed delivery window, with the right items in the right quantities. Each order meets all of those or it does not; there is no partial credit.

5.2. The share of orders that meet them in a calendar month must be at least 97 per cent. For each full percentage point by which a month falls below that, Vetrix receives a service credit of 2 per cent of that month's handling invoice, up to a maximum of 10 per cent.

5.3. In the first contract year the target was 95 per cent, with the same credit rate.

5.4. An order is excluded from the otif count only where the failure was caused by Vetrix, by the receiving party, or by an event outside Quillfern's control listed in the contract, reported within one working day.

5.5. A shortfall in two consecutive months needs a written recovery plan from Quillfern, whatever the credit paid; a shortfall in three brings the otif figure to the half-yearly meeting of senior managers.

5.6. Credits are deducted from the next invoice, not paid in cash.

## 14. The annual look back

14.1. Every partner is scored once a year by Procurement, using the site managers' records and the engineering pool's opinion. The score is out of 100 and covers attendance times, quality of work, safety, paperwork, and conduct on site.

14.2. A partner scoring 65 or more stays on the list. A partner scoring below 65 is put on probation for six months with a written plan of what must improve.

14.3. A partner put on probation in two consecutive years is removed from the list, whatever its score at the end of the second probation.

14.4. A partner may see its score and the records behind it, and may answer in writing before the score is final.

14.5. Scores are not shared with other partners.

## 5. Seeing them at home

5.1. Category A partners are visited at their own premises before approval by someone from Procurement and someone from the engineering pool. The visit looks at the workshop, the tools, the stock of spares, the gas recovery equipment, the training records and the way the firm logs its jobs.

5.2. The visit report scores the firm against a written checklist, and a firm that fails any safety item on the checklist is not approved until it has put it right and been visited again.

5.3. Category B partners are visited only where the engineering pool asks. Category C partners are not visited.

5.4. The visit is unannounced in its timing but agreed in principle: the firm knows a visit will come within a month and agrees to admit the visitors on any working day.

## 15. Customer audits

15.1. Customers may audit the store on ten working days' notice, and for cause at shorter notice. The RP or the QA lead hosts every audit; the store manager joins for the operational parts.

15.2. An auditor may see any record about the customer's own stock and any part of the building. An auditor may not see another customer's stock records or another customer's audit reports.

15.3. The store answers each audit finding within 20 working days with a corrective action, an owner and a date. Answers are written by the QA lead and signed by the RP.

15.4. Findings from customer audits are added to the store's own corrective action register, so that one customer's finding fixes the problem for every customer.

15.5. A customer may ask to observe a mock recall or a self-inspection walk. The request is granted where the customer's own batch is chosen or where the walk does not expose another customer's records.

## 11. Running the relationship

11.1. The account manager and Vetrix's supply chain manager hold an operations review on the second Tuesday of every month, by video call or in person at Ludhiana. The review goes through the monthly report, open excursions, returns, upcoming promotions and any problems either side has seen.

11.2. A steering group of senior people from both companies meets twice a year, in January and July. Quillfern sends its operations head and the account manager; Vetrix sends its head of supply chain and its head of quality. The group sets priorities for the next six months and settles anything the monthly review could not.

11.3. In the first contract year the steering group met once, in October, which both companies agreed at renewal was too seldom.

11.4. Minutes of every meeting are written by the account manager, agreed by both sides within a week, and kept with the contract file.

11.5. The governance meetings are the only place where the measures, the credits or this schedule are changed. An agreement made on a phone call between two managers is not a change until it has been through them, and the record of governance decisions is attached to this schedule.

## 6. References

6.1. Category A and B firms give two references from customers for whom they have done similar work in the past two years. At least one reference is spoken to by phone.

6.2. A reference from a relative of the firm's owner, or from another firm under the same ownership, does not count.

6.3. Procurement writes a short note of each reference call and files it.

6.4. A bad reference does not automatically stop approval, but it is discussed with the firm and the note of that discussion is filed with the reference.

## 12. Passing work on

12.1. A partner may not pass any part of a Quillfern job to another firm without Procurement's written consent before the work is done. A firm that subcontracts without consent is suspended.

12.2. Consent is given only where the other firm meets the same category's requirements in this standard, including the papers in section 4 and police verification where section 7 requires it.

12.3. Specialist work that the partner cannot do itself — crane hire, scaffolding, a manufacturer's own warranty technician — may be brought in with the shift lead's agreement on the day, but the partner remains responsible for it.

12.4. Agency labour sent in place of the partner's own technicians counts as subcontracting.

## What RF-120 may carry

RF-120 carries frozen food only: frozen restaurant-chain loads, frozen peas and
frozen chicken on the Nagpur intercity lanes.

**RF-120 must never be loaded with vaccines, insulin, milk or paneer.** A frozen
body cannot be run warm for a chilled load, and a chilled load in a frozen body
is a product loss whether or not a sensor alarms. If a chilled consignment is
offered to RF-120 at the gate, the dock team refuses the load and calls Fleet
Control; the dock team may not reclassify the stock to make the booking work.

The frozen target, the excursion threshold and the defrost allowance that apply
to RF-120 are in the `owned_reefer_frozen` truck profile of
[the legacy sensor threshold file](02-sensor-thresholds.yaml), and the excursion
definition that governs a dispute is clause 2.4 of
[the Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md). This
file deliberately repeats neither, because the two have disagreed before.

## What RF-118 may carry

RF-118 is a chilled asset. It may carry vaccines, insulin, milk and paneer. It
must not be loaded with frozen food: the body cannot hold the frozen target and
the frozen profile belongs to [RF-120](18-reefer-RF-120-asset-file.md).

This file sets no temperature limit of its own. Every limit and every excursion
duration for the products RF-118 carries is in
[the Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md), and
the sensor configuration is documented in
[the legacy sensor threshold file](02-sensor-thresholds.yaml). Where this file
and the SOP appear to differ, the SOP wins.

## 5. The cold source

5.1. Chilled kits are kept cold by sealed phase-change packs that melt at +3 C, holding the food near that temperature until they have melted. They are conditioned in the Kondhwa cold room for at least 24 hours before use.

5.2. Every chilled kit carries two packs of 600 g each, one under the food and one on top. A kit with frozen items as well carries a third pack, conditioned at -21 C, packed against the frozen items behind the divider.

5.3. The pilot carried three smaller packs and the food between them warmed first.

5.4. Each pcm brick is checked at the line for leaks and swelling and discarded if either is found. Packs are reused only when they come back intact through the box returns, and each pcm brick is retired after 30 uses.

5.5. Gel and ice packs from any other source are never used in a Thali Box kit.

## Cold source

Each pcm brick conditioned for 24 hours. Three packs of 400 g each per chilled kit.

## 8. Storing components

8.1. Shippers, liners and paper components are stored in the ambient store at Kondhwa, on pallets, in the order they arrived. Nothing is stored against the outside walls.

8.2. Phase-change packs are stored and conditioned in the cold room on their own racks, by temperature, with chilled packs and frozen packs on separate racks clearly labelled.

8.3. Stock of each component is counted every Monday. The packaging engineer orders from the approved suppliers when stock falls to two weeks' use.

8.4. Components that have been damaged in storage are set aside and counted, not used to make up numbers.

## 3. The outer shell

3.1. The outer shipper takes the weight of other kits stacked on it in the van and the knocks of the doorstep, and it is the first thing a customer sees. It must still be square and closed when it arrives, after a night in a damp van and a day on a stone floor.

3.2. The shipper is a five-ply corrugated box in a regular slotted style, printed in two colours with the Thali Box design. Its strength in the bct, measured by the testing laboratory on conditioned samples, must be at least 450 kgf.

3.3. The 2025 pilot used a lighter board and a lower strength, and lost corners in the monsoon.

3.4. Every delivery of shippers comes with the box maker's bct certificate for that lot, and the laboratory tests one lot in five again on receipt. A lot that fails is returned whole.

3.5. Corrugated stock is stored off the floor, away from the kitting room's damp walls, and used first in, first out.

## 12. Complaints about packaging

12.1. Complaints from Thali Box customers about packaging, such as a crushed box, a leaking pack or a warm kit, come to Quillfern through Thali Box's customer team. They are logged by customer service and passed to the packaging engineer the same day.

12.2. Each complaint is traced to the kit's order number, the components' lot numbers, the van and the delivery time. The packaging engineer writes a short finding within five working days.

12.3. Complaints are counted per thousand kits delivered and reviewed at the monthly meeting with Thali Box. A component whose complaint rate rises for two months running is reviewed with its supplier.

Three-ply corrugated slotted box, tested by bct. Compression strength at least 300 kgf.

## 8. Frozen breeding stock

8.1. Vetrix sells frozen bull semen to dairy cooperatives and artificial insemination centres. The doses are stored and carried in LN2 at about -196 C and must never warm, even briefly.

8.2. Quillfern holds Vetrix's straws in eight storage dewar units in a separate locked room at Ludhiana DC, and carries them to customers in smaller transport units of the same kind.

8.3. Each storage dewar is topped up with LN2 every 10 days, and its level is measured with a dipstick every day. The level must never fall below 40 per cent of the unit's capacity; a reading below that is topped up the same day and reported to Vetrix.

8.4. LN2 is supplied by Vetrix's approved gas supplier under Vetrix's contract. Quillfern handles it under its own safety rules for cryogenic liquids, which require face shields, cryogenic gloves and a ventilated room.

8.5. Transport units are charged by Quillfern staff trained for the purpose, and their levels are recorded at dispatch and at delivery. Straws are never handled outside a unit.

8.6. In the first contract year the units were topped up every 14 days, and two readings fell below the minimum before a top-up arrived.

## Frozen breeding stock

Straws are held in storage dewar units at Ludhiana DC. Each unit is topped up every 14 days. The level must not fall below 40 per cent of capacity.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

## 14. Ending the contract

14.1. Either company may end the contract by giving six months' written notice, or at once for a serious breach not put right within 30 days of a written demand.

14.2. On ending, Quillfern hands over Vetrix's stock and records to Vetrix or to a new provider named by Vetrix, in an orderly way agreed between the two companies, and continues to meet this schedule until the last stock has left.

14.3. Frozen breeding stock is handed over unit by unit, with the receiving party's trained staff present, and each unit's level is recorded on handover.

## 20. If Ludhiana cannot work

20.1. Quillfern keeps a continuity plan for the account, reviewed with Vetrix each year at the July meeting of senior managers. It names the site that would hold Vetrix's chilled stock if Ludhiana DC could not, the vehicles that would carry it there, and the order in which deliveries would be restarted.

20.2. If Ludhiana DC loses power for longer than its generators can cover, or cannot be reached because of flooding or civil disturbance, the account manager tells Vetrix's supply chain manager within one hour of the decision to invoke the plan, and twice a day after that until normal working resumes.

20.3. Measures in this schedule are suspended for the days on which the plan is in force, provided Quillfern followed the plan. Days on which it did not follow the plan are measured as normal.

20.4. The plan is tested once a year by a desk exercise with Vetrix's team, and the lessons are written into the next version.

## 10. Noise

10.1. The plant room, the generator enclosure and parts of the dock area are loud enough to damage hearing over time. Levels are surveyed with a decibel meter by the safety officer every year and after any new machine is installed, and the results are posted at each entrance.

10.2. Hearing protection is compulsory for everyone, however short the visit, wherever the survey shows a level of 85 or more. Signs mark those areas, and dispensers of earmuffs hang at their doors.

10.3. People who work regularly in those areas wear earmuffs for the whole shift and have a hearing test every 12 months, arranged by HR with an occupational health provider.

10.4. The 2025 rules set the line higher and the tests further apart.

10.5. A person whose test shows a change is told the result in person and moved away from the loudest work while the provider advises. Results are kept by HR, and a decibel reading in a survey is never treated as a personal medical record.

## Monthly report

Each kpi is defined in this schedule. The report and its one-page scorecard reach Vetrix by the 10th working day of the following month.

## 12. Invoicing

12.1. Quillfern invoices Vetrix monthly in arrears, with separate invoices for storage, handling and transport, within five working days of the month's end.

12.2. Service credits appear as a separate line on the next handling invoice, with a reference to the month and the measure that earned them.

12.3. Vetrix pays each invoice within 45 days of its date. Disputed lines are raised within 15 days; the undisputed part is paid on time.

## Liability

The indemnity for one consignment is limited to Rs. 5 lakh. The aggregate in a contract year is limited. The yearly figure is Rs. 40 lakh.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 9. Counting the money

9.1. Every Quillfern site holds a petty cash float for small purchases that cannot wait for a purchase order: courier charges, a replacement padlock, tea for a visiting inspector. It is an imprest: topped back up to a fixed figure against vouchers, never increased because a month was busy.

9.2. The float is Rs. 15,000 at each site and Rs. 25,000 at head office. Internal Audit counts it by surprise twice a year at every site, with the custodian present, and reconciles cash plus vouchers to the fixed figure.

9.3. A petty cash shortage of more than Rs. 500 is reported to the head of Finance the same day, with the custodian's written explanation.

9.4. The counts in 2025 were yearly and each imprest smaller; both changed in this programme.

## How much

The office's petty cash is kept at Rs. 8,000. It works as an imprest: every voucher spent is replaced from the bank at the end of the month, so the box always returns to the same total.

## 15. The customer's own claim

15.1. A customer's claim against Quillfern runs on its own track, under its own contract, and is handled by the account manager and Finance. The claims desk is told of it and links the two files, but the customer's claim is not decided by what our insurer does.

15.2. Customers' contracts set their own limits, claim periods and evidence rules. Those terms, not the policy terms, decide what the customer gets.

15.3. Customers are not told whether Quillfern is insured for a loss, how much the cover is, or what the insurer paid. A customer who asks is told that Quillfern meets its contractual obligations.

15.4. Nobody promises a customer insurance money, a quick settlement or a particular figure. The first written word to a customer about money comes from the account manager after Finance has agreed it.

15.5. Evidence gathered for our own claim may be shown to a customer's surveyor on request, through the account manager, but the claim file itself is not sent to customers.

## 14. The team's own quality

14.1. The team reviews its own work after each engagement: what took longer than planned, where evidence was hard to get, and whether the report's findings were accepted. The notes feed the next year's planning.

14.2. Once every three years an outside firm reviews the team against recognised internal audit standards. The first review is planned for 2028.

14.3. Department heads are sent a short questionnaire after each engagement, asking whether the auditors were clear, fair and courteous. The answers go to the head of the team and, in summary, to the board.

14.4. The head of the team reports to the board once a year on the team's performance: engagements completed against plan, findings by grade, actions closed and overdue, and the results of the questionnaires.

## 16. Keeping the file

16.1. Each claim file is kept, complete, for eight years from the date of final settlement or rejection, whichever comes later. Files involving a court case or arbitration are kept until three years after the case ends, if that is longer.

16.2. Scanned files live in the Finance document store under the TPC26 number. Paper originals are boxed by policy year and kept in the Finance archive room.

16.3. Physical evidence — seals, logger files, damaged packaging — is kept until the claim is closed, then for one more year, and is then disposed of with the desk lead's signature.

16.4. A file is never weeded to save space. If storage runs short, the desk lead asks Finance for more.

## Counting

The office manager counts the box every quarter, on the last working day of March, June, September and December, with one other member of staff present. Cash plus vouchers must equal the fixed total. A shortage of more than Rs. 200 is reported to the regional accountant by e-mail the same day.

## 5. The ride to the hub

5.1. Most chilled returns come back in vehicles that delivered something else first. Putting returns on that backhaul is cheaper than sending an empty van, but a chilled carton that has already been out of the customer's fridge is fragile, and every extra stop warms it.

5.2. A chilled return rides on a delivering vehicle only if Fleet Control's plan puts that vehicle at the hub within 6 hours of the collection. Where it cannot, a dedicated pickup is sent instead, however small the load.

5.3. Fleet Control records the planned arrival time on the collection note, and the receiving team writes the actual arrival time beside it, so that the rule can be checked month by month.

5.4. The interim note allowed a longer window, and the hub's first summer showed that it was too long.

5.5. Frozen returns are never added to backhaul unless the delivering body is itself frozen; consolidation of frozen and chilled returns in one body is not allowed.

5.6. Planners may combine several customers' returns on one dedicated pickup, but the consolidation is planned by Fleet Control and never arranged by drivers on the road.

## Chilled returns

Chilled returns may ride on a delivering vehicle's backhaul. The vehicle must reach the hub within 10 hours of collection. Consolidation of several customers' returns is arranged by Fleet Control.

## 3. Before anything travels

3.1. A customer who wants to return goods asks customer service, which checks the customer's contract and issues an rma, the return number. It carries the customer code, the date and a running count, and it is printed on the collection note and on every carton label.

3.2. An rma is valid for 14 days from the day it is issued. Goods that reach the hub after that date are received, put in the hub's quarantine area and held, and the customer is asked to raise a fresh number before anything else is done with them.

3.3. The interim rules of 2025 allowed twice as long, and the hub found itself holding stock that nobody remembered asking to return.

3.4. A return without any authorisation number at all is not accepted at the gate unless the hub manager agrees by phone. Goods that cannot be refused safely, such as chilled stock on a vehicle that has nowhere else to go, are taken in under the same hold as a late one.

3.5. A second authorisation is never issued for goods already in the building; the first number is extended by customer service instead.

## 3. Customers we are building for

3.1. Godavari Aqua Exports is the anchor for frozen work. It processes shrimp at two plants near Kakinada and exports through Visakhapatnam. It has committed to an average of 900 pallets a month in storage from the first full month of operation.

3.2. Kalinga Biologicals is the anchor for pharma work. Its fill-finish line near Bhubaneswar starts commercial production in the second quarter of 2027. Until then it will send stock from its western plant through the DC.

3.3. Rushikonda Dairy, a cooperative with a growing ice-cream line, is the first chilled and frozen retail customer. Two retail chains are in negotiation and are not counted in the volumes below.

3.4. No customer is promised space it has not contracted for. Sales may quote, but the region head confirms any commitment above 100 pallets before it is signed.

3.5. Customers are told plainly that the satellite does not store goods.

## 4. The calendar

4.1. Civil works at Atchutapuram finished in June 2026. Racking, refrigeration and the electrical fit-out run through the monsoon, with commissioning in October and qualification of the rooms in November.

4.2. The DC receives its first customer stock on 1 December 2026. The date is fixed by Godavari Aqua's contract and it will not move later without the customer's written agreement. Earlier receipts are refused, however much space is ready, because the rooms will not yet have finished qualification.

4.3. The satellite at Bhubaneswar starts cross-dock work on 1 February 2027, eight weeks after the DC, so that the trunk run can be proven with the DC already working.

4.4. Full volume is planned for the end of the first quarter of 2027. From then until the end of 2028, growth is planned in steps tied to signed contracts, not to forecasts.

4.5. Each milestone has a named owner on the project board kept by the region head, and the board is reviewed every Monday.
