title: Talegaon frozen store returns cage - what happens to frozen stock sent back
doc_id: QCL-OPS-NTE-77
owner: Nitin Bhegade
department: Operations
status: in_force
effective_date: 2025-12-15
applies_to: Talegaon frozen store

TALEGAON FROZEN STORE: THE RETURNS CAGE

Frozen stock sent back by restaurants and retailers to the Talegaon frozen store is held in the returns cage at the back of the freezer, behind the yellow mesh.

ON ARRIVAL
The receiving clerk checks the cartons against the return note, probes one carton per pallet and writes the reading on the note. Anything that arrives soft is photographed before it goes into the cage.

THE DECISION
Every line in the cage gets its grading within 72 hours of arrival. The Talegaon team uses three labels rather than letters: KEEP for stock that can go back to the owner's saleable stock, REWORK for stock the owner must decide about, and SCRAP for stock that must be destroyed. Each label is a coloured bucket tag tied to the pallet: green, orange and red.

WHO DECIDES
The shift lead decides on frozen food. Ice cream that has softened at any point is always SCRAP, whatever the owner says, because it cannot be refrozen safely.

TELLING THE OWNER
The owner is told of every REWORK line on the day it is labelled, by e-mail from the store office, and the line waits in the cage until the owner replies.

SPACE
The cage holds twelve pallets. If it is full, the store manager is told at once; nothing is put in the main freezer to make room.

Questions to the store office.

## 7. Sorting what came back

7.1. Grading is a decision about every line, not a valuation, and each decision is checked by a second person.

7.2. Every line is judged within 24 hours of receipt. Bucket A means fit to go back to the owner's saleable stock under the owner's own rules; B means the owner must decide; C means destruction.

7.3. Grading of pharmaceutical lines is done by the QA officer on duty, not by the receiving team, and a pharmaceutical line never goes into A without QA's signature on the returns system.

7.4. Food lines go to C whenever the packaging has been opened, the use-by date has passed, or the temperature history is missing for a chilled or frozen line.

7.5. Lines judged B are reported to the owner the same day. Until the owner replies, they stay in the area for their temperature class, marked with an orange label.

7.6. A line may move from bucket B to A or C on the owner's written instruction only; it never moves because space ran short.

## 15. The hub's own measures

15.1. The hub is judged on how fast it decides, not on how much it holds. Each month the hub manager reports the share of lines judged within the time in section 7, the share of chilled returns that reached the hub within the time in section 5, the number of lines still waiting for an owner's decision, and the age of the oldest of them.

15.2. The report also counts returns that arrived without a valid number, broken seals found at the dock, damage found at receiving that was not noted at collection, and certificates overdue from the waste contractor.

15.3. The measures are read at the operations review each month, alongside the measures of the other sites. A measure that misses its target for three months running gets a written recovery plan from the hub manager, agreed with the operations head.

15.4. Customers are not sent the hub's measures as they stand. An account manager may draw on them for a customer's own service report.

## Sorting

Every line is judged within 48 hours. Grading puts each line in one bucket: A restock, B owner decides, C destroy.

# Bhosari hub: interim rules for returned goods

Interim rules for the first months of the Bhosari hub, until the returns manual is issued.

## 12. People and training

12.1. Everyone who handles returns at the hub completes the company induction and the hub's own half-day course on receiving, labelling and the returns system before handling stock alone.

12.2. The QA officers on duty at Bhosari are trained by the QA function and hold the same authority as QA officers at any other site. They do not take instructions on pharmaceutical decisions from the hub manager or from account managers.

12.3. Receiving clerks are trained to say "I'll check and come back to you" to drivers and customers who ask what will happen to returned goods. The answer comes from customer service.

12.4. Agency staff may count and move cartons but may not scan them into the returns system or judge them.

12.5. Training is refreshed every year and whenever this manual changes.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The hub manager reviews this manual every July with the QA lead and the customer service lead, and sooner when a customer's contract or a company procedure changes what the hub must do.

16.2. Each revision is issued with a short note of what changed and why. Hub staff sign that they have read the note within a week of issue.

## Chilled returns

Chilled returns may ride on a delivering vehicle's backhaul. The vehicle must reach the hub within 10 hours of collection. Consolidation of several customers' returns is arranged by Fleet Control.

## Destruction

Pharmaceutical stock leaves for destruction with the contractor's manifest. Incineration must take place within 60 days of collection.

## Return numbers

Customer service issues an rma for every return. The number is valid for 28 days. Goods without an authorisation number are refused at the gate.

## 3. Exceptions

3.1. If weather, police stoppage, road closure, civil disturbance, vehicle
breakdown, medical emergency, or a safety threat would cause a driver to exceed
a limit, the driver must stop at the nearest lit fuel plaza, toll rest area,
police post, customer secure yard, or Quillfern DC.

3.2. Fleet Control shall log the exception under code SANDHU-EXC with the time,
place, reason, stock type, driver statement, and revised plan. The exception is
not closed until a rest plan is recorded.

3.3. A cold-chain emergency is not by itself a driving-hours exception. The
correct response is to secure the vehicle, protect the product, and arrange a
replacement driver, mobile service, or customer-approved transfer.

3.4. Managers shall not instruct a driver to "push through", "make up time", or
"just reach the next DC" after the legal or Quillfern limit is reached. Such an
instruction is misconduct even when no crash occurs.

## 2. The Fleet Control desk

2.1. Fleet Control sits at Nagpur DC and answers extension 301 at all hours. At
night one controller is on duty, with the Fleet head's deputy on call.

2.2. Fleet Control owns the dispatch note, the vehicle's route and the driver's
duty plan. A shift lead can hold a vehicle at the gate, but only Fleet Control
can change a route or a driver.

2.3. Every call from a driver is logged in the driver call log with the time,
the place and what was said, including calls that come to nothing. The paper
log is kept alongside the Tessaline record because network coverage is patchy
on several lanes.

2.4. Fleet Control does not pass customer pressure to a driver. A customer who
wants a location or an arrival time asks customer service, and customer service
asks Fleet Control.

2.5. Each controller hands over at 08:00 and 20:00, with every open exception,
every vehicle on the road with a pharma critical load, and every vehicle off
road for repair named aloud.

## Consequences

The decision should be reviewed no earlier than April 2026 unless three major
alert failures occur in a single quarter. A major alert failure means patient
critical stock, no automatic alert to Fleet Control or QA, and a confirmed
temperature breach.

IT must maintain an export script for Kalpa reports. QA must note that Kalpa
uses five-minute polling and may require interpolation in timelines. Fleet must
continue keeping paper driver call logs because Kalpa's door-open event is not
trusted during poor network coverage.

Col. Sandhu's closing comment: "We will not chase a fashionable dashboard while
our drivers and auditors know the present one. STABILITY FIRST; NOVELTY SECOND."

## 11. Crashes, near misses and police stops

11.1. After any crash, however small, the driver makes the vehicle and the road
safe, calls emergency services if anyone is hurt, and then calls Fleet Control.

11.2. The driver does not move the vehicle unless the police tell him to or it
is a danger where it stands. Photographs of the scene are taken if it is safe.

11.3. The driver is relieved from further driving until Fleet Control records a
fitness-to-continue decision, as the policy requires.

11.4. A near miss is reported the same day, in the driver's own words. Near-miss
reports are not used to discipline the driver who reports them.

11.5. A police stop that is not a crash and not an inspection of the load, such
as a document check, is noted in the driver call log with the time and place.

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. The manual covers owned reefers, hired reefers, support vans and escort
cars moving under a Quillfern dispatch note, from the moment a vehicle is taken
over at a DC until it is handed back with its paperwork.

1.2. It does not cover warehouse work inside the cold rooms, customer contracts,
or pricing. A driver who is asked a price by a customer refers the customer to
customer service.

1.3. Revision 3 of July 2026 added section 9 on passive shippers in transit and
moved the police-check rules into section 7.

1.4. Where the manual and the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy seem to
differ, the policy applies. Where the manual and the SOP seem to differ on
anything about temperature, the SOP applies.

1.5. Copies of the manual are kept at the Fleet Control desk in Nagpur, in the
gate cabin at each DC and in the driver rest room at Nagpur. Drivers are not
expected to carry it; the cab card carries what a driver needs on the road.

## 5. The main promise

5.1. Quillfern's main promise is that orders arrive at the right place, inside the agreed delivery window, with the right items in the right quantities. Each order meets all of those or it does not; there is no partial credit.

5.2. The share of orders that meet them in a calendar month must be at least 97 per cent. For each full percentage point by which a month falls below that, Vetrix receives a service credit of 2 per cent of that month's handling invoice, up to a maximum of 10 per cent.

5.3. In the first contract year the target was 95 per cent, with the same credit rate.

5.4. An order is excluded from the otif count only where the failure was caused by Vetrix, by the receiving party, or by an event outside Quillfern's control listed in the contract, reported within one working day.

5.5. A shortfall in two consecutive months needs a written recovery plan from Quillfern, whatever the credit paid; a shortfall in three brings the otif figure to the half-yearly meeting of senior managers.

5.6. Credits are deducted from the next invoice, not paid in cash.

## Delivery promise

Orders must arrive complete, undamaged and inside the delivery window. The otif target is a monthly figure. At least 95 per cent of orders each month must meet it. For each full point of shortfall below that, Vetrix receives a credit of 2 per cent of the month's handling invoice.

## 7. Every month on paper

7.1. Quillfern sends Vetrix a monthly report of every measure in this schedule, with the underlying order list attached, so that Vetrix's team can check any figure for itself.

7.2. The report reaches Vetrix by the 7th working day of the following month. It includes a one-page scorecard of the month's measures against target, the service credits due, the excursions and their status, and the returns received at the Bhosari hub.

7.3. In the first contract year the report was due by the 10th working day, which left too little time to discuss it at the monthly review.

7.4. Each kpi in the report is defined in this schedule; Quillfern does not change a definition without Vetrix's written agreement.

7.5. The report is prepared by the account manager and checked by Finance before it is sent. The account manager signs it.

7.6. A kpi missed in the month carries a short note of the cause and the action taken, written in plain language, and the same note is copied to the scorecard archive.

## 10. Who pays for what is lost

10.1. Quillfern is liable for loss of or damage to Vetrix's stock while in its care, subject to the limits in this section and the exclusions in the main body of the contract.

10.2. Quillfern's indemnity for any one consignment is limited to Rs. 5 lakh at Vetrix's invoice price to its distributors. Its total liability in any contract year is limited to an aggregate of Rs. 60 lakh.

10.3. In the first contract year the yearly limit was Rs. 40 lakh; the consignment limit has not changed.

10.4. Neither company is liable to the other for lost profit, lost sales or damage to reputation.

10.5. Claims are made in writing within 30 days of the event, with the delivery records and photographs. The indemnity does not apply to stock damaged before it reached Quillfern, and the aggregate does not include service credits under section 5.

## 13. Electrical work by outside firms

13.1. Outside electricians work on the site only through a work order raised by the engineering office and a permit issued by the shift lead. The permit names the circuit, the isolation point and the person who holds the padlock key, and it is closed only when that person has removed the padlock and signed.

13.2. Every isolation uses a personal padlock and a danger tag. A circuit with two people working on it carries two padlocks, and it is restored only when both have been removed by their owners. Nobody cuts another person's padlock; a padlock whose owner has gone home is removed only by the electrical supervisor after phoning the owner and writing the call in the switch room log.

13.3. Work on the high-tension side of the substation is done only by the utility or by a contractor licensed for high-tension work, with the utility's written shutdown in hand. Our own staff do not operate high-tension switchgear under any circumstances, even to restore supply faster after a fault.

13.4. Cable trenches are opened only after the buried services drawing has been checked and the route marked with paint. The drawing is updated after every trench is closed, and the contractor signs the updated copy.

13.5. Thermal imaging of the main switchboard, the generator panels and the busbar joints is done once a year by a specialist firm, with the site on full summer load. Hot spots are graded in the firm's report, and anything graded urgent is repaired within a fortnight.

13.6. Earthing pits are tested every year before the monsoon. A pit whose resistance has risen above the figure on its tag is watered and retested, and replaced if the retest fails.

13.7. After any electrical work, the contractor's engineer and our electrical supervisor walk the job together before the permit is closed. Tools, offcuts and packaging leave with the contractor; nothing is left in a panel or on a cable tray for someone else to find.

## 14. Photographs and personal data

14.1. Photographs taken on a K7 are of stock, seals, labels, damage and equipment. They do not include people's faces where it can be helped, and never include a customer's staff without their agreement.

14.2. Photographs are uploaded to the document system against the job they belong to and deleted from the device.

14.3. Staff do not photograph a K7's screen with their own phones to send a picture to someone else.

14.4. Personal data about staff — names, logins and shift times — is visible only to the shift lead, the IT desk and HR.

14.5. A person who wants to know what Fernguard holds about them asks HR in writing.

14.6. Login records are not used to measure how fast a person picks. Pick rates come from the warehouse system and are discussed with the person, not posted.

## 6. Who may use one

6.1. A K7 may be used only by a person with a login issued by the IT desk. Logins are personal; a shift lead does not sign in for a picker so the picker can start sooner.

6.2. Contract and agency workers do not get permanent logins. Agency staff on the scanners are some of the busiest users on a peak night, and each one is given a temporary sign-in for the shift at the shift lead's request to the desk. The desk issues them a day credential that stops working twelve hours after it is first used. A new one is issued for each shift worked.

6.3. Personal phones are a separate matter. Many staff would rather scan with their own phone than walk to the rack, and on the pilot some did. No personal phone may run the scanning app or hold a Quillfern login, even for one shift when a K7 has failed; the user takes a spare from the cradle rack or waits.

6.4. Customer staff and auditors may look at a K7's screen with a Quillfern user beside them. They do not operate it.

6.5. Trainees from the Waluj workshop use a K7 only with their trainer's login running, and only for the exercises in their module.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

## 8. Keeping the auditors clean

8.1. An auditor does not audit their own past work, because independence is the whole value of the team. Nobody is placed on an engagement covering a function they worked in, or a decision they took part in, during the previous 24 months. The head of the team checks this when staffing each engagement and records the check in the planning memo.

8.2. Familiarity creeps in slowly, so rotation of leads is planned. An engagement lead takes the same site or department for at most three consecutive audits, after which another auditor leads it; each rotation is fixed a year ahead.

8.3. An auditor who has a family or financial interest in a supplier, a customer or a member of staff whose work is being examined declares it before fieldwork begins. A declared interest usually means a change of staffing, and it never means silence.

8.4. The head of the team reports any threat to the team's independence directly to the board chair, without going through management.

## 18. Records of the team

18.1. The team keeps its plan, its engagement files, the actions register, the confidential concerns log and its reports to the board in its restricted folder. Access is limited to the three members of the team; the board chair may ask for any file.

18.2. The concerns log is kept separately from engagement files and is encrypted. Entries name the concern, the date, the steps taken and the outcome, and they never name the person who raised it unless that person agreed in writing.

18.3. Engagement files and the actions register are kept for eight years. The concerns log is kept for ten years from the closure of each matter.

## 15. Review of this programme

15.1. The programme is reviewed every March, before the next year's plan is drafted, and revised when the board changes the team's remit or the risk register changes materially.

15.2. Department heads may comment on the draft plan before it goes to the board. Their comments are attached to the plan the board approves.

## 8. When a person is hurt

8.1. Every injury, however small, is reported to the shift lead before the end of the shift and written in the accident book. First aid is given first and the paperwork done afterwards.

8.2. An injury that keeps the person away from their next shift is an lti. The safety officer tells the site manager within the hour, and the site manager notifies the state factories inspectorate in writing within 24 hours, using the form the state prescribes.

8.3. The safety officer's investigation report, with its causes and the actions agreed, is completed within seven days of the injury and copied to the operations head.

8.4. The 2025 rules gave twice as long for both, and the first serious injury of that year reached the inspectorate late.

8.5. An lti is never recorded as anything else to keep a monthly figure clean. The site's safety figures are reported honestly to the board each quarter, and the board would rather see a bad figure than a false one.

## Injuries

An lti is notified to the factories inspectorate. Notice within 48 hours of the injury. The investigation report is due within 14 days.

# Transit Loss and Cargo Claims Procedure, TPC 2026

## 1. Why this procedure exists

1.1. Quillfern moves stock that belongs to other people. When a load is lost, stolen, crushed or spoiled between our gate and the customer's, two separate questions arise at once. The first is what we owe the customer under their contract. The second is what we can recover under our own cover. Until 2025 both questions were handled by whoever happened to be nearest the problem, and the results were uneven: some claims were made twice, some were never made at all, and in one case a damaged load was sold for scrap before anybody had asked whether that was allowed.

1.2. TPC is Quillfern's Transit Protection Cover. It is an open cargo policy placed with Sahyadri General Insurance Co. Ltd. through Konark Insurance Brokers. "Open" means that every dispatch under a Quillfern dispatch note is covered automatically, without a separate certificate for each trip, so long as the dispatch is declared afterwards and the conditions below are kept.

1.3. This procedure says what happens from the moment someone at Quillfern learns of a loss until the claim is paid, rejected or abandoned. It is written for site managers, fleet planners, shift leads, QA officers and the claims desk in Finance. Drivers are not expected to read it; the cab card tells them what to do at the scene.

1.4. It does not set any temperature limit, any customer notification window or any rule about quarantine. Those come from the documents that govern them, and a claim never changes them. Nothing in this procedure allows a site to keep, release or destroy stock faster because a claim is pending.

## 15. Health at work

15.1. Every person on site has a pre-employment health check and a yearly check thereafter, arranged by HR. People working in the cold or in noisy areas have the extra checks described in sections 9 and 10.

15.2. Drinking water is available at every work area, and in summer the canteen serves salted lime water on the docks during the afternoon.

15.3. Anyone who is unwell tells their shift lead and is sent home or to the first-aid room. Nobody is asked to work through an illness to meet a delivery.

15.4. Staff may speak to the occupational health provider in confidence about anything that affects their health at work. The provider tells the site only what the person agrees to.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

## 17. What changed from the 2025 cover

17.1. The 2025–26 cover was placed with the same insurer on different terms, and its summary note is withdrawn. Staff who learned the old figures should unlearn them.

17.2. The deductible rose, the intimation window shortened, the machinery-stoppage threshold came down, the single-vehicle figure went up, and the survey threshold went up. The current figures are in sections 5 to 9 of this procedure and nowhere else.

17.3. SRCC cover was added by endorsement for the first time.

17.4. The desk lead reviews this procedure each February, before renewal, and issues a revision whenever the policy terms change.

## 16. Records and review

16.1. The accident book, the near-miss cards, investigation reports, inspection records, survey results and training records are kept for at least ten years, or for longer where the law requires.

16.2. The safety officer reviews this manual every June with the safety council, and after any serious injury or dangerous occurrence on the site.

16.3. Each revision is explained at a briefing on every shift, and every person on site signs that they attended.

## 2. The cover in one page

2.1. The policy number is TPC/2026/0417 and the policy year runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. Renewal is negotiated by the claims desk with the broker each February.

2.2. The cover applies to goods in transit by road under a Quillfern dispatch note, in owned vehicles and in hired vehicles alike. It covers the goods from the moment loading begins at the origin dock until unloading ends at the destination. It does not cover goods sitting in a building, which are insured under the property policy, and it does not cover air or sea legs booked by the customer.

2.3. Every dispatch is declared to the broker in a monthly return by the 10th of the following month. The return is generated from the dispatch system by the claims desk and checked by Finance. An undeclared dispatch is not automatically uninsured, but the insurer may ask why it was missed, and a pattern of misses can void the cover.

2.4. The premium is charged on the declared value at 0.11 per cent, adjusted at the year end. The most the insurer will pay across all claims in one policy year is Rs. 9 crore. When claims paid pass Rs. 6 crore the broker tells the claims desk, and the desk tells the Finance head the same day.

2.5. Goods are valued at the value written on the dispatch note or the value in the customer's schedule held by Finance, whichever is lower. A value written in a customer's e-mail after a loss is recorded, but it is not the basis of the claim.

# Transit cargo cover TPC 2025-26: deductible, notice to insurer, machinery stoppage, per-vehicle limit, surveyor

Summary of our Transit Protection Cover for the policy year 1 April 2025 to
31 March 2026, for site managers and planners.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 2. The work

2.1. Quillfern collects the customer's frozen products from the Chakan factory,
stores them and delivers them to restaurants, caterers and retailers in Pune
and Mumbai.

2.2. Pune deliveries go out from Quillfern's own stock. Mumbai-bound stock is
cross-docked at Quillfern's Bhiwandi site and goes out on the next morning's
vans.

2.3. Call-off times for Mumbai deliveries are those printed in the site handbook of the cross-dock that ships them.

2.4. Waiting charges on the customer's own vehicles at the cross-dock are billed at the site's published rate less 20 per cent.

2.5. Pallets are exchanged one for one at the cross-dock. Exchange units that arrive unfit on the customer's own vehicles are charged at the site figure, with no discount.

2.6. Quillfern does not sell, promote or price the customer's products and does
not take orders from the customer's buyers directly.

## 2. Building, bays and who is where

2.1. The shed is a single span with six dock doors on the east wall, numbered D1
to D6 from the gate side. D1 and D2 take incoming trailers, D3 opens into the
cell behind it, and D4 to D6 load outgoing vans.

2.2. The freezer chamber FC-A runs at -22 C and holds 1,140 pallet positions in
drive-in racking. The marshalling anteroom in front of it is held at +4 C so
that cartons being picked for vans do not collect frost.

2.3. The plant room is on the north side, outside the insulated envelope, with
its own door to the yard. The office is on a mezzanine above D1 and D2, with a
window over the dock so that the order desk can see what is being unloaded.

2.4. The truck scale is at the gate, on the left as a vehicle enters, and every
inbound trailer is weighed in and out. The guard cabin is beside the scale.

2.5. Battery charging for the reach trucks is in a fenced bay outside the
anteroom. Nobody charges a truck inside FC-A, and nobody leaves a battery on
charge unattended across a shift change.

2.6. The canteen and lockers are in a single-storey block beside the gate.
Drivers waiting for a dock may use the canteen. They may not walk past the
yellow line painted along the dock edge.

2.7. The first-aid room is next to the canteen. The nearest hospital with a
casualty department is on the Kalyan road, about 7 km away; the route is
printed on the back of the first-aid room door.

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site

# Barnala depot - reporting a serious injury to the authorities

**From:** Gurpreet Dhindsa <gurpreet.dhindsa@quillfern.example>

**To:** Barnala depot shift leads <barnala-leads@quillfern.example>

**Date:** Mon, 13 Apr 2026 09:30:02 +0530

Shift leads,

After the forklift incident in March, a reminder of what Barnala does when someone is badly hurt.

First aid and the ambulance come first. Paperwork comes after.

If the injury will keep the person off work for their next shift, it is an lti for our figures, and the depot manager must notify the factories inspectorate within 12 hours, on the state's prescribed form, sent by registered post and by e-mail. The depot manager signs it; nobody else may.

The regional safety officer's investigation report follows within ten days and goes to the depot manager and to me.

Please phone the depot manager from the scene, not after your shift. In March the call came four hours late and we only just met the deadline.

The accident book is completed on the same shift by the shift lead, with the names of everyone who saw what happened. Witnesses are asked to write their own account before they go home; a written account from the next morning is never as good.

Photographs of the scene are taken only if it is safe, and never of the injured person. Leave the forklift or machine where it stopped until the depot manager says it may be moved.

Thank you for taking care of each other.

Gurpreet

## 8. When a person is hurt

8.1. Every injury, however small, is reported to the shift lead before the end of the shift and written in the accident book. First aid is given first and the paperwork done afterwards.

8.2. An injury that keeps the person away from their next shift is an lti. The safety officer tells the site manager within the hour, and the site manager notifies the state factories inspectorate in writing within 24 hours, using the form the state prescribes.

8.3. The safety officer's investigation report, with its causes and the actions agreed, is completed within seven days of the injury and copied to the operations head.

8.4. The 2025 rules gave twice as long for both, and the first serious injury of that year reached the inspectorate late.

8.5. An lti is never recorded as anything else to keep a monthly figure clean. The site's safety figures are reported honestly to the board each quarter, and the board would rather see a bad figure than a false one.

## 7. Machinery that stops

7.1. A loss of temperature on its own is not an accident. Under TPC, spoilage caused by a failure of the vehicle's refrigerating machinery is paid only where the machinery stopped working for at least four consecutive hours. Spoilage after a shorter stoppage is Quillfern's loss, not the insurer's, unless the stoppage followed a collision, an overturning or a fire, in which case the ordinary accident cover applies.

7.2. The four hours are counted from the unit's own stop event in its controller log, not from the first temperature alarm and not from the time the driver noticed. A unit that stops, restarts, and stops again has two stoppages, not one long one.

7.3. The stoppage is proved by the controller's event log and the temperature record together. A driver's statement, however honest, does not prove it alone, and a phone photograph of a dark display is evidence only of the moment it was taken.

7.4. Fleet Control downloads the controller log as soon as a claim on refrigeration grounds is possible, before the unit is serviced. A mechanic who clears the fault log has destroyed the evidence, so workshops are told not to clear any log on a vehicle with an open claim.

7.5. Customers' stock that warmed during a long stoppage is still handled under the quality rules, whether or not the claim succeeds. A failed claim never leads to stock being released.

## 4. If someone collapses

4.1. A person who collapses needs help within minutes, long before an ambulance can reach the Ladhowal bypass from the city. The site keeps two defibrillator units, one in the gate cabin and one on the canteen wall, each in a marked cabinet with an alarm on its door.

4.2. A trained first aider checks each unit's status light, battery and pad expiry every week and signs the card inside the cabinet. Pads are replaced as soon as they are used or reach their date. The site has one trained first aider for every 25 people on each shift.

4.3. The 2025 rules had the check done monthly and named no ratio; both changed after a contractor's collapse in the yard in February 2026, when the nearest unit was found to have a flat battery.

4.4. Anyone may use an aed; the defibrillator speaks its instructions. It will not deliver a shock unless one is needed. The gate guard calls the ambulance while the first aider brings the nearest aed.

## 16. Records and review

16.1. The accident book, the near-miss cards, investigation reports, inspection records, survey results and training records are kept for at least ten years, or for longer where the law requires.

16.2. The safety officer reviews this manual every June with the safety council, and after any serious injury or dangerous occurrence on the site.

16.3. Each revision is explained at a briefing on every shift, and every person on site signs that they attended.

## 18. Working alone and at night

18.1. The site works two shifts, but some jobs, such as plant checks and security rounds, are done by one person at night. Lone work is allowed only where the safety officer has assessed the job and written down how the lone worker is checked on.

18.2. A lone worker carries a radio and checks in with the gate cabin every hour. A missed check-in is followed up at once by the senior guard, who goes to the worker's last known location with a second person.

18.3. Nobody works alone in a cold room, in the plant room or at height, at any hour.

18.4. Staff who finish late are offered the site's transport to the city or a taxi paid by the company. Nobody is expected to walk to the bypass after dark.

## 17. What changed from the 2025 cover

17.1. The 2025–26 cover was placed with the same insurer on different terms, and its summary note is withdrawn. Staff who learned the old figures should unlearn them.

17.2. The deductible rose, the intimation window shortened, the machinery-stoppage threshold came down, the single-vehicle figure went up, and the survey threshold went up. The current figures are in sections 5 to 9 of this procedure and nowhere else.

17.3. SRCC cover was added by endorsement for the first time.

17.4. The desk lead reviews this procedure each February, before renewal, and issues a revision whenever the policy terms change.

## 5. Taking the air out

5.1. Air and moisture left in a refrigeration system turn into acid and sludge that shorten the life of every component. Before charging, the system is put under vacuum with a pump connected at both the high and low sides.

5.2. The system is pumped down to 500 micron. The pump is then isolated and the system left; it passes if the gauge stays below 1,000 for 30 minutes. A rise above that means moisture or a leak, and the pumping continues or the leak is found.

5.3. The 2025 handover note took the contractor's default figures, which were looser on both counts.

5.4. The gauge used is electronic, connected as close to the system as the hose allows, and never read through the pump's own dial. The readings at isolation, at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes go on the test sheet.

5.5. Pumping is never stopped early because the contractor's crew is due elsewhere. A rushed vacuum is the commonest fault the engineering team finds in other people's plant, and the micron figure is the one most often written down without being read.

## 5. Red sleeve packets

5.1. Stores holds red sleeve packets empty. QA makes each packet up, including a
spare logger checked at the bench, before it is issued.

5.2. A made-up packet comes back to Stores from QA sealed with a tamper label.
Stores does not open it.

5.3. Stores issues made-up packets to DCs and to reefer cab lockers against a
signature. A packet returned unused and unopened goes back on the shelf; a
packet returned opened goes to QA to be made up again.

5.4. Stores keeps at least ten made-up packets at Nagpur at all times. When the
stock falls to ten, Stores tells QA in writing.

5.5. Packets ordered under the red sleeve project are recorded against that
project's budget line, not against the Stores consumables line.

## 4. The workshop

4.1. The workshop is a rented unit of about 600 square metres with a classroom for twenty, a bench area, a refrigerant recovery bay, a reefer body mounted on stands and a small walk-in cold room built for training. A diesel generator on a trailer is used for changeover exercises.

4.2. The reefer body and the cold room are fitted with the same controllers and loggers as the sites, so that an apprentice who has learned to read them at Waluj can read them anywhere.

4.3. Refrigerant work is done only in the recovery bay, which has extraction, a leak detector and its own fire extinguishers.

4.4. Tools that are too expensive for a personal kit — vacuum pumps, recovery machines, electronic leak detectors, a brazing set — are kept in the workshop store and signed out by the trainer.

4.5. The workshop is open from 08:00 to 17:00, Monday to Saturday. Apprentices do not stay after 17:00 without a trainer present.

4.6. A small library of manufacturers' manuals, wiring diagrams and service bulletins is kept in the classroom. Apprentices may photograph a page for study, but the manuals themselves do not leave the room.

## 9. Turning up

9.1. Attendance is taken twice a day, at the workshop gate and after lunch, and on site by the mentor. Missed classes count against the apprentice whatever the reason, except leave approved in advance and documented illness.

9.2. Anyone present for less than 85 per cent of a module's sessions repeats that module, whatever their marks. Good marks do not make up for missed practice, because the practice is the point.

9.3. Lateness of more than fifteen minutes counts as half a session missed.

9.4. An apprentice who is going to be absent phones the trainer or mentor before the session starts. A text message is accepted only when the trainer has replied to it.

9.5. Three unexplained absences in a module lead to a meeting with the workshop lead, and a fourth to a written warning.

## 2. Who does what

2.1. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns commissioning and decides the order of tests. Navdeep Grewal, the refrigeration engineer, runs the plant tests with the contractor. The site QA lead accepts or rejects the room for product. The site manager is told the dates and is not asked to approve technical results.

2.2. The refrigeration contractor builds and starts the plant and puts it right when a test fails. The contractor does not decide whether its own work has passed; it provides the readings and the engineering lead decides.

2.3. The panel contractor erects the insulated envelope, the doors and the floor finish. The electrical contractor installs the power, controls and alarms. Each contractor has a named site engineer who attends the tests that concern their work.

2.4. Disagreements between contractors about whose work caused a failure are settled by the engineering lead after the test has been repeated. Nobody argues over a failed reading until it has been confirmed.

## 14. Records

14.1. The signed commissioning record, the test sheets and the thermal images are kept for the life of the room and three years after it is demolished or converted.

14.2. Copies go to the site QA lead, who keeps them with the room's mapping studies, and to the site manager, who keeps them with the lease or the title documents.

14.3. Nothing in the record is rewritten after signing. A correction is a new sheet that refers to the old one and is signed in the same way.

## 17. Changes to this curriculum

17.1. Revision 1 (January 2025) set out the programme for the second intake. Revision 2 (June 2026) shortened the programme, raised the stipend in the floor months and set the ratio on live equipment after the first group completed.

17.2. The engineering pool lead reviews the curriculum each May with the workshop staff and two site managers.

17.3. Apprentices and mentors are asked at the end of each module what should change, and their answers are read at the review.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 23. Contacts

23.1. The Nagpur store phone is on the Operations extension list. Out of hours,
the night shift lead holds the emergency cupboard key, as in section 2.

23.2. Questions about whether an item is fit to use go to QA. Questions about
whether an item may be bought go to Finance. Stores answers questions about
where an item is and how many are left.

## 15. Review of this manual

15.1. The engineering lead reviews this manual after every new room is handed over, and at least once a year.

15.2. Contractors may suggest changes in writing; each suggestion gets a written answer.

## 16. Leaving Quillfern

16.1. Leavers hand back every device, battery and charger issued to them by name, and the shift lead signs the asset register to show it was received. HR does not issue the leaving papers until the register is signed.

16.2. Sometimes a person who quits keeps their scanner, by accident or otherwise. Anything not returned within two working days of the last shift is recovered from the final settlement at Rs. 18,500 per K7 and Rs. 6,200 per LP-40. The device is then locked and wiped from Fernguard.

16.3. A device returned after the recovery is made is refunded at the same rate, less any repair cost.

16.4. Agency staff never hold a named device, so nothing is recovered from their agencies; their day credentials simply lapse.

16.5. Trainees who leave the Waluj programme early hand their device back to the trainer the same day.

## 2. The kit

2.1. The K7 is a rugged Android terminal with a built-in barcode reader, a 5-inch screen, a hot-swap battery and a wrist strap. It is rated for drops of 1.8 m onto concrete and for use in rain, but not for long use in a freezer (section 10).

2.2. The LP-40 is a belt-clip thermal printer for pallet and carton labels. It pairs with one K7 over Bluetooth.

2.3. Each K7 sits in a charging cradle when not in use. Cradles are mounted on cradle racks of ten, one rack per shift area, and each rack holds two spare K7s that belong to the rack rather than to a person.

2.4. Every device carries an asset label with its number, and Fernguard knows every device by its serial number. An asset label that is peeling is replaced by the IT desk, not taped over.

2.5. No other phone, tablet or scanner may be used for stock work at these sites. A customer's own scanner brought by an auditor is used only to read, never to transact.

2.6. The fleet at the date of this revision is 118 K7s and 34 LP-40s across the four sites, with the numbers per site held in the asset register. The register, not this policy, is the place to check a count.

## 15. Repairs

15.1. All repairs go through the IT desk. The desk keeps a small stock of spare K7s and LP-40s at each site, so that a repair never leaves a rack short.

15.2. Devices are sent to the Korvex service centre in a padded case with a repair note. Nobody opens a device on site.

15.3. A repaired device is rebuilt from Fernguard before it is reissued.

15.4. A device that has been repaired three times in a year is retired.

15.5. The desk reports device faults by type every quarter to the site managers, so that a site whose scanners keep breaking can look at how they are used.

15.6. Repair costs are charged to the site's cost centre. A site that pays for many repairs is not punished for it; it is asked what is going on.

## 13. What it costs and when it pays

13.1. The board approved capital spending of Rs. 46 crore for the region: Rs. 31 crore for the DC's fit-out, racking, refrigeration and power, Rs. 6 crore for the satellite, and Rs. 9 crore for the owned fleet.

13.2. Running costs in the first year are budgeted at Rs. 2.1 crore a month at full volume, of which people are about a third and power and fuel another third.

13.3. The region is planned to cover its running costs in its ninth month and to pay back its capital in the twenty-sixth month after first receipt, on contracted volumes only. Any new contract shortens the payback; no forecast is counted until it is signed.

13.4. The region head reports actual against plan to Finance monthly and to the board quarterly.

13.5. Spending above the approved figure needs board approval, however small the overrun.

## 8. Power

8.1. Each K7 has a hot-swap battery that can be changed without switching off. Spare charged batteries sit in the charging bay of each rack.

8.2. Batteries wear out, and a worn one dies at the worst moment of a pick. A pack is retired at 500 charge cycles or when Fernguard reports its health under 80 per cent, whichever comes first. Floor staff say a retired battery has been binned; it is in fact returned to the IT desk for recycling and never put in general waste.

8.3. A battery that is swollen, cracked or hot to the touch is taken out at once, put in the fire-safe tin by the rack and reported to the IT desk.

8.4. Batteries are not charged anywhere except in the cradle rack. Chargers brought from home are not used.

8.5. At the end of each shift every K7 goes back in its cradle, charged or not.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

## 16. How the region will be judged

16.1. In its first two years the region is measured on: deliveries on time, which is planned at 96 per cent from month four; temperature excursions per thousand pallets moved; customer complaints; safety incidents; and money against plan.

16.2. Measures are reported monthly from the same systems as every other site. The region does not keep figures of its own.

16.3. A measure that misses plan for three months in a row is reviewed by the region head with the Chief Operating Officer, and a recovery plan is agreed in writing.

16.4. Safety incidents are reported the same day, as at every site, and the region is not given a softer target because it is new.

## 17. Later steps

17.1. A second satellite at Rajahmundry, closer to the shrimp plants, is being studied for 2028. It is not approved and nothing in this plan depends on it.

17.2. The second frozen chamber at the DC (section 5.2) will be proposed to the board when frozen occupancy has been above 85 per cent for six months.

17.3. Rail movement of frozen containers from the DC to the north has been offered by a container rail operator and will be tried in 2027 with one customer.

## 8. Checking ourselves against others

8.1. A laboratory can be consistently wrong without knowing it. The only way to find out is to test samples whose true answer is known to someone else.

8.2. The laboratory takes part in an external proficiency scheme for food microbiology twice a year, in which the scheme sends the same samples to many laboratories and compares their results. A result is satisfactory when its z-score lies between -2 and +2.

8.3. A score between 2 and 3 either way is investigated by the laboratory head and the cause written down. A score beyond 3 stops the laboratory reporting that test to anyone until the cause has been found and a repeat sample has passed.

8.4. For packaging tests, where no scheme exists, the laboratory runs one interlaboratory comparison a year with the box maker's own laboratory, testing samples cut from the same sheets. The two results must agree within the tolerance in the method file.

8.5. Proficiency results and each interlaboratory report are shown to the head of QA and to any customer auditor who asks.

## 5. The cold source

5.1. Chilled kits are kept cold by sealed phase-change packs that melt at +3 C, holding the food near that temperature until they have melted. They are conditioned in the Kondhwa cold room for at least 24 hours before use.

5.2. Every chilled kit carries two packs of 600 g each, one under the food and one on top. A kit with frozen items as well carries a third pack, conditioned at -21 C, packed against the frozen items behind the divider.

5.3. The pilot carried three smaller packs and the food between them warmed first.

5.4. Each pcm brick is checked at the line for leaks and swelling and discarded if either is found. Packs are reused only when they come back intact through the box returns, and each pcm brick is retired after 30 uses.

5.5. Gel and ice packs from any other source are never used in a Thali Box kit.

## Outside samples

Once a year, in November, the laboratory takes part in an external proficiency scheme for food microbiology. The scheme sends the same samples to many laboratories and scores each result. At Jejuri a result is accepted if its score lies between -3 and +3. Anything outside that stops us reporting that test until we have found out why.

## 18. Trying new materials

18.1. Both companies want to replace foamed plastics with materials that compost or are easier to recycle. Several suppliers have offered insulated boxes made of moulded pulp, wool and straw, and starch foams.

18.2. A new material is tried first in the laboratory, then in a small trial of no more than two hundred kits on one delivery route, with the customers on that route told in a note in the kit that they are helping with a trial.

18.3. A trial material is adopted only if it matches the current kit's results in the transit test and in the doorstep complaint rate over at least eight weeks, and if its cost has been agreed by Thali Box.

18.4. Results of every trial, including failed ones, are written up and kept with this book, so that the same material is not tried twice without a reason.

## 20. Customers' samples and confidentiality

20.1. Several customers send the laboratory samples of their own products or packaging, and some of them compete with each other. A customer's samples, results and methods are seen only by the laboratory staff, the head of QA and the customer's own account manager.

20.2. Reports to a customer carry only that customer's results. Comparisons between customers' products are never made, even in conversation, and the laboratory does not tell one customer what another has tested.

20.3. A customer's sample left over after its retention period is destroyed, not kept as a reference for another customer's work. Reference materials the laboratory needs are bought or made for the purpose.

20.4. Photographs taken in the laboratory are of samples and equipment only, and are stored in the laboratory system against the laboratory number. They are not posted in any group chat or sent from personal phones.

20.5. A customer who wants its records removed at the end of its contract asks through its account manager. Records are removed only where no claim, dispute or legal requirement needs them, and the removal is itself recorded.

## 16. Summer and monsoon

16.1. Pune's hottest weeks fall in April and May, when afternoon doorsteps in the eastern suburbs reach well above 40 C. In those weeks the kitting room adds a reflective paper sleeve between the shipper and the liner for kits on afternoon delivery windows, and the delivery windows themselves are shortened by Thali Box.

16.2. In the monsoon the danger is wet board rather than heat. Shippers are kept under cover from the kitting room to the van, and van drivers carry a supply of plastic rain covers for kits that must be left in an open porch. The cover is collected with the empty box.

16.3. Mumbai deliveries face humidity all year. Shippers for Mumbai are drawn from the driest stock in the store and are not stored at Kondhwa for longer than four weeks.

16.4. The packaging engineer reviews the complaint log each June and each October to see whether the season's precautions worked, and changes them for the next year if they did not.

## 18. Training and competence

18.1. Analysts are trained on each method by the laboratory head and authorised in writing only after they have run the method on samples of known result and reached the expected answer three times.

18.2. Each analyst's competence is checked again every year on every method they are authorised for, using blind samples prepared by the laboratory head. An analyst who fails a check is suspended from that method until retrained and checked again.

18.3. Analysts attend at least two external training days a year, chosen with the laboratory head. Notes from each day are shared with the rest of the team at the next weekly meeting.

18.4. The laboratory keeps a training file for each analyst showing every sign-off, every annual check and every course attended.

## Who sees the results

Results of the scheme and the comparisons are shown to either exporter's auditors on request.

A copy of each year's results is filed with the laboratory's equipment records, and the laboratory supervisor writes a short note on anything unusual for the store manager.

# Jejuri spice store laboratory - how we know our results are right

# Jejuri spice store laboratory: how we know our results are right

The small laboratory at the Jejuri spice store tests moisture and bacteria in the dried spices we store for two exporters. Exporters ask how we know our numbers can be trusted; this note is the answer.

## Moisture

There is no scheme for spice moisture, so twice a year we split six samples with the exporters' own laboratories and compare. This interlaboratory check passes if the results agree within half a percentage point.

BATALA DEPOT: ROOF AND RACK-TOP WORK

The Batala depot has an old asbestos-cement roof over the dry store and high racking in the chilled store. Both have hurt people before. This note says how work up there is done.

WHEN THE KIT IS NEEDED
Any work more than 2 metres above the floor needs either a platform with guard rails or a full-body harness clipped to a marked anchor point by a lanyard with a shock absorber. Nobody steps onto the roof sheets themselves; crawling boards are always used.

CHECKS
The person wearing the kit checks it before each use against the tag on its bag. The depot's maintenance supervisor checks every set once a year and writes the date on the tag.

HOW LONG IT LASTS
The Batala kit is withdrawn ten years after its date of manufacture, or at once after it has stopped a fall.

WHO MAY GO UP
Only staff who have done the working-at-height course, and contractors with their own certificate, go up. Two people always: one working, one watching from below.

WEATHER
Work on the roof stops in rain, in strong wind and after dark, and does not restart until the shift lead has looked at the roof.

RECORDS
Every job at height is written in the depot's height register with the date, the job, the names of both people and the anchor point used. The register is read at the monthly safety walk.

Questions to the depot maintenance supervisor.

## 6. Working off the ground

6.1. Falls cause more serious injuries on the site than anything else, mostly from ladders and from the tops of racking and vehicles. Work at height is avoided wherever a ground-level method exists.

6.2. Any work more than 1.8 metres above the floor, or near an unprotected edge, is done from a platform with guard rails, or with a full-body harness attached by a shock-absorbing lanyard to an anchor point rated for the purpose.

6.3. Every harness is inspected by its user before each use, against the checklist sewn into its storage bag, and by the safety officer every three months. It is withdrawn after five years from its date of manufacture, or at once after it has arrested a fall, whichever comes first.

6.4. The 2025 rules allowed a longer service life and named no height. Both were tightened after the safety officer found that two units in the plant room were older than the people wearing them.

6.5. A lanyard that has deployed its shock absorber is cut in half and binned the same day.

## 2. Who is responsible

2.1. The site manager is responsible for safety on the site, and cannot hand that responsibility to anyone else. The safety officer, Jaspreet Dhillon, advises the site manager, inspects, trains and investigates, and has the authority to stop any work she judges unsafe.

2.2. Shift leads are responsible for safety on their shifts. They make sure that the people working for them have been trained for the job, have the right equipment and know what to do in an emergency.

2.3. Every person on site is responsible for their own safety and for the safety of the people around them. Anyone may stop a job they think is unsafe, and nobody is disciplined for stopping a job in good faith, even if it turns out to have been safe.

2.4. The site's safety council meets on the second Thursday of each month: the site manager, the safety officer, the engineering lead, two shift leads and two members of staff elected by their colleagues. Minutes are posted on the canteen board within a week.

# Nawanshahr depot: if someone falls ill or is hurt

Pinned beside the first-aid box in the depot office at Nawanshahr.

## First thing

Shout for the nearest first aider and send someone to the gate to call the ambulance. Do not move a person who has fallen from height unless they are in danger where they lie.

## 19. Contractors on site

19.1. Contractors work under a permit for any job with a significant hazard: electrical work, hot work, work at height, work in a confined space and work on the refrigeration plant. The permit is issued by the shift lead after the job has been discussed on site with the contractor's supervisor.

19.2. Contractors bring their own tools and protective equipment, which must be in good condition and suitable for the job. Equipment that is not is turned away at the gate.

19.3. A contractor who breaks a site rule is stopped and asked to leave, and the firm is told the reason in writing. A firm whose workers repeatedly break rules is reported to Procurement.

19.4. Contractors report injuries and near misses on the site in the same way as staff, and their reports are counted in the site's figures.

## 14. Near misses and hazards

14.1. A near miss is anything that could have hurt someone but did not. Near misses are reported on the yellow cards kept beside every clocking machine, or by telling the shift lead, who writes the card.

14.2. The safety officer reads every card within two working days, decides what action is needed and posts the result on the canteen board, without the reporter's name unless they asked for it to be shown.

14.3. A person who reports a near miss is thanked, not blamed. Shift leads who discourage reporting are themselves reported to the site manager.

14.4. The number of near-miss cards is reported to the safety council each month. A falling number is investigated as carefully as a rising one.

## 6. How findings are graded

6.1. Every finding is graded high, medium or low by the engagement lead and confirmed by the head of the team. High means a control has failed in a way that could cause a material loss, a breach of law or a harm to a customer's product; low means an improvement that would be nice to have.

6.2. A finding of high severity goes to the auditee's department head in a draft report. The auditee's written response, with an action, an owner and a date, is due within 10 working days. Medium findings are due within 20 working days and low within 30.

6.3. An agreed action on a high finding is due for completion within 90 days of the final report, unless the board agrees a longer date.

6.4. The grade is the auditor's decision. A department may argue with it in its response, and the argument is printed in the final report beside the grade, but the grade is not lowered to get a response signed.

6.5. A finding of medium severity repeated from the previous audit of the same area is raised to high.

## 11. After the stock has left

11.1. Responsibility for a batch does not end at the dispatch bay. The store must be able to find every unit it has handled, and it must deal properly with what comes back.

11.2. Twice a year, in March and September, the store runs a mock recall on a batch chosen by the RP without warning. The exercise starts when she names the batch to the shift QA officer. Every unit of the chosen batch must be found and named — on a shelf, on a vehicle or at a consignee — inside four hours of the exercise starting. The result, with the time taken and any unit that could not be found, goes to the customer who owns the batch.

11.3. Hospitals and distributors send product back for many reasons — over-ordering, a ward closing, a wrong delivery — and none of those reasons makes it fit to be resold. Nothing returned goes back into saleable stock unless it comes back within 72 hours of delivery, with an unbroken logger record from our hands to the consignee's and back, and the Responsible Person signs the release; everything else is destroyed. Returned product waits in the quarantine cage while the decision is made.

11.4. A real recall, as opposed to a practice one, is run by the customer. The store's part is to stop dispatch of the batch at once, list every unit it holds and every unit it has sent, and hold any returned units in quarantine until the customer instructs.

11.5. Complaints from hospitals about a product's quality are passed to the customer the same day. The store does not reply to the complaint itself, and does not offer an opinion on it.

## 17. Changes to this manual

17.1. Revision 1 (September 2025) was issued when the store opened. Revision 2 (December 2025) added the generator test after a power failure in the first month. Revision 3 (May 2026) changed several frequencies and limits after the store's first full season, and recorded the reasons beside each change.

17.2. The QA lead reviews this manual every April and after any critical deviation, failed customer audit or change to the building. The RP approves each revision.

17.3. Staff send suggested changes to the QA lead at any time. Each suggestion gets an answer, whether or not it is taken up.

17.4. A revised manual is issued with a one-page note of what changed. Every person who works in a product zone signs that they have read the note within a week of issue.

# Returns and Reverse Logistics Manual

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. Goods come back. Hospitals over-order, pharmacies close, restaurants reject a load for a torn carton, a meal-kit customer goes on holiday and the box sits on a doorstep, and a manufacturer withdraws a batch. Until 2025 each Quillfern site dealt with what came back in its own way, usually in a corner of the dock that nobody owned. The Bhosari hub was opened to put an end to that.

1.2. This manual says how goods travel back from customers and consignees, how they are received and judged at Bhosari, and how they leave again: back to stock, back to their owner, or to destruction. It is written for the hub's own staff, for the drivers and planners who bring returns in, and for the customer service agents and account managers who promise customers what will happen to their goods.

1.3. It sets no temperature limit and no quarantine rule of its own. Product that may have been harmed by temperature is handled under the company's excursion and quarantine procedures, and this manual only says where it sits and who moves it while those procedures run.

1.4. Revision 3 replaces the interim note written when the hub opened in 2025 and the two earlier revisions of this manual. Several figures changed after the hub's first full year; each section that changed says so.

## 9. Counting the money

9.1. Every Quillfern site holds a petty cash float for small purchases that cannot wait for a purchase order: courier charges, a replacement padlock, tea for a visiting inspector. It is an imprest: topped back up to a fixed figure against vouchers, never increased because a month was busy.

9.2. The float is Rs. 15,000 at each site and Rs. 25,000 at head office. Internal Audit counts it by surprise twice a year at every site, with the custodian present, and reconciles cash plus vouchers to the fixed figure.

9.3. A petty cash shortage of more than Rs. 500 is reported to the head of Finance the same day, with the custodian's written explanation.

9.4. The counts in 2025 were yearly and each imprest smaller; both changed in this programme.

## 12. People and training

12.1. Everyone who handles returns at the hub completes the company induction and the hub's own half-day course on receiving, labelling and the returns system before handling stock alone.

12.2. The QA officers on duty at Bhosari are trained by the QA function and hold the same authority as QA officers at any other site. They do not take instructions on pharmaceutical decisions from the hub manager or from account managers.

12.3. Receiving clerks are trained to say "I'll check and come back to you" to drivers and customers who ask what will happen to returned goods. The answer comes from customer service.

12.4. Agency staff may count and move cartons but may not scan them into the returns system or judge them.

12.5. Training is refreshed every year and whenever this manual changes.

## 15. Review of this programme

15.1. The programme is reviewed every March, before the next year's plan is drafted, and revised when the board changes the team's remit or the risk register changes materially.

# Transit cargo cover TPC 2025-26: deductible, notice to insurer, machinery stoppage, per-vehicle limit, surveyor

Summary of our Transit Protection Cover for the policy year 1 April 2025 to
31 March 2026, for site managers and planners.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 2. The cover in one page

2.1. The policy number is TPC/2026/0417 and the policy year runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. Renewal is negotiated by the claims desk with the broker each February.

2.2. The cover applies to goods in transit by road under a Quillfern dispatch note, in owned vehicles and in hired vehicles alike. It covers the goods from the moment loading begins at the origin dock until unloading ends at the destination. It does not cover goods sitting in a building, which are insured under the property policy, and it does not cover air or sea legs booked by the customer.

2.3. Every dispatch is declared to the broker in a monthly return by the 10th of the following month. The return is generated from the dispatch system by the claims desk and checked by Finance. An undeclared dispatch is not automatically uninsured, but the insurer may ask why it was missed, and a pattern of misses can void the cover.

2.4. The premium is charged on the declared value at 0.11 per cent, adjusted at the year end. The most the insurer will pay across all claims in one policy year is Rs. 9 crore. When claims paid pass Rs. 6 crore the broker tells the claims desk, and the desk tells the Finance head the same day.

2.5. Goods are valued at the value written on the dispatch note or the value in the customer's schedule held by Finance, whichever is lower. A value written in a customer's e-mail after a loss is recorded, but it is not the basis of the claim.

## 4. Behind door 3

4.1. The cell behind D3 is BC-1, a blast cell with an air temperature of -35 C
and room for six pallets. It exists because brand owners do not always send
stock as cold as their paperwork says, and a frozen store is not built to pull
warm stock down; it is built to hold cold stock cold.

4.2. Every inbound pallet is probed at the dock: one carton from the middle of
the pallet, probe into the product core. Anything with a core warmer than minus 12 on the arrival probe goes behind door 3 first, whatever the paperwork says.

4.3. The target in the cell is a core of minus 18. It gets six hours from the moment the doors close. A load that has not reached target by then is reported to QA and held, and the customer is told the same day.

4.4. Stock that comes out of the cell is probed again before it goes into FC-A,
and both readings are written on the inbound sheet with their times.

4.5. The cell is never used as overflow storage, however busy the night. A
pallet parked in the cell because FC-A is full blocks the next soft arrival,
and the next soft arrival then sits on the dock warming further.

4.6. The cell's fans put a hard frost on cartons that sit too close to the coil.
Pallets are placed on the painted floor marks and nowhere else.

4.7. Whether cell time is charged depends on the customer's contract, not on
this handbook. The shift lead records the door-closing and door-opening times on
the cell log so that the office can apply whatever the contract says.

4.8. The cell was enlarged from four to six pallet places in March 2026. The two
extra places took space from the apron, which is why the apron now holds nine
vehicles and not eleven.

## 5. Temperatures

5.1. The customer's products are kept at -18 C or colder in storage and in
transit.

5.2. The customer pre-cools each trailer before loading at Chakan and sends the
pre-cool record with the trailer.

5.3. Product that turns up above minus 12 is brought down to temperature at the cross-dock, and that work is invoiced to the customer.

5.4. Quillfern is not liable for product damage caused by temperatures before
handover. Each party may inspect the other's temperature records for its
stock.

## 2. The work

2.1. Quillfern collects the customer's frozen products from the Chakan factory,
stores them and delivers them to restaurants, caterers and retailers in Pune
and Mumbai.

2.2. Pune deliveries go out from Quillfern's own stock. Mumbai-bound stock is
cross-docked at Quillfern's Bhiwandi site and goes out on the next morning's
vans.

2.3. Call-off times for Mumbai deliveries are those printed in the site handbook of the cross-dock that ships them.

2.4. Waiting charges on the customer's own vehicles at the cross-dock are billed at the site's published rate less 20 per cent.

2.5. Pallets are exchanged one for one at the cross-dock. Exchange units that arrive unfit on the customer's own vehicles are charged at the site figure, with no discount.

2.6. Quillfern does not sell, promote or price the customer's products and does
not take orders from the customer's buyers directly.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

## 4. Product, packing and handover

4.1. The customer packs its products in cartons that carry the batch number and
the best-before date on two faces.

4.2. Loaded pallets stand no higher than 1.8 metres including the wooden base. Taller pallets are restacked at the customer's cost before they are
accepted.

4.3. Each pallet is stretch-wrapped and labelled with the customer's pallet ID
on two faces.

4.4. Handover takes place when the pallet crosses the dock edge at the
receiving site. The receiving shift lead's count is the count.
