## 11. Following up actions

11.1. Every agreed action from every report goes into the actions register, with its owner, its due date and its finding's grade. The register is updated by the team on the first working day of each month from the evidence owners send in.

11.2. An action is closed only on evidence. An e-mail saying "done" is not evidence; a revised procedure, a changed system setting, a signed balance check or a trained-staff list is.

11.3. Overdue actions on high findings are listed by name in each quarterly report to the board, together with the owner's explanation. Overdue actions on medium findings are listed by count.

11.4. Each high finding is tested again by the team about six months after its action is closed, to confirm the fix has held. A fix that has not held reopens the finding at its original grade.

11.5. Owners may ask for one extension of an action date, in writing, before it falls due. A second extension needs the board's agreement.

## 9. What the condensers drink

9.1. The site has no municipal supply. Drinking water comes in by tanker to a separate overhead tank with its own filter and is never mixed with the plant supply.

9.2. Water for the evaporative condensers on the plant room roof comes from the borewell at the south-east corner of the plot. Hard water scales a condenser within weeks, so everything drawn from the borewell passes through the softening plant before it reaches the roof.

9.3. Softened water is tested every week by the plant operator, and the reading must stay below 500 ppm; above that, the bleed rate on the condensers is increased the same day and the softener is regenerated.

9.4. Until the second softener was commissioned in May 2026 the limit was looser and the test was monthly; that rule has gone.

9.5. Every weekly reading goes into the water log with the hand-held meter's serial number beside it, and the tds meter itself is checked against a standard solution each month.

9.6. Whatever the tds, condenser sumps are drained and cleaned every three months, and the water-treatment contractor doses biocide under a written chart kept in the plant room.

## 6. Charging and first start

6.1. Refrigerant is charged by weight from the contractor's scale, with the cylinder number and the weight before and after recorded on the test sheet. The charge must match the designer's figure within the tolerance the designer gives.

6.2. The plant is started with the room empty and its doors shut. The contractor's engineer checks motor currents, oil levels, superheat and the operation of every safety cut-out before the plant is left to run.

6.3. Every safety cut-out is tested by causing the condition it protects against, not by reading its setting. A high-pressure switch is tested by blocking the condenser airflow until it trips, with the engineer standing at the isolator.

6.4. The alarm panel is tested at this stage too: each probe's high and low alarms, door alarms, plant fault alarms, and the call-out to the duty phone. A call that reaches nobody is a failed test.

6.5. Defrost is run manually through at least two full cycles and its termination checked.

## 3. Documents before anything starts

3.1. Before the first test is run, the engineering lead issues a commissioning plan listing every test, its acceptance criteria, the readings to be taken, the instruments to be used and their calibration certificates, and the people who must attend.

3.2. Acceptance criteria are written before the test, not after it. A criterion changed once readings are known is a failure to be explained, not a new criterion.

3.3. The plan is sent to every contractor at least two weeks before the first test. A contractor who disagrees with a criterion says so in writing before testing begins; afterwards it is too late.

3.4. Every instrument used to take a reading has a current calibration certificate traceable to a recognised laboratory. The certificate number is written beside each set of readings on the test sheet.

3.5. Drawings of the room, the plant and the controls are issued in their as-built state before acceptance. A room whose drawings still show the design rather than what was built is not accepted.

## 2. Who does what

2.1. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns commissioning and decides the order of tests. Navdeep Grewal, the refrigeration engineer, runs the plant tests with the contractor. The site QA lead accepts or rejects the room for product. The site manager is told the dates and is not asked to approve technical results.

2.2. The refrigeration contractor builds and starts the plant and puts it right when a test fails. The contractor does not decide whether its own work has passed; it provides the readings and the engineering lead decides.

2.3. The panel contractor erects the insulated envelope, the doors and the floor finish. The electrical contractor installs the power, controls and alarms. Each contractor has a named site engineer who attends the tests that concern their work.

2.4. Disagreements between contractors about whose work caused a failure are settled by the engineering lead after the test has been repeated. Nobody argues over a failed reading until it has been confirmed.

## 12. Closing an engagement and reporting

12.1. Fieldwork ends with an exit meeting at which the engagement lead goes through every finding with the department head, before anything is written down as final. Nothing should appear in a final report that the department hears of for the first time on paper.

12.2. The final report is issued within 15 working days of that meeting, to the department head, the Chief Financial Officer and the Managing Director, and to the chair of the board's audit committee, which reads every final report at its next quarterly sitting.

12.3. Until this programme the report was allowed 30 working days, and too many reports arrived after the people involved had forgotten the details.

12.4. The committee may call any department head to explain an overdue action in person, and may ask why any report missed its date after the exit meeting.

## 10. Looking at whole populations

10.1. Some tests are run on every transaction rather than a sample, using data extracted from the finance system. Extracts are taken by the team with read-only access and are never edited; any cleaning is done on a copy and recorded.

10.2. The duplicate payment test runs every month, on the fifth working day, on all supplier payments of the previous month. It looks for the same supplier, amount and invoice number, and for near-matches where one character differs. Every hit is followed up with accounts payable within a week.

10.3. A Benford first-digit test runs once a quarter on staff expense claims, by site and by person. A pattern that departs from the Benford curve is a reason to look, never by itself a finding.

10.4. Results of every run are kept, including runs that found nothing, so that a duplicate missed later can be traced to the run that should have caught it.

# Cold Room Commissioning Manual

## 1. Why commissioning gets its own manual

1.1. A cold room is not finished when the builders leave. It is finished when it has been shown, by tests written down in advance and run by people who did not build it, that it will hold product inside its range on the worst day of the year. Everything between the last panel going up and the first pallet going in is commissioning, and this manual says how Quillfern does it.

1.2. The manual was first written for the opening of Ludhiana DC in 2025 and is now used for the second frozen block at Ludhiana, due for handover in the winter of 2026, and for every new chamber the engineering team builds after it. It applies whether the chamber is built by a turnkey contractor or assembled by our own team from bought-in panels and plant.

1.3. It is written for the engineering lead who runs commissioning, the contractors who build and start the plant, the site QA lead who must accept the room, and the site manager who wants to know when the room can earn money. It does not replace temperature mapping, which follows the company mapping method once commissioning is complete.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the handover note written in a hurry at the end of the first Ludhiana build. Several of that note's figures were the contractor's defaults, accepted without question; this revision sets Quillfern's own.

## 3. Behind the chain-link fence

3.1. The 2 MVA transformer in the substation yard is oil-filled, and its oil is usually the first thing to fail without anyone noticing. Moisture and sludge pull down the oil's dielectric strength long before anything trips.

3.2. A sample is drawn by the approved testing laboratory every six months, in March and September, with the unit on load. The breakdown voltage must read at least 50 kV. A sample below that is filtered on site within seven days and drawn again after filtering.

3.3. The 2025 commissioning note allowed a yearly sample and a lower pass figure; both were tightened after the first monsoon, when condensation was found in the breather.

3.4. The laboratory's report is filed in the substation folder and copied to the engineering lead together with the dielectric figure from each of the last four samples, so that a slow decline is visible before it becomes a failure.

3.5. Nobody opens the transformer enclosure except the electrical supervisor or the utility's linesman, and never alone.

## 2. Who does what

2.1. The engineering lead, Gurmeet Kaur Sidhu, owns commissioning and decides the order of tests. Navdeep Grewal, the refrigeration engineer, runs the plant tests with the contractor. The site QA lead accepts or rejects the room for product. The site manager is told the dates and is not asked to approve technical results.

2.2. The refrigeration contractor builds and starts the plant and puts it right when a test fails. The contractor does not decide whether its own work has passed; it provides the readings and the engineering lead decides.

2.3. The panel contractor erects the insulated envelope, the doors and the floor finish. The electrical contractor installs the power, controls and alarms. Each contractor has a named site engineer who attends the tests that concern their work.

2.4. Disagreements between contractors about whose work caused a failure are settled by the engineering lead after the test has been repeated. Nobody argues over a failed reading until it has been confirmed.

# Refrigeration Technician Development Curriculum

## 1. Why we train our own

1.1. Quillfern's new sites need people who can keep a reefer unit, a walk-in chamber and a standby generator running at three in the morning, and the market does not supply enough of them. Experienced mechanics are hired away by the dairies and the pharma makers as soon as they are any good, and the ones who stay with independent garages rarely know anything about temperature records or why a door left open for ten minutes matters.

1.2. In 2024 the engineering pool therefore started its own apprenticeship, run from a workshop in the Waluj industrial area outside Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (still Aurangabad on most of the signboards). The workshop trains young people in the trade and in the Quillfern way of working, and then places them at the sites that need them.

1.3. This curriculum describes the programme as it runs from the January 2026 intake: who may join, how long it lasts, what the apprentices learn and how they are assessed, what they are paid, and what they may and may not do on live equipment.

1.4. It is written for apprentices, their trainers and mentors, and the site managers who receive them. An apprentice is given a copy on the first day and is expected to have read it by the end of the first week.

## 12. Signing the room into service

12.1. Commissioning ends with a single signed record that gathers every test sheet, every calibration certificate, the as-built drawings, the closed list and the fire contractor's certificate.

12.2. Every test on the record must have been witnessed, and the record carries two signatories for each: the site QA lead and the refrigeration contractor's engineer. The customer whose stock the room will hold may send an observer, whose name is recorded, but the observer does not sign.

12.3. The 2025 note asked for one signature, the contractor's, and nobody from Quillfern could later say who had watched the pressure test.

12.4. A test that was not witnessed by both signatories is void, and is repeated. Neither signature may be added later by phone or by e-mail.

12.5. Once the record is complete the room passes to the site QA lead for temperature mapping.

## 2. Who can join

2.1. Applicants hold an ITI certificate in refrigeration and air-conditioning, or in an electrical or mechanical trade with a refrigeration module, and are between 18 and 25 on the day the intake opens.

2.2. Applicants sit a written test in arithmetic and basic electrical theory and a short practical in the workshop: wiring a contactor, reading a pressure gauge, brazing a joint. The practical counts for more than the written test.

2.3. A medical examination checks eyesight, colour vision and hearing. Colour vision matters because wiring and refrigerant cylinders are colour-coded.

2.4. Applicants must hold, or obtain within the first three months, a two-wheeler licence. Many floor jobs are reached by motorcycle.

2.5. Quillfern does not charge any fee for the programme, the tests or the medical. An agent who asks an applicant for money is reported to the engineering pool lead, and the applicant is not penalised for having been asked.

## 9. Weather from the bay

9.1. The coast between Visakhapatnam and Bhubaneswar is struck by storms from the Bay of Bengal in two seasons: April to May, and above all October to December. In 2014 and in 2019 storms in the region cut grid power to the industrial estates for several days.

9.2. From 1 October each year, and from 1 April, the DC keeps enough diesel on site to run both generator sets at full load for 120 hours. The satellite keeps enough for 72 hours at full load. The figure is checked by dipping the tanks every Monday in those months, and a shortfall is reported to the region head the same day.

9.3. When the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issues a red warning for the district, both sites stop dispatching outbound loads that would be on the road during the warning, and vehicles already on the road are directed to the nearest safe yard. Inbound vehicles are received if they can reach the site before the warning period begins.

9.4. Before landfall, loose items on the yards are tied down or brought inside, the solar plant is isolated, and the duty roster for the next 72 hours is fixed so that the people on it can stay on site safely.

9.5. Customers are told of a red-warning stop by the account managers, not by drivers, and are told again when dispatch restarts.

## 7. Machinery that stops

7.1. A loss of temperature on its own is not an accident. Under TPC, spoilage caused by a failure of the vehicle's refrigerating machinery is paid only where the machinery stopped working for at least four consecutive hours. Spoilage after a shorter stoppage is Quillfern's loss, not the insurer's, unless the stoppage followed a collision, an overturning or a fire, in which case the ordinary accident cover applies.

7.2. The four hours are counted from the unit's own stop event in its controller log, not from the first temperature alarm and not from the time the driver noticed. A unit that stops, restarts, and stops again has two stoppages, not one long one.

7.3. The stoppage is proved by the controller's event log and the temperature record together. A driver's statement, however honest, does not prove it alone, and a phone photograph of a dark display is evidence only of the moment it was taken.

7.4. Fleet Control downloads the controller log as soon as a claim on refrigeration grounds is possible, before the unit is serviced. A mechanic who clears the fault log has destroyed the evidence, so workshops are told not to clear any log on a vehicle with an open claim.

7.5. Customers' stock that warmed during a long stoppage is still handled under the quality rules, whether or not the claim succeeds. A failed claim never leads to stock being released.

## 11. When the grid is told to give way

11.1. In the paddy season and in very cold spells the utility may order large consumers to reduce their load for set hours. Such a curtailment order arrives by e-mail and by phone to the site manager, who tells the engineering lead and the shift lead at once.

11.2. The site's sanctioned load is 1,450 kW against a contract demand of 1,200 kVA. During an order, loads are switched off in this sequence until the site is under the figure the order gives: first the office and canteen air conditioning, then the yard and apron lighting except the gate, then the softening plant, and only last the ambient store's ventilation. Refrigeration, the frozen block and the controls are never shed.

11.3. If shedding all of those still leaves the site above the figure, the generators take the essential load and the site draws only what the order allows from the grid.

11.4. Each curtailment is logged with the order number, the hours, the loads shed and the diesel used, and the sanctioned figures are reviewed with the utility once a year in the light of that log.

## 5. Racking and rooms

5.1. The DC has three temperature zones. The chilled block at +2 to +8 C holds 2,400 pallet positions in selective racking, split into a pharma room of 600 and a food room of 1,800. The frozen block at −22 C holds 1,600 pallet positions in drive-in racking. The controlled-room-temperature store holds 300.

5.2. The frozen block is built so that a second chamber of the same size can be added on the east side without stopping the first. That expansion is not approved and is not in this plan's figures.

5.3. The pharma room has its own anteroom and its own door to the dispatch canopy, so that pharma picking never shares a door with food.

5.4. Every room is temperature-mapped before first stock and again after its first summer. The mapping follows the company method.

5.5. Floor space in the dispatch canopy is for staging only. Nothing waits there longer than it takes to load.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

## 17. What changed from the 2025 cover

17.1. The 2025–26 cover was placed with the same insurer on different terms, and its summary note is withdrawn. Staff who learned the old figures should unlearn them.

17.2. The deductible rose, the intimation window shortened, the machinery-stoppage threshold came down, the single-vehicle figure went up, and the survey threshold went up. The current figures are in sections 5 to 9 of this procedure and nowhere else.

17.3. SRCC cover was added by endorsement for the first time.

17.4. The desk lead reviews this procedure each February, before renewal, and issues a revision whenever the policy terms change.

## 5. What the bill penalises

5.1. The utility bills the site on kilovolt-amperes as well as kilowatt-hours, so a poor power factor costs money every month even when nothing is wrong with the plant. Large compressor motors pull the factor down; the capacitor bank in the switch room pushes it back up.

5.2. The bank is rated at 360 kvar in six automatic steps. The site's target is a monthly average of 0.98. The utility adds a surcharge to any month that averages below 0.90, and gives a small rebate for any month above 0.95.

5.3. When the bank was first installed it had four steps and a lower rating, and the target was 0.95; the extra steps were added in April 2026 after two summer bills carried the surcharge.

5.4. The controller's display, which shows the kvar switched in on each step, is read at every monthly energy review. A step that will not switch in is reported to the electrical supervisor the same day.

5.5. Capacitor cans are never touched until the bank has been isolated and left for the discharge time printed on its door.

## 3. Behind the chain-link fence

3.1. The 2 MVA transformer in the substation yard is oil-filled, and its oil is usually the first thing to fail without anyone noticing. Moisture and sludge pull down the oil's dielectric strength long before anything trips.

3.2. A sample is drawn by the approved testing laboratory every six months, in March and September, with the unit on load. The breakdown voltage must read at least 50 kV. A sample below that is filtered on site within seven days and drawn again after filtering.

3.3. The 2025 commissioning note allowed a yearly sample and a lower pass figure; both were tightened after the first monsoon, when condensation was found in the breather.

3.4. The laboratory's report is filed in the substation folder and copied to the engineering lead together with the dielectric figure from each of the last four samples, so that a slow decline is visible before it becomes a failure.

3.5. Nobody opens the transformer enclosure except the electrical supervisor or the utility's linesman, and never alone.

# Cold Room Commissioning Manual

## 1. Why commissioning gets its own manual

1.1. A cold room is not finished when the builders leave. It is finished when it has been shown, by tests written down in advance and run by people who did not build it, that it will hold product inside its range on the worst day of the year. Everything between the last panel going up and the first pallet going in is commissioning, and this manual says how Quillfern does it.

1.2. The manual was first written for the opening of Ludhiana DC in 2025 and is now used for the second frozen block at Ludhiana, due for handover in the winter of 2026, and for every new chamber the engineering team builds after it. It applies whether the chamber is built by a turnkey contractor or assembled by our own team from bought-in panels and plant.

1.3. It is written for the engineering lead who runs commissioning, the contractors who build and start the plant, the site QA lead who must accept the room, and the site manager who wants to know when the room can earn money. It does not replace temperature mapping, which follows the company mapping method once commissioning is complete.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the handover note written in a hurry at the end of the first Ludhiana build. Several of that note's figures were the contractor's defaults, accepted without question; this revision sets Quillfern's own.

## 5. Taking the air out

5.1. Air and moisture left in a refrigeration system turn into acid and sludge that shorten the life of every component. Before charging, the system is put under vacuum with a pump connected at both the high and low sides.

5.2. The system is pumped down to 500 micron. The pump is then isolated and the system left; it passes if the gauge stays below 1,000 for 30 minutes. A rise above that means moisture or a leak, and the pumping continues or the leak is found.

5.3. The 2025 handover note took the contractor's default figures, which were looser on both counts.

5.4. The gauge used is electronic, connected as close to the system as the hose allows, and never read through the pump's own dial. The readings at isolation, at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes go on the test sheet.

5.5. Pumping is never stopped early because the contractor's crew is due elsewhere. A rushed vacuum is the commonest fault the engineering team finds in other people's plant, and the micron figure is the one most often written down without being read.

## 6. Quick checks on cleanliness

6.1. Not every cleanliness check can wait three days for a plate count. For surfaces that have just been cleaned, such as the inside of a returned meal-kit liner or a reefer floor before loading, the laboratory uses a rapid swab that gives a reading in seconds.

6.2. The swab detects atp, the energy molecule present in food residue and living cells, and the hand-held reader reports it in rlu. A reading of 100 or below is a pass. From 101 to 300 the surface is cleaned again and swabbed again; above 300 it fails, and the cleaning itself is reviewed.

6.3. Until March 2026 the laboratory's pass line was higher, and liners that passed were later found carrying mould.

6.4. A swab reading measures cleanliness, not safety. A surface that passes still goes through any microbiological test that QA has asked for.

6.5. The atp reader is checked each morning with the maker's control swabs, which give a known rlu figure. A reader that fails its check is not used that day.

## 12. Records and review

12.1. The substation folder, the switch room log, the generator log, the water log, the energy review notes and the load-shedding log are kept for five years. Laboratory reports on oil and water are kept for the life of the equipment.

12.2. Records are made at the time, in ink or in the building management system, and corrected only by striking through and initialling.

12.3. The engineering lead reviews this manual every August, after the first full summer of each year's figures, and whenever equipment covered by it is added or replaced. A revised manual is issued with a one-page note of what changed and why.

12.4. Suggestions for the manual come to the engineering office from anyone on site, on paper or by e-mail. Each one gets an answer within a month, whether or not it is taken up.

## 16. Review of this manual

16.1. The laboratory head reviews this manual every June and whenever a method, a piece of equipment or a customer requirement changes.

16.2. Each revision is explained to the analysts at a briefing, and each analyst signs that they have read it.

16.3. Suggestions for changes come from analysts, from the people who send samples and from customers' auditors. Each suggestion is answered in writing by the laboratory head within a month, whether or not it is taken up, and the answers are kept with the manual's revision file.

## 15. Review of this manual

15.1. The engineering lead reviews this manual after every new room is handed over, and at least once a year.

15.2. Contractors may suggest changes in writing; each suggestion gets a written answer.

## 3. Getting a vehicle in and out

3.1. Reefers use the south gate. The east gate is for dry grocery only unless
the DC manager approves an emergency move, as the old wiki page also said.

3.2. School traffic on Temple Street blocks the turn into the south gate between
07:45 and 08:30. Drivers are told on booking to arrive either before 07:30 or
after 08:40. A reefer is never queued across Temple Street; if the apron is
full, the driver goes round the block and comes back.

3.3. Security holds each vehicle outside the south gate until the previous one
has cleared the apron. The apron takes one reefer and one van at a time, no
more, because a reversing reefer cannot see a second one parked behind it.

3.4. Bookings are made in Dockwise, which Coimbatore joined on 1 February 2026.

3.5. Frozen loads are placed before lunch. After about 13:00 the afternoon sun

controls, and they have twice failed to come on in the monsoon.

# Safety and Incident Manual, Ludhiana DC

## 1. What this manual is for

1.1. Ludhiana DC employs about ninety people on two shifts, hosts contractors most days of the year, and receives up to forty vehicles in a day. Every one of those people should go home in the condition they arrived in. This manual says how the site keeps them safe, what happens when something goes wrong, and who is answerable for each part.

1.2. It is written for everyone who works on the site, whether employed by Quillfern, supplied by an agency or sent by a contractor, and for the managers who plan their work. Drivers of visiting vehicles are covered by the gate rules in section 12 and by their own employers' rules.

1.3. The manual does not replace the law. Where the Factories Act, the state rules made under it, or any other law asks for more than this manual, the law applies, and the safety officer tells the site manager what has changed.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the safety rules issued when the site opened in 2025. Several limits in those rules were copied from another company's manual without anyone asking whether they suited a building with freezers at -25 C and a yard full of reversing trucks. This revision sets limits for this site.

## 9. Cold work

9.1. The frozen block at Ludhiana runs at -25 C, colder than most of the company's freezers, and the body loses heat there faster than people expect. Cold slows thinking before it slows hands, which is why the rules below do not depend on how anyone feels.

9.2. Nobody works inside the frozen block for longer than 40 minutes at a stretch, even in a full freezer suit. A 20-minute rewarming break in the canteen or the warm room follows each stretch, with a hot drink available.

9.3. The shift lead keeps the break board for the frozen block and moves names on it; the workers do not keep their own time.

9.4. Signs of hypothermia, such as uncontrolled shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness or confusion, mean the person leaves the cold at once with a colleague and is checked by a first aider. A person who has shown those signs does not go back into the cold that shift.

9.5. In 2025 the stretch was an hour and the rewarming break fifteen minutes, and two cases of mild hypothermia followed; both were changed after the first winter.
